Therefore, a 19-year-old holding a national license for categories "BE", "CE" can obtain an international permit for the same categories after reaching age 21 (Law, art. 27, part 7).

g2-q81.text: According to the Law of the Republic of Armenia on Ensuring Road Traffic Safety, is a person holding a driver’s license for subcategory “C1” permitted to drive a truck whose maximum authorized mass exceeds 8500 kg?
g2-q81.explanation: Subcategory "C1" includes trucks whose maximum authorized mass exceeds 3500 kg but does not exceed 7500 kg. A truck heavier than 8500 kg is outside this limit and requires category "C", so driving it with a "C1" license is not permitted (Law, art. 27, part 1).

g2-q82.text: According to the Law of the Republic of Armenia on Ensuring Road Traffic Safety, which of the following may be operated on public roads?
g2-q82.explanation: By legal definition, a quadricycle is intended for operation on public motor roads, whereas operating all-terrain quadrocycles (ATVs) on such roads is prohibited. The names are similar, but they are different vehicles, so only a quadricycle is permitted (Law, art. 2).

g3-q1.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The remaining tread depth of the tires of a passenger car is 1.8 mm.
The hydraulic brake system is not leak-tight.
g3-q1.explanation: Loss of tightness (leaking) in a hydraulic brake drive is a brake system malfunction that prohibits operation. The residual tread pattern depth of passenger car tires must not be less than 1.6 mm, so 1.8 mm is not a malfunction (for winter tires on icy or snow-covered roads, 4 mm or less is already a malfunction) (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 1, subitem 2; item 4, subitems 1 and 1.3).

g3-q2.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The remaining tread depth of the tires of a truck is 1.6 mm.
The pressure gauge of the pneumatic brake system does not operate.
g3-q2.explanation: A non-functioning pressure gauge on a pneumatic or pneumohydraulic brake drive is a brake system malfunction that prohibits operation. The minimum residual tread pattern depth for truck tires is 1.0 mm, so 1.6 mm is permissible (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 1, subitem 3; item 4, subitem 1).

g3-q3.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: There is movement in steering parts or assemblies that is not provided for by the design, or threaded connections are not tightened.
A fire extinguisher is missing from a truck.
g3-q3.explanation: Both cases prohibit operation. Unintended movement of steering parts and assemblies not provided by design, or untightened threaded connections, are steering malfunctions, and a truck must be equipped with a fire extinguisher (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 2, subitem 2; item 6, subitem 9).

g3-q4.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The exterior lighting devices do not operate in the prescribed mode.
The remaining tread depth of the tires of a motorcycle is 0.6 mm.
g3-q4.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if external lighting devices do not operate in the prescribed mode, and the residual tread pattern depth of motorcycle tires must not be less than 0.8 mm, so 0.6 mm is a malfunction (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 3, subitem 3; item 4, subitem 1).

g3-q5.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The rear fog lights are connected to the vehicle’s brake lights.
The engine coolant temperature gauge does not operate.
g3-q5.explanation: If rear fog lamps are connected to the vehicle's brake lights, operation is prohibited. A non-functioning engine coolant temperature gauge is not on the list of malfunctions prohibiting operation (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 3, subitem 7).

g3-q6.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The tires have localized damage exposing the tire cord.
The interior lighting devices of a passenger car do not operate.
In all of the listed cases.
g3-q6.explanation: If tires have localized damage exposing the cord (punctures, cuts, tears), operation is prohibited. Irregular engine operation is not on the list, and interior lighting devices are listed only for the passenger compartment of a bus, not for a passenger car (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 4, subitem 2; item 6, subitem 6).

g3-q7.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: A motorcycle without a sidecar does not have an emergency warning triangle.
The tires do not correspond to the vehicle model in size or permitted load capacity.
g3-q7.explanation: If tires do not match the given vehicle model in size or permissible load, operation is prohibited. A warning triangle (emergency stop sign) is mandatory in buses, passenger cars, trucks, wheeled tractors, and motorcycles with a sidecar, but not in a motorcycle without a sidecar (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 4, subitem 4; item 6, subitem 9).

g3-q8.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Even one wheel-fastening bolt is missing.
Tires with different tread patterns are installed on the same axle.
g3-q8.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if even one bolt (nut) securing the wheel rim or disc is missing, as well as if tires with different tread patterns are mounted on the same axle (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 4, subitems 3 and 5).

g3-q9.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The head restraints provided by the vehicle’s design are missing.
New and retreaded tires are installed on the same axle.
g3-q9.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if seat headrests provided by design are missing or do not work, as well as if new and retreaded tires are mounted on the same axle (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitem 11; item 4, subitem 5).

g3-q10.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The content of harmful substances in the exhaust gases exceeds the limits established by the legislation of the Republic of Armenia.
The footrests provided by the motorcycle’s design are missing.
g3-q10.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if the content of harmful substances in exhaust gases or their smokiness exceeds the norms established by RA legislation, as well as if footrests provided by design are missing on a motorcycle (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 5, subitem 1; item 6, subitem 12).

g3-q11.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The engine crankcase ventilation system is not leak-tight.
The engine fuel system is not leak-tight.
g3-q11.explanation: Both are engine malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if the crankcase ventilation system is not airtight, as well as if the fuel supply system is not airtight (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 5, subitems 2 and 4).

g3-q12.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The engine crankcase ventilation system is not leak-tight.
Winter and non-winter tires are installed on the same axle.
g3-q12.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if the engine crankcase ventilation system is not airtight, as well as if winter (frost-resistant) and non-winter tires are mounted on the same axle (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 5, subitem 4; item 4, subitem 5).

g3-q13.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The windshield washers provided by the vehicle’s design do not operate.
The engine’s external noise level exceeds the limits established by the standard.
g3-q13.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if the windshield washers provided by design do not work (or the windshield wipers do not operate in the prescribed mode), as well as if the permissible external noise level exceeds the standards set by the standard (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitem 1; item 5, subitem 5).

g3-q14.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The rear fog lights are not connected to the brake lights.
The windshield washers provided by the vehicle’s design do not operate.
In all of the listed cases.
g3-q14.explanation: Operation is prohibited if the windshield washers provided by design do not work. Rear fog lamps, on the contrary, must not be connected to the brake lights, so their not being connected is not a malfunction, and irregular engine operation is not on the list (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitem 1; item 3, subitem 7).

g3-q15.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Items or objects that may cause injury to road users are installed on the vehicle.
g3-q15.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if objects or items posing a risk of injuring road users are installed, as well as if the audible warning device (horn) does not work (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitems 3 and 4).

g3-q16.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: There is excessive play in the connections between the motorcycle frame and the sidecar frame.
Yellow-light fog lamps are installed at the front.
g3-q16.explanation: Operation is prohibited if there is play (looseness) in the frame joints between the motorcycle and the sidecar. Lighting devices with white, yellow, or orange lights are permitted at the front, so fog lamps with yellow light are not a malfunction (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitem 8; item 3, subitem 6).

g3-q17.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: A first-aid kit is missing from a truck.
White reflectors are installed at the front.
g3-q17.explanation: A truck (as well as a bus, passenger car, and wheeled tractor) must carry a first-aid kit, and in its absence operation is prohibited. Reflectors of any color other than white are prohibited at the front, so white reflectors are permitted (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitem 9; item 3, subitem 6).

g3-q18.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: A first-aid kit is missing from a motorcycle with a sidecar.
The trailer support-coupling device is defective.
g3-q18.explanation: Both are malfunctions. A motorcycle with a sidecar must carry a first-aid kit and a warning triangle, and if a tractor's fifth-wheel coupling device is faulty, operation is prohibited (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitems 8 and 9).

g3-q19.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The seat belts provided by the vehicle’s design do not operate.
Items or objects that restrict the driver’s field of vision are installed within the driver’s field of view.
g3-q19.explanation: Both are malfunctions. Operation is prohibited if seat belts provided by design are missing or do not work, as well as if objects or items are installed that restrict visibility from the driver's seat (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitems 4 and 11).

g3-q20.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Changes or modifications have been made to the vehicle’s design without permission from the vehicle registration authority.
Yellow-light turn signals are installed at the front.
g3-q20.explanation: Operation is prohibited if structural modifications (re-equipment) have been made without the permission of the vehicle registration authority. Lighting devices with white, yellow, or orange lights are permitted at the front, so turn signal indicators with yellow light are not a malfunction (Rules, Appendix No. 2, item 6, subitem 17; item 3, subitem 6).

g3-q21.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: A motor vehicle used for practical driving instruction does not have the required identification sign.
The fuel gauge does not operate.
g3-q21.explanation: A motor vehicle used for practical driving instruction must display the "Instructional Vehicle" identification sign; otherwise, its operation is prohibited. Meanwhile, a non-functioning fuel level gauge is not included in the list of malfunctions prohibiting operation (malfunctioning of the speedometer and tachograph is prohibited). (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", items 6, 19)

g3-q22.text: A motorcycle may not be operated if:
options: The safety bars provided by its design are missing.
The minimum remaining tire tread depth is 1.6 mm.
g3-q22.explanation: If the safety bars (crash bars) provided by the motorcycle's design are missing. Safety bars are part of the motorcycle's approved design, and removing them—usually done for appearance or weight reduction—prohibits operating the motorcycle. The criterion is whether the manufacturer provided them: if so, they must be in place. Their purpose becomes obvious the moment a fall occurs: a fallen motorcycle slides with its entire mass across the rider's leg. A safety bar creates a gap between the hot, heavy body and the rider's leg and takes the sliding energy onto metal rather than bone. It also prevents the fuel tank from being crushed and spilling gasoline onto a hot engine. The second option is the numerical trap of this chapter. The permissible residual tread depth depends on the vehicle type: the minimum for a motorcycle is 0.8 mm, for a passenger car 1.6 mm, and for a bus 2 mm. That means 1.6 mm on a motorcycle is not only permissible, it is double the legal limit. A typical mistake is applying the memorized 1.6 figure for passenger cars to all vehicles. Remember these three figures separately: you will encounter them in several more questions in this same chapter. • 1.6 mm is the limit for passenger car tires; for a motorcycle the permissible minimum is 0.8 mm, so a 1.6 mm tread exceeds the legal limit with a safe margin and is not a violation. • Since the second item is not considered a malfunction, the combined option is also excluded.

g3-q23.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Yellow-light turn signals are installed at the front.
Even one wheel-fastening bolt is missing.
g3-q23.explanation: If even one of the wheel mounting bolts is missing. There is no tolerance margin regarding wheel mounting bolts: the absence of even one bolt (or its loosening) prohibits operating the car. Highlight the phrase "even one" in your memory, as that is usually what creates the difference between the right and wrong answer on the exam. The technical logic is simple: the force holding the wheel is evenly distributed across all bolts. Removing one bolt makes the load on the remaining ones both greater and uneven: with each rotation, the wheel turns on those fewer bolts under alternating stress, resulting in metal fatigue and sequential bolt failure. A wheel detaching while driving almost always ends in complete loss of control, and the detached wheel itself becomes a projectile for other cars. The option about yellow turn signals at the front is a trap. Yellow (orange) is precisely the standard color for turn signals—exactly what the rules require. For this chapter, keep a small color table in mind: white or yellow at the front, red at the rear, yellow/orange turn signals on both sides, white reversing lamps, white front reflectors, red rear reflectors. Any option fitting this table is not a violation. • Yellow or orange is the standard color for turn signals, so having them at the front complies with the rules rather than violating them; this option only counts on you mistaking "yellow" for a prohibited color. • Since the first item is not a malfunction at all, the combined option is also incorrect.

g3-q24.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Amber-light turn signals are installed at the front.
The trailer towing device is defective.
g3-q24.explanation: If the towing-coupling device is faulty. The towing-coupling device—the hook, eye, or attachment point provided by the manufacturer on the vehicle for towing—must be serviceable, and its malfunction is included in the list of defects prohibiting operation. It is important to understand that this equipment is needed not only when you are towing another car; on the day your own breaks down, that hook will be the only way to remove it from the road. The load on this part is much greater than it seems. During towing, the rope or bar constantly tightens and slackens, and each jerk delivers a sharp impact to the hook. A cracked or weakened hook, which shows no signs during normal operation, breaks precisely under such an impact, and the snapped rope whips rapidly toward one of the two cars. If the coupling comes undone while moving, the towed car—which also usually lacks brake and steering boosters—is left completely without control. The option about orange turn signals at the front is a trap: orange/yellow is the standard color for turn signals. Whenever you see an option about a lamp color in this chapter, first compare it with the color table and treat it as a violation only if there is a mismatch. • Orange (yellow) is the legal color for turn signals; this option describes a proper condition of the vehicle and is not a malfunction. • Since the first item is not a violation, "in both cases" cannot be the answer either.

g3-q25.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: White reflectors are installed at the front.
The trailer towing device is defective.
g3-q25.explanation: If the towing-coupling device is faulty. A faulty towing-coupling device is one of the explicitly listed items in the catalog of malfunctions under which vehicle movement is prohibited. The criterion is the serviceability and readiness for work of the part; whether you intend to tow anything today does not affect the rule. From a safety standpoint, towing is one of the most dangerous road situations: two vehicles at short distance, one without propulsion and often with heavy brakes and steering, moving in general traffic. The only thing holding them together is the coupling device. If the hook's weld seam has cracked or the bolts securing it to the body have loosened, the first jolt is enough for the coupling to open and leave the rear car stranded in the middle of the road. Therefore, rather than regulating only the towing method, the legislator made the serviceability of the part itself a condition for driving. The option about white reflectors at the front is a color trap. The rule is: front reflectors are white, rear reflectors are red. That means mounting a white reflector at the front is exactly what the standard requires. If they were swapped—a red reflector at the front or a white one at the rear—an oncoming driver would misread the orientation of a parked car in reverse, and that would be the violation. • Front reflectors must be white (and rear ones red), so having a white reflector at the front complies with the rule rather than violating it. • Since the first item is not a violation at all, the combined option is also excluded.

g3-q26.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The seat belts provided by the vehicle’s design are missing.
White-light backup lamps are installed at the rear.
g3-q26.explanation: If the seat belts provided by the car's design are missing. The legal criterion is "provided by design": if the manufacturer equipped the car with seat belts, those belts must be present and functional. Removing a belt—as is sometimes done in older cars or on rarely used rear seats—by itself prohibits operating the vehicle. Remember the safety reason through one simple quantity: in a collision, the body flies forward at the same speed the car was moving. The belt distributes this energy over several tens of centimeters and across the strong bones of the pelvis and ribcage; without a belt, the same energy is released over a few centimeters—against the steering wheel, windshield, or asphalt. An unbuckled rear-seat passenger additionally turns into a projectile and can strike those seated in front. Nor does an airbag replace a seat belt: it is engineered for a body held in the proper position by a belt. The second option is a color trap: reversing lamps must emit white light. Their white color clearly tells the driver behind that the car is backing up; thus, this condition complies with the standard and is not a malfunction. • White light is precisely the standard color for reversing lamps, and placing them at the rear complies with the rules; mixed-up colors, such as a red reversing lamp, are the violation. • Since the second item is not a malfunction, the combined option is also excluded.

g3-q27.text: A motorcycle with a sidecar may not be operated if:
options: The transverse passenger handhold on the seat, as provided by the design, is missing.
The remaining tire tread depth is 0.6 mm.
In all of the listed cases.
g3-q27.explanation: In all listed cases: absence of a transverse grab handle for the passenger, residual tread depth of 0.6 mm, and absence of a first-aid kit. All three items in this question individually appear on the list of malfunctions prohibiting the operation of a motorcycle with a sidecar, so the comprehensive answer is correct. The first option concerns the absence of a transverse grab handle on the seat. A motorcycle passenger has neither a seat belt nor a vehicle body: that handle is their sole point of support. During hard braking or sudden acceleration, a passenger without a handle either leans onto the driver and interferes with steering or slides backward. The second item is numerical: the minimum permissible tread depth for a motorcycle is 0.8 mm, meaning 0.6 mm is below the legal limit and impermissible. A bald motorcycle tire has almost no grip on wet asphalt, and since a motorcycle has only two contact patches, a skid leads directly to a fall. The third item is mandatory equipment: a motorcycle with a sidecar carries a passenger and is required to have a first-aid kit. The exam trap is the number 0.6: if you memorized only 1.6 (which applies to passenger cars), it might seem that 0.6 is "enough" for a motorcycle. Keep the three key values of this chapter together: motorcycle 0.8 · passenger car 1.6 · bus 2 mm. • This item is true on its own: a motorcycle with a sidecar must not operate without a transverse grab handle for the passenger, but it ignores the other two conditions. • A 0.6 mm tread is indeed below the permissible 0.8 mm and creates a prohibition, but choosing it alone leaves the answer incomplete. • Absence of a first-aid kit is also an independent ground for prohibition: again true, but incomplete.

g3-q28.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The interior lighting devices of a passenger car do not operate.
The head restraints provided by the vehicle’s design are missing.
g3-q28.explanation: If the headrests provided by the car's design are missing. A headrest is not a comfort accessory: it is part of the car's passive safety system, and the absence of manufacturer-provided headrests prohibits operating the car. Remember what a headrest does through the mechanism of "whiplash injury": when you are rear-ended, the body and seat are abruptly thrown forward while the head stays behind by inertia; the result is a violent backward snap of the neck and injury to vertebrae and ligaments. The headrest stops this motion and forces the head to move together with the torso. Notably, such injury occurs even in low-speed urban collisions—the classic rear-end hit at a traffic light—and is one of the most common lasting road injuries. The option about interior lighting in a passenger car is a trap, and the exam plays on one exact distinction: passenger car cabin lighting is not on the list of prohibiting malfunctions, whereas a malfunction of a bus's interior lighting is a violation. The reason lies in the difference in function: on a bus, passengers move in the dark along steps and aisles, so interior lighting is part of boarding and alighting safety, whereas in a passenger car it serves only comfort. • Passenger car interior lighting is not on the list of prohibiting malfunctions; this option is tempting because that very same item is indeed a violation for a bus. • Since the first item is not a violation, the "in both cases" option is also incorrect.

g3-q29.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Red reflectors are installed at the rear.
The speedometer provided by the vehicle’s design does not operate.
g3-q29.explanation: If the speedometer provided by the car's design does not work. A non-functioning speedometer is included in the list of malfunctions prohibiting vehicle operation. The reason is straightforward: a large share of traffic rules is built around speed values—limits in built-up areas, limits outside cities, permissible speed on motorways, reduced speeds for heavy vehicles and towing vehicles. Without a speedometer, a driver cannot comply with these rules even with the best intentions. Visual estimation of speed is also unreliable: human hearing and vision adapt to speed, and after driving a few minutes on an open road, 90 km/h feels "slow." That is precisely why most speed limit violations are unintentional and happen right as a driver enters a built-up area while continuing at the open-road pace. The speedometer is the driver's sole objective reference and prevents collisions caused by inappropriate speed. The option about red reflectors at the rear is a trap: rear reflectors must be red so that a parked or unpowered vehicle is visible at night to a driver behind and its orientation is read correctly. This condition complies with the standard. • Rear reflectors must be red; this option describes a proper condition of the vehicle and indicates no malfunction. • Since the first item is not a violation, "in both cases" cannot be the right answer either.

g3-q30.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The total play in the steering system of a passenger car exceeds 10 degrees.
The mud flaps and splash guards provided by the vehicle design are missing.
g3-q30.explanation: Both total free play (slack) in the steering of a passenger car exceeding 10 degrees and the absence of mudguards provided by design. Both items appear on the list of prohibiting malfunctions, and each alone is sufficient to keep the car off the road. Total steering free play is the angle through which the steering wheel turns without any response from the steered wheels. The permissible limit depends on the vehicle type: 10 degrees for a passenger car, 20 degrees for a bus, and 25 degrees for a truck. Exceeding this limit means a lag between the driver's input and the vehicle turning: during an emergency maneuver, this small delay turns steering from a precise action into excessive, oscillating inputs, causing the car to sway laterally. Excessive free play is usually also a sign of worn ball joints and steering gear, meaning there is also a risk of sudden structural failure. Mudguards seem decorative, but they serve a clear safety function: they contain gravel, mud, and spray thrown backward by the tire at speed. Without them, a following car suffers a cracked windshield or zero visibility in rain, and a following motorcyclist becomes a direct target for stones. What is worth remembering: associate the number 10 degrees with the word "passenger car"; if you see the same figure applied to a bus or truck, you are most likely looking at a trap. • True, but incomplete: steering play over 10 degrees on a passenger car indeed creates a prohibition, but this option ignores the mudguards item. • The absence of mudguards also independently belongs on the list; choosing it alone discards the steering control item.

g3-q31.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: A first-aid kit is missing from a passenger car.
Red-light backup lamps are installed at the rear.
g3-q31.explanation: Both the absence of a first-aid kit in the car and the installation of reversing lamps with red light. This question places one item from the "mandatory equipment" category next to one from the "lighting colors" category, and both appear on the list of prohibiting malfunctions. A first-aid kit is mandatory equipment for every car. The logic is that time decides: in road collisions, the interval between the crash and the ambulance's arrival is often the exact window in which severe bleeding becomes fatal. A bandage and tourniquet in the hands of the first driver on scene accomplish what no more advanced equipment can make up for later. There is also a direct rule for the color of reversing lamps: it must be white. White light at the rear of a car carries a specific meaning: "this car is backing up." If a red lamp is installed instead, a driver behind will mistake it for a position light or brake light and will not realize the car ahead is moving toward them; the result is scrapes in parking lots and collisions while reversing. Furthermore, rearward red light is reserved for marking "the rear end of the vehicle," and adding an extra red light source prevents others from reading the car's state properly at night. Short rule: only red at the rear (except reversing lamps and license plate illumination, which are white), and never red at the front. • True, but incomplete: absence of a first-aid kit indeed prohibits operation, but this option leaves aside the reversing lamp color item. • A red reversing lamp is also an independent violation, but choosing it alone makes the answer incomplete.

g3-q32.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The remaining tread depth of the tires on a passenger-car trailer is less than 1.6 mm.
Amber-light turn signals are installed at the rear.
g3-q32.explanation: If the residual tread pattern depth of the tires of a passenger car trailer is less than 1.6 mm. A trailer towed behind a passenger car is subject to the same tire limit as the towing vehicle: the minimum residual tread depth is 1.6 mm. Below this value, operating the combination is prohibited even if the car's own tires are new. The tread performs a simple yet vital task—evacuating water from beneath the tire so contact with the asphalt is maintained. With tread below the permissible limit, the tire skims over a film of water (hydroplaning), and grip drops sharply. On a trailer, this phenomenon is even more dangerous: when the rear wheels of the combination lose grip, the trailer begins swaying laterally and can drag the entire combination into jackknifing and rollover—something the driver is nearly powerless to control. What is worth remembering and what drivers often forget: trailer tires cover few kilometers, yet stand for years in the sun sitting idle; their wear is more rubber aging than abrasion. Before every trip, check the trailer's tread and tire pressure separately from the car. By contrast, an orange turn signal at the rear is precisely the standard color and is not a violation. • Rear turn signals must also be yellow/orange; this option describes a proper condition of the vehicle and has no place on the list of malfunctions. • Since the second item is not a malfunction, "in both cases" is also excluded.

g3-q33.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The hydraulic brake system is not leak-tight.
White-light turn signals are installed at the rear.
g3-q33.explanation: Both loss of tightness (leaking) in the hydraulic brake drive and installing white turn signals at the rear. Both items appear on the list of prohibiting malfunctions: one from the brakes category, the other from lighting colors. A hydraulic brake works on a simple principle: fluid is incompressible, so the force of your foot reaches all four wheels without loss. The moment the circuit's seal is broken and air enters the system or a leak develops, this chain breaks: the pedal becomes spongy, its travel lengthens, and in the worst case it goes to the floor while the car fails to slow down. The main danger of this malfunction lies in its hidden nature: during gentle city braking you will feel only slight softness, yet at the very first emergency stop all braking capability vanishes. Therefore, no degree of leakage can be left unattended. A white turn signal at the rear is also a violation, since the color of turn signals on both ends of a car must be yellow/orange. White light at the rear has a different specific meaning—reversing. Seeing white light, a driver behind will conclude the car ahead is backing toward them when it is merely about to turn; or conversely, will fail to understand the intention to turn and enter its path. Rule: in a vehicle's lighting devices, every color carries a unique message; swapping colors means sending a false message. • True, but incomplete: loss of tightness in the hydraulic brake circuit indeed prohibits operation, but this option ignores the rear white turn signal item. • A white turn signal at the rear is also an independent violation, but choosing it alone excludes the brake malfunction from your answer.

g3-q34.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Tires of different constructions are installed on the same axle.
The engine fuel system is not leak-tight.
g3-q34.explanation: Both mounting tires of different construction on the same axle and damage to the engine fuel supply system. Both items individually appear on the list of prohibiting malfunctions, so the comprehensive answer is correct. Mixing tires of different construction on the same axle—say, radial on one side and bias-ply (diagonal) on the other—means the two wheels of one axle operate with different sidewall stiffness and different behavior under load. The effect does not show during calm driving, but under hard braking or a sharp turn, grip on the two sides becomes uneven, and the car pulls sideways or its rear skids out. The same logic applies to a major difference in wear, size, or tread type (winter and summer tires on one axle). Damage to the fuel supply system is a fire hazard. Even the slightest leak of gasoline or diesel onto a hot manifold or near an electrical spark can ignite the car; fire spreads rapidly inside an enclosed engine bay and, in a collision, deprives occupants of the chance to get out. Therefore, a fuel leak is never "tolerable until the service shop." Exam observation: any option mentioning a fuel leak, brake fluid leak, or mismatched tires on one axle almost always belongs on the list of prohibitions. • True, but incomplete: tires of different construction on one axle are indeed prohibited, but this option leaves aside damage to the fuel supply system. • Damage to the fuel supply system is also an independent ground for prohibition: choosing it alone leaves the answer incomplete.

g3-q35.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The cooling system does not maintain a stable operating temperature for the engine.
g3-q35.explanation: If the audible warning device (horn) does not work. A non-functioning horn appears on the list of malfunctions prohibiting vehicle operation. At first glance the horn seems a minor detail, yet it is the driver's only means of warning someone who does not see them: a pedestrian stepping onto the roadway without looking, a driver in an adjacent car changing lanes into a blind spot, or a child darting out from between parked cars. Its importance grows on mountain roads and blind curves, of which there are many on Armenia's roads: there, two drivers cannot see each other until the last moment, and sound arrives before sight. Remember that the lawful use of the horn is to prevent a collision, not to express frustration; yet a vehicle deprived of this capability lacks a means of warning and therefore has no right to be on the road. The trap in the question is the cooling system. Inability to maintain a stable thermal regime for the engine is a malfunction that harms the engine itself, but it is not included in the closed list of prohibiting malfunctions. Apply this chapter's general rule: everything relating to brakes, steering, visibility, lighting, signaling, and mandatory safety equipment is on the list; malfunctions affecting engine performance and service life are not. • A malfunctioning cooling system harms the engine, but it is not on the list of prohibiting malfunctions; this option is tempting only because it describes a real breakdown. • Since the second item is not on the list, "in both cases" is also incorrect.

g3-q36.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: There is movement in steering parts or assemblies that is not provided for by the design.
White-light turn signals are installed at the front.
g3-q36.explanation: The presence of unintended movement of steering parts and assemblies not provided by design endangers controllability and prohibits operating the vehicle. Turn signal indicators with white lights at the front are permitted, since at the front only lighting devices with colors other than white, yellow, or orange are prohibited. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Steering Systems", item 2; "External Lighting Devices", item 6)

g3-q37.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The tires have localized damage exposing the tire cord.
g3-q37.explanation: If tires have localized damage (punctures, cuts, tears) exposing the tire carcass (cord), operating the vehicle is prohibited, as the risk of tire blowout increases. Irregular engine operation is not included in the list of malfunctions prohibiting operation. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Wheels and Tires", item 2)

g3-q38.text: A passenger-car may not be operated if:
options: The remaining tire tread depth is 2.2 mm.
g3-q38.explanation: In the absence of a first-aid kit, operating a passenger car is prohibited. The minimum permissible residual tread pattern depth for passenger car tires is 1.6 mm, so a measurement of 2.2 mm fully complies with the standard. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Wheels and Tires", item 1.b; "Other Malfunctions", item 9.a)

g3-q39.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: For a bus built on a passenger-car chassis, the total play in the steering system exceeds 10 degrees.
The mudguards and splash guards provided by the vehicle’s design are missing.
g3-q39.explanation: The total free play in the steering system of passenger cars and trucks and buses built on their basis must not exceed 10 degrees (for regular buses 20°, for trucks 25°). Operation is also prohibited in the absence of mudguard aprons and splash guards provided by design; therefore, the prohibition applies in both cases. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Steering Systems", item 1.a; "Other Malfunctions", item 7)

g3-q40.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The cargo-bed door latch provided by the vehicle’s design does not operate.
The cab door latch provided by the vehicle’s design does not operate.
g3-q40.explanation: Operation of vehicles is prohibited if the locks of body or cab doors provided by design do not work. Since both malfunctions are explicitly listed among prohibiting conditions and endanger passenger and driver safety, operation is prohibited in both cases. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", item 6)

g3-q41.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Red-light turn signals are installed at the rear.
The rear protective device provided by the vehicle’s design is missing.
g3-q41.explanation: Operation of a vehicle is prohibited if the rear underrun protective device provided by design is missing. Turn signal indicators with red lights at the rear do not prohibit operation, since red, yellow, and orange colors are permitted for rear lighting devices. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "External Lighting Devices", item 6.b; "Other Malfunctions", item 7)

g3-q42.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The power steering system provided by the vehicle’s design is defective or missing.
The car audio system is not functioning.
g3-q42.explanation: If the power steering unit provided by design is faulty or missing, operating the vehicle is prohibited. Meanwhile, a non-functioning audio player does not prohibit operation, unlike a malfunction of the audible warning device (horn). (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Steering Systems", item 3)

g3-q43.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The parking brake system does not hold the vehicle stationary on the gradient specified by the standard.
The leak-tightness of the transmission seals is compromised.
g3-q43.explanation: In both cases, operating the vehicle is prohibited. A parking brake system that fails to hold the vehicle stationary on the slope established by the standard, and loss of tightness in gearbox seals, are included in the list of malfunctions prohibiting operation. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Braking Systems", item 4; "Other Malfunctions", item 15)

g3-q44.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The spare-wheel holder does not operate.
The leak-tightness of the rear-axle seals is compromised.
g3-q44.explanation: A non-functioning spare wheel carrier can cause the wheel to detach while driving, and loss of tightness in rear axle seals leads to oil leakage and environmental pollution. Both malfunctions directly prohibit operating the vehicle. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", items 13, 15)

g3-q45.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: There are visible tears in the webbing of the seat belts provided by the vehicle’s design.
The vehicle is not equipped with fog lamps.
g3-q45.explanation: The presence of visible tears on the webbing of seat belts provided by design reduces their strength and prohibits operating the vehicle. The absence of fog lamps is not a violation, as they are not mandatory equipment. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", item 11)

g3-q46.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The engine-hood latch provided by the vehicle’s design does not operate.
The rear side windows are curtained and two side rear-view mirrors are installed.
g3-q46.explanation: If the engine hood latch provided by design does not work, operation is prohibited, because the hood can fly open while driving and block visibility. Curtains on rear side windows are permitted if 2 side rear-view mirrors are present. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", item 5.c, item 6)

g3-q47.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The rear side windows are curtained and two side rear-view mirrors are missing.
The window heating and defogging devices provided by the vehicle’s design do not operate.
g3-q47.explanation: In both cases, operating the vehicle is prohibited. Rear side windows may be curtained only when 2 side rear-view mirrors are present, and windshield/window heating and defrosting (blower) devices provided by design must be in working order. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", item 5.c, item 6)

g3-q48.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The fuel-tank cap provided by the vehicle’s design does not operate.
The front side windows are curtained.
g3-q48.explanation: A non-functioning fuel tank cap is dangerous in terms of fuel leakage and fire, and curtaining the front side windows is prohibited regardless of the presence of side mirrors. Consequently, operation is prohibited in both cases. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", item 5.b, item 6)

g3-q49.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The windows provided by the vehicle’s design are missing.
g3-q49.explanation: Operation of a vehicle is prohibited both when the audible warning device (horn) does not work and when windows provided by design are missing. Both conditions are explicitly established in the list of prohibiting malfunctions. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", items 2, 3)

g3-q50.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: There are cracks in a wheel rim or wheel disc.
There are visible distortions in the shape or dimensions of the wheel-rim mounting holes.
g3-q50.explanation: Cracks on a wheel rim or disc, as well as visible distortions in the shape and size of mounting holes, compromise secure wheel fastening. In both cases, operating the vehicle is prohibited. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Wheels and Tires", item 3)

g3-q51.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The exterior lighting devices and reflectors are dirty.
The front and rear protective devices are dirty.
g3-q51.explanation: If external lighting devices and reflectors are dirty, they do not ensure proper visibility, so operating the vehicle is prohibited. Dirty front and rear protective devices are not grounds for prohibiting operation (only the absence of a rear protective device is prohibited). (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "External Lighting Devices", item 3)

g3-q52.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Lamps or lenses are missing from the lighting devices.
Lenses or lamps that do not correspond to the type of the lighting device are used.
g3-q52.explanation: In both cases, operating the vehicle is prohibited. It is not permitted to operate lighting devices without bulbs or lenses (diffusers), or to use lenses or bulbs that do not match the type of the given lighting device. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "External Lighting Devices", item 4)

g3-q53.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The exterior lighting devices and reflectors are dirty.
Exterior lighting devices from a different make of vehicle are installed on a discontinued vehicle.
g3-q53.explanation: If external lighting devices and reflectors are dirty, operating the vehicle is prohibited. Meanwhile, on vehicles discontinued from production, it is permitted to install external lighting devices of other makes and models, so the second option is not a violation. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "External Lighting Devices", items 1, 3)

g3-q54.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Tires with different tread patterns are installed on the same axle.
The remaining tire tread depth of a passenger car is 1.6 mm.
g3-q54.explanation: Mounting tires with different tread patterns on the same axle is prohibited, as this impairs the vehicle's stability and handling. The residual tread depth of passenger car tires must not be less than 1.6 mm; therefore, a height of exactly 1.6 mm is still permissible. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Wheels and Tires", item 1.b, item 5)

g3-q55.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The remaining tire tread depth of a truck is 1.4 mm.
Yellow reflectors are installed at the front.
g3-q55.explanation: At the front of a vehicle, it is prohibited to install retroreflective devices of any color other than white (including yellow), so in the second option operation is prohibited. The minimum permissible tread depth for truck tires is 1.0 mm; therefore, 1.4 mm complies with the standard. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "External Lighting Devices", item 6.a; "Wheels and Tires", item 1.c)

g3-q56.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Yellow reflectors are installed at the rear.
Yellow reflectors are installed at the front.
g3-q56.explanation: At the rear of a vehicle, only red retroreflective devices may be installed, and at the front only white ones (except license plates, distinguishing marks, and identification signs). Consequently, installing yellow retroreflective devices is prohibited both at the front and at the rear. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "External Lighting Devices", item 6)

g3-q57.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: An “Oversized Cargo” identification sign with white and red reflective stripes is installed at the rear.
The remaining tire tread depth of a moped is 0.7 mm.
g3-q57.explanation: According to items 162 and 175 of the Rules, the "Oversize Load" identification sign marks cargo protruding beyond the established limit, whereas installing a panel with white and red retroreflective stripes on the rear of a vehicle without grounds violates the rear reflector color requirement. In addition, the minimum permissible tread depth for moped tires is 0.8 mm, so at 0.7 mm operation is prohibited. (Rules, items 162, 175; Appendix No. 2, "Wheels and Tires", item 1.d; "External Lighting Devices", item 6.b)

g3-q58.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: The “Doctor” identification sign is missing from an automobile driven by a physician-driver.
The fuel-tank cap provided by the vehicle’s design does not operate.
g3-q58.explanation: If the fuel tank cap does not work, operating the vehicle is prohibited. Meanwhile, displaying the "Doctor" identification sign is optional—done at the driver's discretion—so its absence does not prohibit operation. (Rules, item 175; Appendix No. 2, "Other Malfunctions", item 6)

g3-q59.text: A vehicle may not be operated if:
options: Tires with different tread patterns are installed on the same axle.
A “Transportation of Children” identification sign with a yellow reflective background and red reflective border is installed at the front.
g3-q59.explanation: Mounting tires with different tread patterns on the same axle prohibits operating the vehicle. Meanwhile, the ban on non-white reflectors at the front does not apply to identification signs, and the "Children Transport" sign specifically has a yellow background and red border, so mounting it at the front is permitted. (Rules, Appendix No. 2, "Wheels and Tires", item 5; "External Lighting Devices", item 6)

g4-q1.text: When making a right turn, is it permitted to enter the lane indicated by this sign?
options: Permitted if the lane is not separated from the rest of the roadway by a solid pavement marking.
g4-q1.explanation: Shown is sign 5.14 "Lane for Public Transport Vehicles". Entering the indicated lane to make a right turn is permitted only if it is separated from the rest of the roadway by broken rather than solid road markings, which rules out unconditional answers 1 and 2 (Rules, item 124, sign 5.14).

options: A section of road where a sidewalk or pedestrian path is present.
A section of road where a pedestrian crossing is present.
A section of road where there is no sidewalk or pedestrian path.
g4-q2.explanation: Shown is warning sign 1.22 "Pedestrian Crossing", informing of approaching a road section where a pedestrian crossing is located. It has nothing to do with the presence or absence of a sidewalk or pedestrian path, so options 1 and 3 are incorrect (Rules, sign 1.22).

g4-q3.text: Which sign prohibits vehicles from proceeding with a distance between them that is less than the distance shown on the sign?
g4-q3.explanation: Sign number three—the minimum distance sign of 70 meters. Sign 3 depicts two cars one behind the other with the number 70 m above them: it means entering this section of road with a longitudinal following distance of less than 70 meters from the vehicle ahead is prohibited. This sign speaks about the "distance between two vehicles," not the dimensions of the vehicle itself—and the entire question hinges on that distinction. Such a restriction is usually installed on bridges, in tunnels, on structures with limited load capacity, and on long mountain descents. It has two safety reasons: first, reducing the simultaneous load on a single span of a structure; second, ensuring braking distance where a sudden stop of a column ends in chain-reaction collisions. On a descent, a heavy vehicle's braking distance is several times longer than usual, and a short distance means an unavoidable impact. For quick recognition on the exam, separate the sign families: signs that use opposing arrows to restrict one dimension of the vehicle itself (width, height, length), and the sign depicting two separate cars. Wherever there are two vehicles on a sign, it is about following distance. • Sign 1 with opposing arrows and the number 2.7 m limits the permissible width of a vehicle; it has nothing to do with the distance between cars. • Sign 2 depicting a truck and the number 10 m limits the length of a vehicle: again a single dimension of the vehicle itself, not distance. • Sign 4 is a supplementary plate showing the length of the main sign's zone of application; by itself it creates no prohibition. • Sign 5 is a blue square with the number 50, i.e., recommended speed; by nature it is informational and creates no prohibition at all.

g4-q4.text: Within populated areas, how far before a hazardous section of road are these signs installed?
g4-q4.explanation: 50–100 meters before the dangerous section of the road. All five signs in the image belong to the warning family: railway crossing with a barrier, railway crossing without a barrier, intersection of equal-priority roads, traffic light control, and "other dangers". A single placement rule applies to all of them: in built-up areas, 50–100 meters before the hazard; outside built-up areas, 150–300 meters. The logic behind these two figures is the distance needed to react. Outside the city, at speeds near 90 km/h, a driver needs a greater distance to see, decide, slow down, and stop if necessary. In the city, speed is lower, while the density of intersections, courtyard exits, and signs is high: a sign placed too far away loses its mental link to the hazard, and the driver forgets about it before reaching it. Remember this as a pair: "50–100 inside, 150–300 outside." Note that these distances apply to warning signs; prohibitory and priority signs are usually placed immediately before where they take effect, and this rule does not apply to them. • 15–25 meters is so short that at city speed it is covered in about one second; practically no time remains to react. • 25–50 meters is also less than needed for effective speed reduction and does not fall into either regulatory range. • 100–150 meters is an ambiguous range falling right between the two correct values; for that reason it is the most deceptive. • 150–300 meters is the correct answer, but for locations outside built-up areas; the question asks about a built-up area, and this substitution is the main trap.

options: Prohibits all motor vehicles except two-wheeled motorcycles without sidecars.
Prohibits all vehicles except wheeled tractors.
g4-q5.explanation: Shown is prohibitory sign 3.6 "No Tractors". It prohibits the movement of tractors and self-propelled machines in both directions and does not apply to all other motor or non-motor vehicles (as stated in options 1 and 2) (Rules, sign 3.6).

g4-q6.text: Which sign requires a driver to yield to vehicles entering or approaching the narrow section of road from the opposite direction?
g4-q6.explanation: Sign 3—the "Priority for Oncoming Traffic" sign. Sign 3 is a red-bordered circle with two arrows: a large black arrow pointing down (the oncoming flow) and a small red arrow pointing up (you). It means that on a narrow road section, vehicles moving from the opposite direction have priority: you must stop before entering the narrowing and let them pass. Such a sign is usually placed before single-lane bridges, roadwork zones, or sections where the roadway width is insufficient for two cars to pass simultaneously. The safety logic is that a joint decision by two drivers in a narrowing reaches a deadlock: both enter, meet in the middle, and one is forced to reverse—on a bridge or beside a parapet. The sign removes this ambiguity in advance and assigns the duty one-sidedly: the red color of your arrow means "prohibited specifically for you," not merely a warning. What is worth remembering and where the classic exam trap lies: this symbol has two versions. Round with a red border means you yield; a blue square with a large white arrow means you have priority. Take the background color as your criterion: red and round = duty, blue and square = priority. Whenever you see this pair, look first at the shape and color, then at the arrow directions. • Sign 1 is "No Motor Vehicles"; it says nothing about priority, it prohibits entry. It is chosen only because it is also round and red. • Sign 2 is the inverted "Give Way" (Yield) triangle, which applies to an intersecting road, not to a narrowing and oncoming flow. The similarity of "yielding" is deceptive, as its place of application is an intersection. • Sign 4 is the warning triangle for an intersection; it only informs that an intersection is ahead and creates no duty to yield by itself. • Sign 5 is a supplementary plate with a two-way arrow. A supplementary plate never has independent meaning: it only defines the length or direction of the main sign above it.

g4-q7.text: Which sign warns of an approaching intersection of roads of equal priority?
g4-q7.explanation: Sign number five—the black cross with two arms of equal thickness. In the family of warning signs for intersections, line thickness is the language of the sign. On sign 5, both arms of the cross are the same size and thickness: meaning neither road has priority over the other, and ahead of you is an intersection of equal-priority roads. At such an intersection, right-of-way is determined not by a sign, but by the "right-hand rule": you must yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. The safety reason for placing this warning is precisely so the driver knows in advance that they are entering an intersection where no one has guaranteed priority. An equal-priority intersection is the most dangerous type of uncontrolled intersection, since both drivers may assume they are on the main road. The sign compels you to slow down, look right, and be ready to stop. What is worth remembering: wherever you see one thick line on a triangular sign, that line is your road and the thinner one is the secondary road, meaning you have priority. Only when both lines are the same thickness is it about equal priority and the right-hand rule. • Sign 1 has a thick vertical line (your road) and a thin horizontal line (secondary): meaning an intersection with a minor road where you have priority—the exact opposite of equal priority. • Sign 2 is from the same family and merely shows a minor road joining from one side; here too your road is the main one. • Sign 3 is the inverted "Give Way" (Yield) triangle and belongs to the priority family; its meaning is that your road is minor, not equal-priority. • Sign 4 with two opposing arrows informs of the start of two-way traffic and has nothing to do with an intersection.

g4-q8.text: Which sign is installed immediately before the intersection of roadways?
g4-q8.explanation: Sign number two, i.e., "No Right Turn". Sign number two is round with a red border and an arrow drawn on it, meaning it is prohibitory. Prohibitory signs restricting a maneuver at an intersection are placed immediately before the crossing of roadways, since their effect starts at that exact point and the driver must make a decision right there. If this sign stood a hundred meters earlier, it would be unclear which intersection the prohibition applies to. The other four signs are triangular, warning signs, and their function is different: they inform rather than prohibit. A warning sign must be placed at some distance from the hazard so the driver has time to slow down, shift gears, and prepare to pass; placing it right at the hazard is useless. Therefore, warning signs are always placed tens or hundreds of meters before the hazard, and outside built-up areas this distance is greater because speeds are higher. The rule to remember is this exact division: a red triangle means "something like this is ahead, get ready" and is placed at a distance; a red circle means "not allowed from here" and is placed at the point where the prohibition applies. The exam trap is that an "intersection" sign is also present in the image, and one's mind is drawn to it; yet that sign only informs of the presence of an intersection and is placed ahead of it. • Sign 1 only informs of approaching an intersection and, as a warning sign, is placed in advance, not immediately before the crossing of roadways. • Sign 3 warns of exiting onto an embankment or shore and has nothing to do with an intersection. • Sign 4 warns of a railway crossing without a barrier: this is where a road crosses railway tracks, not two roadways, and it is placed at a distance. • Sign 5 warns of a drawbridge and, like the other triangles, is placed ahead of the hazard.

options: Straight ahead, to the right, and by making a U-turn.
g4-q9.explanation: In the image, sign 3.2 "No Vehicles" (Traffic Prohibited) is installed with supplementary plate 8.3.2 "Direction of Application" pointing left. This combination prohibits traffic only to the left; therefore, at the intersection it is permitted to proceed straight, turn right, and make a U-turn (reverse direction), which rules out restrictive options 1, 2, and 3 (Rules, signs 3.2, 8.3.2).

g4-q10.text: Which sign gives a driver the right-of-way over oncoming vehicles?
g4-q10.explanation: Sign number four, i.e., "Priority over Oncoming Traffic". Sign number four is a blue rectangle with one large white arrow pointing up and one small red arrow pointing down. The blue color means good news for you: at the narrow section ahead, you go first while the oncoming vehicle must wait. Sign number two is its mirror image: round, with a red border and a large red arrow, it means you must yield. What to remember: on both signs, the large arrow belongs to whoever has priority, while the red arrow always represents the oncoming flow. If the red arrow is small, the right is yours; if the red arrow is large, you must stop. Shape also helps: a circle with a red border is duty and prohibition, a blue rectangle is information and priority. This pair of signs is installed on narrow bridges, in gorges, and on sections where road width is insufficient for two cars to pass simultaneously. If the legislator did not assign priority for such a place, two drivers would enter the narrowing from both ends and either get stuck in the middle or reverse: both outcomes on a mountain road are dangerous. One-sided assignment of priority removes the decision from split-second negotiations between two drivers. • Sign 1 is merely a "Two-Way Traffic" warning and gives priority to no one: it simply informs that oncoming traffic exists. • Sign 2 is the exact opposite of the right answer: under it, you are required to yield to oncoming traffic. • The yellow diamond means main road and gives priority only at intersections over minor roads, not over traffic coming toward you. • Sign 5 shows lane movement directions and dedicates one lane to public transport vehicles; its subject is lane allocation, not priority over oncoming traffic.

g4-q11.text: What does the supplemental plaque below the sign indicate?
options: The distance from the sign to the beginning of the first turn.
The distance from the first turn to the beginning of the second turn.
The length of the road section with hazardous turns.
g4-q11.explanation: Below sign 1.12.2 "Dangerous Bends" is supplementary plate 8.2.1 "Distance/Zone of Application" with arrows pointing upward on both sides ("↑ 100 m ↑"). The plate with arrows indicates the length of the road section with dangerous bends (100 m), not the distance to the first or second bend (Rules, signs 1.12.2, 8.2.1).

g4-q12.text: What does the following combination of signs indicate?
options: Motorcycle traffic to the right is prohibited.
Motorcycle traffic to the right is permitted.
g4-q12.explanation: Shown is a combination of prohibitory sign 3.5 "No Motorcycles" and supplementary plate 8.3.1 "Direction of Application" pointing right. This means motorcycle traffic to the right is prohibited, so option 2 ("permitted") is incorrect (Rules, signs 3.5, 8.3.1).

g4-q13.text: Which sign prohibits parking on even-numbered days of the month?
g4-q13.explanation: The sign numbered five — with two vertical bars on a blue background. The last two signs in the image form a pair that differ only in the number of vertical bars on them: one bar means parking is prohibited on odd days of the month, and two bars mean on even days. The way to remember this is simple counting: count the bars and match that number to the parity of the day of the month. The fifth sign has two bars, meaning it closes even dates. The logic behind these two signs is to keep one side of the street clear on alternating days. On narrow city streets, if both sides are constantly filled with parked cars, the passage width narrows to a single lane, ambulances and fire trucks cannot pass, and cleaning and snow removal become virtually impossible. With these two signs, one side of the street is clear every day, while parking is not completely banned. The exam trap is that all five signs in the image look alike, and attention is drawn to the supplementary plates under the 2nd and 3rd signs. However, those plates refer to working days and weekends, not the parity of the date. The only place where the day of the month matters is those vertical bars inside the sign itself. • The 1st sign prohibits parking without specifying a date: on any day of the month, even or odd. • The plate under the 2nd sign indicates working days and has nothing to do with the parity of the date. • The plate under the 3rd sign applies to weekends and holidays, not the day of the month. • The 4th sign has only one vertical bar, meaning the exact opposite — parking is prohibited on odd days of the month.

options: Permits driving only at the indicated speed or higher.
Prohibits driving at a speed higher than the speed shown on the sign.
Indicates the speed recommended for driving on this section of road.
g4-q14.explanation: It permits movement only at a speed of 50 km/h or higher. The blue background and round shape place this sign in the mandatory signs family — that is, signs that tell you what to do, not what not to do. The number 50 on a round blue background means the minimum permitted speed: on this stretch of road you cannot travel slower than 50 km/h. Remember the difference between these three signs once and for all: a white circle with a red border and a number means maximum speed, and exceeding it is prohibited; a blue circle with a number means minimum speed, and driving slower is prohibited; a blue square with a number means recommended speed and is not mandatory. All three have a number, and it is this similarity that causes mistakes on the exam: make your decision by shape and color, not by the number. The safety reason behind a minimum speed limit is also important: a very slow vehicle on a high-speed road becomes an obstacle itself. It forces drivers behind to brake sharply and make repeated overtakes, and a large difference in speed between vehicles is a known crash factor. If your vehicle cannot maintain this speed for technical reasons or due to weather, this road is not suitable for it. • This is the definition of the maximum speed sign, which is round and white with a red border: the blue background reverses the sign's meaning. • Recommended speed is placed on a blue square sign and is not mandatory, whereas this round blue sign is a mandate.

g4-q15.text: Which of the following signs requires a driver to yield to oncoming vehicles?
g4-q15.explanation: The 2nd sign — the 'Priority for oncoming traffic' sign. The 2nd sign is the circle with a red border where the large black arrow points down and the small red arrow points up. This is the only sign in the set that obliges you to give way to oncoming vehicles: on a stretch of road not wide enough for simultaneous passage, you must stop before entering to let the oncoming flow pass. The most dangerous option in this question is the 5th sign, because it has the exact same two arrows, but with reversed colors and inside a blue square frame: a large white arrow up (you) and a small red one down (oncoming flow). Its meaning is the exact opposite — you have priority. So if you only keep 'two opposite arrows' in your head, you will get it wrong half the time on the exam. The key to telling them apart is the color and shape of the frame: a round sign with a red border creates an obligation, while a blue square grants priority. A second way to distinguish them is the color of your own arrow: on the 2nd sign, the arrow for your direction is red, meaning 'you stop'; on the 5th sign, the arrow for your direction is white and large, meaning 'you go'. Remember this single point and you will answer several questions from this family without hesitation. And on the real road, slow down before entering a narrowing even when the sign gives you priority: the oncoming driver may not have seen their sign. • The 1st sign is the 'Two-way traffic' warning triangle: it only informs you that oncoming traffic exists from this point and creates no obligation to yield. Its two arrows also lead to confusion with the correct sign. • The 3rd sign is the 'STOP' sign: it obliges you to come to a full stop and give way to the intersecting road, not to vehicles approaching you head-on. • The 4th sign is blue and relates to 'traffic directions by lanes': it only shows where each lane goes and has nothing to do with priority. • The 5th sign has the exact opposite meaning: the blue background and the large white arrow in your direction mean you have priority over oncoming traffic. This is the most tempting wrong option in the question.

options: Advance indication for going around an obstruction.
Advance indication for changing to another roadway.
Advance indication for entering the oncoming traffic lane.
g4-q16.explanation: The advance lane-change indicator. The yellow background of this sign shows that it is temporary and installed for the duration of road works. The image on it shows the traffic lanes from above: one of the lanes is closed by a round red symbol, while an arrow coming from below directs the flow into the adjacent lane. The word 'advance' in the sign's name is the core of its meaning: the sign is placed ahead of the actual merge point so the driver knows in advance that they will need to change lanes. This 'advance notice' is the sign's safety function. The most dangerous situation in a road-works zone is when a driver stays in the closed lane until the last moment and then, seeing the cones, swerves or brakes sharply. The result is a side impact with a car in the adjacent lane or a rear-end collision. The advance sign gives you time to reduce speed, check your mirrors and blind spot, turn on your indicator, and smoothly change lanes. On the exam, the option describing the maneuver itself is tempting because it sounds practically accurate. But the question asks for the name of the sign, and this sign's name points to the lane change. When answering, always associate yellow signs with road works and temporary traffic management. • The obstacle bypass sign shows the obstacle itself on the path and indicates which side to pass it on; here it is about directing traffic into another lane. • This wording describes the maneuver rather than the sign's name: the sign announces an upcoming lane change.

g4-q17.text: Which sign requires a driver to yield to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road?
g4-q17.explanation: The 3rd sign — the inverted 'Give way' triangle. The 3rd sign is a white inverted triangle with a red border and no symbol inside — 'Give way'. This sign obliges you to give way to vehicles traveling on the intersecting road. Unlike the 'STOP' sign, coming to a complete stop is not mandatory, but you must slow down enough to stop if necessary, and you must not force any driver on the intersecting road to change their path or speed. The key distinction in this set is between a 'warning sign' and a 'priority sign'. The 1st, 2nd, and 4th signs are upright triangles with a red border, and they only inform you that something awaits ahead: none of them creates a legal duty to yield. Only the single sign with its own unique shape — the inverted triangle — creates an obligation. The reason this sign is inverted and has no symbol worldwide is safety: a driver must recognize it from a distance, in fog, at night, and even when snow has stuck to its face and symbols have become illegible. No other sign has this shape, so ambiguity is zero. What to remember for the exam: use shape, not color, as your criterion. Upright triangle = warning, inverted = give way, octagon = stop. • The 1st sign is the 'Intersection of roads of equal importance' warning triangle: it only tells you there is an intersection ahead where priority is determined by the 'right-hand rule', not by this sign. • The 2nd sign warns of 'traffic light control'. Your obligation is set by the traffic light, not by this sign; the sign itself only prompts you to slow down. • The 4th sign — a triangle with an exclamation mark — means 'Other dangers': this is the most general warning sign, and it creates no specific priority duty. • The 5th sign applies to a road narrowing and obliges you to give way to oncoming traffic, not to the intersecting road. The similarity is in the verb 'give way', but the place of application is completely different.

g4-q18.text: Which of the following signs permits driving only at the indicated speed or higher (km/h)?
g4-q18.explanation: Number 3 shows the blue round mandatory sign 4.6 'Minimum speed limit', which permits driving only at the indicated speed (50 km/h) or higher. 1 is the maximum speed limit (3.24), 2 is its end (3.25), 4 is the end of the minimum speed limit zone (4.7), and 5 is the recommended speed (6.2) (Rules, sign 4.6).

g4-q19.text: Which sign indicates a section of one-way road?
g4-q19.explanation: The sign numbered three — the blue rectangle with a single white arrow pointing upward. The sign numbered three is a blue rectangle with one plain white arrow, and it means that traffic across the entire width of this carriageway moves in only one direction. This is an information sign about the road's status, not an instruction regarding your maneuver: it tells you there is no oncoming traffic and you may use the full width of the carriageway. The main trap in this question is sign number 5 — the blue circle with a white arrow. The shape, color, and arrow look similar, but the meaning is completely different: a blue circle is a mandatory sign, telling you that from this point you must proceed straight only, without saying anything about one-way traffic for the entire road. Remember the general rule: a circle defines your obligation, while a rectangle and square describe the condition of the road. The other two signs in the image disqualify themselves. The signs for priority over oncoming traffic and yielding to oncoming traffic both assume that oncoming traffic exists — i.e., that the road is two-way. On a one-way road, oncoming traffic makes no sense at all, and this contradiction immediately rules out both options. • The red triangle in the image warns of the road narrowing from the right and says nothing about the direction of traffic. • The 2nd sign grants priority over oncoming vehicles: the presence of oncoming traffic means the road is two-way. • The 4th sign obliges you to yield to oncoming traffic: here too, the underlying assumption is a two-way road. • The blue circle with an arrow is the 'Proceed straight only' mandatory sign, and it governs your action at that point, not the traffic regime of the entire road.

g4-q20.text: What does the supplemental plaque used with the main sign indicate?
options: The length of the narrow section of road.
The distance from the sign to the location where the restriction begins.
The distance to the location for going around the narrow section of road.
g4-q20.explanation: Under the prohibitory sign 3.14 'Width limit' ('2.7 m'), there is a plate without arrows, 8.1.1 'Distance to object' ('300 m'). A plate without arrows shows the distance from the sign to the point of the restriction (300 m), rather than the length of the narrow section, for which plate 8.2.1 with arrows is used (Rules, signs 3.14, 8.1.1).

g4-q21.text: This traffic sign warns that ahead there is:
options: A road section with a water crossing that has no bridge or ferry.
A road section crossing water by means of a drawbridge.
A location where the road reaches a riverbank or shoreline.
g4-q21.explanation: A place where the road leads onto an embankment or shore. The image inside the red triangle shows a car going off the edge of a vertical wall toward the water. This sign warns that the road ahead ends at an embankment, quay, or shore — that is, a place where the carriageway surface abruptly ends and immediately beyond it is water or a drop-off. The safety reason for this sign is straightforward: such places usually lack a solid reliable barrier, road markings at night also poorly define the edge, and in rain or fog the water surface can be mistaken for a continuation of the road. A minor braking or steering mistake here is irreversible, as the car enters the water and rescuing those inside is extremely difficult. Seeing this sign, you must slow down, avoid overtaking and unnecessary maneuvers, and at night stay away from the edge of the carriageway. The exam point is that water also appears on several other triangular signs, which creates confusion. Tell them apart by the main element of the picture: if a car is falling off the edge into water, it is an embankment or shore; if a bridge span is raised, it is an opening bridge; and if a boat is shown, it is a ferry crossing. • This description refers to a ferry crossing without a bridge, which has a separate sign depicting a boat rather than a car falling off an edge. • The opening bridge sign shows the bridge itself with a raised span: there is no bridge at all in this image.

g4-q22.text: Which of the following indicates the area of effect of traffic signs prohibiting stopping and parking?
g4-q22.explanation: Number 4 shows plate 8.2.2 'Zone of validity' with an upward-pointing arrow and the inscription '10 m', which is used with signs prohibiting stopping and parking (3.27–3.30) and indicates their effective zone. 1, 2, and 3 are prohibitory signs (width, length, and minimum distance limits), while 5 is the recommended speed sign 6.2 (Rules, sign 8.2.2).

g4-q23.text: Which sign indicates the length of a hazardous road section covered by the warning signs?
g4-q23.explanation: Number 4 shows plate 8.2.1 'Zone of validity' with two arrows ('↑ 100 m ↑'), which when paired with warning signs indicates the length of the dangerous stretch of road. 2 (8.1.1) and 5 (8.1.2) indicate the distance to an object or a 'STOP' sign, 1 shows recommended speed (6.2), and 3 shows a route number and direction (Rules, sign 8.2.1).

options: A one-way road on which only trucks are permitted.
A lane designated only for trucks.
The recommended direction of traffic for trucks.
g4-q24.explanation: Recommended direction of movement for trucks. This sign belongs to the information signs family: a blue rectangular field, an upward white arrow, and a truck silhouette beside it. Its message is route advice — meaning movement in this direction is considered suitable for freight vehicles. It neither obliges a truck to take this route nor excludes passenger cars from it. The safety logic behind this sign is simple: the shortest route is not always the right route for a truck. A narrow street, a bridge with limited load capacity, a steep grade, and a residential neighborhood are places where the passage of a heavy vehicle means a longer braking distance, a wider turning radius, and heightened danger for pedestrians. By placing this sign, the traffic authority guides freight traffic onto a suitable road before it reaches that bottleneck, without banning anything. The exam trap in this question is color and shape. Every prohibition is framed by a red circle, and every mandate by a blue circle; a blue rectangle means 'information and guidance'. This rule alone separates the three options: an arrow inside a blue rectangle never creates an obligation or exclusivity, it only informs. If you use the sign's shape rather than the wording of the options as your criterion, you will always solve this class of questions correctly. • 'One-way traffic' is announced by a separate sign without a truck symbol; moreover, this sign does not prohibit passage for any other vehicles and creates no exclusivity. • Reserving a lane for a specific type of vehicle is announced by a special lane sign placed above that lane; this sign refers to the direction of the entire road, not a single lane of the carriageway.
