g4-q25.explanation: Number 3 shows service sign 7.9 'Hotel or motel' with a bed silhouette. The other signs show: 1 — 'Hospital' (7.2), 2 — 'Refreshments' (7.7), 4 — 'Camping site' (7.10), and 5 — 'Rest area' (7.11) (Rules, sign 7.9).

g4-q26.text: Vehicles displaying this identification sign are:
options: Driven by deaf or deaf-mute drivers.
Driven by drivers with less than 3 years of driving experience.
g4-q26.explanation: Vehicles driven by deaf or deaf-mute drivers. The sign in the image is a yellow circle with three black dots arranged in a triangle. This identification sign is placed on a vehicle whose driver is deaf or deaf-mute and must be visible to other drivers from the front and rear. Its safety reason is entirely practical: a significant share of everyday road warnings are auditory — a horn, an ambulance or police siren, the sound of braking, and the sound of a car in your blind spot. A driver with such a sign hears none of these. Seeing a yellow circle on a car ahead or alongside, you must assume that sounding your horn is useless: instead, increase your following distance, switch on your turn signal well in advance, use your headlights to signal your presence, and never start a maneuver like overtaking or changing lanes relying on your horn. This change in behavior alone prevents 'I thought they heard me' crashes. It is worth remembering how to distinguish this family of identification signs by color and shape: a yellow circle with three dots means the driver cannot hear; a wheelchair symbol means a driver with a disability; a colored rectangular plate means dangerous goods; and the novice driver sign is something else. The exam constantly swaps these four signs for one another. • The dangerous goods sign is a rectangular plate with a colored section and a black border showing the hazard code, not a yellow circle; the similarity of yellow and orange makes this option tempting. • A vehicle of a driver with a disability is marked with a wheelchair symbol: plain dots contain no reference to physical disability. • A novice driver is marked by a different sign, and its subject is driving experience, not hearing: these two signs are confused only because both are yellow.

g4-q27.text: Which sign indicates the end of a zone with a maximum speed limit of 50 km/h?
g4-q27.explanation: The sign numbered two — the same maximum speed 50 sign crossed out with diagonal lines. The end of a restriction is shown by repeating the image of the restricting sign itself, but crossed out diagonally and without red color. For a sign to mean 'end of 50 limit', two conditions must be met simultaneously: the same number 50 must be repeated on it, and the diagonal lines must indicate cancellation. Keeping the number is not accidental: several different restrictions may be in force on a route at the same time, and the end sign must clearly specify which exact one is ending. A common trap in this question is the 'end of all restrictions' sign — a circle with several diagonal lines and no number at all, which lifts all previously introduced restrictions at once. If there is no number on the sign, it is not the answer to this question. A practical note for Armenia's roads: an explicit end sign is not always installed; a speed limit may also end upon reaching the next intersection, at a sign leaving a built-up area, or upon installation of a new speed sign with a different number. Thus, the absence of a cancelling sign by itself proves nothing: keep these three indicators in mind as well.

g4-q28.text: What do this sign and supplemental plaque warn about?
options: Stopping on the shoulder is prohibited because of roadwork.
Entering the shoulder is dangerous because of roadwork.
Parking on the shoulder is prohibited because of roadwork.
g4-q28.explanation: Pulling onto the shoulder is dangerous due to road repair works. Read the two elements of the image together. At the top is a triangle with a red border and the symbol of a worker with a shovel: the 'Road works' warning sign. At the bottom is a rectangular plate showing a car whose right side has dropped onto a broken, uneven shoulder. The combination of these two elements means: road repairs are ahead, and driving onto the shoulder is dangerous. The decisive rule is sign classification. A triangle with a red border only warns: by itself, it never prohibits anything. The plate beneath it only specifies the subject of the warning rather than creating a new ban. Therefore, any option starting with 'prohibited' is suspect before you even finish reading it. The safety reason here is also physical: in a repair zone, the shoulder is usually dug up, covered with gravel, or loose, and sits at a different level from the carriageway. If you take the right wheels onto such a shoulder at speed, one side of the car will get less traction, the vehicle will be pulled toward the shoulder, and trying to correct it with a sharp turn of the steering wheel will end in a rollover or veering into the oncoming lane. So you must reduce speed, stay on the carriageway, and find a safer spot for an emergency stop. • A triangle with a red border only warns and sets no prohibition: a stopping ban is announced by a round sign, not by a road-works warning sign. • This option also attributes a prohibition to a warning sign; moreover, the difference between 'parking' and 'stopping' is not the subject of this sign at all, and the plate below speaks of the danger of the shoulder, not permission to be there.

g4-q29.text: Vehicles displaying this identification sign are:
options: Driven by deaf or deaf-mute drivers.
g4-q29.explanation: It carries dangerous goods. The sign in the image is a rectangular plate with a black border: the left side is white, the right side is colored (orange-red), divided horizontally into two halves. This plate is mounted on the front and rear of a vehicle carrying dangerous goods — fuel, gas, chemicals, flammable or toxic substances — and its colored part displays the hazard code and substance identification number. The safety function of this sign has two layers. The first is for you as an ordinary driver: keep a greater distance behind such a vehicle, do not rush to overtake it, avoid staying alongside it in a tunnel or dense traffic, and know that this vehicle has its own speed and route restrictions and does not stop abruptly. The second layer is for emergency services: in a crash, the number on the orange plate determines whether firefighters extinguish with water or foam and how wide to set the evacuation zone. Therefore, the sign must always remain clean and legible. A common trap is confusing this plate with other identification signs. Keep a simple criterion: a rectangle with a colored section and black border means dangerous goods; a yellow circle with three dots means a deaf driver; a wheelchair symbol means a driver with a disability; and a square with diagonal red-and-white stripes means an oversized load. • The sign for a driver with a disability bears a wheelchair symbol: there is no symbol of an occupant on this plate, and it refers to the vehicle's cargo, not the driver. • An oversized load is marked with diagonal red-and-white stripes (and, if needed, flags and lights): the shared red color is what leads to confusing these two signs. • The deaf driver sign is a yellow circle with three black dots, and it is not rectangular at all.

g4-q30.text: Which sign cancels all previously imposed restrictions?
g4-q30.explanation: The 4th sign — a white circle with diagonal lines and no symbol inside. The rule that solves this question is: on 'end of restriction' signs, diagonal lines cancel only what is drawn inside the circle. That means if there is no symbol inside the circle, no specific restriction is selected, and the sign lifts all previously imposed restrictions at once. The 4th sign is just that — an empty circle with several diagonal lines. Each of the remaining signs in the image cancels one and only one thing. On the 1st sign there are two passenger cars — end of no-overtaking zone. On the 2nd sign there are a truck and a passenger car — end of no-overtaking zone for trucks. On the 3rd sign there is the number 50 — end of the 50 km/h speed limit. The 5th sign is a crossed-out yellow diamond, which does not belong to the restrictions family at all, but announces the end of a priority road. The safety logic of this rule is simple: restrictions are introduced for a reason, and lifting them unintentionally is dangerous. If a single 'end' sign could vaguely cancel everything, a driver leaving a hazard zone would not be sure which rule still applies. Therefore, only one sign has the authority to cancel everything, and only with a blank symbol. A phrase to remember: 'only what is inside the circle is cancelled; an empty circle means all'. • The 1st sign announces only the end of the overtaking ban: a speed limit or any other previously imposed prohibition is not lifted by it. • The 2nd sign announces the end of the overtaking ban only for trucks: its scope is even narrower than that of the 1st sign. • Inside the 3rd sign is the number 50, meaning it cancels only that 50 km/h speed limit: this is the most common wrong answer to this question. • The 5th sign — the crossed-out yellow diamond — means the end of the priority road: this sign is about priority and does not belong to the restrictions family at all.

g4-q31.text: In which case has the driver correctly complied with the requirements of this sign?
options: The driver yielded to motor vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road.
The driver yielded to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road.
g4-q31.explanation: They have yielded to all vehicles traveling on the intersecting road. The sign in the image is the inverted triangle with a red border — 'Give way'. The requirement of this sign is absolute and allows no exceptions by vehicle type: that is, approaching the intersection, you are obliged to give way to everything moving along the intersecting road, not only motor vehicles. The difference between the two options lies in one word: 'vehicle' is a broader concept than 'motor vehicle', and includes bicycles, mopeds, and animal-drawn carts. If you read the text of the law as 'motor', you reach the wrong conclusion that you may pull out in front of a cyclist. The safety reason is right here: the most vulnerable road user at an intersection is the cyclist. They have no bodywork or airbag, no engine noise to draw your attention, and in a mirror they appear small and inconspicuous. An inexperienced driver's eye scans for a 'car' and fails to process a bicycle: most collisions with cyclists at intersections happen this exact way. One more practical point: 'Give way' is not the same as 'Stop'. This sign does not oblige you to come to a full stop: if the intersecting road is clear, you can proceed without stopping. The real requirement is that nobody on the intersecting road should be forced to change speed or direction. • The word 'motor' narrows the scope, and that is what makes the option tempting: you are also obliged to give way to bicycles, mopeds, and animal-drawn carts moving on the intersecting road.

g4-q32.text: Which of the displayed signs is used as the identification sign for a road train?
g4-q32.explanation: The right-hand sign — three orange lights arranged in a horizontal row on the cab roof. In the image, two trucks are seen from the front. On the roof of the right-hand cab, three orange lights sit side by side at equal spacing: this arrangement of three lights is the identification sign of a road train — that is, a vehicle towing a trailer or semi-trailer whose total length is much greater than that of an ordinary truck. On the roof of the left-hand vehicle there is merely a triangular orange symbol, which is a different sign and has nothing to do with a road train. The safety reason for this sign is overtaking. At night or in rain, a driver behind sees only the rear lights and underestimates the true dimensions of the combination. Overtaking a road train requires two to three times as much clear distance, and if a driver realizes mid-maneuver that they misjudged the length, there is no turning back. Three orange lights give this warning from afar: this is a long vehicle, and overtaking needs more time and space. The exam trap is the 'both signs' option, since both symbols are orange and both are mounted on the roof. The true criterion is not color, but quantity and arrangement: three lights in a row. • On the roof of the left-hand vehicle is a triangular orange symbol, which is a different sign: the orange color is shared, but the road-train sign is always three lights in a row. • Both signs are orange and mounted on the roof, which makes them look similar, but only the row of three lights signifies a road train: accepting both means losing the identification criterion.

g4-q33.text: Which sign requires a driver to yield to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road?
g4-q33.explanation: The 4th sign — the inverted 'Give way' triangle. The 4th sign is a white inverted triangle with a red border meaning 'Give way': before entering the intersection, you must yield to vehicles traveling on the intersecting road. In practice, this means a minor road is under your wheels and the intersecting road is the priority road: you must reduce speed enough so that your entry does not force any driver to brake or swerve. The other three signs in this set are unrelated to intersections and serve only as filler: one is a supplementary plate, another is a mass limit for trucks, and the third concerns road narrowing. The only serious rival is the 2nd sign, which also refers to an intersection, but only warns. This distinction must be locked in: a warning sign says 'be aware of what is ahead', while a priority sign says 'here is what you must do'. The reason this sign exists is simple: at an intersection with no signs at all, priority is decided by the 'right-hand rule', and that rule works only when both drivers can see each other. At intersections with limited visibility or where one road is clearly busier, the law removes the uncertainty and places the duty on the minor road. What to remember: the inverted triangle is the only sign with a unique shape so that it can be recognized even from behind and in the worst visibility. • The 1st sign is a plate with a two-way arrow. A plate never creates an obligation on its own: it only specifies the length or direction of the main sign above it. • The 2nd sign is the intersection warning triangle, and it is tempting precisely because its subject is an intersection. However, it only warns: at such an intersection, priority is determined by the 'right-hand rule'. • The 3rd sign applies to road narrowing and obliges you to yield to oncoming vehicles, not to the intersecting road. • The 5th sign is a mass limit for trucks and says nothing about priority at all: it merely prohibits the movement of vehicles heavier than the stated limit.

g4-q34.text: Which of the following signs (supplemental plaques) indicates how a vehicle must be positioned when parked?
g4-q34.explanation: The 3rd plate — the car standing with the wheels on one side on a raised curb. The 3rd plate shows a car at an angle with the wheels of one side on the raised surface of the street edge. This image is an instruction, not a description: within the zone of a parking sign, the car must be positioned exactly as drawn on the plate. If the plate shows the car halfway onto the curb, parking entirely on the carriageway is a violation, and vice versa. The reason for this rule is street geometry. In narrow passages, if every car parks across its full width on the carriageway, the remaining width will not be enough for two-way traffic and, more importantly, for an ambulance or fire truck. On the other hand, unregulated parking on the sidewalk pushes pedestrians out into the middle of the road. The parking-method plate sets this exact balance point, and therefore must be followed literally. What to remember: a parking-method plate always shows the car's relationship to the edge and curb. If the image on the plate does not show the car's relationship to a curb or sidewalk edge, that plate is not about parking. • The 1st plate shows a car with a red symbol crossed out: its subject is a restriction related to the car's condition, not how to position it next to the carriageway. • The 2nd plate shows a car near an uneven, sunken shoulder: this is the 'Dangerous shoulder' warning, and it does the opposite — telling you to stay away from the edge, not park there. • The 4th plate shows a car on a bridge-like structure, and its relationship to a curb or sidewalk is not shown: thus it does not define a parking method. • The 5th plate is simply the silhouette of a passenger car and indicates which type of vehicle the main sign applies to: it specifies the vehicle type, not its position.

g4-q35.text: Is it permitted to stop in the lane indicated by this sign to pick up passengers?
options: Permitted if the lane is located along the right edge of the roadway and is not separated from the rest of the roadway by a solid pavement marking.
g4-q35.explanation: Permitted, provided that this lane is at the right edge of the carriageway and is not separated from the rest of the carriageway by a solid marking line. The sign in the image is a blue square with an upward white arrow and a bus symbol — a lane for public transit vehicles. The general rule is that other vehicles have no right to drive or stop in this lane, but the law makes a limited exception for boarding and alighting passengers. This exception has two conditions, and both must be met simultaneously: the dedicated lane must be at the right edge of the carriageway and must not be separated from the rest of the carriageway by a solid marking line. In addition, your stop must not obstruct the movement of public transit vehicles. The logic of both conditions is safety. A solid line means crossing it is prohibited: if you enter the dedicated lane across such a line, you will have to cross it and stop right in front of a bus moving at steady speed and not expecting an obstacle. The 'at the right edge' condition exists so that passengers step directly onto the sidewalk rather than crossing traffic lanes. The exam trap is that both unconditional options — 'prohibited' and 'permitted' — sound simple and decisive, whereas the correct answer is conditional. In questions about dedicated lanes, always look for the option that states both conditions together: the right edge and the absence of a solid line. • An unconditional ban ignores the law's explicit exception for boarding and alighting passengers: this option merely repeats the general rule on dedicated lanes. • Unconditional permission is even more dangerous: if the dedicated lane is separated by a solid line or is not at the right edge, entering and stopping on it is a violation.

g4-q36.text: When this traffic sign is present:
options: Passing by all types of vehicles is prohibited, except when passing slow-moving vehicles, animal- drawn carts, two-wheeled motorcycles without sidecars, mopeds, and bicycles.
Trucks with a maximum authorized mass not exceeding 3.5 metric tons are permitted to pass.
Passing is permitted if the speed of the passing vehicle does not exceed 30 km/h.
g4-q36.explanation: Overtaking is prohibited for all types of vehicles except for overtaking slow-moving vehicles, animal-drawn carts, motorcycles without a sidecar, mopeds, and bicycles. This sign introduces a general ban with a closed list of exceptions, and the criterion for an exception is the type of vehicle you are overtaking. The logic of the list is simple: all five are either very slow or very narrow. The speed difference with a bicycle, moped, or cart is large and their width is small, so the overtaking maneuver is completed in a few seconds and sometimes does not even require fully entering the oncoming lane. Banning such overtakes would only create long, tiring queues behind slow-moving vehicles without reducing real danger; whereas overtaking a passenger car or truck traveling close to your speed is the exact maneuver the sign is placed to prevent. The exception does not exempt you from other rules: a solid line, limited visibility, intersections, and pedestrian crossings remain in force. On rural and mountain roads in Armenia, where tractors and carts are not uncommon, this exception is the most practical part of the rule, though it is performed only with sufficient visibility of the oncoming lane. • The exemption by truck mass applies to the 'No overtaking by trucks' sign: on this sign, the criterion is the type of vehicle being overtaken, not the mass of the overtaking vehicle. • There is no such numerical condition in the list of exceptions: a 'slow-moving vehicle' is a specific class with an identification sign, not just any car currently traveling slower than 30 km/h.

g4-q37.text: Which sign indicates “Intersection with a Bicycle Path”?
g4-q37.explanation: Number 2 shows the triangular warning sign with a red border 1.24 'Cycle track crossing'. 1 is the mandatory sign 4.4.1 'Cycle track', 3 prohibits cycling (3.9), 4 is a vehicle-type plate (8.4.7), and 5 prohibits motorcycles (3.5) (Rules, sign 1.24).

g4-q38.text: Which sign indicates the end of the no-passing zone?
g4-q38.explanation: Number 1 shows sign 3.21 'End of no-overtaking zone' (silhouette of two passenger cars crossed by diagonal black lines). 2 cancels only the overtaking ban for trucks (3.23), 3 cancels the speed limit (3.25), 4 cancels all restrictions (3.31), and 5 is sign 2.1 'Priority road' (Rules, sign 3.21).

g4-q39.text: Which sign indicates the permitted directions of traffic at a T-intersection?
g4-q39.explanation: The 2nd sign — the red rectangular panel with white arrows pointing left and right. The 2nd sign is a rectangular panel with a red background and a row of white arrows pointing both left and right. This panel is placed directly facing the driver at the end of the stem of a T-intersection — right where the road ahead ends and the only continuation is to the left or right. Its message is directional: there is no straight path from here. The safety reason is visibility at night and in bad weather. The end of a road is the most dangerous type of road termination: if a driver realizes this too late, they will run straight off the intersection. The red background and retroreflective white arrows are visible from a long distance and sooner than a car's headlights illuminate the road markings, giving the driver time to slow down. That is why such a panel is usually installed together with a warning sign. The exam trap is confusing 'indicating direction' with 'mandating direction'. A blue round sign gives a movement mandate and can stand anywhere; the red panel with arrows refers specifically to the point where the road ends. If you take the geometric shape of the sign as your criterion — red rectangle versus blue circle — this question is solved in seconds. • The 1st sign is a blue circle with left and right arrows: this mandatory sign sets the permitted direction of movement and can stand at any intersection, meaning it is not specific to a T-intersection. • The 3rd sign is a warning triangle for a minor road joining from the left: in that case you are on the through road, and your road does not end. • The 4th sign announces a dead end: a dead end means the road has no continuation at all, whereas at a T-intersection the route continues left and right. • The 5th sign is a blue circle with two diverging arrows and refers to passing an obstacle on either side: its subject is an obstacle on the carriageway, not the end of a road at an intersection.

options: The direction of traffic toward a destination located within a populated area.
The end of an acceleration lane or an additional lane on an uphill grade.
g4-q40.explanation: A road without through passage — that is, a dead end. This sign is rectangular and blue: a white vertical line ending in a horizontal red bar. It is a simple diagram of what lies ahead: a road you enter that is closed at the end. The red bar depicts that very wall or blocked end of the route. The key point tested on the exam is that this sign belongs to the information family, not the prohibitory family. Entry into a dead-end street is free: the sign only informs you that you have no exit that way and will have to make a U-turn to come back. That is why the background is blue and there is no red ring around it. The reason for placing this sign is clear: a driver who enters a dead end unaware is forced to turn around in a narrow alley usually filled with parked cars, or reverse for a long distance. Prolonged reversing in a tight space is one of the most frequent sources of hitting pedestrians, especially children, and colliding with parked cars. Announcing a dead end before entry completely eliminates this maneuver. A common trap is confusing it with the 'No entry' sign (a red circle with a horizontal white bar). That sign prohibits entry; this one only informs. There are also versions of this same sign with a horizontal branch showing that the road to the right or left at the intersection ahead is a dead end. • 'Direction toward an object in a built-up area' is shown by a sign with a guiding arrow and, as a rule, the name of the destination: in this image there is no arrow at all, and the end of the line is closed by a red bar. • 'End of an auxiliary lane or acceleration lane' is depicted as a diagram of several lanes, one of which merges: here we have a single route closed at the end.

g4-q41.text: Which vehicles are permitted within the area where this sign is in effect?
options: Vehicles whose maximum speed exceeds 40 km/h.
g4-q41.explanation: Shown is the special regulation sign 5.3 'Road for motor vehicles'. Within the zone of this sign, only cars and motorcycles are permitted, while the entry of tractors, self-propelled machines, mopeds, bicycles, and vehicles whose speed is below 40 km/h is prohibited, which rules out the other options (Rules, items 116–117, sign 5.3).

g4-q42.text: Which of these traffic signs is not a prohibitory sign?
g4-q42.explanation: The sign numbered 2 — the inverted triangle with a red border, i.e., 'Give way', which belongs to the priority signs. The key to this question is shape and color, not the symbol inside the sign. In this system, prohibitory signs are all round with a thick red border. In the image, signs 1 (horn prohibited), 3 (no overtaking), 4 (no stopping — a blue circle with a red cross inside a red ring), and 5 (maximum speed 50 km/h) have this exact format and prohibit one behavior or another. The 2nd sign is the only one that is not a circle at all: a white inverted triangle with a red border. Across the entire sign system, this shape is reserved for only one sign, and its message is 'Give way'. That is, it prohibits nothing, but determines the order of crossing the intersection and belongs to the priority signs group. The safety logic of such coding is important: at real driving speed, a driver first recognizes the shape and color of a sign from afar and only then reads the symbol inside. An inverted triangle is recognizable from any angle and even when snow or mud has stuck to the sign; that is why it was given a unique shape. A common exam trap is the 5th sign. The number 50 inside a red circle is a prohibition, whereas the same number on a blue square is merely a recommended speed. Color and shape decide, not the number. • The 1st sign is 'No audible warning devices' — a red circle with a crossed-out horn symbol, a fully prohibitory sign. • The 3rd sign is 'No overtaking' — two cars inside a red circle, one painted red to indicate the overtaking vehicle. • The 4th sign is 'No stopping': the blue field inside the red ring must not mislead you, as the red border keeps it in the prohibitions group. • The 5th sign is 'Maximum speed 50 km/h', and it prohibits driving faster.

g4-q43.text: What does this identification sign indicate?
options: Ahead is a section of road with an uneven roadway surface.
Ahead is a section of road with three lanes for traffic in this direction.
The motor vehicle is equipped with studded tires.
g4-q43.explanation: The vehicle is equipped with studded tires. Before you is a white triangle with a red border and the letter 'Ш' in the middle. This is not a roadside sign: it is a vehicle identification sign placed on the rear window of a car. The letter 'Ш' is the initial letter of the word for 'studs' (shipy), and it serves as the sole means of recognition. The safety logic goes back to the physics of braking. A studded tire has much greater grip on ice and packed snow and shortens braking distance, but on dry or wet asphalt it performs worse than an ordinary tire. That means the braking behavior of such a car differs from what you expect from a normal one. A driver following behind must know that on an icy road the vehicle ahead may stop much sooner than expected, and therefore must keep a greater distance. This sign is placed specifically to make such behavior predictable. The exam trap is the triangular shape and red border, which pull you toward the warning road signs group and make options like 'uneven road surface' or 'three lanes' look plausible. The rule for telling them apart is simple: a road sign is mounted on a post beside the road and bears a graphic symbol; an identification sign is placed on the vehicle's body and here bears a letter of the alphabet instead of a picture. • 'Uneven carriageway' has its own separate warning sign showing a bump, not a letter of the alphabet. • 'Three lanes in this direction' is announced by a blue rectangular sign depicting traffic lanes: no triangular sign carries such a message.

g4-q44.text: Which sign is called “End of One-Way Road”?
g4-q44.explanation: The sign numbered four — a wide white arrow pointing up on a blue field, crossed out by a red diagonal stripe. In the group of blue information signs, a simple rule applies: the sign itself announces the start of a traffic regime, while the same sign with a red diagonal stripe announces the end of that regime. The 'One-way road' sign is a wide arrow pointing up on a blue field; therefore, 'End of one-way road' is the exact same arrow crossed out by a red stripe — sign 4 in the image. This sign is not a mere informational formality: from the moment you pass it, the road's status changes completely. Up to that point, the entire width of the carriageway belonged to your direction and you could use any lane; beyond it, the left half of the road belongs to oncoming traffic. That means you must immediately return to the right half and stop using the left for overtaking or U-turns. The deadliest crashes caused by this mistake are head-on collisions with a car the driver did not expect. To remember it, keep this distinction fixed: one arrow means one-way traffic, while two arrows in opposite directions mean reversible traffic. Sign 1 in the image has just such two crossed-out arrows, and it is the most frequent distractor in this question. • Sign 1 has two arrows in opposite directions: this means 'End of road with reversible traffic', not one-way. The only visual difference is the number of arrows, which makes the option tempting. • The 2nd sign depicts a bus and several lanes and marks the end of a road with a lane for public transit vehicles, not the end of one-way traffic. • The 3rd sign has no red stripe at all: its arrow crosses along a dashed line onto a parallel carriageway and does not 'end' any regime. • The 5th sign has an upward arrow together with a bus, and it marks the beginning of a road with a lane for public transit vehicles — the opposite of 'end'.

g4-q45.text: Which sign requires a driver to yield to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road?
g4-q45.explanation: The 2nd sign — the inverted 'Give way' triangle. The 2nd sign is a white inverted triangle with a red border and no symbol, and it is the only sign in the set that obliges you to give way to vehicles traveling on the intersecting road. It is usually installed slightly before the intersection so you have time to reduce speed: you must enter in such a way that no driver on the priority road is forced to brake or change path. The trap in this question is the 3rd sign. It also creates an obligation to 'give way', but in a completely different situation — a road narrowing and oncoming traffic, not an intersection. If you only memorized the phrase 'which sign means give way', you will confuse these two. Remember the difference by 'place of application': inverted triangle for an intersection, circle with two arrows for a narrowing. The safety point behind this sign is that an intersection without assigned obligations is the most dangerous spot in the road network: angled impacts cause the greatest injuries to occupants because the side of a car has the least protective structure. The 'Give way' sign removes this uncertainty before the intersection and from a safe distance. Remember that this sign is not the same as 'STOP': a full stop is not required here, though in poor visibility you will have to stop in practice. • The 1st sign is 'No motor vehicles': it prohibits entry and says nothing about priority at all. Its visual similarity (round and red) is the only reason for a wrong choice. • The 3rd sign obliges you to yield to oncoming vehicles on a narrowed stretch of road. This is the most attractive wrong option because it also creates a duty to yield, just not at an intersection. • The 4th sign is the intersection warning triangle: its subject is an intersection, but it only informs. At such an intersection, priority is decided by the 'right-hand rule', not by the sign. • The 5th sign is a plate with a two-way arrow and has no independent meaning: it only specifies the length or direction of the main sign above it.

options: A parking place 30 meters away for automobiles displaying the “Disabled” identification sign.
A parking place within a 30-meter-long area for vehicles, except motorized wheelchairs.
A parking place within a 30-meter-long area for motorized wheelchairs and automobiles displaying the “Disabled” identification sign.
g4-q46.explanation: Shown are signs 6.4 'Parking area', 8.17 'Disabled', and 8.2.1 'Zone of validity' with two arrows ('↑ 30 m ↑'). This combination indicates a parking area over a 30 m zone for motorized invalid carriages and cars equipped with the 'Disabled' identification sign, which rules out the incorrect 1st ('in 30 meters') and 2nd ('except motorized invalid carriages') options (Rules, signs 6.4, 8.17, 8.2.1).

g4-q47.text: Which of these signs is considered a vehicle identification sign?
g4-q47.explanation: Number 3 shows the vehicle identification sign 'Transporting children' (a yellow square with a red border and a silhouette of running children), which is mounted on vehicles carrying organized groups of children. 1 (1.23 'Children') and 2 (4.5.1 'Pedestrian path') are road signs (Rules, items 155, 175).

g4-q48.text: Traffic of which vehicles is prohibited by this traffic sign?
g4-q48.explanation: The movement of motor vehicles. The sign is a circle with a red border and a picture of a car in the middle. The red border places it in the prohibitory signs group, and in this sign system the car image symbolizes the entire family of motor vehicles, not only the specific type drawn. That is, motorcycles, vans, trucks, and buses are covered by the same prohibition. This distinction is the core of the question. The sign designer has to draw one symbol, and the simplest and most recognizable symbol of a motor vehicle is a passenger car. If a ban were meant to be restricted to one specific class, a separate sign with that class exists for it — for example, signs that directly prohibit trucks or motorcycles. From a safety standpoint, this sign is usually placed where an area is not designed for motorized traffic at all: a park zone, pedestrian route, protected area, or narrow passage that cannot withstand motorized loads. In such places, a pedestrian does not expect to encounter a motor vehicle and does not exercise ordinary roadside caution: the entry of any motorized transport — passenger car or motorcycle — creates the same danger. Thus a ban covering only cars makes no sense. A rule to remember: the picture on a sign is an 'example', not a 'closed list'. • 'Only cars' narrows the scope of the ban without reason: if this were true, a motorcycle could enter freely and the entire point of the sign would be lost. • 'Only passenger cars' is even narrower than the previous option and relies solely on the outward shape of the picture, whereas the picture represents the entire class of motor vehicles.

g4-q49.text: Which sign indicates that an obstruction may be passed on either the right or the left?
g4-q49.explanation: The sign numbered five — a blue circle with two arrows diverging upward to the right and left. The obstacle-bypass sign belongs to the mandatory family, hence the blue circle with a white symbol. This sign is usually placed directly on the obstacle itself — a dividing island, road-works site, construction equipment, or anything blocking part of the carriageway. Two arrows diverging from one point to the right and left mean the obstacle may be passed on either side, and the choice of side is yours. The reason for placing it is to eliminate last-second hesitation. A stationary obstacle on the carriageway is noticed late, especially at night or in rain: a driver who sees it at short distance either brakes sharply or swerves abruptly into the adjacent lane. Both maneuvers cause crashes. A bright retroreflective sign on the obstacle makes the decision in advance. The biggest trap in this question is the 1st sign. It is also a blue circle, and it also has arrows to the right and left, but its arrows emerge from a vertical stem and form a 'T' shape — meaning 'turn right or left' at the intersection ahead and a ban on going straight. On the 5th sign there is no stem at all, and the two arrows diverge diagonally. This stem makes all the difference: a stem means an intersection, no stem means an obstacle. • On the 1st sign the arrows sit on a vertical stem, establishing 'turn right or left' at an intersection: the shared blue circle and two directions make it the most tempting option. • The 2nd sign is a blue rectangle with a single white arrow pointing right, announcing the direction of traffic: it does not refer to bypassing an obstacle. • The 3rd sign is a red warning triangle for a minor road joining from the left, meaning its subject is priority, not bypassing. • The 4th sign is the blue dead-end sign, telling you the road ahead has no exit — the opposite of 'may be passed on either side'.

g4-q50.text: Which sign is placed on the front and rear of vehicles transporting organized groups of children?
g4-q50.explanation: At the front and rear of vehicles transporting organized groups of children, identification sign number 1 'Transporting children' must be mounted. 2 is the 'Disabled' identification sign, while 3 (4.5.1) and 4 (1.23) are road signs and are not mounted on vehicles (Rules, item 155).

g4-q51.text: What do the indicated traffic signs show?
options: The priority road continues to the left at the intersection.
The priority road continues straight ahead and to the left at the intersection.
g4-q51.explanation: The priority road continues to the left beyond the intersection. On the right side of the image, two elements are mounted on the same post: a yellow diamond with a white border meaning 'Priority road', and directly beneath it a supplementary plate showing the layout of the intersection ahead. On this plate, a thick line rises from below — that is, from the route you are traveling on — and turns left; the straight road and the right-hand road are drawn with thin lines. The thick line is always the priority road, and the thin line is the minor road. The practical message of this combination is vital: you are currently on the priority road, but the priority road does not continue straight through this intersection. If you go straight, you leave the priority road, and at that point you no longer have priority: you must give way to vehicles traveling along the priority direction. Conversely, by turning left, you remain on the priority road and have priority, though you must switch on your left turn signal. The safety reason for this plate lies right here. Most drivers' mental assumption is that 'going straight means continuing on the same road', and on that basis they enter an intersection without slowing down. When the priority road bends, this assumption proves false, and the result is a side impact in the middle of the intersection — the most crash-prone pattern of urban intersections. The direction plate is installed specifically to break this assumption. • If the priority road continued both straight and left, the plate would have to show the thick line in both directions; in the image, however, the straight continuation is drawn as a thin line and only the left branch is thick.

g4-q52.text: What do the indicated traffic signs show?
options: Within the area of effect of the supplemental plaque, drivers must proceed at a speed higher than the speed shown on the sign.
Within the area of effect of the supplemental plaque, drivers are advised to proceed at the speed shown on the sign.
g4-q52.explanation: Within the sign's effective zone, drivers are recommended to travel at 50 km/h. In the image, a blue square sign with the number 50 is placed beside the street, and underneath it is a plate with '800 m' between two arrows. Color and shape determine the message: a blue field means an information sign, and a number on a blue field means a recommended rather than a mandatory speed. The plate below tells you this recommendation applies for the next 800 meters. The difference between this sign and the round 'Maximum speed' sign with a red border is fundamental. That sign sets a legal limit, and exceeding it is a violation; this one suggests the speed that yields the best result on that specific stretch. A recommended speed is usually set to coordinate with sequential traffic lights or for a section with a certain curve radius and limited visibility. If you travel at this speed, you generally avoid hitting red lights and having to brake sharply, and reducing sharp braking is what lowers rear-end collisions. Note that the fact that this number is a recommendation does not mean complete freedom: general speed limits, including the built-up area ceiling visible in the image, remain in force. A common exam trap is that the mind instantly translates the number 50 as 'speed limit'. The true criterion is background color: red and round means obligation, blue and square means recommendation. • No sign requires a driver to travel faster than the number written on it: the 'Minimum speed' sign is also a blue circle and means 'do not go slower', not 'go faster'.

g4-q53.text: Which signs apply only during the period when the roadway surface is wet?
g4-q53.explanation: Only sign C — the 50 km/h speed limit together with the 'Wet surface' plate. The plate under sign C bears an image of a cloud with raindrops, and its job is to restrict the temporal scope of the main sign: the 50 limit applies only while the carriageway surface is wet. On a dry road, the same sign has no effect, and the general limit for that section applies. The safety logic here works in two directions. On wet asphalt, the friction coefficient drops sharply, and braking distance at the same speed becomes much longer; the risk of aquaplaning also increases. Yet if the same limit applied in dry weather, it would create a sign that seems pointless most of the time, and drivers would gradually start ignoring it — and then fail to obey it on a rainy day as well. Making the sign conditional preserves its authority. The main trap is sign A. It depicts a car skidding on a slippery surface, and the mind immediately translates that as 'wet road'. However, slipperiness can also be caused by ice, mud, leaves, or an oil spill: this sign is not conditional and applies at all times. A rule to remember: a restriction under specific conditions is announced only by a plate below the sign, never by the picture on the sign itself. • 'Only A and C' is appealing because sign A depicts skidding on a slippery surface; however, that sign has no conditional plate and also applies on a dry icy or oily road. • 'Only B' is wrong: sign B warns of loose gravel thrown up from under wheels and has nothing to do with pavement wetness. • 'All' would mean all three signs are conditional on wetness, whereas the wet-surface plate is only under sign C.

g4-q54.text: What should the driver do in this situation?
options: Move into the part of the roadway intended for oncoming traffic.
g4-q54.explanation: In the image, sign 3.2 'No vehicles' is mounted above the right carriageway, and on the right is the temporary yellow sign 6.19 'Advance indicator of changing to another carriageway'. It indicates that to bypass the section closed to traffic, the driver must move onto the oncoming carriageway, so continuing straight is prohibited (Rules, signs 3.2, 6.19).

g4-q55.text: What do the following traffic signs indicate?
options: There is a narrowing of the road from the right 150–300 m beyond the sign, and the narrowed section is 100 m long.
There is a narrowing of the road from the right 100 m beyond the sign.
g4-q55.explanation: Shown are warning sign 1.20.2 'Road narrows' (from the right) and plate 8.2.1 'Zone of validity' with two arrows ('↑ 100 m ↑'). Outside built-up areas, a warning sign is placed 150–300 m before the start of the hazardous section, while plate 8.2.1 shows the length of the narrowed section (100 m), not the distance to the narrowing (Rules, signs 1.20.2, 8.2.1).

g4-q56.text: In which direction is the driver permitted to proceed?
options: To the right and left only.
Straight ahead and by making a U-turn.
g4-q56.explanation: Straight ahead, as well as in the opposite direction (U-turn). The round white sign with a red border is 'No vehicles', but the plate underneath limits its scope: a horizontal two-way arrow means this prohibition applies to the roads going right and left at the intersection ahead. Thus entry onto the intersecting road — both right and left — is closed, while the straight route remains open. A U-turn is also not prohibited, because when making a U-turn you do not enter the intersecting road and remain on the road you are already traveling on. The general rule this question teaches: a plate never creates an obligation on its own; it only states where and to what the sign above it applies. If the plate is ignored, the sign is read as many times stricter than it is, making it seem the road is closed altogether. The use of this combination in a city is obvious: it allows closing side alleys or minor streets at an intersection — a residential zone, market, or narrow street — to through traffic without cutting off the road's main flow. A common exam trap is that the test-taker automatically puts a U-turn on the list of bans, whereas neither the sign nor the plate said anything about a U-turn. • This is the exact opposite of the truth: right and left are the very two directions that the two-way arrow plate assigned to the ban. • 'Straight only' is half right and therefore tempting, yet it needlessly excludes a U-turn, since a U-turn is not entering the intersecting road.

g4-q57.text: What do the indicated traffic signs show?
options: Stopping is prohibited on Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays.
g4-q57.explanation: Stopping is prohibited on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays. The main sign is a blue circle with a red border and a red cross — 'No stopping'. This sign is stricter than the no-parking sign because it bans both parking and brief stopping. However, the white plate beneath it with a red asterisk-like symbol limits the time of the ban to Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. That means on working days this same edge of the carriageway is open for stopping. The logic of such a time restriction is straightforward: on certain streets, traffic load rises only on non-working days — near a market, church, park, or event venue — and a car stopped at the curb blocks visibility and eats up the usable width of the carriageway. Rather than closing the street permanently, the law closes only those days. The image shows a narrow street with houses right next to the carriageway, which a single row of parked cars would easily block. The trap in this question is entirely visual: the plate's symbol looks like a snowflake and steers the mind to 'during snowfall', whereas no plate announces weather conditions. Remember the pair of 'day' plates together: crossed hammers mean work and thus working days; the asterisk-like symbol means non-working days. • The plate does not announce a single day: Saturday is part of the non-working days set, not all of it. • The same objection applies as to the previous option: Sunday is also just one day in that set and omits Saturday and holidays. • Supplementary plates do not refer to weather. The resemblance of this symbol to a snowflake is coincidental, and the exam author is counting on that resemblance.

g4-q58.text: Which traffic sign prohibits a U-turn?
g4-q58.explanation: The 3rd sign — the crossed-out U-turn arrow. All three signs are white circles with a red border and a crossed-out arrow — meaning all three prohibit a particular maneuver and differ only in the shape of the arrow. The arrow on the 1st sign points right, on the 2nd left, and on the 3rd turns 180 degrees: this full reversal is the U-turn symbol. Thus the answer is the 3rd sign. The most important point of this question is a distinction tested in various ways on the exam: 'No left turn' and 'No U-turn' are two separate signs, and neither replaces the other. Where only the no-U-turn sign is installed, a left turn remains permitted. The reason for prohibiting a U-turn is that of all maneuvers, a U-turn occupies the carriageway for the longest time: the car must cross the width of the road and the lanes of both directions, moving very slowly the entire time and exposed to a side impact. That is why this maneuver is closed in places with poor visibility, on busy roads, and near lively intersections even where a left turn is still considered safe. • The 1st sign closes only a right turn and has nothing to do with a U-turn: its connection to the question is zero. • The 2nd sign is the most tempting option, since a U-turn begins as a leftward movement; however, that sign prohibits only turning onto the road to the left, while a U-turn has its own sign.

g4-q59.text: What do these traffic signs indicate?
options: Entering the shoulder is dangerous because of roadwork.
Roadwork is being carried out on the road.
g4-q59.explanation: In the image, sign 1.25 'Road works' is mounted on the right with plate 8.12 'Dangerous shoulder'. That combination specifically warns that pulling onto the shoulder is dangerous due to repair works, so the 2nd option mentioning only repairs is incomplete (Rules, signs 1.25, 8.12).

g4-q60.text: What must the driver do when the following traffic sign is installed before an intersection?
options: Proceed through the intersection while maintaining safety.
Yield to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road.
Stop before the sign and yield to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road.
g4-q60.explanation: They must come to a complete stop before the sign and then give way to vehicles on the intersecting road. The red octagonal sign reading 'ԿԱՆԳ / STOP' is the only sign that makes a full stop mandatory: no merely slowing down and no 'look and roll'. The vehicle must stop completely at the stop line — or, if no stop line is marked, before the sign and at the edge of the carriageway of the intersecting road — and then must give way to any vehicle moving along the intersecting road, proceeding only when your entry will not force any driver to brake or change path. The key point is that this requirement does not depend on traffic being present: even if the intersecting road is completely empty, stopping is still mandatory. There are two reasons. First, a complete stop guarantees that you actually looked: a driver creeping forward has practically no chance of spotting a fast car or motorcycle. Second, this sign is usually installed where visibility is restricted, and the only proper vantage point is that very edge of the intersecting carriageway. A common trap is confusing this sign with the inverted 'Give way' triangle. That sign only requires yielding, and if the road is clear you may proceed without stopping; at a 'STOP' sign, stopping is unconditional. The unique octagonal shape was chosen for the same reason: even when the sign is covered with snow or mud and the inscription cannot be read, it is recognized by shape. • 'Proceed while maintaining safety' reduces the 'STOP' sign to the level of advice: this sign is a precise, verifiable duty, not a general call for caution. • Giving way is necessary, but not sufficient. That phrasing is the exact meaning of the 'Give way' sign, and it omits what sets the 'STOP' sign apart — coming to a full stop.

g4-q61.text: Which traffic signs do not apply to public transit vehicles?
g4-q61.explanation: Only the fourth sign. The first three signs concern stopping and parking: the 1st sign is no parking, the 2nd is no parking on odd days of the month, and the 3rd is no stopping. These bans also apply to public transit vehicles: their only concession is that they may stop at designated stops to pick up and drop off passengers. Outside those stops, a bus falls under the ban just like any other car. The 4th sign belongs to a different family: a white circle with a red border and a car image, meaning a ban on motor vehicle traffic. Traffic bans do not apply to public transit vehicles. The logic is simple: the goal of such a sign is to remove general car traffic from a street (narrow street, residential zone, old quarter), not to cut off a bus route that the residents of that very neighborhood depend on. Public transit drivers are also professionals following a fixed and familiar route. A distinction worth keeping in mind: a traffic ban does not affect public transit vehicles, whereas stopping and parking bans do, because the reason for a 'No stopping' sign is the hazard of a specific spot — blocked sightlines, narrowed carriageway, proximity to an intersection — and a bus stopped there creates the exact same hazard as a passenger car. • 'None' assumes public transit vehicles have no exceptions at all, whereas the fourth sign is precisely their exception. • The 1st sign is a parking ban, and contrary to this option, it is among the signs that also bind public transit vehicles.

options: At the intersection, traffic must proceed to the left or to the right.
Reversible traffic is established on the intersecting road.
One-way traffic is established on the intersecting road.
g4-q62.explanation: In the image, before the intersection, there is the blue rectangular sign 5.10 'Entering a road with reversible traffic' (with a horizontal two-way white arrow). It informs you that reversible traffic is organized on the intersecting road, which rules out options about one-way traffic or a mandatory turn (Rules, sign 5.10).

g4-q63.text: In this situation, must the driver yield to the truck?
g4-q63.explanation: Must yield: when exiting a residential zone, priority belongs to vehicles moving along the road. The blue sign on the right side of the image depicting a car, a pedestrian, and a playing child, crossed out by a red diagonal line, is the 'End of residential zone' sign. That means you are leaving a residential zone and entering a public road — the very carriageway along which the white truck is moving on the left side of the frame. The rule is simple and allows no exceptions: a driver exiting a residential zone yields to all vehicles and pedestrians moving along the road. The safety reason is clear: speeds inside a residential zone are very low, while outside on the road they are normal. A car emerging from this low-speed environment usually has limited visibility of the carriageway and its speed is not matched to the flow: if it tries to go first, a side impact is almost inevitable. A truck with its mass and longer braking distance is the worst possible candidate for a 'maybe I can slip through' thought. What to remember: exiting a residential zone, courtyard, parking lot, or any adjacent area is not an intersection of two roads. Thus the 'right-hand priority' rule does not come into play here at all: you yield in every case. The side mirror is needed only to make sure the space behind is clear, not as an excuse to rush. • 'Not obliged' would be right if you were entering an intersection from a road of equal importance; however, the end-of-residential-zone sign tells you that you are leaving an area in which no priority is established for you.

g4-q64.text: What do the following traffic signs indicate?
options: When the road is icy, traffic must proceed at a speed of 40 km/h.
When the roadway surface is wet, the maximum permitted speed is 40 km/h.
g4-q64.explanation: Shown are sign 3.24 'Maximum speed limit' ('40') and plate 8.16 'Wet surface' (depicting a raincloud). They require driving at no more than 40 km/h when the road surface is wet, while the 1st option is wrong because the plate refers to a wet surface, not icing (Rules, signs 3.24, 8.16).

g4-q65.text: What do the following traffic signs indicate?
g4-q65.explanation: Stopping is prohibited on working days. A blue circle with a red border and a red cross means 'No stopping' — both parking and brief stopping. The plate below it with two crossed hammers defines the time scope of this ban: working days. That is, on days officially considered working days, this edge of the carriageway is closed to stopping, whereas on holidays it is open. Link the symbol to its meaning so you do not forget: a hammer is a sign of work, so a plate with hammers means working days. Its counterpart is the plate with an asterisk-like symbol, which means Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. On the exam, these two plates are deliberately given with nearly identical images and close options to find out whether you know the symbol or are guessing. The safety logic of a working-day ban is also predictable: on a street beside an office, school, or busy morning route, a car stopped at the curb knocks out a traffic lane and creates a bottleneck right at rush hour; on weekends, when there is no such load, there is no reason for the restriction either. Note: the plate limits only the operating time, not the strictness of the ban: on working days the ban is complete, and not even a brief stop is allowed. • Saturday is a non-working day, not a working day: this option reads the plate's meaning backward. • Sunday is also on the opposite side of 'working day' and belongs to the non-working days plate, not the hammers symbol.

g4-q66.text: What do the following traffic signs indicate?
options: On this section of road, the maximum permitted speed is 50 km/h.
A speed of 50 km/h is recommended on this section of road.
Driving is permitted only at the speed indicated on the sign or higher.
g4-q66.explanation: On the right side of the image is the blue square sign 6.2 'Recommended speed' ('50') (sign 1.29 'Crosswind' is also visible ahead). Sign 6.2 only recommends traveling at 50 km/h on this stretch and does not set a mandatory maximum or minimum speed limit (Rules, sign 6.2).

g4-q67.text: Which traffic sign requires a driver to proceed only to the left or to the right?
g4-q67.explanation: The 3rd sign — the arrow branching left and right. All three signs are round and blue — that is, from the mandatory family, setting permitted directions of travel. To answer, it is enough to check whether each sign has an upward arrow, meaning permission to go straight. The 1st sign permits straight and right, the 2nd straight and left, and only the 3rd sign has no straight arrow at all: it has two arrows, one going left and the other right. Thus only this sign obliges the driver to turn one way or the other at the intersection. These signs apply to the intersection immediately following their placement, and after passing that intersection their requirement is fulfilled. There is also a subtle point that earns exam marks: a mandatory sign permitting a left turn also permits a U-turn. So under the 3rd sign you may make a U-turn, while you have no right to go straight. The reason for placing such a sign is usually the road layout itself: the road ahead may be one-way in the oncoming direction, a dead end, or under repair. Instead of the driver discovering this in the throat of the intersection and having to brake hard or make a sudden U-turn, the sign makes the decision before reaching the intersection and keeps traffic flowing smoothly. • The 1st sign also permits going straight, meaning it forces no one to turn: the only thing it closes is a left turn. • The 2nd sign is the mirror image of the 1st sign, and it also has a straight arrow: a test-taker who sees only the left arrow and misses the upward one goes wrong right here.

g4-q68.text: What do the following traffic signs indicate?
options: When the roadway surface is wet, a speed of 40 km/h is recommended.
When the roadway surface is wet, the maximum permitted speed is 40 km/h.
g4-q68.explanation: When the road surface is wet, a speed of 40 km/h is recommended. This combination unites two things: a recommended speed and a conditional plate limiting the recommendation's effect to a wet road surface. That means when the asphalt is wet, 40 km/h is the speed the road suggests for that condition, not a ceiling whose exceedance brings a penalty. The difference between these two on the exam is created by one word: if 'maximum' is added to the sentence, the sign's nature changes from advice to prohibition, and the answer comes out wrong. A recommendation sign neither sets a legal ceiling nor raises it: the permitted ceiling for that stretch of road applies independently of this sign. Remember the number 40 together with the 'wet surface' condition. A practical note: the same 40, if it were on a round sign with a red border, would be a mandatory ceiling. So look at the sign's shape before reading the number. • Adding the word 'maximum' turns a recommendation sign into a mandatory limit: such a sign does not establish a legal ceiling.

g4-q69.text: The effect of these traffic signs applies:
options: On the left side of the road.
On the right side of the road.
On the side of the road where they are installed.
g4-q69.explanation: Shown are prohibitory signs 3.29 ('No parking on odd days of the month') and 3.30 ('No parking on even days of the month'). According to the rules, the effect of these signs extends only to the side of the road on which they are installed (rather than always only the right or left side) (Rules, signs 3.29, 3.30).

g4-q70.text: In this situation, along which path or paths is it permitted to go around the obstruction?
g4-q70.explanation: Both trajectories — 'a' and 'b': the obstacle may be passed on the right or on the left. On the obstacle in the middle of the road — that red divider under the bridge — there is a round blue sign with two arrows, one going left and the other right. That is exactly what the sign means: pass the obstacle on the right or left. Hence trajectory 'a', which passes on the right, and trajectory 'b', which passes on the left, are both permitted, and the choice is yours. This sign has two siblings with a single arrow that allow only one side: tell them apart by the number of arrows, not by habit. This is where a common exam trap hides: many people, recalling the general rule to keep right, immediately choose 'right only', whereas the two-arrow sign explicitly overrides that rule at this point. The reason such a sign exists is practical: when a bridge pier or central island divides the carriageway into two passable openings, closing one of them would only create congestion and unnecessary stops. Still, 'permitted' does not mean 'safe': before choosing a side, assess the width of the opening, oncoming cars, and pedestrians. In this very picture, two people with bicycles are standing on the left under the bridge, so if you choose trajectory 'b', you must slow down and leave sufficient lateral clearance. • Trajectory 'a' is indeed permitted, which makes the option deceptive: its flaw is exclusivity. The two-arrow sign also left the left side open, and there are no grounds to exclude 'b'. • Trajectory 'b' is also permitted, but if the sign required passing only on the left, its arrow would be one-sided and point left; here both sides are indicated.

g4-q71.text: What should the driver do in this situation?
options: Stop at least 5 meters before the first railroad track.
g4-q71.explanation: They must come to a full stop before the second sign — that is, the 'ԿԱՆԳ/STOP' sign placed right next to the rails. In the image, two separate signs stand one behind the other: first the red-and-white cross on the right edge beside the car, marking an unguarded railway crossing, and then the octagonal 'ԿԱՆԳ/STOP' right before the railway track; railcars are visible on the tracks. The first sign is only a warning and creates no duty to stop: the duty to stop is created by the second sign. Thus the correct stopping place is immediately before the 'STOP' sign, and only after coming to a full stop and making sure the track is clear may you proceed. The safety reason is obvious: an unguarded crossing has no physical barrier, and the only thing that saves you is stopping and looking. A train can neither stop in a short distance nor swerve: if you end up on the rails, you are no longer the one making the decision. Stopping at the right point means stopping where your view along the track is open in both directions: stopping earlier leaves your sightline blocked by trees and road slope, while stopping later puts your car on the rails. What to remember: wherever there is a 'STOP' sign, the stopping place is defined by the sign itself (or the stop line); do not start measuring distance to the rails. • The first sign is a warning sign, not a mandatory one: stopping by it is unnecessary and unsafe, as visibility of the tracks is not yet sufficient and drivers behind do not expect a stop at that point. • The figure 5 meters refers to the stopping distance from a barrier at crossings without a sign and without a stop line, and it stuck in the test-taker's memory in the right form; however, a 'STOP' sign is installed here, and the sign itself determines where to stop.

g4-q72.text: What should the driver do if intending to make a right turn at the intersection?
options: The driver may change into the right traffic lane and then make the right turn.
The driver may approach the intersection and then make the right turn.
g4-q72.explanation: Both methods are permitted. Mounted above the carriageway are two blue 'Lane directions' signs. The left sign, applying to the left lane, shows both a straight arrow and a right-turn arrow; the right sign shows only a right turn. That means turning right is permitted from both lanes, and the driver has two paths: either change into the right lane in advance and turn from there, or approach the intersection in their own lane and turn right. The general rule states that before turning right you must take a position as close as possible to the right edge of the carriageway. However, this default rule yields to 'Lane directions' signs or arrow markings wherever they are present. At busy urban intersections, these signs are used for this exact purpose — so two lanes can turn right simultaneously and the traffic light queue is shorter. The safety reason is also clear: the biggest hazard of a right turn is a gap left to the right of a car and a cyclist or motorcyclist slipping into it. When a sign allows both lanes to turn, cars turn along parallel, predictable trajectories and that dangerous gap disappears. The exam trap is that the first two options each look right on their own: since neither is wrong, the answer is 'both'. • This is permitted, but not the only permitted path: since the sign above the left lane also permits a right turn, choosing this option throws away half of the correct answer. • This is also permitted, precisely because of that 'straight or right' sign above the left lane; on its own, however, it is an incomplete answer and needlessly treats changing into the right lane as an error.

g4-q73.text: In this situation, at a distance of 200 m from the sign, is the driver permitted to make a U-turn?
g4-q73.explanation: They have the right: the sign has announced a permitted U-turn area in 200 meters. The sign on the right side of the image is blue and rectangular with a U-turn arrow, and the plate below it shows '200 m'. This combination means 'U-turn area in 200 meters'. The blue sign belongs to the information family and essentially prohibits nothing; on the contrary, it informs you that 200 meters ahead there is a spot equipped where you can legally and safely make a U-turn. Hence the answer is affirmative. The safety logic behind this sign is tied to intercity roads like the one you see in the image: high speed, two opposing directions, and limited visibility on bends and crests. Making an arbitrary U-turn on such a road is the most dangerous maneuver possible, since the car effectively blocks the width of the road. Instead of hoping drivers will guess a suitable spot themselves, the road authority builds one engineered point with open sightlines and enough space, and notifies the driver in advance with a sign. What to remember: at a spot marked by this sign, only a U-turn is permitted, not a left turn. Color and shape are also a reliable guide: prohibitions are round and white with a red border, not blue and rectangular. • This answer would be right if the sign were a white circle with a red border and a crossed-out U-turn arrow: the blue sign in the image works the exact opposite way and marks a permitted U-turn area.

g4-q74.text: In this case, must the driver stop at the location indicated by the traffic controller?
options: No, because the sign prohibits stopping.
g4-q74.explanation: Must obey: the traffic controller's instruction takes priority over the 'No stopping' sign. In the image, the traffic controller stands in the middle of the carriageway and points with their hand to a stopping spot, while at the right edge of the street there is a 'No stopping' sign (blue circle with a red cross). The contradiction is apparent rather than real: in the hierarchy of traffic control devices, the signals and instructions of a traffic controller stand at the highest level — above traffic lights, signs, and markings. When a traffic controller gives an instruction, the sign temporarily steps aside, and you must stop where they indicate. The safety reason for this order is important: signs are designed for ordinary, pre-planned situations, whereas a traffic controller appears precisely when the situation is extraordinary — a crash, traffic light failure, convoy passage, flooding, or route closure. At such a moment, the only person with the full picture is the traffic controller. If every driver cited a local sign and disobeyed them, control of the situation would collapse. What to remember for the exam: the order of priority is traffic controller, then traffic light, then signs, and lastly road markings. In practice, any question in which a traffic controller is present is solved in this exact order. • The option's reasoning is valid under normal conditions, which makes it tempting; however, before a traffic controller's instruction, a sign loses force, and citing the sign to disobey a traffic controller is itself a violation.

g4-q75.text: What should the driver do in this situation?
options: Proceed through the railroad crossing while ensuring safety.
Proceed through the railroad crossing without stopping.
Stop before the sign and then, while ensuring safety, proceed through the multiple-track railroad crossing.
g4-q75.explanation: In the image, before a railway crossing without a barrier, signs 1.3.2 'Multi-track railway' and 2.5 'Stop' ('ԿԱՆԳ STOP') are installed, while 'Stop line' marking is absent. In that case, the driver must stop immediately before the sign and, maintaining safety, cross the multi-track railway crossing (Rules, item 111, signs 1.3.2, 2.5).

g4-q76.text: What does the pavement marking on the roadway indicate?
options: The boundaries of lanes designated for vehicles proceeding in the same direction.
The boundaries of a reversible traffic lane.
g4-q76.explanation: Boundaries of traffic lanes with reversible traffic. The key to recognition is the shape of the marking: two parallel broken lines side by side. The boundary between lanes going in the same direction is drawn with a single broken line; when you see two broken lines side by side, it means the direction of travel in the adjacent lane can change at different times of day. The image provides a second proof as well: special lane traffic lights are mounted above the carriageway — one with a red cross (lane closed) and another with a green downward arrow (lane open). The safety reason for this marking is serious. In a reversible lane, a car that was moving in your direction a few minutes ago may now be driving toward you: that is, the risk of a head-on collision sits right beside you. The double marking tells the driver 'you cannot rely on habit here' and forces them to read the overhead signal before changing lanes. If the signal is off or you cannot see it, you must act as if the lane is prohibited and stay in your right lane. What to remember: one broken line means lanes in the same direction, two broken lines mean reversible traffic. This simple distinction answers several exam questions. • This definition belongs to a single broken line: the two parallel broken lines and the overhead signals with a cross and arrow in the image are precisely what distinguish reversible traffic from an ordinary street.

g4-q77.text: In which direction or directions is the passenger car permitted to proceed?
options: To the left and by making a U-turn.
Straight ahead, to the left, and by making a U-turn.
g4-q77.explanation: Straight, left, and in the opposite direction (U-turn). The sign on the right side of the image consists of two parts. The upper part is a blue rectangle with a white arrow pointing left: the street ahead is one-way, and its permitted direction is to your left. The lower part depicts a bus with an arrow pointing right: to the right, only public transit vehicles (buses and the like) travel in a dedicated lane against the general direction. For a passenger car, the conclusion is simple: turning right is prohibited, as it would mean entering a one-way road against its direction. Meanwhile, going straight, turning left (which matches the one-way direction), and making a U-turn are none of them prohibited. The reason for banning the right turn is the very thing these signs are meant to prevent: a head-on crash on a street where drivers expect no oncoming car at all, and worse, a crash with a bus coming head-on in a dedicated lane whose existence a newcomer does not know. A common trap is that bus symbol: the test-taker thinks that because there is traffic to the right, the road is two-way and 'any direction' is allowed. However, permission for that lane is granted only to public transit vehicles, not to you. • Turning left and making a U-turn are identified correctly, but going straight is excluded without reason: no sign in the image prohibits crossing the intersection straight ahead. • 'Any direction' also includes turning right, whereas the road to the right is one-way against your direction, and a passenger car is prohibited from entering it.

g4-q78.text: What should the driver do in this situation?
options: If necessary, yield to a vehicle proceeding on the intersecting road.
Stop and yield to a vehicle proceeding on the intersecting road.
g4-q78.explanation: They must come to a full stop and then give way to the vehicle traveling on the intersecting road. The red octagonal 'ԿԱՆԳ / STOP' sign on the right and the thick white line crossing the carriageway right in front of you together give one instruction: stop. This stop is not conditional: whether the intersecting road is busy or empty, whether visibility is good or poor, the car must stop completely so the wheels stop turning. The stopping point is that very stop line; if there is no marking, then the edge of the intersecting carriageway. The reason for such strictness is what is called 'stopping for sight'. In the image, buildings and trees come right up to the corner of the intersection, and until you pull forward, a large part of the intersecting road is hidden from view. A full stop gives you a few seconds to turn your head left and right and judge the true speed of approaching cars — something that practically never happens while creeping slowly. A common exam trap lies here: the wording 'yield if necessary' is the text for the triangular 'Give way' sign, not the 'STOP' sign. With the triangular sign you may pass without stopping at low speed if the road is clear; with a 'STOP' sign, never. Always review these two signs as a pair and in comparison with each other. • The option is tempting because in practice you will end up having to yield anyway; however, 'if necessary' implies permission to pass without stopping, which is the exact thing the 'STOP' sign prohibits.

g4-q79.text: Outside populated areas, at what distance before the beginning of a hazardous section is this warning sign installed?
g4-q79.explanation: Shown is warning sign 1.12.2 'Dangerous bends'. Outside built-up areas (without plate 8.1.1), warning signs are placed 150–300 m before the start of the hazardous section, whereas a distance of 50–100 m applies inside built-up areas (Rules, sign 1.12.2).

g4-q80.text: In which direction is traffic permitted?
options: Straight ahead and to the right.
Straight ahead, to the right, and to the left.
g4-q80.explanation: In the image, in front of the red car is the blue rectangular sign 5.5 'One-way road'. On a one-way road at an intersection, proceeding straight, right, and left is permitted, whereas making a U-turn is prohibited (due to driving against traffic), which rules out the 4th option (Rules, item 50, sign 5.5).

g4-q81.text: Which of the following traffic signs prohibits entering an intersection area if congestion has formed ahead in the direction of traffic, except when making a right or left turn?
g4-q81.explanation: Marking number 3 — the yellow square with a cross inside, i.e., 'intersection area'. The four elements in the image are intentionally taken from four different families to make recognition harder. Number 1 is a blue circle with a red cross — stopping prohibited altogether along the entire stretch of road. Number 2 is a white circle with a red border and a crossed-out U-turn arrow — no U-turn. Number 4 is a red triangle with a black cross — warning of an intersection with a minor road, which only informs and prohibits nothing. Only number 3 — the yellow square with a cross — marks the intersection area and prohibits entering it in congestion, unless you are going to turn left or right.
