The reason for the turn exception is also logical: a car turning left or right leaves the intersection and does not block the cross path for long, whereas a car going straight and stuck in a queue stops right in the middle of the perpendicular flow and blocks the entire intersection. At rush hour, a blocked intersection quickly spreads congestion to subsequent intersections and also blocks emergency services' routes. What to remember: link the yellow color and square shape with 'keep the intersection clear'. • The absolute no-stopping sign applies to stopping at the edge of the carriageway, not entering an intersection: it has nothing to do with congestion or the turn exception. • The no-U-turn sign removes just one specific maneuver and says nothing about the traffic situation ahead. • This is a warning sign that merely informs you of approaching an intersection with a minor road: warning signs do not create prohibitions.

g4-q82.text: At what maximum distance may the “Intersection Area” traffic sign be installed at a complex intersection if it cannot be installed at the boundary of the intersection?
g4-q82.explanation: Shown is warning sign 1.35 'Intersection area'. If at complex intersections it is impossible to install this sign directly at the boundary of the intersection, it is placed at a maximum distance of 30 m from the intersection boundary (the 10 m and 20 m options are incorrect) (Rules, sign 1.35).

g4-q83.text: What does the following traffic sign warn about?
options: Entering the intersection area is prohibited if congestion has formed ahead in the direction of traffic and would force the driver to stop.
Entering the intersection area is prohibited if congestion has formed ahead in the direction of traffic.
g4-q83.explanation: Entering the intersection area when congestion ahead will force you to stop inside the intersection. The yellow square with a cross marks the intersection area, and its message fits in one phrase: do not occupy this square with your car unless you are sure you can clear it. That means before entering you must see free space on the far side of the intersection, not just a green light. If the queue ahead is such that you will stop in the middle of the intersection, you must stop before entering and wait. The safety and traffic-management reason is the phenomenon of gridlock (blocking the intersection). A car stuck in the middle of a crossing keeps the perpendicular flow's path blocked when their light turns green: they in turn get stuck too, and within a few light cycles the intersection stops working altogether. Worse than delay is blocking the route of ambulances and fire trucks. The key point and main trap of this question is the qualification 'will force you to stop'. The mere presence of a queue in your direction does not prohibit entry: if the queue is moving and you judge you will clear the intersection before the red signal, proceeding is permitted. The criterion is the outcome of your maneuver, not the outward look of the traffic flow. • This marking says nothing about stopping at the edge of the carriageway: a stopping ban has its own separate sign (a blue circle with a red cross). • The option is very close to the right answer and is a trap for that very reason: it dropped the decisive qualification 'such that you will be forced to stop' and extended the ban to any congestion.

g4-q84.text: What does the following pavement marking indicate?
options: A section of an intersection that may not be entered if congestion has formed ahead in the direction of traffic and would force the driver to stop.
g4-q84.explanation: Shown is the yellow grid horizontal marking 1.26. It marks the section of an intersection onto which entry is prohibited if congestion has formed ahead in the direction of travel that would force the driver to stop and obstruct cross traffic (Rules, items 88, 170, marking 1.26).

g4-q85.text: Which of the following pavement markings indicates a section of an intersection that may not be entered if congestion has formed ahead in the direction of traffic and would force the driver to stop?
g4-q85.explanation: Marking number 3 — the yellow box-junction grid. Marking number 3 is the yellow crisscross grid applied to the intersection surface, and its meaning comes down to one thing only: do not enter this zone until you are sure you can clear it completely. If congestion has formed ahead in your direction and your entry would leave you stopped in the middle of the intersection, entry is prohibited even on a green signal. The safety and operational reason for this marking is intersection blockage. A car stuck in the middle of an intersection blocks the path of perpendicular traffic; that flow gets stuck at the next intersection, and within minutes the entire street network locks up. More important than traffic jams is that the route for ambulances and fire trucks gets blocked, and drivers trapped behind the stuck car resort to nervous and risky maneuvers. The yellow grid visually turns this zone into a 'no-stopping zone' so no excuses remain for entering blindly. What to remember: keep the yellow color and grid pattern together. A green light gives you permission to proceed, not to enter a full intersection. The final decision is yours: if there is nowhere to exit, stay behind the line. • Parallel yellow lines are pedestrian crossing markings: they mark where pedestrians cross and have nothing to do with entering an intersection during congestion. • A chevron pattern marks a channelizing island — a place where traffic flows split or merge, and vehicle entry there is prohibited altogether, not only during congestion.

g4-q86.text: Making a U-turn from the indicated lane is:
g4-q86.explanation: Prohibited. The sign above the carriageway sets the permitted directions of travel separately for each lane. According to the image, the left lane — the one your car is in — has a straight arrow and a right arrow, while the right lane has only a right arrow. Neither of these lanes has a left arrow, and that settles the question: a U-turn is permitted only from a lane that has a left arrow. Permission to turn left from the leftmost position of the carriageway carries with it permission to make a U-turn; the absence of that arrow means no permission for a U-turn. The safety reason is straightforward: a U-turn means crossing the entire width of oncoming traffic at minimum speed and occupying the intersection for the longest time. Where the road designer has not provided for a left turn, no traffic light phase is allocated for it, and there is neither sufficient sightline nor room for the maneuver: a car making a U-turn at such a spot is a completely unexpected obstacle for an oncoming driver. What to remember: before any U-turn, first read the arrows above the lanes or the markings on the asphalt. Keep the rule simple: left arrow present = U-turn allowed; no left arrow = no U-turn either. • This option assumes a U-turn is a free maneuver unless explicitly prohibited; however, where a lane-directions sign is installed, that sign closes the list of permitted actions, and a left turn is not on it.

g4-q87.text: Along which path is it permitted to make a U-turn?
g4-q87.explanation: In the image, sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight' is installed before the intersection, and the intersecting road has two carriageways separated by a dividing strip. Since the effect of sign 4.1.1 applies only to the first intersection of carriageways, a U-turn along trajectory B is prohibited, while at the second intersection — along trajectory A — it is permitted (Rules, sign 4.1.1).

g4-q88.text: Along which path is it permitted to make a U-turn?
g4-q88.explanation: In the image, signs 5.6 'End of one-way road' and 1.21 'Two-way traffic' are installed on the right, meaning the driver is still on a one-way road. On a one-way road, both making a U-turn before the intersection (B) and turning back onto the same road from the intersection (A) will result in driving against traffic, so neither trajectory is permitted (Rules, item 50, signs 5.6, 1.21).

g4-q89.text: Which vehicle driver may continue straight ahead through this intersection?
g4-q89.explanation: In the image, mandatory sign 4.1.2 'Turn right' is installed before the intersection. This sign requires turning right only, but its effect does not extend to public transit vehicles, so only the driver of the latter may continue straight (the motorcycle and bicycle must turn right) (Rules, sign 4.1.2).

g4-q90.text: Along which path is a U-turn permitted?
options: At the intersection, along path A.
Before the intersection, along path B.
g4-q90.explanation: The effect of sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight', installed at the beginning of the road section (on the right), extends up to the nearest intersection. For this reason, making a U-turn before the intersection (along trajectory B) is prohibited, while at the intersection (along trajectory A) the sign's effect ends and a U-turn is permitted (Rules, sign 4.1.1).

g4-q91.text: Must you stop before the “Stop Line”?
g4-q91.explanation: In the image, the green permissive signal of the traffic light is on at the intersection, and below it is sign 2.5 'Stop' (Proceeding without stopping prohibited). When a traffic light signal contradicts the requirement of a priority sign, the driver must follow the traffic light signal, so on a green light they are not required to stop at the 'Stop line' (Rules, item 173, sign 2.5).

options: Only in directions A or B.
g4-q92.explanation: In the image, mandatory sign 4.1.4 'Proceed straight or turn right' is installed before the intersection. It permits driving only in directions A (right) or B (straight) and prohibits turning left (C), which rules out the 1st and 3rd options (Rules, sign 4.1.4).

options: The distance from the end of the tunnel.
The distance from a location hazardous to children.
The location of an emergency exit and the distance to it.
g4-q93.explanation: The green indicator shown (depicting a running person, a door, a left arrow, and '150 m') in a tunnel indicates the direction to an emergency exit and the distance from it to the sign (150 m). It has nothing to do with the end of the tunnel or a place hazardous for children, so the 1st and 2nd options are wrong (Rules, information signs).

options: We must yield to the truck driver.
We may proceed through the narrow section first.
g4-q94.explanation: In the image, before a narrow section of road, sign 2.7 'Priority over oncoming traffic' is installed on our side. It indicates that when driving through the narrow section, the driver has priority over the oncoming truck and may proceed first, so the 1st option is wrong (Rules, sign 2.7).

g4-q95.text: After these signs, the driver of a truck with a maximum authorized mass not exceeding 3.5 metric tons may proceed at a maximum speed of:
g4-q95.explanation: In the image, sign 3.24 'Maximum speed limit' (80 km/h) is installed with plate 8.4.3 'Type of vehicle' depicting a passenger car. Plate 8.4.3 extends the sign's effect to passenger cars and trucks with a maximum permissible mass not exceeding 3.5 tons, so this truck is permitted to travel at a maximum speed of 80 km/h (Rules, item 70, signs 3.24, 8.4.3).

g4-q96.text: What is prohibited by this traffic sign?
options: Proceeding at a speed greater than 20 km/h.
g4-q96.explanation: Shown is sign 5.33 'Pedestrian zone' (with the inscription 'ZONE' and a pedestrian image). Within the area marked by this sign, only pedestrian movement is permitted; consequently, driving all vehicles (not only motor vehicles or those moving faster than 20 km/h) is prohibited (Rules, sign 5.33).

g4-q97.text: Where must the driver stop in order to comply with the sign?
options: Before the intersection of the roadways (C).
g4-q97.explanation: In the image, sign 2.5 'Stop' (Proceeding without stopping prohibited) is installed before the intersection, while 'Stop line' marking is absent. At intersections where a 'Stop line' is absent, the driver must stop immediately before the edge of the intersecting carriageway — in front of line C, rather than at the sign (A) or at the start of the intersection (B) (Rules, sign 2.5).

g4-q98.explanation: Number 2 shows sign 5.21 'Residential zone', within whose effective zone speed is limited to 20 km/h. 1 is a priority sign (2.4), 4 is a warning sign (1.18), and 3 is sign 6.2 'Recommended speed', which only indicates a preferred speed and does not impose a mandatory limit (Rules, item 68, signs 5.21, 6.2).

g4-q99.text: Which sign applies only to the lane above which it is installed?
g4-q99.explanation: Only in option A is plate 8.14 'Traffic lane' with a downward black arrow installed under sign 3.24 'Maximum speed limit' ('50'), limiting the sign's effect to that lane only. Signs B (4.6) and C (6.2) without plate 8.14 apply to the entire road in that direction (Rules, signs 3.24, 8.14).

g4-q100.text: Parking at the indicated location is:
g4-q100.explanation: In the image, the effect of sign 3.28 'No parking' installed on the right extends, in the absence of an intersection, to the end of the built-up area. Since the car is parking on the right shoulder past sign 5.24.2 'End of built-up area', where the effect of sign 3.28 has already ended, parking is permitted (Rules, item 78, signs 3.28, 5.24.2).

g4-q101.text: Has the truck driver violated the parking rules?
options: Yes, if the maximum authorized mass exceeds 3.5 metric tons.
g4-q101.explanation: In the image, plate 8.6.3 showing the manner of parking on the sidewalk curb is installed under sign 6.4 'Parking area', and a truck is parked beneath it. Parking at the sidewalk edge in this manner is permitted only for passenger cars, motorcycles, mopeds, and bicycles, so the truck driver (regardless of mass) has violated the parking rules (Rules, item 81, signs 6.4, 8.6.3).

g4-q102.text: In which direction is traffic permitted?
options: Straight ahead and by making a U-turn.
g4-q102.explanation: Straight ahead and U-turn (movement in the opposite direction). The sign on the right is 'No left turn' — a white circle with a red border and a leftward-bent arrow crossed by a red line. The key point is that this sign closes a left turn and nothing else: it does not prohibit a U-turn. If a U-turn also needed to be banned, a separate 'No U-turn' sign would have to be installed. Now look at the intersection itself: the intersecting road joins this street only from the left. On the right there is a solid curb, metal fence, grass strip, and building wall, and there is no road to turn right into. That means out of all possible movements, the left turn is closed by the sign, the right turn by the road geometry itself, and straight ahead and U-turn remain. The lawmaker's logic in this distinction is the destination, not merely crossing oncoming traffic. A left turn takes you onto a street where entry from this side is undesirable due to one-way traffic, tram tracks, or pedestrian density. A U-turn leaves you on the same street in the opposite direction and creates no prohibited destination. A common exam trap lies here: most test-takers cautiously pick 'straight only', assuming a left-turn ban also covers a U-turn. That assumption is wrong. Remember: every prohibitory sign closes exactly the movement depicted on it and nothing more. • 'Straight only' is overly cautious: the sign did not prohibit a U-turn, and excluding it from the answer is reading more into the sign than it says. • 'All directions' ignores the sign: a left turn is directly prohibited, and there is no road on the right at all.

g4-q103.text: Which sign does not apply to you if you reside within the area where the sign is in effect?
g4-q103.explanation: Shown are signs: A — 3.2 'No vehicles', B — 3.1 'No entry', and C — 3.3 'No motor vehicles'. The effect of signs 3.2 and 3.3 does not extend to vehicles belonging to citizens residing in that zone, whereas sign 3.1 provides no exception for residents (Rules, signs 3.1, 3.2, 3.3).

g4-q104.text: What does the supplemental plaque indicate?
options: The distance from the sign to the intersection when a “Yield” sign is installed immediately before the intersection.
The distance from the sign to the intersection when a “STOP” sign is installed immediately before the intersection.
The location of a border checkpoint.
g4-q104.explanation: The distance to the intersection before which the 'Stop' (Proceeding without stopping prohibited) sign is installed. The white inverted triangle with a red border is the 'Give way' sign, and the plate under it shows the word STOP and the number 250 m. This combination has one specific, predefined meaning: the 'Distance to object' plate, used only with the 'Give way' sign, informs you that 250 meters ahead, at the intersection, a 'STOP' sign is installed and a mandatory stop applies there — not that you must stop here. Look at the photo itself: an intercity road with a grade and curve, a metal guardrail on the right, and limited forward visibility. A driver approaching at highway speed and seeing the 'STOP' sign for the first time at 30 meters would have to either brake hard or overshoot the stop line and enter the priority road. Hard braking on a downgrade and in a curve, especially for a loaded truck, means skidding and leaving the road. Giving notice at 250 meters eliminates both this hard braking and blind entry into the intersection. What to remember: wherever you see the word STOP and a number under a 'Give way' triangle, read it as 'mandatory stop in so many meters'. The exam trap is that the test-taker confuses the triangle with the 'STOP' sign itself and thinks the number gives the distance from the 'Give way' sign to the intersection; whereas the word STOP on the plate directly tells you what awaits at the intersection. • The option is tempting because the upper sign really is 'Give way'; however, if that same sign stood at the intersection, there would be no need to write STOP on the plate — it is that word that announces the mandatory stop. • A border control post has its own separate sign, and it is never written under a 'Give way' triangle with a distance in meters.

g4-q105.text: Stopping at the indicated location is:
g4-q105.explanation: Stopping at this point is permitted because the sign's effective zone ended before it. A round blue sign with a red border and a cross means 'No stopping'. But look not only at the sign: look at the edge of the curb. In the image, a solid yellow line runs along the right curb, and farther along this line ends: the white arrow points to a spot right beyond the end of that line, and from there the curb is ordinary, unpainted. The rule is this: when a 'No stopping' sign is used together with a yellow line along the curb, the length of that marking determines the sign's effective zone. Normally, this sign's effective zone stretches from where it is installed to the nearest intersection (or end of the built-up area) and applies only to the side of the road on which the sign is placed; however, the yellow line shortens that zone. Since the indicated spot lies outside the yellow line, stopping there is permitted. The safety reason for this technique is practical: a sign is a single point in space and is easy to miss at night, in rain, or behind a truck, whereas the yellow line runs beneath your wheels along the entire length of the ban and shows its boundary accurately and continuously. With this line, both illegal stops decrease and drivers do not needlessly drive on to the next intersection. The exam trap is seeing the red cross and immediately answering 'prohibited'. Always check first how far the yellow marking goes and on which side of its end the indicated spot lies. • The red cross immediately pushes the mind toward 'prohibited', but the yellow marking accompanying the sign ended before the indicated point, and this point is no longer within the sign's effective zone.

g4-q106.text: Which signs remain in effect in the direction of traffic up to the nearest intersection?
g4-q106.explanation: The effect of the shown prohibitory signs B — 3.24 ('50') and D — 3.28 ('No parking') extends from the place of installation to the nearest intersection. Meanwhile, the effect of the 'ZONE' signs A (5.31) and C (5.27) is not interrupted by an intersection and applies up to the signs marking the end of the respective zone (Rules, signs 3.24, 3.28, 5.27, 5.31).

g4-q107.text: What speed regulation is established on the road by these signs?
options: Minimum speed in the left lane proceeding in the same direction: 50 km/h.
g4-q107.explanation: In the image, above the left lane in the same direction, the blue round sign 4.6 'Minimum speed limit' ('50') and plate 8.14 'Traffic lane' are mounted. Plate 8.14 restricts the effect of sign 4.6 to that lane only, establishing a minimum speed of 50 km/h in the left same-direction lane (Rules, signs 4.6, 8.14).

g4-q108.text: Which of the signs prohibits making a left turn?
g4-q108.explanation: Sign A — 5.13.1 shows that the main flow goes right, while to the left there is only an oncoming lane for public transit vehicles, so turning left is prohibited, just as with sign C — 6.3.1 'U-turn area'. Meanwhile, sign B — 3.19 'No U-turn' prohibits only a U-turn and does not prohibit turning left (Rules, signs 5.13.1, 3.19, 6.3.1).

g4-q109.text: Is the driver permitted to make a left turn?
g4-q109.explanation: In the image, information sign 6.8.2 'Dead end' installed on the right only informs you that the road leading right has no through passage, and does not prohibit turning in any direction. There is a broken marking line in the middle of the carriageway and no signs prohibiting a left turn, so turning left is permitted (Rules, sign 6.8.2).

options: Within a 150 m section of road, there is a danger of pedestrians entering the roadway.
There is an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing 150 m ahead.
g4-q110.explanation: Shown are warning sign 1.22 'Pedestrian crossing' and plate without arrows 8.1.1 'Distance to object' ('150 m'). They inform you that 150 m after the sign there is an unguarded pedestrian crossing, whereas the length of a hazardous section would be indicated by plate 8.2.1 with arrows (Rules, signs 1.22, 8.1.1).

g4-q111.text: Along which paths is traffic permitted?
g4-q111.explanation: In the image, sign 4.3 'Roundabout' is installed before the intersection, requiring traffic to move around the island in the direction shown by the arrows (counterclockwise). Trajectory C is opposite to the roundabout direction, and A bypasses the circle (and sign 3.18.1 is installed on the right), so movement is permitted only along trajectory B (Rules, sign 4.3).

g4-q112.text: Which of the signs prohibits proceeding at a speed below 40 km/h?
g4-q112.explanation: On roads marked with the shown signs A — 5.1 'Motorway' and B — 5.3 'Road for motor vehicles', traffic is prohibited for vehicles whose speed, due to technical specifications or condition, does not exceed 40 km/h. Meanwhile, sign C — 6.2 'Recommended speed' establishes no prohibition (Rules, items 116, 117, signs 5.1, 5.3, 6.2).

g4-q113.text: With which sign must you yield to oncoming traffic at a narrow section?
g4-q113.explanation: When oncoming passing is difficult under the shown sign A — 1.13 'Steep descent', the driver descending must yield the road, while sign C — 2.6 'Priority for oncoming traffic' directly obliges yielding to oncoming traffic on a narrow stretch. Signs B (1.14 'Steep ascent') and D (2.7), by contrast, grant priority (Rules, item 46, signs 1.13, 2.6).

g4-q114.text: In which direction or directions may you continue through this intersection if you are driving a truck with a maximum authorized mass of 3.5 metric tons?
options: To the right, to the left, or by making a U-turn.
g4-q114.explanation: You may continue driving in any direction. The round sign with a red border and a truck image mounted above the straight direction in the picture is 'No trucks'. The key point is that when no number is written on this sign, it covers only trucks whose maximum permissible mass exceeds 3.5 tons. Your truck is exactly 3.5 tons, no more: that means this ban does not apply to you at all, and you can continue driving in any direction — straight, right, left, or U-turn. The blue sign on the right with a left arrow and a truck image is 'Direction of movement for trucks' — that is, the route set specifically for those heavy trucks that are not allowed to go straight. When the prohibitory sign does not cover you, this directional sign is not mandatory for you either. The lawmaker's logic is that the division must be made by permissible mass, not by the vehicle's outward appearance: residential streets, bridges, and road surfaces are not built for heavy axle loads, and a heavy truck there also has a longer braking distance and takes up more room on turns. A common exam trap is this threshold number. '3.5 tons' means 'at the limit', and the limit is not included in the ban: the ban begins at 'over 3.5 tons'. If the question said 3.6 tons, the answer would be completely different. • 'Left only' is inferred from the blue direction sign for trucks; however, that sign shows the route for trucks over 3.5 tons and creates no obligation for a 3.5-ton truck. • This answer is right for a truck whose permissible mass exceeds 3.5 tons and which cannot go straight: your vehicle sits right at the limit and is not covered by the sign.

g4-q115.text: Is a right turn onto the unpaved road permitted?
g4-q115.explanation: Sign 1.11.2 'Dangerous bend' (to the left) installed on the right in the image only warns of a bend ahead and does not prohibit turning right. Where the dirt road joins on the right, the shoulder line breaks and there are no signs prohibiting a turn, so turning right is permitted (Rules, sign 1.11.2).

g4-q116.text: Is stopping at the indicated location to pick up a passenger permitted?
g4-q116.explanation: Yes: this sign prohibits only parking, not stopping. The sign on the right is a blue circle with a red border and a single diagonal line — 'No parking'. Under it is a plate with '50 m', which defines the length of the sign's effective zone ahead of where it is installed. The entire answer rests on the difference between two terms. Stopping is the intentional cessation of movement for up to 5 minutes, or longer if necessary for boarding and alighting people or loading and unloading. Parking is ceasing movement for more than 5 minutes not related to boarding, alighting, or loading. The sign in this picture closes only the second category. In the photo, the very thing that remains permitted is happening: a white car has stopped at the curb and a passenger is getting out. The safety logic of the rule: a car left at the edge of the carriageway for hours reduces the usable width of the road, blocks sightlines for drivers and pedestrians, and forces others into the adjacent lane or even onto the oncoming carriageway. A brief stop while the driver sits at the wheel and can move at any moment creates no such hazard; therefore the law did not ban it. What to remember: a red cross = 'No stopping', stricter; one diagonal line = 'No parking', milder. The exam trap is that the test-taker perceives any crossed-out blue circle as an absolute ban. • Because the sign is crossed out and looks 'prohibitory', the answer 'no' feels natural; however, a single diagonal line closes only parking, while stopping — including dropping off a passenger as seen in the picture — remains permitted.

g4-q117.text: Which sign indicates a pedestrian path?
g4-q117.explanation: Under letter B is the blue round mandatory sign 4.5.1 'Pedestrian path'. A is the prohibitory sign 3.10 'No pedestrians', and C is the special regulation sign 5.19.1 'Pedestrian crossing', so the 2nd and 3rd options are wrong (Rules, sign 4.5.1).

options: Warns of an approaching narrow section.
Requires the driver to yield to oncoming traffic at narrow sections.
g4-q118.explanation: It obliges you to give way to the oncoming vehicle in the narrow section. The sign is round with a red border, a wide black arrow pointing down, and a narrow red arrow pointing up — 'Priority for oncoming traffic'. The key to reading this sign is color, not direction: the red arrow is your direction of travel, and its being red means it is not your turn; the black arrow is the oncoming flow, which has priority. This sign does not merely warn: it creates an obligation. The scene in the photo is the exact situation for which the sign was created: a narrow bridge on a forest road with side railings, too narrow for two vehicles to pass simultaneously, and a blue car approaching from the opposite side. Your duty is to stay back before the narrow section and let it pass. The safety reason: in a narrow section there is neither a shoulder nor room to fix a mistake: if both drivers enter, one will have to reverse across the bridge, usually with a queue of cars behind. Instead of leaving the decision to split-second negotiations between two drivers, the law assigns priority in advance and conclusively. What to remember: this sign has a pair — the blue square sign with a large white arrow, which is its opposite and gives priority to you. Find the color of the arrow referring to you: red = wait, white = go. • The 'Road narrows' warning is a different sign — a triangle with a red border — and it only informs; the sign in this image is round and, besides informing, creates a duty to yield. • This sign does not prohibit passage altogether: it only sets the order of passage. A ban on passage has its own separate sign.

g4-q119.text: What should you do if you need to reverse your direction of movement?
options: Make a U-turn at this intersection.
Proceed straight through the intersection and then make a U-turn.
g4-q119.explanation: Installed on the right before the intersection is mandatory sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight', whose effect applies to this intersection of carriageways and requires moving straight only. For this reason, making a U-turn directly at this intersection is prohibited, and to change direction you must pass straight through the intersection and then make a U-turn at a permitted place. (Rules, sign 4.1.1)

g4-q120.text: Parking at the indicated location is:
g4-q120.explanation: On the right side of the carriageway, sign 3.28 'No parking' is installed, whose effect extends from the place of installation to the nearest intersection. Although there is a break in the dividing strip ahead equipped with sign 6.3.1 'U-turn area', a break in the dividing strip and a U-turn area do not interrupt the effect of sign 3.28. Consequently, parking at the spot indicated by the arrow is prohibited. (Rules, sign 3.28)

g4-q121.text: When this supplemental plaque is used, the sign with which it is used applies to:
options: Passenger cars and trucks with a maximum authorized mass not exceeding 3.5 metric tons.
g4-q121.explanation: Shown is supplementary information plate 8.4.3 'Type of vehicle' with the silhouette of a passenger car. It extends the effect of the sign used with it to passenger cars as well as trucks with a maximum permissible mass of up to 3.5 tons. The effect of this plate does not extend to motorcycles. (Rules, sign 8.4.3)

options: Stopping on the shoulder is prohibited.
Entering the shoulder is dangerous because of roadwork.
Stopping is permitted only on the roadway.
g4-q122.explanation: Installed on the right are warning sign 1.25 'Road works' and plate 8.12 'Dangerous shoulder'. This combination warns drivers that pulling onto the shoulder is dangerous due to repair works being carried out, but it is not a sign prohibiting stopping. (Rules, signs 1.25, 8.12)

g4-q123.text: In which direction or directions is traffic permitted from the indicated lane?
options: Straight ahead and to the left.
Straight ahead, to the left, and by making a U-turn.
g4-q123.explanation: The car is in the leftmost lane, above which sign 5.15.2 'Lane directions' with straight and left arrows is mounted. According to the rules, sign 5.15.2 permitting a left turn from the leftmost lane also permits a U-turn from that lane. Therefore, from the indicated lane, proceeding straight, left, and in the opposite direction is permitted. (Rules, sign 5.15.2)

g4-q124.text: In which of the indicated directions may you continue through this intersection?
g4-q124.explanation: The intersecting road has two carriageways separated by a dividing strip, and sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight' is installed before the first intersection of carriageways. Since sign 4.1.1 applies only to the first intersection following it, it prohibits turning right in direction C, but does not extend to the second intersection. Consequently, after passing the first intersection straight, you may continue both straight (B) and to the left (A). (Rules, sign 4.1.1)

options: Recommends proceeding at a speed of 40 km/h.
Permits proceeding only at a speed of 40 km/h or higher.
Prohibits proceeding at a speed higher than 40 km/h.
g4-q125.explanation: This sign prohibits driving faster than 40 km/h. A round sign with a white field and a red border belongs to the prohibitory group, and the number inside it is a speed ceiling, neither a recommended speed nor a lower limit. From the point of installation to the end of the zone — the nearest intersection or a cancelling sign — moving faster than 40 km/h is a violation; driving slower is permitted provided you do not unnecessarily obstruct traffic. Keep the identification criterion in color and shape: a red circle means a prohibition, a blue circle means an obligation (for example, minimum speed), and a blue rectangle means information or advice. If the same number 40 were inside a blue circle, the meaning would flip: driving slower than 40 would be prohibited. So always remember the number 40 together with the sign's shape and color, since that exact pair is what gets swapped on the exam. In Armenia, this sign is often found at village entrances along intercity roads, in repair zones, and on mountain descents, and fixed speed cameras use this very ceiling as the basis for fines. • 'Recommendation' is the job of blue recommended-speed signs: a red circle is mandatory, and exceeding its number is a violation and triggers a fine. • That is the meaning of the minimum speed sign (blue circle with a white number) and the exact opposite of the current sign: here 40 is the ceiling, not the floor.

g4-q126.text: Which supplemental plaques indicate the area of effect of the sign with which they are used?
g4-q126.explanation: Plates B (8.2.1) and C (8.2.2) are called 'Zone of validity' and use arrows to show the length of the effective zone of the sign installed with them (the length of a hazardous stretch or a stopping/parking ban zone). Meanwhile, plate A (8.1.1 'Distance to object') shows only the distance to the start of the sign's effect, not the effective zone. (Rules, signs 8.1.1, 8.2.1, 8.2.2)

g4-q127.text: Which yard is the driver permitted to enter?
g4-q127.explanation: At the start of the road section, sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight' is installed, whose effect extends to the nearest intersection. Sign 4.1.1 installed in this position does not prohibit turning right into courtyards and other areas adjacent to the road, but prohibits turning left and making a U-turn. Consequently, the driver is permitted to enter only the right courtyard. (Rules, sign 4.1.1)

g4-q128.text: Which sign takes effect immediately from the location where it is installed?
g4-q128.explanation: In options A (sign 3.24 and plate 8.2.1 'Zone of validity') and B (sign 3.24), the speed limit takes effect immediately from the place where the sign is installed. In option C, however, sign 3.24 is combined with plate 8.1.1 'Distance to object' ('200 m'), meaning the restriction begins 200 m ahead rather than at the sign's location. (Rules, signs 3.24, 8.1.1, 8.2.1)

g4-q129.text: Along which path is it permitted to continue?
g4-q129.explanation: At the break in the dividing strip, information sign 6.3.1 'U-turn area' is installed. This sign permits continuing straight (A) and making a U-turn (along trajectory C or D), but prohibits turning left (in direction B — into the courtyard). Therefore, driving along any trajectory except B is permitted. (Rules, sign 6.3.1)

g4-q130.text: What does this traffic sign warn about?
options: An approaching slippery section of road.
An approaching wet and dirty section of road.
An approaching section of road where loose gravel may be thrown up by vehicle tires.
g4-q130.explanation: Installed on the right is warning sign 1.18 'Loose gravel'. It warns of approaching a section of road where gravel or stones may be thrown up from under vehicle wheels, rather than a slippery or dirty surface. (Rules, sign 1.18)

g4-q131.text: Within the area of effect of which sign do the traffic rules applicable in populated areas not apply?
g4-q131.explanation: Signs A (5.23.1) and B (5.23.2) have a white background and mark the beginning of a built-up area where the rules governing traffic in built-up areas apply. Sign C — 5.25 'Beginning of built-up area' (with a blue background) — indicates the beginning of a built-up area where the traffic rules for built-up areas do not apply on that road. (Rules, sign 5.25)

g4-q132.text: In which direction or directions is the passenger-car driver permitted to proceed in this situation?
options: Straight ahead and to the right.
g4-q132.explanation: Under sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight' installed before the intersection, plate 8.4.1 'Type of vehicle' depicting a truck is used. This plate extends the sign's effect only to trucks with a maximum permissible mass exceeding 3.5 tons and vehicle combinations. Therefore, the driver of a passenger car is permitted to proceed in any direction. (Rules, signs 4.1.1, 8.4.1)

g4-q133.text: Unloading an automobile within the area where this traffic sign is in effect is:
options: Permitted if it takes no more than 5 minutes.
g4-q133.explanation: Permitted, regardless of duration. The sign on the right is a blue circle with a red border and a single diagonal line — 'No parking'. To answer, you must know the exact definition of parking: parking is ceasing movement for more than 5 minutes when it is not connected with boarding or alighting people or loading or unloading cargo. That means as long as you are genuinely unloading cargo, your stop is legally 'stopping' rather than 'parking', no matter how long it takes. Thus, unloading cargo within this sign's effective zone is permitted with no time limit. There is, however, a fine boundary: as soon as unloading finishes and the car remains in place, your stop turns into parking and becomes a violation. The safety reason is visible right in the photo: a narrow sloped street in a residential area, with a wall and curb on both sides and a pedestrian walking directly on the carriageway on the right. A car left there for hours eats up the usable width of the road, blocks drivers' view of that very pedestrian, and forces others into the oncoming lane. A car whose driver is working alongside it can be moved at any moment and creates no such hazard. What to remember: the law's criterion is 'what are you doing?', not 'how long are you standing?'. The 5-minute figure matters only for stops completely unrelated to loading or boarding and alighting. • The 5-minute figure is real and therefore tempting, but it applies to a stop unrelated to loading and unloading: while you are unloading cargo, no time ceiling applies to you. • This sign prohibited parking, not stopping: unloading cargo falls under the legal definition of stopping and is not prohibited.

g4-q134.text: Which of the signs prohibits a U-turn?
g4-q134.explanation: Shown are signs 5.7.1, 5.7.2 'Entering a one-way road' (A, B) and 5.13.1, 5.13.2 'Entering a road with a lane for public transit vehicles' (C, D). They prohibit turning against the oncoming flow or onto the lane for public transit vehicles, yet none of them prohibits making a U-turn at the intersection. (Rules, signs 5.7.1, 5.7.2, 5.13.1, 5.13.2)

g4-q135.text: Is it permitted to enter the indicated yard?
g4-q135.explanation: Sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight' installed on the right is located immediately before the intersection, so its effect extends only to that intersection. The indicated courtyard is located beyond the intersection, where sign 4.1.1 no longer applies; therefore, after passing straight through the intersection, turning left into the courtyard is permitted. (Rules, sign 4.1.1)

g4-q136.text: In this situation, stopping to pick up a passenger is:
g4-q136.explanation: On the right side of the carriageway, sign 3.27 'No stopping' is installed with plate 8.2.4 'Zone of validity' (two-way vertical arrow), which informs you that you are within the sign's effective zone. This means stopping (including to pick up or drop off a passenger) is prohibited both before the sign and after it. (Rules, signs 3.27, 8.2.4)

g4-q137.text: After which signs is proceeding prohibited without permission?
g4-q137.explanation: Further movement without permission is prohibited past signs B (3.17.1 'Customs') and C (3.17.2 'Danger'). Meanwhile, A (7.12 'Traffic police patrol post') is a service sign, and D (6.16 'Stop line') only marks the place to stop on a prohibitory signal from a traffic light or traffic controller. (Rules, signs 3.17.1, 3.17.2)

g4-q138.text: What is the minimum distance from the location of this sign at which an intersection of roads of equal priority may be encountered?
g4-q138.explanation: The image shows a built-up area where warning sign 1.6 'Intersection of roads of equal importance' is installed on the right. In built-up areas, warning signs are placed 50–100 m before the start of the hazardous section, so the minimum distance is 50 meters. (Rules, sign 1.6)

g4-q139.text: In which of the directions indicated by the arrows may towing continue?
g4-q139.explanation: The blue car is towing a motorcycle with a sidecar. At the start of direction B, sign 3.7 'No trailers' is installed, which also prohibits towing motor vehicles. Consequently, towing may be continued only in direction A by turning before the sign. (Rules, sign 3.7)

g4-q140.text: From what point do the requirements regulating traffic in a populated area take effect?
options: After the “Beginning of Populated Area” sign with a white background.
Only after signs with a white or blue background that contain the name of the populated area.
Only after the beginning of the developed area.
g4-q140.explanation: The requirements establishing the traffic regime in a built-up area (such as the 60 km/h speed limit) take effect past signs 5.23.1 and 5.23.2 'Beginning of built-up area' with a white background. Where sign 5.25 with a blue background is installed, the built-up area traffic regime does not apply on that road, and the mere presence of a built-up area without a sign does not establish that regime. (Rules, signs 5.23.1, 5.23.2, and 5.25)

options: Warns of an intersection with tram tracks.
Warns of an approaching tram stop.
Requires yielding to the tram operator.
g4-q141.explanation: It warns of the carriageway intersecting a tram line. The sign's shape settles the question: a white triangle with a red border belongs to the warning signs family, and its role is solely to announce a hazard ahead. The symbol inside the triangle is a tram car: meaning further ahead tram tracks cross your path, and you must reduce speed and be ready to stop. In the image, the street curves left immediately after the sign, and a hedge and tall building block your view of the crossing; that is why the sign is placed before the bend. The safety reason for this warning is twofold: first, a tram runs on rails, cannot swerve, and has a braking distance several times longer than a passenger car's; second, the rails themselves and the cobblestones around them are slippery in rain, and hard braking on them can spin or overturn a car. What to remember: a warning sign never grants priority and never takes it away. The fact that at an intersection of roads of equal importance a tram has priority over trackless vehicles is a separate rule in the traffic code and does not follow from this triangle. On the exam, these two topics are usually mixed intentionally in the options. • Approaching a tram stop is announced by a rectangular blue information sign, not a red warning triangle: the sign in the image is triangular. • A duty to give way is imposed by priority signs (inverted triangle or 'Minor road' sign): a warning sign creates no such duty.

g4-q142.text: These signs require you to maintain between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead:
options: A distance of up to 70 m over a 900 m section of road.
A distance of at least 70 m over a 900 m section of road.
A distance of 70 m after proceeding 900 m.
g4-q142.explanation: Shown are sign 3.16 'Minimum distance limit' ('70 m') and plate 8.2.1 'Zone of validity' ('900 m'). Sign 3.16 prohibits driving if the distance between vehicles is less than 70 m, and plate 8.2.1 establishes that this requirement applies over a 900 m stretch. Other options misinterpret the minimum distance or the length of the effective zone. (Rules, signs 3.16, 8.2.1)

g4-q143.text: In which direction or directions may you continue from the indicated lane?
options: To the left and straight ahead.
To the left, straight ahead, and by making a U-turn.
g4-q143.explanation: From this lane, you may only go straight or turn left. Above each lane is a blue 'Lane direction' sign, and these signs — not habit or markings — define your obligation. The sign above your lane has two arrows: one straight, the other left. The left sign has only a left arrow, and the right sign has straight and right. That means your lane is not the leftmost one: beside you is a lane dedicated entirely to left turns. This point makes up the entire answer: a U-turn is permitted only from the leftmost position on the carriageway, and even then only when a sign permits a left turn from that very lane. Since the adjacent leftmost lane serves that role, the left arrow on your sign means only a left turn and does not grant the right to make a U-turn. The safety reason is also tangible: a U-turn from the middle lane traces a wide arc that simultaneously crosses the path of cars in the left lane; a driver waiting to turn in the left lane does not expect someone to turn around in front of them from the right. The image also shows a double line down the middle of the road, which cannot be crossed. The exam trap is that the test-taker automatically equates a left arrow with 'left and U-turn'. • 'Straight only' would require a sign with a single upward arrow: the sign above your lane has two arrows and explicitly permitted a left turn. • This option links a U-turn with a left arrow, but that permission applies only to the leftmost position on the carriageway, and that lane has its own separate sign in the image.

options: There is a three-track railroad crossing ahead.
There is a railroad crossing without a barrier gate 150–300 m ahead.
There is a railroad crossing 50–100 m ahead.
g4-q144.explanation: Shown are signs 1.2 'Railway crossing without a barrier' and 1.4.1 'Approach to a railway crossing' (with three slanted red stripes). Outside built-up areas, sign 1.4.1 is installed under the first sign 1.2 at a distance of 150–300 m from the crossing (one stripe corresponds to 50–100 m, and the number of stripes does not refer to the number of tracks). (Rules, signs 1.2, 1.4.1)

g4-q145.text: Is parking permitted at the indicated location?
options: Permitted only for residents of the indicated area.
g4-q145.explanation: Yes: from this point the restriction is lifted, and parking is permitted. The crossed-out sign on the post is indeed 'No stopping', but the plate beneath it changes the meaning of the entire scene: an arrow with its tip only at the bottom means 'End of sign's zone of validity'. The restriction behind you has ended, and the road ahead of you is free of that sign's requirements: thus neither a brief stop nor parking in the zone of interest raises any objection. This single plate generates three different questions, and its three forms must be recognized without hesitation: an upward arrow means the zone starts here; a two-way arrow means you are inside the zone; and a downward arrow means the zone closes here. This is precisely the exam trap: seeing a crossed-out circle, the test-taker instinctively picks 'no' and does not look at the plate at all. The lawmaker's logic in marking the end of a zone is also instructive: a stopping ban is a costly tool and is applied only to the stretch where a real problem exists — in front of an entrance, on a bend, at a narrowing, or at a transit stop. Rather than stretching the ban to the next intersection, this plate announces right where its job is done so drivers do not needlessly hunt for parking farther on and roadside space is not wasted. • A 'residents only' exception is announced by a separate plate, which is absent in the image: no such meaning follows from a downward arrow. • If the plate had an upward arrow or a two-way arrow, the right answer would be 'no'; however, a downward arrow announces the end of the ban.

g4-q146.text: Which sign requires the driver of a 5-metric-ton truck to make a right turn at the intersection?
g4-q146.explanation: Only sign B — 4.1.2 'Turn right' — is mandatory and requires all vehicles, including a 5-ton truck, to make a right turn at the intersection. Sign A (5.7.1 'Entering a one-way road') does not prohibit going straight, while sign C (6.15 'Direction of movement for trucks') is only a recommended direction and is not mandatory. (Rules, signs 4.1.2, 5.7.1, 6.15)

g4-q147.text: In which direction or directions may you continue through the indicated intersection if you are driving a truck with a maximum authorized mass of 3 metric tons?
options: Straight ahead and to the right only.
g4-q147.explanation: You may continue driving in any direction. The round blue sign with an upward arrow means 'Proceed straight only'. Right beneath it, however, is a white plate depicting a truck, and this small plate changes the whole equation: the vehicle-type plate limits the main sign's scope to trucks whose permissible mass exceeds 3.5 tons. Your truck is 3 tons, meaning the 'Proceed straight only' sign does not cover you, and you may continue driving in any direction. The logic of this combination is managing heavy transport. A city wants heavy trucks to follow a designated route and stay off minor streets, yet there is no reason to send a van or light truck along that same mandatory route: if all vehicles were restricted, traffic would needlessly concentrate on one route and collision risk there would rise. What to remember: always read the plate before the main sign. A truck symbol on a plate means by default 'a truck with a permissible mass over 3.5 tons', not just any vehicle that looks like a truck. This single rule solves several exam questions at once. The exam trap is that the eye sees only the large blue arrow and misses the small white plate beneath it. • This answer would be right if the van's permissible mass exceeded 3.5 tons: at 3 tons, the plate takes you outside the scope of the main sign. • This option confuses the 'Proceed straight only' sign with the 'Proceed straight or turn right' sign; moreover, the sign does not apply to a 3-ton truck at all.

g4-q148.text: In this situation, the horn may be used:
options: Only to warn of an intention to pass.
Only when necessary to prevent a traffic accident.
In both of the listed cases.
g4-q148.explanation: Although the road is outside a built-up area, sign 3.26 'No audible warning devices' is installed on the right. Within this sign's effective zone, using a horn is permitted only to prevent a traffic accident, and is prohibited to warn of overtaking. (Rules, item 136, sign 3.26)

g4-q149.text: Which sign is used to mark a speed hump?
g4-q149.explanation: A speed bump itself (its boundaries) is marked with special regulation sign A — 5.20 'Speed bump'. Sign B (1.17 'Speed bump') is installed in advance to warn of approaching a speed bump, while sign C (1.16 'Uneven road') warns of an uneven section of road. (Rules, sign 5.20)

g4-q150.text: Along which path may you continue?
g4-q150.explanation: The intersecting road has two carriageways separated by a dividing strip, and sign 4.1.2 'Turn right' is installed before the first intersection. The sign's effect applies specifically to the first intersection, so the driver must turn right onto the first carriageway (along trajectory A) and cannot continue to the second intersection (B). (Rules, sign 4.1.2)

g4-q151.text: At an uncontrolled intersection, which signs give the driver the right-of-way over vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road?
g4-q151.explanation: At an unguarded intersection, priority over vehicles traveling on the intersecting road is granted by priority signs A (2.1 'Priority road') and C (2.3.1 'Intersection with a minor road'). Sign B (2.7 'Priority over oncoming traffic'), however, grants priority only over oncoming vehicles on a narrow road section, not at an intersection. (Rules, signs 2.1, 2.3.1, 2.7)

g4-q152.text: Is passing permitted in this situation?
options: Yes, if the motorcycle is proceeding at a speed below 30 km/h.
g4-q152.explanation: Yes, overtaking is permitted in this situation. An overtaking ban is never absolute: its exceptions are determined by the type of vehicle ahead, not by its instantaneous speed. Slow-moving vehicles (marked with their own special red triangle), animal-drawn carts, bicycles, mopeds, and two-wheeled motorcycles without a sidecar are on that list, and overtaking them is allowed. Thus the right question is 'what is moving ahead of me?', not 'how many kilometers per hour is it going right now?'. However, permission by vehicle type does not cancel the general conditions for overtaking: the oncoming lane must be clear for a sufficient distance with open visibility, nobody must be overtaking you, the vehicle ahead must not be signaling a left turn, and you must not cross a solid line or maneuver at an intersection, pedestrian crossing, bridge, or tunnel. On Armenia's two-lane roads between Yerevan and nearby towns, motorcyclists and slow-moving tractors are common: this exception prevents long queues from forming behind them. • The figure 30 refers to the definition of a 'slow-moving vehicle', not to a condition for overtaking a motorcycle. Permission is tied to the vehicle type rather than its instantaneous speed: regardless of how fast the motorcycle is going, the conclusion does not change. • A total ban applies when no exception is in effect: here the situation falls within the list of exceptions, and the general conditions for overtaking pose no obstacle either.

g4-q153.text: Has the truck driver violated the parking rules?
options: Yes, if the maximum authorized mass exceeds 3.5 metric tons.
g4-q153.explanation: The truck parked on the edge of the sidewalk under sign 6.4 'Parking area' and plate 8.6.3 'Manner of parking a vehicle'. According to item 81 of the Rules, parking at the edge of the sidewalk is permitted only for passenger cars, motorcycles, mopeds, and bicycles. Consequently, the truck driver violated the parking rules regardless of its maximum permissible mass. (Rules, item 81, signs 6.4, 8.6.3)

g4-q154.text: Along which path is the U-turn permitted?
g4-q154.explanation: Before the intersection on the right is sign 4.1.1 'Proceed straight', whose effect extends only to this intersection. A U-turn along trajectory A is prohibited by sign 4.1.1 (as well as due to crossing a solid marking line), whereas after passing straight through the intersection the effect of sign 4.1.1 ends, and a U-turn may be made across the broken line along trajectory B. (Rules, sign 4.1.1)

g4-q155.text: On odd-numbered dates of the month, is parking permitted at the indicated location?
g4-q155.explanation: Yes, but only after 19:00. On both sides of the street, two signs from the same family are installed: both are blue circles with a red border and a single diagonal line — meaning 'No parking' — with the difference that the number of white vertical bars inside the circle differs. One bar means parking is prohibited on odd days of the month, two bars mean on even days. When these two signs are used together opposite each other, the lawmaker's intent is simple: every day the car must be moved to the opposite side. Moving a car, however, requires a time window: if one side's ban started right at midnight simultaneously with the other opening, no driver could comply. Therefore, during evening hours — from 19:00 to 21:00, known as the 'repositioning period' — parking is permitted on both sides of the street. The safety and municipal purpose of this arrangement is also clear: every day one side of the street remains free so fire trucks and ambulances have enough width and cleaning and snow removal are possible. Exam note: remember the number of bars inside the sign — one bar equals odd days — and remember that the answer to such a question is never an unconditional 'yes' or 'no', but depends on the time. • An unconditional 'yes' ignores the presence of the odd-days sign: during daytime hours, parking on this side is a violation. • 'No' is true only until 19:00 and misses the evening repositioning window.

g4-q156.text: Which signs indicate the section where drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing the roadway?
g4-q156.explanation: An immediate area with a duty to yield to pedestrians is marked by signs B (5.19.1 'Pedestrian crossing') and C (5.21 'Residential zone', where pedestrians may move on the carriageway and have priority). Sign A (1.22 'Pedestrian crossing'), meanwhile, only warns of approaching a pedestrian crossing ahead. (Rules, items 103, 119, signs 5.19.1, 5.21)

g4-q157.text: Which sign warns that you are approaching the beginning of a road with two-way traffic?
g4-q157.explanation: Approaching the start of a road section with oncoming traffic is warned of only by warning sign A — 1.21 'Two-way traffic'. Sign B (5.8 'Reversible traffic') marks the start of a section with reversible traffic, while sign C (5.15.7 'Traffic directions by lanes') shows the number and directions of lanes. (Rules, sign 1.21)

g4-q158.text: Are you permitted to enter your workplace located within the area where these signs are in effect?
g4-q158.explanation: Installed are sign 3.2 'No vehicles' and plate 8.5.2 'Working days'. The effect of sign 3.2 does not extend to vehicles belonging to citizens who work in the designated zone (on working days you may enter on that basis), while on non-working days sign 3.2 does not apply due to plate 8.5.2. Therefore, entering to reach your workplace is permitted on all days. (Rules, signs 3.2, 8.5.2)

g4-q159.text: Is a passenger car towing a trailer permitted to proceed straight ahead through the intersection?
options: Permitted only for persons residing within the area where the sign is in effect.
g4-q159.explanation: Ahead on the right is sign 3.7 'No trailers'. This sign prohibits the movement only of trucks and tractors with any type of trailer (as well as towing), but does not prohibit passenger cars towing a trailer. Consequently, proceeding straight is permitted. (Rules, sign 3.7)

g4-q160.text: In which of the indicated directions is traffic permitted?
g4-q160.explanation: Opposite the intersection is sign 5.7.2 'Entering a one-way road', which indicates that traffic on the intersecting road moves from right to left. Consequently, proceeding straight (A), turning left in the direction of one-way traffic (B), and making a U-turn (C) are all permitted. (Rules, sign 5.7.2)

options: Indicates the directions of traffic at the intersection.
g4-q161.explanation: Ahead at the T-intersection is warning sign 1.34.3 'Direction of turn'. It shows the permitted directions of travel at the intersection (right or left) and does not prohibit driving through the intersection. (Rules, sign 1.34.3)

g4-q162.text: Which sign indicates the length of the lane provided for making a U-turn?
g4-q162.explanation: Sign B — 6.3.2 'U-turn zone' — shows the length of the zone intended for making a U-turn (15 m). Combination A (sign 6.3.1 'U-turn area' with plate 8.1.1 '50 m'), however, informs you of the distance to the U-turn area rather than the length of the zone. (Rules, sign 6.3.2)

g4-q163.text: At what minimum distance from the sign will a slippery section of road begin in a populated area?
g4-q163.explanation: At least 50 meters after the sign. The triangular sign in the image depicts a car with tire skid marks—the "Slippery road" warning. However, the question is not about the hazard itself; it is about the placement distance of warning signs. The rule has two numbers, and those are the ones to remember: in a built-up area a warning sign is placed 50–100 meters before the hazard, and outside a built-up area 150–300 meters before it. This means that in a town or city, the earliest point where the slippery section can begin is 50 meters after the sign. The reason for the difference between these two ranges is speed. The distance must be enough for the driver to see the sign, understand its meaning, and smoothly reduce speed without harsh braking. At lower urban speeds 50 meters is enough for this, whereas on an intercity road at high speed the same task requires several times greater distance, so the sign is placed much earlier. Look at the wet asphalt and damp sidewalk in the image: after this sign, you should increase the following distance from the vehicle ahead, avoid abrupt braking and steering, and reduce speed before reaching the slippery section rather than on it. A common trap is choosing "immediately after the sign." • 100 meters is the upper limit of the placement range in a built-up area, not its minimum; the question asks for the minimum distance. • A warning sign is never placed right next to the hazard, because then the driver would have no opportunity to slow down.

g4-q164.text: Which vehicles are not subject to the “No Stopping” sign in this situation?
options: Only motorized wheelchairs and automobiles displaying the “Disabled” identification sign.
g4-q164.explanation: Vehicles of persons with disabilities: that is, motorized carriages for persons with disabilities and cars bearing the "Person with a Disability" identification sign. The crossed-out round sign in the image is "Stopping prohibited," but the white plaque beneath it plays the decisive role: a wheelchair symbol crossed out with a red diagonal line means "Except persons with disabilities." This plaque lifts the sign's restriction for one specific group while leaving it unchanged for everyone else. Pay attention: the correct option does not mean an ordinary motorcycle—it refers to motorized carriages for persons with disabilities and cars equipped with the "Person with a Disability" identification sign. The logic of this exception is both humane and related to safety: a driver unable to walk far, if forced to stop farther away, would have to cover a greater distance along the roadway or traffic flow; the legislator preferred that the car stop closer to the destination so the person is not put in danger. Keep two exam points together. First, no exception exists on its own: if there were no plaque under the sign, stopping would be prohibited for everyone. Second, using this exception depends on whether the official "Person with a Disability" sign is mounted on the car, not merely on having a passenger with reduced mobility inside: only this single plaque is posted in the image, and no other exception is declared. • Taxis hold a special position in many stopping rules, making that option tempting; however, the plaque in the image grants an exception only for persons with disabilities and makes no mention of taxis. • If the sign applied to no vehicles at all, placing it would be pointless: the plaque removes the prohibition for one group, not for everyone.

g4-q165.text: At the next intersection, in which of the indicated directions may you continue?
g4-q165.explanation: At the start of the road section (immediately after the intersection just passed), sign 4.1.1 "Proceed straight" is posted. When sign 4.1.1 is placed at the beginning of a road section, its effect extends up to the nearest intersection and does not apply to that intersection itself. Therefore, at the next intersection you may continue driving in all indicated directions: A, B, and C. (Rules, sign 4.1.1)

g4-q166.text: Within the area of effect of which sign may you proceed at a speed of 60 km/h?
g4-q166.explanation: Sign A—3.24 "Maximum speed limit"—prohibits driving faster than 50 km/h, so 60 km/h is not permitted. Sign B (4.6 "Minimum speed limit") requires driving at 50 km/h or higher, while sign C (6.2 "Recommended speed") is purely advisory. Therefore, you may drive at 60 km/h in the zone of signs B and C. (Rules, signs 3.24, 4.6, 6.2)

g4-q167.text: Which driver has violated the parking rules?
options: The motorcycle operator and the passenger-car driver.
g4-q167.explanation: At the right edge of the roadway, sign 6.4 "Parking area" is posted with plaque 8.6.1 "Method of placing a vehicle in parking areas," which provides for parking on the roadway parallel to the curb (without driving onto the sidewalk). Parking in this manner is permitted for all vehicles, and all three drivers shown—of the motorcycle, passenger car, and truck—have parked correctly: no one has violated the rules. (Rules, signs 6.4, 8.6.1)

g4-q168.text: Which of the indicated directions is permitted?
g4-q168.explanation: Before the intersection, sign 3.18.1 "Right turn prohibited" is posted, so turning right along trajectory D is prohibited. Trajectory B is also prohibited because it leads onto the left side of the median strip—into the oncoming roadway. Only a U-turn (A) and proceeding straight (C) are permitted. (Rules, item 41, sign 3.18.1)

g4-q169.text: When used with which supplemental plaque does the sign apply to the driver of a truck with a maximum authorized mass of less than 3.5 metric tons?
g4-q169.explanation: Plaque A—8.4.1 "Vehicle type"—applies only to trucks with a permissible maximum mass exceeding 3.5 tons. Plaque B (8.4.3) applies to passenger cars and trucks with a mass up to 3.5 tons, and plaque C (8.6.1—parking parallel to the edge of the roadway) applies to all vehicles, including trucks up to 3.5 t. Therefore, the correct answer is B and C. (Rules, signs 8.4.1, 8.4.3, 8.6.1)

g4-q170.text: Which case indicates a railroad crossing with two or more tracks?
g4-q170.explanation: Signs A (1.1 and 1.4.3) and B (1.2 and 1.4.1) warn of approaching a railway crossing with a barrier and without a barrier, respectively, but do not indicate the number of tracks. Only sign C—1.3.2 "Multi-track railway"—informs of an unbarriered railway crossing with two or more tracks. (Rules, sign 1.3.2)

g4-q171.text: A U-turn along the indicated path is:
g4-q171.explanation: On the right, mandatory sign 4.3 "Roundabout" is posted, whose arrows indicate the mandatory direction of circular traffic (counterclockwise). Making a U-turn by turning left along the indicated trajectory contradicts the direction of the sign's arrows and is prohibited. (Rules, sign 4.3)

g4-q172.explanation: Before the overpass on the right side, sign 3.28 "Parking prohibited" is posted. Since the effect of sign 3.28 extends from its point of installation to the nearest intersection and is not interrupted after crossing the overpass, parking at the indicated location is prohibited. (Rules, sign 3.28)

options: An approaching railroad crossing with a barrier gate.
A railroad crossing without a barrier gate.
g4-q173.explanation: They indicate an approach to a railway crossing with a barrier. Read both elements together. First, the red triangle on the right with the symbol of a fence or closed gate: this sign means the railway crossing ahead has a barrier. If the crossing had no barrier, the symbol inside the triangle would be a locomotive—that single visual difference already answers the entire question. Second, the white posts with diagonal red stripes placed on both sides of the road at three consecutive distances: the number of stripes decreases as you get closer to the crossing and works as a countdown—the three-stripe post stands by the first warning sign, and the one-stripe post is closest. The reason for all these layered warnings is simple: a train can neither swerve nor stop in a short distance—its braking distance is measured in hundreds of meters. That means the entire burden of prevention rests on the driver, who must reduce speed and be ready to stop before the crossing long before seeing the rails. In the image, dense forest and fog have shortened your sight distance and the asphalt is wet—the exact conditions these signs were designed for. The exam trap is that the candidate mistakes the presence of a barrier for "less danger, no caution needed," whereas the duty to slow down and be ready to stop remains. • The symbol inside the triangle is a crossing barrier, not a construction site sign: roadworks are marked by a sign depicting a worker with a shovel. • A crossing without a barrier has its own sign whose symbol is a locomotive, not a barrier gate.

g4-q174.explanation: Sign A (4.1.3 "Turn left") mandates a left turn, yet also permits a U-turn. Sign B (3.18.2 "Left turn prohibited") prohibits only a left turn, and sign C (5.7.1 "Entry onto a one-way road") shows the direction of one-way traffic, and none of them prohibits a U-turn. Therefore, all three signs permit a U-turn. (Rules, signs 3.18.2, 4.1.3, 5.7.1)

g4-q175.text: From the indicated lane, traffic is permitted:
options: To the left and by making a U-turn.
g4-q175.explanation: The car is in the leftmost lane, above which sign 5.15.2 "Lane directions" is posted, permitting movement to the left. Since sign 5.15.2 permitting a left turn from the leftmost lane also permits a U-turn from that lane (and proceeding straight is not indicated), turning left and making a U-turn are permitted from this lane. (Rules, sign 5.15.2)

g4-q176.text: This sign indicates that you are approaching a tunnel:
g4-q176.explanation: On the right, warning sign 1.31 "Tunnel" is posted. It informs of approaching a tunnel that lacks artificial lighting (or whose entrance portal visibility is limited), and does not relate to the absence of road markings. (Rules, sign 1.31)

g4-q177.text: At which of the indicated locations is stopping permitted?
options: Stopping is prohibited at all of the indicated locations.
g4-q177.explanation: On the right before the intersection, signs 2.3.3 "Side road junction" and 3.27 "Stopping prohibited" are posted. Location A is within the zone of sign 3.27 (after the sign up to the intersection), so stopping there is prohibited. After the intersection with the secondary road, the effect of sign 3.27 ends; therefore, stopping is permitted only at location B. (Rules, signs 2.3.3, 3.27)

g4-q178.text: With which sign may you make a left turn?
g4-q178.explanation: Sign A (5.7.1 "Entry onto a one-way road") shows that traffic on the intersecting road moves from left to right, so a left turn is prohibited. Sign B (6.8.2 "Dead end") merely informs of a road on the left without through passage, and sign C (5.13.2) shows the general traffic flow moving to the left. Therefore, a left turn may be made under signs B and C. (Rules, signs 5.7.1, 5.13.2, 6.8.2)

g4-q179.text: This sign gives advance warning of:
options: The need to yield to bicyclists.
An intersection with a bicycle path.
g4-q179.explanation: About a road intersection with a cycle path. A triangle with a red border and a bicycle symbol is a warning sign, and it informs that slightly ahead a cycle path crosses the roadway. The image shows the same thing: the road is narrow, lined with trees, visibility is short due to foliage on both sides, and transverse cycle-crossing markings are visible on the pavement not far ahead. The safety reason for this warning is the difference in speeds and the small size of the object. A cyclist is narrow, silent, and moves faster than a driver assumes: on a road like the one in the image, where vegetation comes right up to the edge of the roadway, a cyclist becomes visible only one second before reaching the crossing line. The sign warns you before that second so that you reduce speed, keep your foot ready over the brake, and look both ways. The key point tested on the exam: triangular warning signs never establish priority. They only warn of a hazard; who must yield is determined by priority signs and markings at that location. That means the mere appearance of this sign neither gives you priority nor takes it away. • Establishing a requirement to yield is the job of priority signs, not a warning triangle: if yielding were required here, a "Give way" sign would be posted. • A "bicycle square" is not defined among traffic signs at all: the image on this sign is a single bicycle, and it warns of a crossing, not a square.

g4-q180.text: Which vehicle drivers are subject to these signs?
g4-q180.explanation: Sign 6.4 "Parking area" is shown with plaque 8.6.3 "Method of placing a vehicle in parking areas," which provides for parking partially onto the sidewalk curb. According to item 81 of the Rules, the combination of sign 6.4 with plaques 8.6.2, 8.6.3, and 8.6.6–8.6.9 applies only to passenger cars and motorcycles (as well as mopeds and bicycles). (Rules, item 81, signs 6.4, 8.6.3)

g4-q181.text: Under which sign, after stopping, may you not resume proceeding without permission?
g4-q181.explanation: The 1st (2.5 "Stop without stopping prohibited" / "Stop") requires stopping and continuing after yielding, the 2nd (1.35) is the intersection area sign, the 3rd (6.16) marks the stop line, and the 4th (3.1) prohibits entry. Only with the 5th sign—3.17.2 "Danger"—is further movement prohibited, and after stopping, traffic may resume only upon receiving permission. (Rules, sign 3.17.2)

g5-q1.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The passenger car, the bus, then the trolleybus.
The trolleybus and the bus, then the passenger car.
The trolleybus, the passenger car, then the bus.
g5-q1.explanation: Trolleybus, passenger car, bus. The yellow diamond on the right of the image tells you this is the main road, and the square plaque beneath it shows the direction of the main road: the main road does not continue straight, but turns at the intersection. The trolleybus coming from the left is on this very main road, and its trajectory arrow shows a right turn along the main road. At the bottom right, the yellow passenger car is also on this main road, but coming from the opposite direction and turning left. The yellow bus on the right enters the intersection from a secondary road. From this, the order becomes clear. The trolleybus turns right and crosses no one's path, so it goes first. The passenger car, although on the main road, is turning left and must yield to the oncoming vehicle: that means it is second. The bus remains last because it enters the main road from a secondary road. The main trap in this question is the names of the vehicles. Both the bus and the trolleybus belong to public transit, and the mind mistakenly attributes priority to them. The only vehicle that has priority over trackless vehicles under equal conditions is a tram: a trolleybus, despite its overhead wire, is an ordinary vehicle when it comes to priority. Here the trolleybus goes first because it is on the main road, not because it is a trolleybus. • "Passenger car, bus, trolleybus" puts the left-turning vehicle first and places secondary-road traffic ahead of main-road traffic: both contradict the rule. • "Trolleybus and bus together" is tempting because both are public transit; however, one is on the main road and the other is on the secondary road, so them going simultaneously makes no sense.

g5-q2.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection first?
g5-q2.explanation: The green car. All four cars in the image have indicated their intentions with turn signals. The small green car on the left has turned on its right indicator and wants to turn right. The yellow car opposite it is signaling left. The red sports car on the oncoming road is also signaling left, while the blue van beside it, with no indicator, is going straight. The key to this image is one invariable rule: a driver turning left always yields to oncoming vehicles. That means the yellow car, although on the same road and oncoming to the green car, must wait until the green car completes its maneuver. On the other hand, a right turn is the least conflict-prone maneuver at an intersection: the green car does not leave the right edge of the roadway, crosses no one's path, and exits the intersection at the very first outlet. Therefore, it goes through first, and the rest follow after it. The safety reason behind this order is more important than memorizing it. A left turn is the most dangerous maneuver at an intersection because the car simultaneously crosses the oncoming stream and the transverse path, while the driver's field of view is minimal during the turn. The law curbs this danger with one simple rule: whoever turns left goes later. An exam tip: first count the turn signals. In questions of this type, the answer is almost always the car that is either going straight or turning right. • The red car is signaling left: a left turn is the most conflict-prone maneuver at an intersection, and it does not open the sequence. • The blue van is going straight, which makes it appealing, but its straight path conflicts with others' maneuvers, and going straight by itself does not create priority. • The yellow car is the most tempting option because it is stopped directly opposite the green car; however, it is signaling left and must yield to oncoming traffic.

g5-q3.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection last?
g5-q3.explanation: The blue car. At this intersection there is no traffic light, no yellow diamond of a main road, and no "Give way" triangle: the roads are of equal priority. None of the three vehicles is signaling a turn, meaning all are going straight. In such a situation, your only tool is the "right-hand rule." To build the sequence, you must start where someone has no one on their right. The green truck on the right side of the frame is approaching from a road with empty space on its right, so it goes through first. The red car moving from the bottom of the frame has the truck on its right and must wait: it is second. The blue car on the left has the red car on its right, meaning it leaves after the red car and ends up last. The point worth keeping in mind is this: at an equal-roads intersection, never jump straight to the question "who goes first?" First look at who has empty space on their right: the chain opens from there and lines up the rest one after another. The safety reason for the rule itself is also clear: a driver has better visibility and more control on the right, and driver-side impacts—the most dangerous type of side collision—are rarer under this order. • The green truck is the exact one with empty space on its right: it goes through first, not last. • The red car yields only to the truck and goes before the blue car, so it is in the middle of the sequence.

g5-q4.text: The blue automobile will proceed through the intersection:
