g5-q4.explanation: First. The traffic light on the right of the image is green, meaning entry into the intersection is permitted for both cars. Now look at the red car: both of its left turn signals are on, and it wants to turn left. The blue car is coming from the oncoming direction—with no indicators, straight ahead. The rule here is short and allows no exceptions: a driver turning left must yield to vehicles approaching from the opposite direction going straight. That means the blue car crosses the intersection first, and the red car turns behind it. Safety reason: during a left turn, a car crosses the oncoming stream at an acute angle, and in the event of a mistake the impact strikes the occupant zone—where there is the least space to crumple. Judging an oncoming car's speed from behind the wheel is also very difficult, and drivers usually underestimate it. By placing the entire risk on the left-turning driver, the law neutralizes this perception error. The trap in the question is the yellow diamond and the main-road direction plaque next to the traffic light. Priority signs only define the relationship between two intersecting roads and give you no advantage over an oncoming car; moreover, at an intersection with a working traffic light, the crossing order is set by the traffic light, not the signs. • "Second" would be correct if the blue car were also preparing to turn left or were coming from a secondary road; in the image, the blue car is going straight with no indicators, and priority belongs to it.

g5-q5.text: Which answer correctly states the order in which the vehicles will proceed through the intersection?
options: The bus, the passenger car, the bicycle.
The passenger car, the bus, the bicycle.
The bicycle, the bus, the passenger car.
g5-q5.explanation: An uncontrolled intersection of equal roads is shown. There are no vehicles on the cyclist's right and the cyclist is going straight, so the bicycle will pass first. The bus must yield to the cyclist approaching from its right and pass second, while the blue car making a left turn yields to the bus approaching from its right and to the oncoming cyclist, passing last. (Rules, items 98, 99)

g5-q6.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q6.explanation: The tram. The yellow diamond on the right tells you that you are on the main road, and the square plaque below it shows that the main road does not continue straight, but turns left at the intersection. The blue car ahead of you is signaling left, meaning that with its left turn it stays on the main road. The tram and the red car are approaching from the opposite road, which is secondary relative to this intersection. From here comes the order: the blue car, being on the main road, passes first, then it is the tram's turn, and last is the red car. The reason the tram goes before the red car is that under equal conditions—that is, when both approach from roads of the same priority—a rail vehicle has priority over a trackless vehicle. The reason for this priority is technical, not ceremonial: a tram can neither swerve off its path nor stop in a short distance—tens of tons of weight slide for tens of meters on wet rails. So the cheapest solution is for cars to yield to it. A common exam trap is the phrase "a tram always goes first." That phrase is wrong: a tram's priority applies only under equal conditions. A tram coming from a secondary road yields to a vehicle on the main road, just like any other vehicle. That is precisely why the tram is second here, not first. • The red car approaches from the same secondary road as the tram and, under equal conditions, must yield to the rail vehicle: thus it passes third. • The blue car is on the main road and passes first, not second: its left turn also follows that same main road.

g5-q7.text: In which direction is traffic prohibited?
options: To the right through the first passage.
To the right through the second passage.
To the right through the first and second passages.
g5-q7.explanation: Turning right into the second entrance. The only prohibitory sign in this image is the red circle on the right with a right-turn arrow drawn on it. The zone of action of such a sign is the intersection or entrance immediately following it—not entrances before it and not all entrances after it. In the image, the sign's post is placed after the mouth of the first entrance and right by the mouth of the second. That means the first entrance ended before you reached the sign and remains open, while turning right into the second entrance is closed. The reason for this placement method is entirely about safety: a driver must see the prohibition sufficiently ahead of the maneuver point to decide without harsh braking and without hasty lane changing. If the sign covered entrances behind it, the driver would not yet see the sign while passing them—a rule impossible to obey. The blue sign in the middle of the image belongs to the mandatory family and shows how to move inside the intersection itself: it prohibits nothing and plays no part in answering this question. A common trap is imagining that the prohibition continues "all the way" from the sign's location. Turn-prohibition signs are very short-lived—just one intersection. • The first entrance lies before the sign's post: the sign does not act backward, and turning right at that point remains permitted. • To close both entrances, a sign would have to be placed before the first one as well: one turn-prohibition sign closes only one intersection or one entrance.

g5-q8.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q8.explanation: The red car. The yellow diamond in the middle of the image faces the red car: the road it is driving on is the main road, and the opposite road, from which the blue car is approaching, is a continuation of the same main road. The red triangle on the right says "Give way" to the green car: that means the green car is on a secondary road. Now look at the turn signals. The red car is signaling left, while the blue car is going straight with no indicators. Both are on the main road, so the signs do not decide between them, and another rule applies: a driver turning left must yield to an oncoming vehicle. Therefore, the blue car passes first, the red car turns second, and the green car stopped behind the triangle remains last. The key point is that the main-road sign clarifies the relationship between two intersecting roads, not the relationship between two cars facing each other on that same main road. Many candidates, seeing the yellow diamond, assume the car by the sign goes first: that is exactly where the trap is set. For two oncoming cars on the same road, always follow the indicators: the one going straight is ahead, and the one turning left is behind it. • In front of the green car stands the "Give way" triangle, and it approaches from a secondary road: it passes last. • The blue car is going straight on the main road, meaning it passes first, not second.

g5-q9.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q9.explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads, drivers must yield to vehicles approaching from the right. The road on the right side of the green car is clear, so the green car will pass first. The blue car will pass second (yielding to the green car on its right), and the red minibus will yield to the blue car approaching from its right and pass last. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q10.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
options: The white automobile, simultaneously with the yellow automobile.
g5-q10.explanation: The red car. Two signs explain the entire image. The yellow diamond on the right faces the red car: the red car's road is the main road, and the opposite road, from which the green car is approaching, continues the same main road. The red triangle in the middle of the image announces "Give way" to the white car, meaning the white car's road and the road of the yellow car opposite it are secondary. Thus, the two cars on the main road pass first, followed by the two on the secondary road. Between the green and red cars, the green car is going straight without indicators while the red car is signaling left: a left turn yields to an oncoming vehicle. So the green car is first, and the red car is second. The pattern worth taking from this question is two-step: the first step is the signs separating the main road from the secondary road; the second step is the turn signals establishing the order within each group. Mixing up these two steps leads to options like "the two cars on the secondary road go simultaneously," which seem logical at first glance. Going simultaneously only makes sense when two cars' trajectories do not intersect at all, not merely when both are on the same road. • "White simultaneously with yellow" is appealing because both are on the secondary road, but the secondary road gets its turn after the main road, so those two cannot go second. • The green car is going straight along the main road, and the left-turning red car must yield to it: thus the green car is first, not second.

g5-q11.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection last?
g5-q11.explanation: The green car. The yellow diamond in the middle of the image shows that the road the blue car is driving on is the main road; consequently, the opposite road, from which the red car is approaching, is a continuation of the same main road. The red triangle on the right announces "Give way" to the green car: the green car's road and the road of the yellow small truck opposite it are secondary. Thus, the sequence has two layers. First, the two cars on the main road—blue and red—pass through. Then comes the turn of the secondary road, and here the second layer applies: the green car is signaling left, while the small truck opposite it is going straight with no indicators. A left turn must yield to an oncoming vehicle, so the small truck passes before the green car, and the green car passes last. The green car effectively steps back twice: once because it is on a secondary road, and a second time because it is turning left. Such a combination—secondary road plus left turn—almost always means "last" on the exam: seeing both features together in the image, you can place that car at the end of the line without further calculation. The safety reason is also clear: that car must cross both the main-road flow and the traffic oncoming to itself; the greatest number of conflict points means the lowest priority. • The blue car stands right by the yellow diamond and on the main road: it is among the first, not the last. • The yellow small truck is also on the secondary road, which makes it tempting, yet it is going straight with no indicators and the green car must yield to it: so it is one place ahead of the green car. • The red car is on the main road, and the main road passes before the secondary road.

g5-q12.explanation: The car driver. The blue car has signaled and is leaving the roadway toward the adjacent road: the black arrow on the pavement shows the exact path it must take, and that path passes directly in front of the cyclist. The rule is simple: any driver changing direction must yield to a vehicle moving straight in its lane, and by law a bicycle is a full-fledged vehicle, not a minor obstacle you can squeeze past. That means priority belongs to the cyclist, and the car driver must wait until the cyclist passes. The safety reason behind this rule is visible in urban crash statistics: the most dangerous collision with a cyclist happens at the exact moment a car turns. The driver's eyes are focused on the open space of the intersecting road and other cars, while the narrow silhouette of a bicycle disappears behind the windshield pillar or in the mirror's blind spot. A cyclist has neither a crumple body nor an airbag: an impact that is a scratch for a car means the hospital for them. What to remember: "turning means a duty to yield." When turning right, you must yield to a cyclist and motorcyclist traveling in the same direction on your right, and when turning left, to all oncoming vehicles, including bicycles. The exam trap is assuming that because a bicycle is smaller and slower, it should wait for the car: size and speed create no priority whatsoever. • The cyclist is riding straight in their lane and crosses no one's path: small size or low speed does not deprive them of priority.

g5-q13.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection first?
g5-q13.explanation: The red car. The yellow diamond "Main road" is placed opposite the blue car's path, and its pair stands in the opposite corner along the red car's path: that is, the main road is the exact axis along which the red and blue cars travel. By contrast, in front of the green car stands the triangular "Give way" sign, and the yellow truck shows the back of the same sign in the corner on its side. That means the crossing order has two stages: first the two vehicles on the main road, then the vehicles on the secondary road. It remains to resolve the red and blue cars, which face each other. The red car turns right, while the blue car is signaling left. A driver turning left crosses the entire width of the oncoming lane and must therefore yield to an oncoming vehicle going straight or turning right. Result: the red car crosses the intersection first, and the blue car follows it. Safety reason: a left turn is the most dangerous maneuver at an intersection because the turning trajectory cuts across the oncoming flow at an angle that produces a "front-to-side" impact at combined speed. The law places the burden of waiting on the one who crosses that path, not on the one going straight. Way to remember: first read the signs and separate the main road from the secondary road, then within each group order the vehicles using the left-turn rule and the right-hand rule. Reversing these two stages is the most common mistake on such pictures. • In front of the green car is the "Give way" sign: it is on the secondary road and has no right to enter the intersection until the main road clears. • The blue car is also on the main road, making it tempting, but by turning left it must first yield to the oncoming red car and passes second. • The yellow truck is on the secondary road, and large dimensions grant no priority: it moves off after both cars on the main road.

g5-q14.text: In what order will the vehicles proceed through the intersection?
options: The motorcycle, the automobile, the tram.
The tram, the automobile, the motorcycle.
The tram, the motorcycle, the automobile.
g5-q14.explanation: Signs 2.1 "Main road" and 8.13 "Direction of main road" show that the motorcycle and the blue car are on the main road, while the tram is on the secondary road. Since the tram is on the secondary road, it must yield to those traveling on the main road and will pass last. Between the motorcycle and the car traveling on the main road, the right-of-way-to-the-right rule applies: the car yields to the motorcycle approaching from the right, so the order is: the motorcycle, the car, the tram. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

g5-q15.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q15.explanation: The blue car. At this intersection there is no traffic light, no "Main road" sign, and no "Give way" sign: that is, the roads are equal, and the sole tool for deciding is the right-hand rule—yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. Apply this rule to all three vehicles. To the right of the green truck it is empty, meaning no one is ahead of it and it moves off first. To the right of the blue car is the truck, and it must yield to it; yet the blue car itself is to the right of the red car, so the red car must stay behind it. The chain is complete: the green truck, then the blue car, and last the red car. The blue car crosses the intersection second. Safety reason: at an unmarked intersection, two drivers reach the conflict point almost simultaneously. If both stop, traffic locks up; if both go, a "front-to-side" impact occurs—the very crash with the least crumple space, where the blow lands directly on an occupant. One simple convention, identical for everyone, removes this decision from spur-of-the-moment discretion. How to act on the exam: instead of analyzing the whole scene, ask just one question about each vehicle: "who is on its right?" The vehicle with empty space on its right is always first, and the rest line up behind it. A common trap is assuming that the largest vehicle or the car closest to the center of the intersection goes first. • The red car is last, not second: the blue car approaches from its right, and it must yield to it. • The green truck is first because its right is empty: if you are looking for the "second" vehicle, you must skip past it.

g5-q16.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection last?
g5-q16.explanation: The red car. Neither signs nor a traffic light appear in the image: that is, all three roads are equal, and the crossing order is set solely by the right-hand rule. Start with the car whose right is empty: the blue car, entering from the right in the image, has no vehicle on its right, so it moves off first. On the right of the green car is the blue car, and it must yield to it. The red small truck, in turn, sees the green car on its right and must stay behind it. The chain comes out as blue, green, red—meaning the last vehicle is the red small truck. All three drivers are signaling left, and that is what makes the scene look overloaded, yet it does not change the order: two cars facing each other and both turning left do not cross each other's paths, so the only remaining criterion is the right-hand rule. Safety reason: at an unmarked intersection, if every driver acted at their own discretion, a "front-to-side" impact would follow—the deadliest kind of urban crash because the side of a car has almost no crumple zone. One firm convention applying to everyone eliminates this uncertainty. Quick exam method: first find the car whose right is empty and build the chain from it—the final link of the chain is the answer to "which vehicle is last?" • The green car is second: the blue car is on its right, yet it moves off before the red small truck. • The blue car is the direct opposite of the answer: since its right is empty, it is first, not last.

g5-q17.text: Which automobile will proceed through the intersection last?
g5-q17.explanation: The red car. The yellow diamond by the road means "Main road," and the white plaque below it shows that the main road does not continue straight, but turns at the intersection. According to the diagram on that plaque, the main road runs from the right branch to the branch from which the green car is approaching. That is, the green and blue cars are on the main road, while the red car, approaching from the left branch, is on the secondary road. That single sentence already gives the answer: a driver on a secondary road must yield to all vehicles on the main road regardless of where they turn. Thus, the red car passes last. Between the two cars on the main road, the right-hand rule settles it: the blue car is to the right of the green car, so the blue car goes first, followed by the green car. The trap in this question is the green car's turn signal. The green car is signaling left and leaving the main road; the thought pops into a candidate's head: "since it is leaving the main road, it loses priority." No such rule exists. Priority is determined by the road you are on now, not where you are heading. Practical rule: wherever you see a main-road sign with a direction plaque, first determine from which branch to which branch the main road runs—after that, everything else falls into place by itself. • The blue car is on the main road and also to the right of the green car: by both criteria it passes first, not last. • The green car is also on the main road and must yield only to the blue car on its right, so its place is second: leaving the main road does not cancel priority.

g5-q18.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection first?
g5-q18.explanation: The green car. In the image there is neither a traffic light nor a priority sign: that means the intersection is "equal," and the crossing order is determined solely by the right-hand rule—yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. To the right of the green car the road is empty and no one approaches from that side, so there is no restriction for it and it enters the intersection first. The blue car sees the green car on its right and must wait; to the right of the red car, in turn, is the blue car, and it is last. The entire chain: green, blue, red. The safety reason for this rule is a clear division of responsibility. At an unmarked intersection two drivers reach the crossing point nearly simultaneously: if both stop, the intersection locks up, and if both go, a "front-to-side" impact occurs. The "priority to the right" convention takes the decision out of guesswork and courtesy, and everyone knows how the other will act. What to remember for the exam: in every image, first look for the vehicle whose right is empty—it is always first. A vehicle's size, its cargo, whether it is a truck or a passenger car, and even its distance from the intersection line play no role in the crossing order. • The red car is last: the blue car is on its right, and it must yield to it. • The blue car is second because the green car approaches from its right, and it must let it pass first.

g5-q19.explanation: The bus driver. This intersection is equal: it has no traffic light, no "Main road" sign, and no "Give way" sign. At such an intersection, the only criterion is the right-hand rule. The bus approaches the intersection along its road, while the motorcyclist approaches from the road located to the right of the bus. That means priority belongs to the motorcyclist, and the bus driver must slow down and let them pass. If these two vehicles swapped places, the answer would swap too: a vehicle's color, size, and type do not enter into this calculation. Two common traps are packed into this single image. First, a bus is a large public transit vehicle, and many believe size or public service grants priority: it does not. A bus receives priority in only one specific case—when pulling away from a marked stop in a built-up area, which is not the case here. Second, the rails laid along the bus's road do not by themselves make that road "main": tram priority belongs specifically to a tram, and there is no tram in this scene. Safety reason: the motorcyclist is the most vulnerable participant at this intersection, and the bus is the heaviest. A strict right-hand rule removes the decision from split-second bargaining, and the duty to yield is assumed by the driver with better visibility and better braking capability. • The motorcyclist enters the intersection from the right: they are the one who receives priority, not the one who yields it. A motorcycle's small dimensions create no duty to yield.

g5-q20.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection first?
g5-q20.explanation: The blue car. Beside the blue car stands the yellow diamond "Main road," and directly under it is the white "Direction of main road" plaque with its thick bent line: this plaque says that the main road changes direction right at this intersection and does not continue straight. That means both the blue and green cars are on the main road, and the main road runs from one's path onto the other's path. When both vehicles are on the main road, the sign is no longer the arbiter between them, and general rules must be applied: the blue car is to the right of the green car, so the blue car crosses the intersection first. The green car, which is signaling left and intends to cross the blue car's path, must wait. Safety reason: the "Direction of main road" plaque was created for this exact moment. A driver seeing only the yellow diamond imagines they own the road across the entire intersection and enters at speed; the plaque shows them the shape of the intersection and from which side to expect a vehicle of their own rank. This single piece of information reduces "front-to-side" impacts at angled intersections. Trap: in such images there is always a vehicle that is not in the queue at all. First determine who is actually approaching the intersection, then read the signs, and only after that apply the right-hand rule. • The red car is on the opposite side and moving away from the intersection: it does not enter the crossing sequence at all. • The green car is also on the main road, but the blue car is on its right, and moreover it intends to turn left: thus it is second.

g5-q21.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q21.explanation: An uncontrolled intersection of equal roads is shown, where all three cars are preparing to make a left turn. No vehicle approaches from the green car's right, so it passes first. The blue car will pass second, yielding to the green car on its right, while the red truck will yield to the blue car on its right and pass third. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q22.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection third?
g5-q22.explanation: The yellow car. The signs divide this intersection into two groups: on the side from which the green and blue cars approach, the yellow diamond "Main road" is posted, while on the side of the red and yellow cars stands the "Give way" triangle. The crossing sequence is strictly two-step: first all vehicles on the main road, then the vehicles on the secondary road; and within each group the sequence is determined by general rules—namely the right-hand rule and the left-turn rule. Thus, the two cars on the main road—green and blue—take first and second place, and only after the passage clears does the turn reach the secondary road. Between the red and yellow cars, which face the "Give way" sign, the right-hand rule applies again: the yellow car is to the right of the red car, so yellow is the third vehicle and red is the fourth. Safety reason: the "Give way" sign does not merely transfer one right of way—it creates a two-tier order. A driver on the secondary road knows they must let the entire main-road stream pass, then sort out their turn among equals. If this order is violated, a car speeding along the main road strikes the side of a car emerging from the secondary road—the very crash that claims the most lives at signed intersections. Exam trap: do not apply the right-hand rule before the signs. The right hand only matters between vehicles of the same priority rank. • The blue car is on the main road and is among the first two cars, not third. • The green car is also on the main road and crosses the intersection before both cars on the secondary road. • The red car is also on the secondary road, but the yellow car is on its right: thus it moves off after the yellow car, in fourth place.

options: Has the right-of-way because it approached the roundabout from the right of the blue automobile.
Must yield to the blue automobile proceeding on the roundabout.
g5-q23.explanation: Before the intersection, sign 4.3 "Roundabout" is posted. According to item 98.1 of the Rules, when entering a roundabout intersection equipped with sign 4.3, a driver must yield to vehicles already circulating in that intersection. Therefore, the red car must yield to the blue car moving along the roundabout. (Rules, item 98.1, sign 4.3)

g5-q24.text: The automobiles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The yellow automobile, the green automobile, the blue automobile.
The blue automobile simultaneously with the green automobile, then the yellow automobile.
g5-q24.explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads, the blue car is moving straight and there is no vehicle on its right, so the blue car has priority. The green car has turned on its right turn signal and is making a right turn whose trajectory does not intersect the path of the blue car going straight, so the green car can pass simultaneously with the blue car. The yellow truck must yield to the blue car approaching from its right and will cross the intersection last. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q25.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection third?
g5-q25.explanation: The blue car. The yellow diamond placed in the middle of the image announces "Main road," but the white plaque below it is more important: it shows that the main road does not pass straight through this intersection, but approaches from the green car's side and turns toward the red car. That means the green and red cars are on the main road, while the blue and yellow cars are on the secondary road; at that same secondary entrance on the right, the "Stop without stopping prohibited" sign is also posted. The sequence is built from here. The main road goes first: between green and red, the green car is to the right of the red car, so the red car must yield to it—green is first, red is second. Then comes the turn of the secondary road, and the same right-hand rule applies between blue and yellow: the blue car is to the right of the yellow car, so blue passes third and yellow fourth. The safety logic of this sequence is clear: as long as even one vehicle remains on the main road, pulling out from a secondary road means an angled collision with a car traveling faster and having no expectation of stopping at all. A common exam trap is that the candidate sees only the yellow diamond and fails to read the direction plaque below it: without that plaque, you imagine the main road goes straight and build the whole sequence backward. • The yellow car is tempting because it stands right at the intersection and looks ready to pull out; however, it is on a secondary road with a "Stop" sign and the blue car is on its right, so it is last, not third. • The red car is on the main road, which leads many to put it earlier, but it must yield to the green car on its right: its place is second. • The green car is on the main road and has no vehicles on the main road to its right, so it passes first and cannot be third.

g5-q26.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection first?
g5-q26.explanation: The red car. In the image there is no sign, no traffic light, and no priority marking: that means before you is an intersection of equal roads without control, and the sole decision tool is the right-hand rule—every driver yields to a vehicle approaching from the right. There are three vehicles in the scene. To the right of the red car is empty, so no one is ahead of it and it crosses the intersection first. To the right of the green car is the red car, and it must wait: it moves off second. To the right of the blue car, in turn, is the green car, so it is third and last. The chain unravels easily because one of the intersection's branches is empty. Remember the method for solving such questions: instead of starting from yourself, first look for the vehicle whose right is empty—it is always first. Then remove it from the scene and ask the same question again. The safety reason is also clear: an uncontrolled intersection is a place where visibility from both sides is blocked by buildings, trees, and roadside bushes—just like the yellow house on the corner in this very image. If no order is set, two drivers enter simultaneously and a side impact follows—a collision in which the passenger on the struck side has virtually no protection. • The green car is close to the intersection and looks like it will arrive first, but the red car is on its right and it must yield to it: green's place is second. • On the blue car's right is the green car, and it must go last: being close to the intersection gives it no rights.

g5-q27.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The red automobile, the green automobile, the blue automobile, the black automobile.
The green automobile, the red automobile, the black automobile, the blue automobile.
The green automobile, the red automobile, the blue automobile, the black automobile.
g5-q27.explanation: Red, green, blue, black. The yellow diamond with the direction plaque is posted beside the red car. That means the main road approaches from the red car's side, turns at the intersection, and goes onto the road where the green truck stands. Thus, red and green are on the main road; the blue and black cars are on the secondary road, and the "Stop" sign on the right of the image applies to that same secondary entrance. The first stage is resolved between the two vehicles on the main road: the red car is to the right of the green truck, so green must wait—red is first, green is second. The second stage is between the two vehicles on the secondary road, and again the right-hand rule applies: the blue car is to the right of the black car, meaning blue is third and black is fourth. The driver of the black car, in addition to yielding, must come to a complete stop before the stop line, rather than merely slowing down. Safety point: the turn of the main road forces its vehicles' path across the intersection and blocks the view of secondary-road drivers; if the secondary road enters first, a collision occurs in the intersection's blind zone. To remember, keep the two stages separate: first all vehicles on the main road, then all vehicles on the secondary road, and within each group the right-hand rule. • That sequence puts the green truck ahead of the red car; yet both are on the main road, and red is to the right of green, so green must yield. • Here green is again placed first. In this option the order of the two secondary-road vehicles is correct, but that single swap of the two main-road cars makes the entire answer wrong.

g5-q28.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The tram, the yellow automobile, the green automobile.
The tram and the green automobile, then the yellow automobile.
The green automobile, the yellow automobile, the tram.
g5-q28.explanation: An uncontrolled intersection of equal roads is shown, where the tram and the green car are moving straight in opposite parallel directions. The tram has priority over trackless vehicles, while the green car's trajectory does not intersect the tram's path and at the same time lies to the right of the yellow car. Therefore, the tram and the green car will pass first (simultaneously), while the yellow car will yield and pass last. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q29.explanation: An uncontrolled intersection of equal roads is shown (the presence of a median strip does not make a road a main road). The red car approaches the motorcycle from the right side, so the motorcyclist must yield. Therefore, the car driver has the right of priority passage. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q30.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q30.explanation: The green car. At this intersection neither a priority sign nor a traffic light is posted: that means the roads are equal, and the crossing order is established solely by the right-hand rule—yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. One branch of the intersection is empty, and that is what unties the knot. There are no vehicles to the right of the red car, so red passes first. To the right of the green car is red, and it must wait: it is the second vehicle. To the right of the blue truck, in turn, is green, and it goes third. The sequence is complete: red, green, blue truck. A reliable way to solve such questions is first to look for the vehicle whose right is empty—that is the loose end of the thread. Then remove it and ask the same question again until the sequence finishes. The safety reason is also clear: at an uncontrolled intersection most crashes are side impacts, meaning the blow lands directly on the passenger door, where a car's structure offers the least protection. A common exam trap is vehicle size: the candidate subconsciously pushes the blue truck forward, whereas a vehicle's dimensions and mass play no role in priority. • The red car is correctly identified as having priority, but it is the first vehicle, not the second: its right is empty and nothing blocks its movement. • The blue truck is tempting because of its size, but the green car is on its right and it must wait: the truck's place is third.

g5-q31.explanation: The car drivers: both the blue truck and the red car must yield to the tram. At an intersection of equal roads, a tram has priority over all trackless vehicles, and this priority does not depend on the tram's direction of movement: whether it goes straight or its track curves within the intersection, it still passes first. In the image, the rails enter the intersection from the left and change direction, and both vehicles—the blue truck and the red car beside it—want to cross those very rails. That means both drivers must stop and yield. The reason for this priority is technical, not ceremonial. A tram weighs tens of tons, is locked to rails, and under no circumstances can steer around an obstacle; its braking distance is also several times longer than a passenger car's. If a car remains on the rails, all the tram driver can do is brake, and in many cases that is not enough. A collision between a tram and a car almost always ends badly for the car. The trap in this question is thinking in the singular: the candidate looks for "one" driver who must yield and usually picks the truck because it is larger and closer. Yet vehicle mass and size play no role in priority: anything without rails yields to a tram. • This option is tempting because the tram's path changes within the intersection, and many assume a turning vehicle must yield; however, a tram keeps its priority regardless of direction of travel. • The blue truck truly must yield, yet this option is incomplete: the red car is also a trackless vehicle and has the exact same duty. An answer naming only one of the two is incorrect.

g5-q32.text: The red automobile will proceed through the intersection:
g5-q32.explanation: First. The traffic light is green, and the green car in the foreground has turned on its left turn signal: that means it wants to turn left at the intersection. The rule is simple: a driver turning left on a green signal must yield to vehicles moving straight or turning right from the opposite direction. The red car approaches from that exact opposite direction, so it crosses the intersection first, while the green car must wait inside the intersection. The yellow diamond "Main road" and the direction plaque below it, posted on the right side of the image, are the exact trap of this question. When an intersection is controlled by a traffic light, priority signs do not determine the crossing order: those signs only matter when the traffic light is off or operating in flashing yellow mode. And a green signal does not mean "the road is clear"—it only permits entry into the intersection. The safety reason for this rule is the geometry of a left turn: a car turning left crosses the entire width of the oncoming lane, and at that same moment the bodies of oncoming cars and intersection pillars block the driver's view. A left-turn crash with an oncoming car is one of the most frequent and deadliest urban collisions because the impact is head-on at high relative speed. • This option seems right if you take the main-road sign near the traffic light as a sign of the green car's priority or think the red car should wait for the left turn to finish; however, on a green signal it is the turning car that yields to oncoming traffic.

g5-q33.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The passenger car, the bus, the bicycle.
The bus, the bicycle, the passenger car.
The bus, the passenger car, the bicycle.
The bicycle, the bus, the passenger car.
g5-q33.explanation: Bicycle, bus, passenger car. The yellow diamond at the bottom of the image is posted opposite the cyclist's path: that is, the bicycle is traveling on the main road and is the first vehicle to cross the intersection. From the opposite side, the red "Give way" triangle faces the blue car, meaning the blue car is on a secondary road and must go after everyone else. The yellow bus remains between these two: its turn signal is on and it is turning, and in any case it must both yield to the bicycle on the main road and pass before the blue car since it enters the intersection to the right of it. The sequence comes out as: bicycle, bus, passenger car. What to remember: a bicycle is also a vehicle, and on the main road it has the exact same priority as a truck. The law does not distinguish vehicles by size, mass, or speed. The safety reason lies right here. A cyclist is small, silent, and easily lost in a bus's mirrors and blind spot; if the bus driver fails to see them while turning and ignores their priority, a collision occurs with the worst possible outcome. That is the exam trap: the candidate's eye sees the large yellow bus and does not take the bicycle in the corner of the picture seriously. • This option puts the bicycle last and the passenger car first, directly opposite to the signs. The blue car has the "Give way" sign, while the bicycle is on the main road. • Here the bus is placed first, but the bus cannot enter the intersection ahead of the bicycle on the main road: vehicle size grants no priority. • This option also puts the bus first and additionally places the blue car with the "Give way" sign ahead of the bicycle: both parts are wrong.

g5-q34.text: Which vehicle driver has the right-of-way?
g5-q34.explanation: The cyclist. Both signs in the image are the yellow diamond "Main road" with a direction plaque beneath them: that means the main road does not stay straight at this intersection, but changes direction. The blue car and the cyclist are both moving along this same main road toward each other: the arrow beside the bicycle shows its direction of travel, and the blue car's active turn signal shows that this driver intends to turn left. The key point here: following the direction of the main road does not exempt you from the left-turn rule. A driver turning left must yield to vehicles coming from the opposite direction along the same road, even if the turning driver is also on the main road. Thus, the cyclist passes first and the blue car waits. There are two common traps in this question. First, the candidate sees the yellow diamond and concludes "I am on the main road, so priority is mine," whereas when both are on the main road the sign no longer decides. Second, failing to count a bicycle as a vehicle. A bicycle is a vehicle, and its priority is full and valid. From a safety standpoint as well, a cyclist is narrow, quickly disappears behind a mirror pillar or in a truck cab's blind spot, and has no protection in a collision: that is why ignoring a cyclist's priority almost always ends in injury. • The driver of the blue car is on the main road and following its direction, which leads many to consider them the winner; however, they are turning left and must yield to oncoming traffic—namely this cyclist.

g5-q35.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The tram, then the automobile and the bus simultaneously.
The tram, the bus, the automobile.
The bus, the tram, the automobile.
g5-q35.explanation: The tram is on the main road marked by sign 2.1 "Main road," so the tram will cross the intersection first. The green car (in front of which sign 2.4 "Give way" is posted) and the bus are on the secondary road and are moving straight in opposite directions without crossing each other's paths. Therefore, after the tram, the car and the bus will cross the intersection simultaneously. (Rules, item 96, signs 2.1, 2.4)

options: The driver of the blue automobile.
The driver of the red automobile.
g5-q36.explanation: The driver of the blue car. The blue and red cars are moving along the same road toward each other. The blue car's turn signal is on and shows that this driver wants to turn left and enter the adjacent road on the left. The rule is straightforward: before turning left, you must yield to all vehicles approaching from the opposite direction—whether they are going straight or turning right. That means the driver of the blue car is the one who must stop and let the red car pass. The safety reason behind this rule lies in the geometry of movement. A vehicle turning left crosses the entire width of the oncoming lane in an instant, and at that same moment its own body and cars behind block its view. If the driver misjudges the oncoming car's speed by a few kilometers per hour, a head-on impact follows at high relative speed—one of the deadliest types of intersection crashes. What to remember: when turning left, nothing—not larger vehicle dimensions, not reaching the intersection earlier, not an empty side road—takes the place of priority. That is also the common exam trap: because the candidate sees a freight vehicle as heavier and "more important," they put it first; yet mass and dimensions play no role in priority. • The red car's turn signal is on and it looks as if it is also maneuvering, which makes this option tempting; however, it approaches from the opposite direction, and the one turning left must yield to it, not the other way around.

g5-q37.explanation: The motorcyclist. The yellow diamond beside the red car means "Main road," and the inverted red triangle in front of the motorcyclist means "Give way." Those two signs by themselves clarify the whole matter: the red car's road is main, while the motorcycle enters the intersection from a secondary road and must therefore slow down, stop if necessary, and let the red car pass first. Beneath both signs is a plaque showing the direction of the main road because at this intersection the main road does not continue straight, but turns. The safety reason is obvious: when a main road changes direction within an intersection, a driver cannot tell from the shape and width of the road alone which direction has priority. Without this plaque, both drivers would assume priority was theirs, and a side impact would follow—the most dangerous kind of intersection crash, as the side of a vehicle offers the least protection. A common exam trap is reaching for the "right-hand rule." The right-hand rule applies only when both roads are equal. As soon as a priority sign appears in the image, the sign has the final say, and left and right do not matter. A motorcycle's small size and maneuverability grant no priority either: priority depends on the road, not the vehicle type. • Tempting because the motorcycle enters the intersection from the car's right; however, the yellow diamond by the red car's road has made that road the main road, and the right-hand rule is powerless against a priority sign.

g5-q38.text: Which vehicle driver is entering the roundabout correctly?
g5-q38.explanation: Both drivers are entering correctly. Entering a roundabout is permitted from any lane. In the image, the passenger car in the left lane and the bus in the right lane approach the circle side by side, and the two black arrows show their paths into the ring; above the entrance, the round blue sign with three circular arrows is also posted. Neither of them is violating anything. The logic of this freedom is traffic throughput. Traffic entering a roundabout yields to vehicles inside the ring anyway, speeds are low, and all trajectories point in the same direction; therefore, allowing two lanes to enter simultaneously creates no new conflict point and only shortens the queue behind the entrance. That same freedom does not exist at the exit, however, and that is the most important thing to remember: exiting a roundabout is done only from the rightmost lane. If someone cuts straight from the inner ring toward an exit, they cross the trajectory of a car in the outer lane and cause a side collision. So remember this pair together: entry is free from any lane, exit is only from the right. On the exam these two cases are usually asked back-to-back to test whether you confuse them. • This option would be right if entry were allowed only from the right lane; however, no such restriction exists for entering a roundabout, and the passenger car in the left lane is also moving lawfully. • The bus enters the roundabout in the right lane in the most natural way possible: no rule prohibits large vehicles from entering a roundabout.

options: The red automobile, because it is entering the roundabout from the right of the blue automobile.
The blue automobile, because it is proceeding on the roundabout.
g5-q39.explanation: Before the intersection, sign 4.3 "Roundabout" is posted. Since when entering a roundabout intersection equipped with sign 4.3 a driver must yield to those circulating in the roundabout, the blue car has priority, not the red car entering from the right. (Rules, item 98.1, sign 4.3)

g5-q40.text: Indicate the order in which the vehicles will proceed through the intersection:
options: The blue automobile, then the red and green automobiles simultaneously.
The red automobile, the blue automobile, the green automobile.
The red and green automobiles simultaneously, then the blue automobile.
g5-q40.explanation: The red and green cars are on the main road (sign 2.1 "Main road") and are traveling without crossing each other's paths, so they will cross the intersection first and simultaneously. Before the blue car, sign 2.5 "Stop" is posted, which requires it to stop and yield to traffic on the main road, so options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, item 96)

g5-q41.text: The driver of the green automobile:
g5-q41.explanation: Has priority of passage. No priority sign is posted in the image, and both roads are equal: at such an intersection, the only applicable rule is the "right-hand rule"—every driver must yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. The red bus approaches from the road to the left of the green car, and conversely the green car is to the right of the bus. That means the green car—which moreover has its right turn signal on and continues its path from the adjacent lane—has priority, and the bus must wait. The safety reason for the right-hand rule is that it provides one simple, indisputable reference point for all unmarked intersections. Within a couple of seconds a driver cannot assess a road's width or status, but they can always turn their head to the right. That single consistent glance prevents side impacts in the middle of the intersection. The trap in this question is the "bus." A public transit vehicle has no general priority at an intersection. The sole recognized exception is a bus in a built-up area pulling away from a marked stop with its turn signal on: in that case you must yield to it. Here there is neither a stop nor a marking: that means the bus is subject to the right-hand rule just like any other car. • "Must yield" would be right if the bus approached from the green car's right or if a sign made the bus's road a main road: neither is present in the image.

g5-q42.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection last?
g5-q42.explanation: The green car. In the image, the yellow diamond "Main road" stands facing us right in the middle of the frame, and the back of the same sign is also visible near the orange building: those two signs mark both ends of a single main road—the road along which the red and blue cars move toward each other. Above the green car, however, stands the inverted "Give way" triangle: meaning the green car enters from a secondary road. The conclusion is clear without further calculation: the green car must yield to both cars on the main road and crosses the intersection last. The fact that the green car has signaled and wants to turn changes nothing: a maneuver grants no priority. The sequence of the other two cars is also instructive: the red car is signaling left and turning left on the main road, so it must yield to the blue car, which is coming straight toward it along the same main road. Hence the full order: blue, then red, and finally green. The safety logic of this layout is simple: the main road carries a continuous fast flow; if secondary entrances could cut across it, both a bottleneck would form and a driver approaching at main-road speed would have no time to react. Common trap: many candidates apply the "obstacle on the right" rule and, because green is on the right, send it first. That rule applies only to equal roads; the presence of a main-road sign completely disables it. • The red car is on the main road: even with its left turn, only one vehicle (blue) is ahead of it, and it is never last. • The blue car is going straight on the main road, and no one precedes it in this image: it actually passes first, not last.

g5-q43.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
options: The red automobile simultaneously with the blue automobile.
g5-q43.explanation: The red car simultaneously with the blue car. No sign is visible at this intersection, so all roads are equal and the crossing order is established solely by the right-hand rule. The green car is on the road located to the right of both the blue and red cars, so it crosses the intersection first. Next comes the turn of the blue and red cars, and finally the yellow car, because the blue and red cars enter the intersection from its right. Why the red and blue cars pass "simultaneously" is the main point of this question: both enter the intersection from the same road and in the same direction—the blue car goes straight from the right lane, while the red car turns left from the left lane with its indicator on. Their paths do not intersect, so there is no reason for one to queue behind the other. A left turn must wait only when an oncoming vehicle is approaching, and there is nothing on the road opposite the red car. The practical method for the exam and real driving is these two questions in sequence: first "who is on my right?", then "whose path crosses mine?" If your path does not cross the adjacent car's path, holding back simply clogs the intersection; if it does cross, never rely on assuming "they will definitely stop." • The green car is not second, it is first: its road lies to the right of the blue and red cars, and those two must wait for it. • The yellow car is last, not second: the blue and red cars enter the intersection from its right, and it must yield to both.

g5-q44.text: The automobiles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The blue automobile, the green automobile, the red automobile.
The red automobile, the blue automobile, the green automobile.
The green automobile, the red automobile, the blue automobile.
g5-q44.explanation: Red, blue, green. The yellow diamond on the left shows that the horizontal road—the one along which the red and blue cars travel—is the main road, while the inverted red triangle on the right tells the green car it must yield. Thus the green car is last in any case and has no right to enter until the main road clears. Between the two cars on the main road, the red car is going straight while the blue car, with its left indicator on, is turning left. A driver turning left must yield to vehicles coming from the opposite direction going straight: hence the sequence is red, blue, green. The safety reason for this rule is clear: it is the turning car that crosses the oncoming stream, so the burden of decision and observation rests on it, not on the one simply continuing straight. What to remember: being on a main road does not give a right to turn carelessly. A main-road sign only puts you ahead of cars from the secondary road; before oncoming traffic on that same main road, you must still yield. The green car must also check both directions of the main road before starting to move, not just one of them. • "Blue, green, red" puts the turning car ahead of straight traffic: the blue car must yield to the oncoming red car, and the green car with the "Give way" sign cannot be second either. • "Green, red, blue" sends first the car facing the inverted red triangle: the green car may enter only after both cars on the main road have passed.

g5-q45.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection second?
g5-q45.explanation: The green car. The yellow diamond together with the plaque below it indicates that the main road does not continue straight through this intersection: the main road approaches from the green car's road and turns to its right—onto the very road from which the blue car approaches. That means the green and blue cars are both on the main road, while the red car, approaching from the horizontal road on the left, is on the secondary road. When multiple vehicles are all on the main road, the sign is no longer the arbiter between them, and they must apply the right-hand rule to one another. The blue car enters the intersection from the green car's right, so the blue car goes first and the green car second. The red car, being on the secondary road, goes after both: the green car's left indicator changes nothing, because it is the road you are on that decides, not the direction you want to go. That exact structure is the main trap of the question: many see only the yellow diamond and conclude, "I am on the main road, so I go first." Always read the plaque under the diamond: its thick line shows the course of the main road and determines who shares your rank. Two drivers of the same rank resolve the conflict by the right hand. • The blue car is not second: since it is on the same main road and approaches from the green car's right, it is the first vehicle to cross the intersection. • The red car approaches from the secondary road and must yield to both cars on the main road: thus it is last, not second.

g5-q46.text: The red automobile will proceed through the intersection:
options: Second, simultaneously with the blue automobile.
Third, after the green and yellow automobiles.
g5-q46.explanation: Second—simultaneously with the blue car. No priority sign is posted at this intersection: the roads are equal, and the crossing order is determined by the right-hand rule. The green car approaches from the road located to the right of both the blue minibus and the red car, so it passes first. Then it is the turn of the blue and red vehicles, while the yellow car remains last because the blue and red vehicles enter the intersection from its right. The red and blue vehicles approach from the same road and in the same direction: the blue minibus turns left from the left lane with its indicator on, while the red car continues its path from the adjacent lane. Their paths do not intersect, so they cross the intersection simultaneously and neither needs to wait behind the other. That is why the correct answer is "second—simultaneously with the blue car." The safety reason for this view matters: an intersection is a place to clear as quickly as possible. If drivers queue behind one another needlessly, following cars get stuck inside the intersection and the cross street gets blocked. Remember that vehicle size—minibus, bus, or truck—creates no priority; you merely need to respect their longer braking distance and poorer visibility. • "Second—after the yellow car" reverses the order: the yellow car must yield to the red and blue vehicles approaching from its right and passes last. • "Third—after the green and yellow cars" assumes the yellow car passes before the red car: under the right-hand rule, that is impossible.

g5-q47.text: The yellow automobile will proceed through the intersection:
g5-q47.explanation: Last. The yellow diamond in the middle of the image with the plaque beneath it shows that the main road turns at this intersection: it approaches from the red car's side and goes onto the green car's road. The blue car's road and the yellow car's road are both secondary, and in front of the yellow car stands the red octagonal "Stop" ("Proceeding without stopping prohibited") sign. That means the cars on the main road pass first: between those two the right-hand rule applies, and since the green car approaches from the red car's right, green is first and red is second. Then it is the turn of the two cars on the secondary road: the blue car enters the intersection from the yellow car's right, so blue is third and yellow is last. The "Stop" sign adds one condition to "Give way": you must come to a complete stop before the stop line or edge of the roadway, even if the road appears clear. The reason is limited visibility at such intersections: a full stop gives time to turn your head and truly see both directions of the main road. The exam trap is thinking the yellow car goes early because it stands to the right of others: being on a secondary road and having a stop sign completely cancel that advantage. • "First" would mean the yellow car has priority, whereas the stop sign obliges it to stop completely and yield to everyone. • "Second" would only be possible if the yellow car were on the main road: the plaque shows the main road turning from the red side toward the green side, and the yellow car's road is secondary. • "Third" would mean the yellow car goes before the blue car, yet the blue car approaches from its right, and the right-hand rule also applies between the two vehicles on the secondary road.

g5-q48.text: Which answer correctly states the order in which the vehicles will proceed?
options: The motorcycle, the bus, the truck.
The bus, the motorcycle, the truck.
The bus, the truck, the motorcycle.
g5-q48.explanation: At this uncontrolled intersection there are no priority signs, so the equal-roads rule of yielding to traffic approaching from the right applies. First to pass will be the motorcycle, which has no vehicle on its right; then the yellow bus (which must yield to the motorcycle approaching from its right); and last the truck, from whose right the bus is approaching. Options 2 and 3 violate this sequence. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q49.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The passenger car, the bus, the tram.
The tram, the bus, the passenger car.
The tram, the passenger car, the bus.
g5-q49.explanation: Tram, passenger car, bus. At equal intersections, a tram has priority over trackless vehicles regardless of the direction it is moving. In this image, the tram enters the intersection on rails and is the first vehicle to pass, even though its track changes direction within the intersection. After the tram comes the turn of the passenger car and the bus, and here the right-hand rule decides again: the passenger car is to the right of the bus, so the bus must yield to it. Final order: tram, passenger car, bus. A tram's priority is rooted in physics, not courtesy: a tram cannot swerve away from an obstacle, its path is completely locked to rails, and its braking distance on steel rails is several times longer than a rubber-tired car's. Blocking a tram's path means creating an unavoidable collision. Two common traps are combined in this question: first, the idea that a turning tram must yield to straight traffic—no, a tram's priority does not depend on its direction of travel; second, pushing the bus ahead as public transit, whereas at an intersection a bus is evaluated by the right-hand rule just like a passenger car. • "Passenger car, bus, tram" puts the tram last: at an equal intersection, a tram always has priority over trackless vehicles. • "Tram, bus, passenger car" starts right, but swaps the order of the next two vehicles: the passenger car is to the right of the bus and must go first.

g5-q50.explanation: The bus driver. This is an unmarked intersection: there is no priority sign in the image, meaning both roads are equal and the right-hand rule applies. The bus enters the intersection from a road running between buildings, while the passenger car is to its right; therefore, the bus driver must yield and let the car pass first. The main trap here: many believe public transit vehicles always have priority. No such rule exists. The only case that grants a bus priority is pulling away from a marked stop in a built-up area: there, drivers must yield to a bus that has signaled and is leaving the stop. No such priority exists at an intersection. A bus's size and mass do not change the rule, though they matter in practical behavior: a bus's braking distance is longer, it accelerates more slowly, and it has large blind spots along its sides. If you are the passenger car driver, keep your eyes on the bus even when you have priority and be ready to slow down: priority is something granted to you, not something worth risking your safety on. • The passenger car driver has priority because they enter the intersection from the bus's right: the bus's public-transit status does not reverse this order.

g5-q51.explanation: The red car. The round blue sign with circular arrows posted beside the red car right at the entrance is the "Roundabout" sign. It means the circular roadway is considered the main road relative to this entrance: thus the red car must yield to the blue car, which is already moving inside the roundabout. In practice this means: approach the entrance with your right indicator on, reduce speed enough to be able to stop completely, look left, and enter only when no vehicle on the circular roadway will reach you. Stop completely before the entrance if necessary. Careless entry into a roundabout is one of the most frequent urban collisions, and it is almost always attributed to the entering car. That is the legislator's exact reason: a roundabout works only when its circle continuously clears. If entrances had priority, every entrance would cut off the circular flow, queues would form inside the intersection itself, and the entire junction would lock up. The exam trap is also clear: forget "the red car approaches from the right"—the right-hand rule does not apply at a roundabout entrance. • The blue car is already on the circular roadway and has priority: anyone moving inside the roundabout does not stop for an entering vehicle.

g5-q52.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The yellow bus, the truck, the green bus.
The truck, the yellow bus, the green bus.
The yellow bus, the green bus, the truck.
g5-q52.explanation: The truck, then the yellow bus, and last the green bus. The key to this image is the pair of signs on the post on the right: the "Give way" triangle and below it the "Direction of main road" plaque. On this plaque, the thick line enters the intersection from the opposite road and turns right; the thin lines mean the road on the left and the road from which the yellow bus approaches are both secondary. The blue truck moves along this exact arc of the main road, so it crosses the intersection first and the rest must wait. Once the intersection clears, the two buses remain—both approaching from secondary roads and of equal rank. Between vehicles of equal rank, only one criterion applies: yield to the one approaching from the right. The yellow bus is to the right of the green bus, so the green bus must stop and move after it. The safety logic of this order is straightforward: the main road carries a continuous fast stream, and if anyone from a secondary road could jump into the middle of it, angled collisions—the most dangerous type of urban crash—would occur in the heart of the intersection. A common exam trap lies right here: the yellow bus is big and close in the image, and the mind puts it first, yet closeness and size create no priority. First read the sign, then look at the vehicles' positions. • Here the yellow bus is placed first because it is big and close in the image; however, that bus is on a secondary road and has no right to move until the truck on the main road has passed. • Here both buses are placed ahead of the truck, and the main-road direction plaque is effectively ignored: a vehicle whose entire path lies on the main road is never last.

g5-q53.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The bus, then the passenger car and the truck simultaneously.
The passenger car and the truck simultaneously, then the bus.
g5-q53.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13 "Direction of main road" show that the main road turns from the left upward, and the yellow bus is on the main road. The truck and the passenger car are on secondary roads, so they must yield to the bus and, without obstructing each other, pass after it simultaneously; option 2 is incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97)

g5-q54.text: In what order will the vehicles proceed through the intersection if the traffic signals are not operating?
options: The trolleybus and the motorcycle, then the bus and the passenger car.
The motorcycle, then the bus and the passenger car, then the trolleybus.
The bus and the passenger car, then the trolleybus and the motorcycle.
g5-q54.explanation: The traffic lights are not working and there are no priority signs, so the intersection is equal (sign 5.7.1 "Entry onto a one-way road" grants no priority). The motorcycle turning right is to the right of the bus and passenger car going straight from the left and does not cross the trolleybus's path, so it will pass first, while the bus and passenger car going straight will pass second. The oncoming trolleybus is not a rail vehicle and when turning left must yield to straight-going traffic, passing last, which rules out options 1 and 3. (Rules, items 95, 98, 99)

g5-q55.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The truck, then the tram and the bus, then the motorcycle and the passenger car.
The tram and the bus, then the motorcycle and the passenger car, then the truck.
g5-q55.explanation: The truck, then the tram and bus, and last the motorcycle and car. The "Give way" sign is posted with the main-road direction plaque below it. On this plaque, the thick line approaches from the opposite road and turns left: that means the main road enters the intersection along the blue truck's path and continues to the left. All other vehicles—the tram, the yellow car, the motorcycle, and the bus on the right—are on secondary roads. Thus, the truck passes first. After that, all the remaining ones are equal in rank, and here two rules operate simultaneously. First, the tram is a rail vehicle and under equal conditions has priority over all trackless vehicles regardless of which side it approaches from. Second, the bus approaches the intersection to the right of the motorcycle and car, so those two must yield to it as well. The tram's trajectory and the bus's trajectory do not conflict, and they can pass one after the other without dispute; the motorcycle and car remain last. What to remember: a tram's priority is not absolute. A tram, too, if it is on a secondary road, yields to the main road just like everyone else. A tram has priority only when the roads are equal. There is also a technical reason: a tram is locked to rails, cannot swerve, and has a long braking distance, so under equal conditions it makes sense for the burden of decision to fall on the driver with better steering and braking. • Here the tram and bus are placed ahead of the truck. A tram's priority makes sense only at an intersection of equal roads: when a tram is on a secondary road, it must, like everyone else, yield to the truck on the main road.

g5-q56.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The ambulance, the tram, the motorcycle, the bus, the passenger car.
The motorcycle, the bus, then the tram and the ambulance, then the passenger car.
g5-q56.explanation: Motorcycle, then bus, then tram and ambulance, and last the car. The "Give way" sign and the main-road direction plaque show that the main road approaches from the opposite side and turns left. The motorcycle on the left and the bus opposite are on this main road, so they cross the intersection first; and since both are on the main road, they apply the right-hand rule between themselves, and the motorcycle, being to the right of the bus, goes ahead. Then it is the turn of the secondary road—the tram and the ambulance. The tram is a rail vehicle and under equal conditions has priority over trackless vehicles; the ambulance, in turn, approaches from the yellow car's right. Consequently, the yellow car goes last. The main trap in this question is the ambulance. An ambulance has special priority only when its blue flashing beacon is turned on and its siren is sounding: in that state everyone else must clear the way. In this image, the ambulance has no warning signal switched on and is not on an emergency call, so it is treated just like an ordinary car. Remember: a red cross on the bodywork gives no priority—priority is given by an active beacon and a sounding siren. • Here the ambulance is placed first: yet without a beacon and siren, an ambulance has no priority and counts as an ordinary vehicle on a secondary road. Moreover, the tram is also on a secondary road and cannot go ahead of the motorcycle and bus on the main road.

g5-q57.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The truck and the motorcycle, then the bus, then the trolleybus.
The truck and the bus, then the motorcycle, then the trolleybus.
g5-q57.explanation: The truck and motorcycle together, then the bus, and last the trolleybus. On the post on the right, the "Give way" sign and the main-road direction plaque are visible: the thick line enters the intersection from the opposite road and turns right. The blue truck and the motorcycle riding beside it are both on this main road, and their trajectories do not conflict, so they cross the intersection together and first. The white-and-green bus in the foreground and the yellow trolleybus on the left both approach from secondary roads and are equal in rank. Here the right-hand rule settles the matter: the white-and-green bus is to the right of the trolleybus, so the trolleybus must yield to it and go last. The most important trap in this question is the trolleybus itself. Many confuse it with a tram and imagine it holds tram priority. A trolleybus is not a rail vehicle: it runs on rubber tires, has a steering wheel, and can swerve to some extent, so it is treated just like an ordinary bus. Only a tram counts as a rail vehicle. Remember this distinction, because the exam asks about it repeatedly with similar pictures. • Here the bus is placed simultaneously with the truck; however, the bus approaches from a secondary road and does not enter the intersection until the main road clears. Moreover, the motorcycle, which is beside the truck on the main road, does not take second place.

g5-q58.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The truck, the passenger car, the bus, the tanker truck.
The truck, the bus, the passenger car, the tanker truck.
g5-q58.explanation: The truck, then the passenger car, then the bus, and last the tanker truck. The yellow diamond "Main road" together with the plaque shows that the thick line approaches from the road on the right and turns onto the road where the white car is located. That means the main road enters the intersection from the right and continues in the white car's direction: the truck on the right and the white car are both on the main road, while the yellow minibus on the left and the tanker truck opposite are on the secondary road. Since the main road changes direction within the intersection, these two drivers apply the right-hand rule between themselves: the truck is to the right of the white car, meaning first the truck, then the car. Next is the turn of the secondary road, and the same rule repeats: the minibus is to the right of the tanker truck, meaning first the minibus, and last the tanker truck. A reliable way to solve this type of question is two-step: first divide all vehicles into the "main road" and "secondary road" groups, then within each group apply only the right-hand rule. Never mix the groups. The exam trap is that the tanker truck is large and heavy and the mind pushes it forward; however, vehicle mass and size play no role in priority. • Here the bus is placed ahead of the passenger car: the bus is on the secondary road while the white car is on the main road, so the bus never goes before it.

g5-q59.text: The passenger car will proceed through the intersection:
g5-q59.explanation: According to sign 2.1 "Main road" and plaque 8.13, the main road turns to the left, so both the bus and the dark passenger car are on the main road, whereas the truck is on the secondary road and yields to both. The bus and the passenger car on the main road are governed relative to each other by the equal-roads rule: the bus is to the right of the passenger car, so it will pass first and the passenger car second, ruling out answers 1 and 3. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

g5-q60.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The passenger car, the bus, the truck.
The bus, the truck, the passenger car.
The bus, the passenger car, the truck.
g5-q60.explanation: The bus, then the truck, and last the car. On the post on the right, only the triangular "Give way" sign is installed without a main-road direction plaque below it. This means the main road passes through the intersection without changing direction: the street along which the yellow minibus travels is the main road, and the street perpendicular to it, at either end of which stand the red car and the truck, is secondary. Thus, the minibus passes first. After that, the red car and the truck remain facing each other on the same secondary road. The right-hand rule does not apply here because neither approaches from the side. The applicable rule is this: a driver turning left must yield to oncoming vehicles going straight or turning right. The red car turns left and the truck turns right, so the truck is second and the car is third. The safety reason for this rule matters: a left turn means crossing the entire trajectory of oncoming traffic and staying in the middle of the intersection longer, whereas a right turn merely follows the edge of the road. The burden of waiting is placed on the one whose trajectory is more dangerous. The exam trap is the truck's size; yet here the type of movement decides, not size. • Here the car is placed first: the red car is on a secondary road and moreover is turning left, meaning it must yield twice. Under no circumstances is it first. • Here the car is placed ahead of the truck; yet between those two, the one turning left yields to the one facing it, so the truck goes ahead.

g5-q61.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The truck, the passenger car, the bus.
The bus, the truck, the passenger car.
The bus, the passenger car, the truck.
g5-q61.explanation: The truck, then the car, and last the bus. Read the yellow diamond "Main road" and the plaque below it together: the thick line approaches from the road on which the red car sits and turns right. That means the main road enters the intersection along the red car's path and continues in the white truck's direction; the bus opposite is on the secondary road.
