The red car and the truck are both on the main road, and since the main road changes direction within the intersection, they treat each other as at an intersection of equal roads. The truck is to the right of the red car, so the truck passes first. In addition, the red car is turning left and must also leave the truck's through path clear. The bus, approaching from the secondary road, moves off after both. What to remember: a main-road sign frees you only from competing with the secondary road, not with someone else who is also on the main road. Whenever you see the thick line turn on the plaque, know that you may also have to yield to another vehicle on the main road. The exam trap is putting the big bus opposite first: yet it approaches from a secondary road, and that same mistake repeats in every option starting with the bus. • Here the bus is placed first: the bus enters from a secondary road and must yield to both vehicles on the main road. • Here the bus from the secondary road is sent ahead again, and moreover the car is placed ahead of the truck while the truck is to the right of the car.

g5-q62.text: May the vehicles make left turns simultaneously?
options: No. The passenger-car driver must yield.
No. The truck driver must yield.
g5-q62.explanation: The paths of the truck and the passenger car making left turns from opposite directions do not intersect and do not obstruct each other. Therefore, both drivers can perform the maneuver simultaneously, and options 2 and 3 are incorrect because neither driver incurs a duty to yield. (Rules, item 99)

g5-q63.text: To whom must you yield in this situation?
g5-q63.explanation: To no one: priority is yours. Two signs on the right clarify the situation: the yellow diamond "Main road" and below it the main-road direction plaque, which shows that the thick line approaches from your road and turns left at the intersection. The straight road opposite is drawn with a thin line, meaning it is secondary. Your left indicator is on, and you are following this exact arc of the main road. Thus, the dark car coming from the opposite direction is on a secondary road and must yield to you, not you to it. The green bus is also on the main road—to your left—but when the main road changes direction, drivers on the main road apply the right-hand rule between themselves, and the bus is to your left, not your right. Therefore, it must wait. A common trap is that upon hearing "left turn," a driver automatically thinks they must yield to oncoming traffic. That rule holds only when the oncoming vehicle is of equal or higher rank; here the oncoming vehicle is on a secondary road. The right habit is: first read the main-road direction plaque and see from where to where its arc runs, then decide. At the same time, legal priority is not a license for carelessness: before turning, make sure the oncoming driver understood the situation the same way. • Here only the bus is chosen; yet the bus is to your left, and between two vehicles on the main road priority belongs to the one on the right, not the left. • Here the oncoming passenger car is chosen: that car travels on a secondary road and according to the sign must yield to you.

g5-q64.text: In this situation, when making a left turn:
options: You will proceed through the intersection first.
You must yield to the truck driver.
g5-q64.explanation: You cross the intersection first. At this spot your road meets a T-intersection: ahead are a fence and a building, and the road continues only left and right. Neither a priority sign nor a traffic light appears in the image, meaning this is an intersection of equal roads. Your left indicator is on, and the blue truck approaches the intersection from the left branch with its left indicator also on. At an intersection of equal roads, the sole criterion is this: yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. To your right it is empty and the truck is on your left, so priority is yours. From the truck's point of view, you are also on its right, and it must wait. In addition, the truck itself is turning left, and a left turn crosses others' paths anyway. A common trap has two parts. First, the misconception "whenever turning left I must yield to everyone": that rule applies to an oncoming vehicle, not to one approaching from the left branch. Second, the truck's size intimidates the mind, yet mass and size do not affect priority. Even so, before turning check that the truck driver has actually slowed down: legal right is no substitute for eye contact. • The truck is large and the mind assumes priority for it; however, the truck is to your left, and at an equal-roads intersection priority belongs to the one on the right, so it must yield to you.

g5-q65.text: In this situation, when making a right turn:
options: You will proceed through the intersection first.
You must yield to the passenger-car driver.
g5-q65.explanation: You cross the intersection first. At this intersection there is neither a priority sign nor a traffic light, meaning the roads are equal. Your right indicator is on and you are turning right; the red car opposite is signaling left and wants to turn left, meaning you are both entering the same street and your paths intersect. The rule is simple: a driver turning left or making a U-turn at an intersection must yield to vehicles moving straight or turning right from the opposite direction. Thus, the red car must wait and you pass first. The motorcycle emerging from the street on the right does not cross your path either, because you enter the near lane of that street while it travels in the oncoming lane. Remember the safety reason behind this rule: a right turn is short and runs along the edge of the roadway, whereas a left turn crosses the entire width of the intersection and stays inside it longer. The law puts the burden of waiting on the one whose movement carries greater risk. The exam trap is "since the car is opposite, it has priority"; whereas the direction of the turn decides, not merely being opposite. Also check your mirror and right blind spot when turning right. • It seems logical because the red car approaches from the opposite direction; however, that car is turning left, and by law a vehicle turning left yields to an oncoming vehicle turning right or going straight.

g5-q66.text: When making a left turn, you must yield to:
options: The passenger-car driver and the operator of tram A.
Only the operator of tram A.
g5-q66.explanation: By signs 2.1 and 8.13, the main road turns left, so tram A and the passenger car approaching from the left are also on the main road, while tram B approaching from the right is on the secondary road and must yield to us. On the equal-priority main road, tram A has priority over trackless vehicles, whereas relative to the passenger car we are on the right and have priority. Therefore we yield only to tram A, and options 1, 3, and 4 are incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97, 100)

options: You will proceed through the intersection first.
You will proceed after the passenger car has passed.
g5-q67.explanation: The intersection is uncontrolled and there are no priority signs, so the roads are equal. When driving straight we must yield to the white passenger car approaching from the right, whereas the motorcycle approaching from the left must yield to us. Therefore the passenger car will pass first and then we will, ruling out option 1. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q68.text: In this situation, when making a U-turn, you must yield to:
g5-q68.explanation: Only to the oncoming passenger car. The yellow diamond by the road shows that you are on the main road, while the road on which the tanker truck stands is secondary. Your left indicator is on and you intend to make a U-turn, meaning you must cross the entire width of the roadway and return in the opposite direction. During a U-turn there are two separate duties. First—to yield to vehicles moving along the same main road from the opposite direction: this is the dark passenger car opposite you. The second duty does not arise here at all, because the truck enters from a secondary road and must itself yield to any vehicle moving along the main road: thus you do not yield to it. The safety reason is clear: a U-turn is the slowest and longest maneuver at an intersection, leaving the car sideways and without speed across the path of oncoming traffic for a long time. That is why the law does not allow this maneuver to cut across oncoming traffic. The exam trap is the size and closeness of the tanker truck; yet its position on a secondary road creates no priority. Practical point: before starting a U-turn, make sure you have enough room and will not have to reverse partway through the maneuver to straighten out. • Here the tanker truck is also added; however, that truck is on a secondary road and by the main-road sign must yield to you, not vice versa.

g5-q69.text: In this situation, must we avoid interfering with pedestrians?
g5-q69.explanation: When making a left (or right) turn at an intersection and exiting the intersection, a driver must not obstruct pedestrians crossing the roadway, regardless of whether crosswalk markings or a sign are present. Therefore we must not obstruct pedestrians, and option 2 is incorrect. (Rules, item 87)

g5-q70.text: When congestion has formed immediately beyond the intersection, entering the intersection is permitted:
options: If you intend to continue straight ahead.
If you intend to make a turn or a U-turn.
In all of the listed cases.
g5-q70.explanation: It is prohibited to enter an intersection if congestion has formed ahead that will force stopping in the intersection and obstruct the movement of other vehicles. Since the congestion is in the straight direction, entering the intersection when going straight is prohibited (options 1 and 3 are incorrect), whereas when turning or making a U-turn the congestion does not force us to stop in the intersection. (Rules, item 88)

g5-q71.explanation: Sign 2.1 "Main road" and plaque 8.13 show that the main road goes straight. Continuing along the main road, we have priority over the motorcycle approaching from the left and the passenger car approaching from the right on secondary roads. Therefore we have no duty to yield to anyone, ruling out options 1 and 2. (Rules, item 96)

g5-q72.text: When proceeding through the intersection, the driver must yield to:
options: The passenger-car driver and the operator of tram B.
g5-q72.explanation: According to signs 2.1 and 8.13, the main road turns right, so the passenger car and tram B approaching from the right are on the main road, while tram A approaching from the left is on the secondary road. We have priority over tram A, but we must yield to the passenger car and tram B approaching from the right on the main road. The remaining options are incorrect because they omit yielding to the passenger car or include tram A. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98, 100)

g5-q73.text: In this situation, when making a left turn, we must yield to:
g5-q73.explanation: To no one: at this intersection priority is yours. The yellow diamond on the right tells you your road is the main road, and the plaque beneath it shows the layout of the intersection: the thick line rises from below—from the exact path you are on—and turns left. That means the main road changes direction at this intersection, and by turning left you remain on the main road. The white-and-red bus is on the right branch: on the plaque that branch is drawn with a thin line, meaning it is secondary and its driver must yield to you. The dark car on the left is on the main road, but when the main road changes direction within an intersection, drivers on the main road act toward each other according to the rules of an equal-roads intersection: that is, "priority to the right." That car is to your left, so it must wait. The safety reason for this plaque is precisely so you know where the main road goes before reaching the intersection line: hesitation in the middle of an intersection is the exact moment a side impact happens. The exam trap is also obvious: the eye falls first on the big bus, and the mind says "yield." Vehicle size is not the criterion: first read the plaque, then decide. • The passenger car is indeed on the main road, making it deceptive, but it is to your left, and by the right-hand rule it must yield to you. • The bus is close and large, but it is on the secondary branch of the intersection: a secondary road has no priority over the main road.

g5-q74.explanation: At the uncontrolled intersection there are no priority signs, so the roads are equal. At such an intersection, the tram approaching from the left has priority over trackless vehicles regardless of direction, while we must yield to the blue truck approaching from the right under the right-of-way-to-the-right rule. Therefore we yield to both drivers, and options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, items 98, 100)

g5-q75.explanation: Signs 2.1 and 8.13 show that the main road turns right, so we are on the main road. Both the bus approaching from opposite and the passenger car approaching from the left are on secondary roads and must yield to us—regardless of our left turn. Therefore we yield to no one, and options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, item 96)

g5-q76.text: In this situation, when proceeding through the intersection, must you yield?
g5-q76.explanation: No: in this situation there is no need to yield to anyone. Neither a priority sign nor a traffic light is visible in the image, meaning this is an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads, and the only rule deciding the matter is "priority to the right." The secondary road joins yours from the left, and the white car is stopped on that same road to your left with its turn signal on. To your right it is empty: there are only a curb, sidewalk, and greenery, and no vehicle is entering the intersection. That means no one is on your right for whom you would have to stop; on the contrary, that white car must wait until you pass. The logic of the right-hand rule is simple: at an unmarked intersection there must be one definite and indisputable criterion so two drivers do not enter simultaneously—the "right side" is that criterion. The trap in this question is the white car's active indicator: signaling creates no priority and merely announces the driver's intention. Still, "having priority" does not mean "driving through carelessly": reduce speed and do not enter the intersection until you are sure that driver has seen you. • "Yes" would be right if a vehicle were approaching from the right or if your road were declared secondary by a sign: neither is present in the image, and the active indicator on the car to the left grants it no priority.

g5-q77.text: In this situation, when proceeding through the intersection:
options: We have the right-of-way to proceed first.
We must yield to the tram operator.
We must yield to the truck driver.
We must yield to all drivers.
g5-q77.explanation: You have the right to pass first. Two elements in the image decide everything. First—the yellow diamond "Main road" placed directly beside your car on the right: meaning the road you are driving on is the main road. Second—the traffic light, showing only flashing yellow. Flashing yellow means "traffic is permitted, but the intersection is considered uncontrolled": that is, the traffic light does not determine the crossing order, and the matter returns entirely to the signs. Thus, this is an intersection of main and secondary roads, and the rule is simple: a driver approaching from a secondary road must yield to all vehicles on the main road regardless of the direction they subsequently choose. Both the tram on the left and the truck on the right approach the intersection from a secondary road, so both must wait. The most important thing to remember here: a tram's priority is not absolute. A tram has priority over trackless vehicles only at an intersection of equal roads. When a tram enters from a secondary road while you are on the main road, that priority is lifted and priority is yours. Even so, safety requires not relying blindly on your legal right. A tram weighs tens of tons, runs on rails, and cannot swerve; its braking distance is several times greater than a passenger car's. If you see its driver is not slowing down, having priority will not save you. Assess the speed of both vehicles before entering. • Here the tram's general priority is recalled, but not its proviso: that priority applies only at an intersection of equal roads, whereas a tram entering from a secondary road yields to the main road. • The truck also approaches from a secondary road, and its dimensions create no legal priority: there is only one criterion—main road or secondary road. • Lumping all options together seems safe, yet it directly contradicts the main-road sign beside you.

g5-q78.text: When entering a roundabout marked with the “Roundabout” traffic sign, the driver of a vehicle:
options: Must yield to vehicles proceeding within the roundabout.
Has the right-of-way over vehicles proceeding within the roundabout.
g5-q78.explanation: When entering a roundabout intersection equipped with sign 4.3 "Roundabout," a driver must yield to vehicles already circulating in that intersection (inside the circle). An entering driver does not have priority of passage. (Rules, item 98.1)

g5-q79.text: In this situation, when making a left turn, we must yield to:
options: The bus driver and the passenger-car driver.
g5-q79.explanation: To the bus driver and the passenger car driver. The inverted red triangle means "Give way": your road is secondary. The plaque beneath it tells you which branches the main road runs through: the thick line approaches from the opposite branch, where the yellow bus stands, and turns right toward the branch where the silver car stands. Your branch and the left branch are drawn with thin lines. Thus, the yellow bus and the silver car are both on the main road, and you must yield to both. However, the motorcycle on the left is on a secondary road equal to yours: between two equal roads, priority belongs to the one on the right, and the motorcycle is to your left. That means it must yield to you, not vice versa. What to remember: the "Give way" sign by itself does not tell you specifically whom you must yield to—the plaque beneath it determines the main branches. And the exam trap is the "to all drivers" option: because the sign declared your road secondary, the mind tends to treat everyone as having priority and include the motorcyclist on the list too. A motorcycle is a full-fledged vehicle and must be noticed, yet here it is moving along the secondary left branch. • "To all drivers" treats the motorcycle as having priority too; however, the motorcycle is on the secondary left branch and under the right-hand rule must yield to you. • The passenger car is on the main road and you must yield to it, yet this option leaves out the yellow bus: the bus is moving along the same main road.

g5-q80.text: Which driver must not interfere with pedestrians?
g5-q80.explanation: When making a right or left turn at an intersection, a driver must not obstruct pedestrians crossing the roadway onto whose crosswalk the driver is exiting the intersection. There are pedestrians in the path of both the truck turning left and the passenger car turning right, so both drivers must not obstruct them, ruling out answers 1 and 2. (Rules, item 87)

g5-q81.text: In this situation, may the driver make a left turn?
options: Yes, if the driver does not interfere with the truck driver.
g5-q81.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13 show that we are on a secondary road, while the main road turns from the top to the right, along which the truck is traveling with a left-turn signal. A driver on a secondary road may make a left turn provided they do not obstruct the driver of the truck traveling on the main road, so options 1 (without the condition) and 3 (complete prohibition) are incorrect. (Rules, item 96)

g5-q82.text: In this situation, when making a left turn, the driver:
options: Will proceed through the intersection first.
g5-q82.explanation: You must yield. Neither a priority sign nor a traffic light is installed at this intersection, and both roads are paved and of the same character: meaning the intersection is equal. At an equal intersection, the sole criterion is which side the other vehicle approaches from, and the dark car in the image approaches the intersection from your right. Consequently, you must stop, let it pass first, and then make the left turn. One important structural point is also tested here: the shape of an intersection creates no priority. The fact that your road meets a cross street and seems to "end" does not make that street a main road. A main road is defined only by a sign or a difference in surface (asphalt versus dirt), not by visible geometry. Safety reason: a left turn is the most dangerous maneuver at an intersection because it covers the longest path inside the intersection, and throughout that time the side of the car—the weakest part of the body in an impact—is exposed to cross traffic. For that reason, the law places the burden of caution on the driver turning left. Remember: without a sign and without a traffic light, always look right—that single glance is the answer to most such questions. • This option assumes that because you reached the intersection earlier or your road meets a cross street, priority is yours: at an unmarked intersection only the direction of entry matters, and the car is to your right.

options: After 200 m, you must yield to traffic proceeding on the intersecting road.
Over the next 200 m, you must yield to all vehicles.
g5-q83.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" with plaque 8.1.1 "Distance to object" ("200 m") informs that at the intersection starting 200 meters ahead, it is necessary to yield to vehicles traveling on the intersecting road. Option 2 is incorrect because plaque 8.1.1 indicates the distance to the intersection, not the length of the zone of action. (Rules, signs 2.4 and 8.1.1)

g5-q84.text: When making a left turn at the second crossing, the driver:
options: Must yield to the other drivers.
Must yield to the bus driver.
g5-q84.explanation: Sign 2.1 "Main road" (without plaque 8.13) means the main road goes straight, so the oncoming bus is also on the main road, while the passenger car approaching from the right is on a secondary road (sign 2.4 is visible from the reverse side). When making a left turn into the second passage, we must yield to the oncoming bus going straight along the main road, whereas the car on the secondary road yields to us; options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97, 99)

g5-q85.text: When proceeding straight through the intersection, the driver:
g5-q85.explanation: You must yield to the tram. The traffic light on the right is green, and you are driving straight through the intersection. From the opposite direction, the red-and-white tram and the white passenger car have both signaled and want to turn. Instinct says: "I am going straight, so both must yield to me"; yet regarding the tram, that instinct is wrong. The rule is this: when a traffic light permits movement for a tram and trackless vehicles simultaneously, the tram has priority—regardless of its direction of movement. That means even a tram coming from the opposite direction and turning left has priority over you going straight. The white car, however, is an ordinary vehicle, and to turn left it must yield to vehicles moving straight from the opposite direction: thus it stays behind you. The reason for this exception is physics. A tram runs on fixed rails, cannot swerve or pull aside, weighs tens of tons, and has a braking distance several times longer than a passenger car's. The only way to prevent a collision is for others always to adjust to the tram, not the other way around. Moreover, a tram usually carries dozens of standing passengers who get injured during sudden braking. What to remember: in this question two vehicles have signaled simultaneously, and that pairing is the trap. The right comparison is "rail versus trackless," not "straight versus turning." • Here the valid rule "going straight has priority over turning" is used, yet that rule is overridden before a tram: a tram has priority regardless of its direction of movement. • Here the white car is also treated as having priority, whereas to turn left it must yield to you going straight from the opposite direction.

g5-q86.text: When making a left turn, to whom must the driver yield?
g5-q86.explanation: To the bus driver. The yellow diamond means your road is the main road, and the plaque beneath it shows that the main road changes direction at this intersection: the thick line approaches from your path and continues up and right—onto the very road where the bus is located. The left branch is drawn with a thin line, meaning it is secondary. You are signaling left, meaning you are leaving the main road and turning onto the secondary branch. The bus stays on the main road and approaches the intersection from your right: when the main road changes direction, drivers on it apply the equal-roads intersection rules between themselves, and in those rules priority belongs to the one on the right. Thus, you must yield to the bus. The silver car on the left is on a secondary road and, conversely, must yield to you. What to remember: "main road" is not a permanent label exempting you from yielding across the entire intersection; if your path leaves the main road, your priority ends right there. The exam trap is the "to no one" option, which stems from that exact misconception. And do not forget the crosswalk marking in front of your car. • The passenger car approaches from the left branch, which is drawn with a thin line on the plaque, meaning it is secondary: it must yield to you. • "To no one" would be right if the main road continued straight; however, by turning left you leave the main road while the bus remains on it.

g5-q87.text: When entering this intersection, the driver:
g5-q87.explanation: Before the intersection, sign 4.3 "Roundabout" is posted. When entering such an intersection, a driver must yield to all vehicles already moving in the roundabout intersection—both the motorcycle and the minibus—so options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, item 98.1)

g5-q88.text: When making a left turn, to whom must the driver yield?
g5-q88.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13 show that we are on a secondary road, while the main road runs from the left toward the oncoming right direction. Both the passenger car approaching from the left and the bus are traveling on the main road, so when making a left turn we must yield to both drivers, ruling out options 2 and 3. (Rules, item 96)

g5-q89.text: In this situation, we must yield to:
options: Only the truck approaching in the oncoming lane.
g5-q89.explanation: Sign 1.6 "Intersection of equal roads" warns that an intersection of equal roads lies ahead. When making a left turn we must yield both to the truck with the orange tanker approaching from the right (under the rule of yielding to traffic from the right) and to the blue truck moving straight in the oncoming lane, so option 2 is incomplete. (Rules, items 98, 99, sign 1.6)

options: You will proceed through the intersection first.
g5-q90.explanation: At the uncontrolled intersection there are no priority signs, so the roads are equal. For the silver car approaching from the left, we are on the right side, so it must yield to us, and when making a left turn we will cross the intersection first; option 2 is incorrect. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q91.text: In this situation, when making a right turn, we:
g5-q91.explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads, when making a right turn the white passenger car approaching from the left must yield to us (since we are on its right side), while our path does not intersect that of the oncoming motorcycle (and if turning left, it would have to yield to us as well). Therefore we will cross the intersection first, and options 2 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, items 98, 99)

g5-q92.explanation: You may pass first. No priority sign is visible in the image: no main-road sign, no "Give way," no "Stop." That means this intersection is equal, and the "obstacle on the right" rule applies: every driver must yield to a vehicle approaching from the right. Relative to the car visible near the intersection on the left side of the image, you are to its right: meaning it must wait, while you with your right indicator on may complete the maneuver. A right turn is also the least dangerous maneuver at an intersection: it starts from the right edge of the roadway and reaches the right edge of the next road without crossing oncoming lanes. That is why the legislator placed no additional waiting requirement on it. Still, do not forget one practical warning: having priority means a legal right, not a guarantee of others' behavior. Before turning the steering wheel, make sure the driver on the left has genuinely slowed down and does not intend to enter the intersection. A common trap in this question is confusing the mere appearance of a car in the frame with a "duty to yield": the criterion is that car's position relative to you, not its presence. • "Give way" is right when you have a "Stop" or "Give way" sign, or when a car approaches from the right: neither is present in this image, and the car is to your left.

g5-q93.text: When making a left turn, you must yield to:
options: The bus driver and the driver of the motorcycle.
g5-q93.explanation: To everyone—the motorcycle, the bus, and the passenger car. The "Give way" sign has made your road secondary, and the plaque below it says the main road approaches from the left branch and turns upward: meaning the motorcycle on the left and the yellow bus opposite are both on the main road, and you must yield to both. There remains the silver car on the right. That branch is drawn thin on the plaque, meaning it is secondary just like your road. However, between two equal roads priority belongs to the one on the right, and that car is located directly to your right. Thus it also has priority, and overall you must yield to all three. The answer "to everyone" comes from adding two different rules together, not just one: that is what distinguishes it from a similar question with a different plaque. The exam trap is that the motorcyclist looks small in the corner of the image and the mind does not take them seriously, or conversely the silver car is excluded because it is on a secondary road. Make it a habit to inspect each branch of an intersection separately: first check on the plaque whether it is main or secondary, then assess whether it is to your right or left. • The bus and motorcycle are selected rightly, yet the silver car on the right is omitted: between two equal roads, priority belongs to the vehicle on the right. • "Only the bus" means you ignored both the motorcycle on the main road and the car on the right: both have priority ahead of you.

options: You will proceed first, simultaneously with the passenger car.
You will proceed after the motorcycle.
g5-q94.explanation: At this uncontrolled intersection there are no priority signs, so the roads are equal. When making a left turn we must yield to the motorcycle approaching from the right, so we will cross the intersection after the motorcycle, ruling out answer 1. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q95.text: When proceeding straight ahead, you must yield to:
g5-q95.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13 inform us that we are on a secondary road, while the main road turns from the top to the right. The bus approaching from opposite and the passenger car approaching from the right are on the main road, so when driving straight we must yield to both drivers; options 2 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 96)

g5-q96.text: Must we yield to the tram?
g5-q96.explanation: Yes: you must yield to the tram. At this intersection there is neither a traffic light nor a priority sign: meaning this is an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads. At such an intersection, a rail vehicle has priority over trackless vehicles regardless of which side it approaches from. The red tram approaches the intersection from your right, so you must stop both because it is a rail vehicle and by the right-hand rule. The safety reason for this priority is purely technical: a tram has no steering and cannot change its path; the only thing it can do is brake, and braking on steel rails requires a distance several times greater than rubber on asphalt. If a tram is forced into an emergency stop, standing passengers inside the car also suffer injuries. For this reason, the legislator placed the burden of decision on the driver who can stop easily and at lower cost. What to remember: a tram's priority applies only at an equal intersection. If you are on the main road and a tram approaches from a secondary road, priority is yours. That is also the common exam trap: some candidates think a tram has priority always and everywhere, while others think that because a tram is slow you can cut in front of it. Neither is right: first determine whether the roads are main or secondary. • "No" would be right if your road were declared the main road by a sign: there is no priority sign in the image, meaning the intersection is equal and priority belongs to the tram.

g5-q97.text: In this situation, when is a right turn permitted?
options: At the same time as the truck passes, provided you do not interfere with the truck.
g5-q97.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" obliges a driver not to obstruct traffic on the intersecting road (one-way under sign 5.7.1), but does not require stopping if no obstruction is created. Since the blue truck is driving in the far left lane while we make a right turn into the near right lane, we may turn simultaneously with its passage provided we do not obstruct the truck; options 1 (without the yielding condition) and 3 (unnecessary waiting) are incorrect. (Rules, sign 2.4, items 41, 96)

g5-q98.text: When proceeding straight through the intersection, you must yield to:
options: Only the operator of tram A.
Only the operator of tram B.
g5-q98.explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads, a tram driver has priority over trackless vehicles regardless of direction of travel. Therefore, when crossing the intersection straight, we must yield both to tram B approaching from the left and to tram A approaching from the opposite direction, ruling out options 1, 2, and 4. (Rules, items 98, 100)

g5-q99.text: When making a left turn, you must yield to:
g5-q99.explanation: Only to the bus driver. The yellow diamond tells you your road is the main road, but the plaque beneath it tells you something more important: the thick line rises from your path and turns right—meaning the main road continues to the right, onto the branch where the white-and-red bus stands. The left branch is drawn thin and is secondary. You are signaling left, meaning you are leaving the main road and turning onto the secondary one. The bus remains on the main road and approaches from your right: when the main road changes direction within an intersection, its drivers apply the equal-roads intersection rules between themselves, and in those rules priority belongs to the one on the right. Thus, you must yield to the bus. The dark car on the left is on the secondary branch, and it must yield to you. This question has almost the exact same image as the one whose answer was "to no one": only the direction of the thick line on the plaque changed. That single small detail changes the answer from "to no one" to "to the bus." Therefore, never answer from visual memory on the exam: every time, trace the thick line on the plaque and check from which branch to which branch the main road runs. • "Both drivers" treats the car on the left as having priority too, whereas that car is on the secondary branch and must yield to you. • "To no one" stems from the idea that the main-road sign always exempts you from yielding; however, by turning left you leave the main road while the bus remains on it.

g5-q100.text: Who will proceed through the intersection first?
options: The rules do not regulate this situation. The drivers should proceed while showing mutual respect.
g5-q100.explanation: At an uncontrolled four-way intersection of equal roads, vehicles have approached simultaneously from all four directions, and to the right of each there is another vehicle. The rules do not prescribe a crossing order in such a situation, so drivers will cross the intersection by showing mutual courtesy (options 1 and 2 are incorrect, and there is no trolleybus in the image anyway). (Rules, item 98)

g5-q101.text: The driver must not interfere with pedestrians:
options: Only when making a left turn.
Only when making a right turn.
g5-q101.explanation: The same in both cases—both when turning left and when turning right. The image shows an intersection with crosswalks marked on both sides and pedestrians walking across them; the yellow diamond additionally tells you that you are on the main road. The key point is that being on the main road gives you no priority whatsoever over a pedestrian. Main-road priority matters only against vehicles from a secondary road. When you turn—left or right—you enter the roadway that the pedestrian is crossing, and in both cases you must allow them to finish crossing. Safety reason: a large share of pedestrian strikes happen specifically during turns because the driver's attention is occupied by crossing vehicles and finding a gap, and at that exact moment they fail to see the crosswalk ahead of them. During a right turn, the car's front pillar can additionally hide a moving pedestrian completely for several seconds. What to remember: every time you turn the wheel, look separately and deliberately at the crosswalk before entering the new roadway. That glance must become a habit, not a reaction. • A left turn feels longer and more dangerous, so only it sticks in memory; however, the duty toward pedestrians does not depend on the direction of the turn. • A right turn is short, and a driver thinks they meet a crosswalk only there; yet at the end of a left turn there is also a crosswalk in front of you.

g5-q102.text: When making a right turn, you must yield to:
g5-q102.explanation: When making a right turn before exiting the intersection, our path is crossed both by the cyclist riding along the path marked by sign 4.4.1 "Cycle path" (and plaque 8.14) and by pedestrians crossing via the pedestrian crosswalk. Under the Rules we must yield to cyclists and not obstruct pedestrians, so option 2 is incomplete. (Rules, item 87)

g5-q103.text: When making a left turn, you must yield to:
options: The passenger-car driver and the bus driver.
g5-q103.explanation: Only to the passenger car driver. The yellow diamond by the road means you are on the main road, yet the small plaque below it drawing the shape of the intersection says the main road does not continue straight and turns right at this exact intersection. Thus, only two branches are main: the road you came from and the road on the right. The road opposite, from which the yellow bus approaches, and the road on the left, where the motorcycle sits, are both secondary. The applicable rule is this: when the main road changes direction within an intersection, drivers traveling on the main road treat one another as at an intersection of equal roads—that is, by the right-hand rule. The passenger car on the right is on this same main road and approaches from your right, so priority is its. The bus and the motorcycle are on secondary roads and must yield to you, even when you turn left. The exam trap is that bus opposite: as soon as a driver sees a vehicle ahead of them, they automatically apply "yield to oncoming when turning left"; however, that rule applies only between two drivers traveling on roads of equal rank. The right decision order is always one: first the rank of the roads, then the direction of travel. Make a habit of reading the small plaque under the yellow diamond as well: without it, this very same image gets a completely different answer. • The bus is large and stopped directly opposite you, so you attribute priority to it; however, the bus travels on a secondary road and must itself yield to you. • "To no one" would be right if the main road continued straight: since the main road turns right, the car on the right is equal to you in rank and approaches from your right hand.

g5-q104.text: When a driver cannot determine whether the road has a paved surface (at night, because of mud, snow, etc.) and there are no priority signs:
options: The driver must consider that he/she is on a secondary road.
The driver must follow the rules for proceeding through an intersection of roads of equal priority.
g5-q104.explanation: If in the dark, due to mud, snow, or another reason, a driver cannot determine the type of road surface and priority signs are absent, they must assume they are on a secondary road. This eliminates the safety risk where the intersecting road may have a paved surface and be the main road. (Rules, item 101)

g5-q105.text: In this situation, we must yield to:
g5-q105.explanation: To all drivers. Where you are stopped, there is no intersection: you are exiting onto the roadway from an adjacent area—from a building courtyard and the lot by a shop—and you are signaling left. Exiting from an adjacent area, courtyard, parking lot, or gas station never creates priority: in this situation you must yield to all vehicles traveling along the roadway as well as pedestrians crossing your path, without exceptions. The safety reason is simple: a car exiting a courtyard usually has limited visibility—a wall, hedge, parked cars—and joins at low speed a stream moving several times faster. If such a car were given priority, every courtyard exit would turn into an uncontrolled intersection. Turning left makes matters worse because you must cross both directions of the roadway: the trajectory of the blue truck on the left and the trajectory of the cars on the right. A common trap is that a driver subconsciously reaches for the right-hand rule and tells themselves: "the truck is coming from the left, so priority is mine." The right-hand rule only makes sense at an intersection of equal roads, and here there is no intersection at all. Before starting to move, pull up to the edge of the roadway, stop, and check both directions separately. • The truck is the closest and largest vehicle in the image, yet not the only one: limiting priority to it means ignoring the cars on the right and pedestrians. • The passenger car on the right must also pass unhindered, yet it is not the only one: when exiting an adjacent area you must yield to everyone.

options: The bus driver and the passenger-car driver.
g5-q106.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13 show that the main road turns from the top to the right, so the bus and the white passenger car are on the main road and we must yield to them. The motorcycle approaching from the left is on the secondary road together with us, and since we are on its right side, it must yield to us; options 1 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

g5-q107.text: When making a U-turn at this intersection:
options: I will perform the maneuver first.
I must yield to the other driver.
g5-q107.explanation: You must yield to the other drivers. A green left arrow is lit on the instrument panel and the car's left indicator is flashing: meaning you intend to make a U-turn. At the same time, the blue car approaches the intersection from the left with its indicator on and wants to enter your roadway. The governing principle is worth remembering as a general rule: a maneuver never creates priority. A driver making a U-turn changes direction and before starting the maneuver must make sure they do not obstruct other road users. A U-turn is the worst case in this regard because the car's trajectory sweeps across the entire width of the roadway and crosses every flow present at the intersection—both the oncoming lane and the car emerging from the road on the left. The safety reason lies right in that. A U-turn keeps the car at nearly zero speed and sideways in the middle of the intersection for several seconds: in that position the side of the car faces every vehicle approaching at speed, and the side is the weakest part of the structure. Therefore, the legislator places the entire burden of decision on the one initiating the maneuver. Practical point: before a U-turn you must have room for the entire maneuver, not just its start. If you have to stop midway through a U-turn, you have blocked the intersection. Wait until the blue car finishes its maneuver, then begin. • The thought "since I reached the intersection earlier or signaled, I perform the maneuver first" is common; yet neither arriving earlier nor signaling is a source of priority, and a U-turn is a maneuver that must be executed in a clear gap.

g5-q108.text: When the traffic signal is flashing yellow, while proceeding straight through the intersection we must:
options: Stop and wait for the permissive green signal.
g5-q108.explanation: A flashing yellow traffic light signal permits traffic and renders the intersection uncontrolled (option 1 is incorrect), so signs 2.1 and 8.13 apply, according to which the main road turns right. The tram approaching from the left is on a secondary road and must yield to those on the main road (option 3 is incorrect), whereas the passenger car approaching from the right is also on the main road and is located to our right, so we must yield to the passenger car. (Rules, items 7, 95, 96, 97, 98)

options: We may proceed through the intersection first.
g5-q109.explanation: You must yield. No priority sign is installed in the image, and both roads have a hard surface: that is, this is an intersection of equal roads. At such an intersection the sole criterion is the side from which the other vehicle approaches: any vehicle approaching from the right has priority. The truck approaches the intersection from the road on the right, so even when going straight you must stop and let it pass first. The safety reason for this rule is simple: unmarked intersections are numerous in residential neighborhoods and secondary routes, and without a firm convention two drivers would enter simultaneously and a side impact would follow—the crash with the least structural protection because the blow lands directly on the door beside a person. The right-hand rule is a single law without exceptions for all such intersections. Remember two points. First, going straight by itself grants no priority: the priority of going straight over turning only applies between oncoming vehicles, not against one approaching from the side. Second, the truck's active indicator changes nothing: an indicator is a statement of intent, not a waiver of priority. Reduce speed before an unmarked intersection so you have time to decide. • The width of your road and the open path ahead create the feeling that the main road is under your wheels, yet no sign confirms it: at an equal intersection priority belongs to the truck on the right.

g5-q110.text: When making a U-turn, to whom must you yield?
g5-q110.explanation: According to signs 2.1 and 8.13, the main road turns right, so we and the truck approaching from the right are on the main road, while the passenger car approaching from opposite is on the secondary road. When making a U-turn we must yield to the driver of the truck approaching along the main road from our right, whereas the passenger car yields to us, ruling out options 2 and 3. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

g5-q111.text: When making a left turn, must we yield to the tram?
g5-q111.explanation: Yes, you must yield to the tram. Under equal conditions a tram has priority over all trackless vehicles regardless of the direction in which it travels. In this image the tram is to your left and the rails run down the middle of the roadway; the blue sign overhead additionally shows that a left turn is made from the left lane. To make that turn, you will inevitably have to cross the rails and the tram's trajectory, so you must let the tram pass first. The logic of this priority is technical, not ceremonial: a tram can neither steer around an obstacle nor stop within a short distance. A mass of several tens of tons and steel wheels on steel rails mean its braking distance is several times longer than a passenger car's. That is why the law places the burden of decision on the driver who is actually able to stop or change their path. What to remember: a tram's priority does not depend on its direction of travel—whether it moves in the same direction, oncoming, or turning. The sole case when this priority is removed is a tram exiting a depot. On the exam, tram questions usually try to distract you by adding a sign or marking: first check whether conditions are equal, then apply the tram rule. • Because the tram travels in the same direction and slower, a temptation arises to turn ahead of it; however, same-direction travel does not cancel a tram's priority, and by turning left you cross its rails.

g5-q112.text: At this intersection, we do not have to yield to the truck approaching from the unpaved road because:
options: We must yield because it is approaching from our right.
A paved road is considered the priority road relative to an unpaved road.
g5-q112.explanation: A paved road (asphalt concrete) is considered the main road relative to an unpaved dirt road regardless of the absence of priority signs. Therefore, the truck approaching from the right from an unpaved road is on a secondary road and must yield to us, so option 1 is incorrect. (Rules, item 1, sub-item 1, item 96)

g5-q113.text: When the traffic signal is flashing yellow:
options: We must wait for the green signal.
We will proceed through the intersection after yielding to the driver of the animal-drawn cart.
You will proceed through the intersection simultaneously with the passenger car.
g5-q113.explanation: Under a flashing yellow traffic light signal, the intersection is considered uncontrolled and traffic is permitted (option 1 is incorrect). Due to the absence of priority signs, the equal-roads rule of yielding to traffic approaching from the right applies, so we must yield to the driver of the animal-drawn cart approaching from the right, which also rules out option 3. (Rules, items 7, 95, 98)

g5-q114.text: When making a left turn, we must yield to:
g5-q114.explanation: By signs 2.1 and 8.13, the main road turns left, so the yellow bus approaching from opposite and the white passenger car approaching from the right are on secondary roads and yield to us. Although the motorcycle approaching from the left is also on the main road, we are on its right side, so it must yield to us. Therefore we yield to no one, and options 1, 2, and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

options: We must yield to the truck driver.
We may proceed through the intersection simultaneously with the tram.
g5-q115.explanation: You must yield to the truck driver. No priority sign is visible at this intersection, meaning the roads are equal and the right-hand rule applies. The blue truck approaches from the road on the right, so priority belongs to it and you must stop. The more important part of the question is the tram on the left. At an intersection of equal roads, a tram has priority over all trackless vehicles regardless of its direction of movement. That means the tram may enter the intersection before you and even before the truck, while you still must stop for the truck. That is precisely why "passing simultaneously with the tram" is wrong: you and the tram operate under two different rules, and its movement is not permission for yours. This is the exact behavioral trap that also leads to crashes on the street: instead of reading the intersection, a driver interprets the movement of an adjacent vehicle as a "way is clear" signal and pulls out behind it. The tall tram beside you additionally blocks your view to the left, so following it is doubly dangerous. Always make the decision yourself: look at the signs, determine the rank of the roads, then look right. • The tram indeed has the right to pass before you, making it tempting to move alongside it; however, the tram's priority belongs strictly to itself, and you still must yield to the truck on the right.

g5-q116.text: When proceeding through the intersection, we must yield to:
options: The driver of the motorcycle and the bus driver.
The bus driver and the passenger-car driver.
g5-q116.explanation: Sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13 show that we are on a secondary road, while the main road turns from the left upward, from where the motorcycle and bus are approaching. Besides yielding to traffic on the main road, we must also yield to the yellow passenger car approaching from the right on the secondary road equal to ours, so we yield to all drivers, and options 1, 2, and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

g5-q117.text: In this situation, you must yield to:
options: The passenger-car driver and the tram operator.
g5-q117.explanation: To the passenger car driver and the tram driver. The yellow diamond on the right together with the small plaque below it says you are on the main road, yet the main road does not continue straight and turns right at this exact intersection. Going straight, you effectively leave the main road and enter the secondary road opposite. Two have priority ahead of you. First—the passenger car on the right: it is also on the main road and approaches from your right, and when the main road changes direction, its drivers apply the equal-intersection rule—that is, the right-hand rule—between themselves. Second—the tram on the left: under equal conditions a tram has priority over trackless vehicles, and at this intersection the rails additionally turn right and pass across in front of you. Conversely, the car approaching from the opposite direction is on a secondary road and must yield to you: therefore "to all drivers" is the wrong answer. What to remember: being on the main road guarantees nothing by itself; as soon as the main-road direction plaque turns, you must think simultaneously of both the right-hand rule and tram priority. Make a habit of reading the small plaque first before an intersection, then tracing the course of the rails. • The tram indeed has priority, yet it is not your only obstacle: the passenger car on the right also travels on the main road and approaches from your right hand. • The passenger car is named rightly, yet incompletely: a tram's priority under equal conditions applies regardless of the side from which it approaches, and it cannot be ignored. • The oncoming car is on a secondary road and must itself yield to you, so "to all drivers" is too broad.

g5-q118.text: In this situation, when making a left turn:
options: You will proceed through the intersection first.
After entering the intersection, you will yield to the driver of the motorcycle and then complete the maneuver.
g5-q118.explanation: Upon entering the intersection, yield to the motorcyclist, then complete the turn. During a left turn, priority belongs to vehicles moving straight or turning right from the opposite direction. In the image, the motorcycle approaches from the opposite direction in a straight line while your left indicator is on: that means you cross its path and must wait. The second part of the option is no less important: waiting does not mean stopping before the intersection. You may enter the intersection, move forward toward the point where the trajectories intersect, stop there, and complete the turn after the motorcycle passes. A driver who has entered an intersection must complete their maneuver: aborting the maneuver or reversing in the middle of an intersection is itself a violation and a hazard. Take the safety reason seriously: a motorcycle is narrow, and the human eye underestimates the distance and speed of a narrow object. That is why "turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle" is one of the most frequent and deadliest urban crashes: a motorcyclist has no protective cage and strikes directly into the car's body. Practical rule: instead of estimating their speed, ask yourself "what if they are faster than they look to me?", and if in doubt, wait. • The width of the road and the motorcycle's small apparent size create the illusion that you have time; however, its path is straight while yours crosses it, so priority belongs to it.

g5-q119.text: When proceeding straight through the intersection, you must yield to:
g5-q119.explanation: According to signs 2.4 and 8.13, the main road turns from the left upward, from where the passenger car is approaching, so we must yield to it. In addition, the truck approaching from the right is on the secondary road together with us, and under the rule of yielding to traffic from the right we must yield to it as well. Therefore we yield to both drivers, and options 1 and 2 are incomplete. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

options: You will proceed through the intersection first.
You will yield to the passenger-car driver.
You will yield to both drivers.
g5-q120.explanation: The intersection is uncontrolled and there are no priority signs, so the roads are equal. We must yield to the white passenger car approaching from the right, whereas the motorcycle approaching from the left must yield to us. Therefore, options 1 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q121.explanation: According to sign 2.4 "Give way" and plaque 8.13, we are on a secondary road, while the main road turns from the left upward. Both the bus approaching from the left and the passenger car approaching from ahead are on the main road, so we must yield to both drivers, ruling out options 2 and 3. (Rules, item 96)

options: You will yield to the truck.
g5-q122.explanation: Both roads have a hard surface and there are no priority signs at the intersection, so it is an intersection of equal roads. The blue truck approaches from our right side, so we must yield to the truck, and option 1 is incorrect. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q123.text: Must we yield to the tram operator?
g5-q123.explanation: You must yield to the tram driver. The blue tram is to your left, its right indicator is on, and the rails turn right at this exact intersection: meaning the tram passes in front of you and crosses your path. There is no priority sign either, meaning conditions are equal, and under equal conditions a tram has priority over all trackless vehicles regardless of its direction of travel. It is on this exact wording "regardless of direction" that most candidates make a mistake. They recall the right-hand rule and, because the tram is on the left, conclude priority is theirs. Yet the right-hand rule applies only among trackless vehicles: a tram stands outside that sequence and passes before everyone. The technical reason for this priority is the tram's physical limitation: it is locked to rails, cannot steer around an obstacle, and because of its large mass and the low friction of steel on steel, its braking distance is much longer than a passenger car's. The law entrusts the decision to the one truly able to stop. The sole exception is a tram exiting a depot: in that case it must yield itself. When a tram is beside you, before starting to move make sure you have properly read its indicator and the curve of the rails. • Because the tram is to your left, a temptation arises to rely on the right-hand rule; however, that rule operates among trackless vehicles and does not cancel the tram's priority.

g5-q124.text: When making a left turn, you must yield to:
g5-q124.explanation: To the truck driver. The traffic light at this intersection is switched off, so the signs resolve the priority question. The yellow diamond without a direction plaque means the main road continues straight, and you are on it. The white car on the right is on a secondary road and must yield to you: therefore "to both drivers" is the wrong answer. However, the blue truck is coming from the opposite direction along the same main road with its right indicator on. When turning left, you must yield to vehicles moving straight or turning right from the opposite direction: the truck's right turn falls into this exact category. Thus, stop, let the truck finish its maneuver, then turn. Two points to remember. First, the oncoming vehicle's active right indicator does not transfer priority to you: it still has priority. Second, a switched-off traffic light does not make an intersection "free": it merely returns it to the order of intersections governed by signs, and if there were no signs either, it would have to be treated as an intersection of equal roads. A loaded truck takes a wider radius when turning, and the edge of its cargo can swing outside the lane boundaries: waiting for its turn to finish is both the law and common sense. • The white car on the right draws attention, yet it is on a secondary road and must yield to you: adding it to the answer means ignoring the main-road sign. • "To no one" would be right if the truck were also on a secondary road: the truck moves from the opposite direction along the same main road, and your left turn crosses its trajectory.

g5-q125.explanation: There are no priority signs at the intersection, so the roads are equal. We are on the right side of the passenger car approaching from the left, so it must yield to us, and there is no road to our right, so we will cross the intersection first; option 1 is incorrect. (Rules, item 98)

g5-q126.text: When proceeding straight ahead, must we yield to the tram?
g5-q126.explanation: With sign 2.1 "Main road" (without plaque 8.13), the oncoming tram is also on the main road—of equal priority with us. At uncontrolled intersections, a tram has priority over trackless vehicles traveling on an equal road regardless of direction, so during its left turn we must yield; option 2 is incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 100)

g5-q127.text: Must we yield to the tram?
g5-q127.explanation: Yes: you must yield to the tram. At this intersection there is neither a traffic light nor a priority sign: meaning this is an uncontrolled intersection of equal roads. At such an intersection, a rail vehicle has priority over trackless vehicles regardless of which side it approaches from. The red tram approaches the intersection from your right, so you must stop both because it is a rail vehicle and by the right-hand rule. The safety reason for this priority is purely technical: a tram has no steering and cannot change its path; the only thing it can do is brake, and braking on steel rails requires a distance several times greater than rubber on asphalt. If a tram is forced into an emergency stop, standing passengers inside the car also suffer injuries. For this reason, the legislator placed the burden of decision on the driver who can stop easily and at lower cost. What to remember: a tram's priority applies only at an equal intersection. If you are on the main road and a tram approaches from a secondary road, priority is yours. That is also the common exam trap: some candidates think a tram has priority always and everywhere, while others think that because a tram is slow you can cut in front of it. Neither is right: first determine whether the roads are main or secondary. • "No" would be right if your road were declared the main road by a sign: there is no priority sign in the image, meaning the intersection is equal and priority belongs to the tram.

g5-q128.text: In this situation, a right turn is permitted:
options: Only after the truck has passed.
At the same time as the truck, provided this does not interfere with the truck driver.
g5-q128.explanation: Simultaneously with the truck, provided you do not obstruct the truck driver. In the image, the triangular "Give way" sign is posted facing you, while the road on which the truck is located is the main road. Yet "yielding" has a precise definition in the law: you must do nothing that forces the other driver to suddenly change speed or direction. Nowhere does this definition say maneuvers must be carried out strictly one by one: if your U-turn trajectory does not conflict with the truck's trajectory, staying stopped until its maneuver is completely finished is not mandatory. An important technical point about heavy vehicles: a truck has a large turning radius due to its length and wheelbase, sometimes swings slightly to the opposite side before turning, and the edge of its cargo sweeps a wider path than the front of the cab. That means "not obstructing" a truck means leaving it more space than you judge by eye and staying out of its side and rear blind spots. The exam trap here: the option that sounds more absolute and cautious is not necessarily the correct answer. The law sets "not obstructing" as the criterion, not an unconditional stop. If you lack sufficient space or are unsure of the truck's path, waiting is the only safe choice. • "Only after the truck" creates a stricter condition than the law itself: the legal criterion is not obstructing, not unconditionally waiting for another's maneuver to finish.

g5-q129.text: To which tram operator must we yield?
g5-q129.explanation: At this uncontrolled intersection there are no priority signs, so the roads are equal. Since trams have priority over trackless vehicles regardless of direction of movement, we must yield both to tram A approaching from the left and to tram B approaching from the right, ruling out options 1 and 2. (Rules, items 98, 100)

g5-q130.text: When proceeding straight ahead, you must yield to:
g5-q130.explanation: By signs 2.1 and 8.13, the main road turns right, so the white passenger car approaching from the right is also on the main road, while the motorcycle and truck are on secondary roads. Those traveling on secondary roads yield to us, yet we must yield to the passenger car approaching along the main road from our right; options 2 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, items 96, 97, 98)

g5-q131.text: In this situation, you must yield to:
g5-q131.explanation: To both drivers. The downward-pointing triangle means "Give way": you are on a secondary road, and the road crossing in front of you is the main road in both of its directions. The green bus on the left and the blue truck on the right are both traveling along this same main road, so you must yield to both and wait until the way clears. At an unequal intersection the right-hand rule is canceled. Remember this as a firm order: first the rank of the roads, then internal rules. As long as the sign has placed you on a secondary road, it does not matter whether the other vehicle approaches from the right or the left, goes straight or turns: you yield. The truck's active indicator changes nothing either. An indicator is only a statement of intent: it could have been left on by mistake or the driver might change their mind, so until the maneuver has actually begun, do not take it as a reason to pull out yourself. The safety reason for the whole rule is the same: the main road carries a continuous flow, while a car pulling out from a secondary road has low speed and low acceleration; a mistaken exit means a side impact, where the car body provides the least protection. Pull up to the edge of the roadway, stop, and check both directions separately. • The bus indeed has priority, yet it is only one of two vehicles on the main road: limiting the answer to it means ignoring the truck on the right. • The truck approaches from the right, tempting you to treat only it as having priority; however, the bus on the left is also on the main road, and at an unequal intersection the side of approach does not matter.

g5-q132.text: Under which sign must you give way at an intersection to drivers approaching from the left?
g5-q132.explanation: Option B has sign 2.4 "Give Way" and plate 8.13, which require yielding to drivers approaching on the main road (including from the left). Sign 2.3.3 in image A indicates that we are on the main road and others must yield to us, while sign 5.13.1 "Exit onto a road with a lane for route vehicles" in image C does not regulate priority, so options 1, 3, and 4 are incorrect. (Rules, signs 2.4 and 8.13, item 96)

g5-q133.text: In which image is the priority road shown?
options: In the lower and left images.
g5-q133.explanation: Roads marked with sign 2.1 "Main Road" in the left image and sign 2.3.1 "Intersection with a secondary road" in the bottom image are considered main roads. Sign 6.8.2 "Dead End" in the top right image does not make a road a main road, so options 1 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 1, sub-item 1, signs 2.1 and 2.3.1)

g5-q134.text: In which image is the priority road shown?
options: In the right and lower images.
g5-q134.explanation: A main road is shown in the right image with sign 2.1 "Main Road" and in the bottom image with sign 2.3.3 "Junction with a secondary road." Sign 2.7 "Priority over oncoming traffic" in the top left image applies only to a narrow section of road and does not make the road a main road, so options 1 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 1, sub-item 1, signs 2.1 and 2.3.3)

g5-q135.text: In which image is the priority road shown?
g5-q135.explanation: The two top images show main roads with signs 5.1 "Motorway" (on the left) and 2.3.2 "Junction with a secondary road" (on the right). Sign 5.5 "One-way road" in the bottom image does not indicate a main road, so options 1, 2, and 4 are incorrect. (Rules, item 1, sub-item 1, signs 5.1 and 2.3.2)

g5-q136.text: At an intersection, which road is considered the priority road?
options: A paved road (asphalt concrete, cement concrete, stone materials, etc.) relative to an unpaved road.
A three-lane road relative to a road having one lane in each direction.
An asphalt-concrete road relative to a road paved with slabs.
g5-q136.explanation: At an intersection, a road with a hard surface (asphalt concrete, cement concrete, stone materials, etc.) is considered the main road in relation to an unpaved (dirt) road. The number of traffic lanes or differences between types of hard surface (for example, asphalt concrete and cobblestones) do not by themselves grant main-road priority. (Rules, item 3, sub-item 1)

options: The blue, green, and white automobiles.
The white, blue, and yellow automobiles.
g6-q1.explanation: The traffic controller's arms are extended to the sides: under this signal, traffic from behind (the green car) and from the front/chest (the white car) is prohibited, while non-rail vehicles approaching from the sides are permitted to proceed only straight ahead and to the right. Although the blue truck is on the side, it has turned on its left turn signal, which is prohibited, whereas the red car (turning right) and the yellow car (going straight) are allowed to proceed, so options 1 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q2.text: Which drivers are permitted to proceed straight ahead?
options: The bus driver and the motorcycle operator.
The passenger-car driver and the truck driver.
g6-q2.explanation: The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward: under this signal, traffic from the right side (the truck) and from behind (the bus) is prohibited, from the chest side (the motorcycle) only a right turn is permitted, and from the left side (the red passenger car) non-rail vehicles are permitted to proceed in all directions. Therefore, only the driver of the passenger car has the right to drive straight ahead, which rules out options 1 and 2. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q3.explanation: The tram driver. The traffic light facing the blue car shows a solid green, while the traffic light on the tram's side shows a lit main red and only a green arrow in the additional section on the right. The rule here is: when the main signal is red and only the additional-section arrow is lit, movement is permitted only in the direction of that arrow, and the driver must yield to vehicles proceeding from other directions on the main green. The safety reason for this rule is clear: an additional-section arrow is a conditional permission, not an independent traffic-light phase. At that same moment, another stream is crossing the intersection on a full green, and that driver does not expect to stop. If the one with the arrow enters the intersection without checking, they will strike the side of a car passing at through speed; a side impact at an intersection is one of the deadliest crashes because the crumple zone on the side of the body is almost zero. The exam trap is that a tram normally has priority over trackless vehicles. However, that priority only applies when signals or priority indicators are equal. A tram moving on an additional-section arrow loses its priority at that moment. Remember this phrase: an additional-section arrow means permission to move, not priority—even for a tram. • The blue car has the main green and its path is completely open; this option is built on the misconception that a tram has priority under all circumstances.

g6-q4.text: If the traffic controller’s right arm is extended forward, traffic of non-rail vehicles is permitted:
options: From the left side, to the left and by making a U-turn.
From the right side, to the right only.
From the left side, in all directions.
From the rear, to the right only.
g6-q4.explanation: When the traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, non-rail vehicles approaching from the left side are permitted to proceed in all directions (straight, right, left, and U-turn). From the chest side only a right turn is permitted, and from the right side and from behind movement is prohibited. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q5.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The tram and the bus, then the passenger car.
The tram, the passenger car, the bus.
The passenger car, then the tram and the bus.
g6-q5.explanation: The red passenger car proceeds on the main green traffic-light signal, while the tram and the bus move in the direction of the green arrow in the additional section lit simultaneously with the red signal. When moving on an additional section, both the bus and the tram must yield to vehicles coming from other directions, so the passenger car will pass first, followed by the tram and the bus; options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, items 91, 92)

g6-q6.text: Which answer correctly identifies the vehicle or vehicles permitted to proceed?
options: The passenger car and the truck.
g6-q6.explanation: The traffic controller's arms are lowered, which has the same meaning as arms extended to the sides: from the chest side (the motorcycle) and from behind (the bus) movement is prohibited, while from the sides only straight ahead and right are permitted. The yellow truck is on the side, but with its left turn signal on it intends to turn left, which is prohibited, so only the red passenger car is permitted to proceed, ruling out the other options. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q7.explanation: The car driver. The motorcycle on the left of the image is moving on a solid green, but in front of the red car the main red is lit and only the green arrow of the additional section is glowing for it; moreover, the car's indicator shows a right turn. In this combination, the car has the right to begin a right turn, but before doing so it must yield to the motorcycle proceeding on the full green. The safety logic of this rule points directly to this very scene. A driver who sees a green arrow subconsciously reads it as "it's my turn" and focuses on the turning path rather than the crossing stream. In addition, a motorcycle is narrow, looks small against an urban background, and its speed is usually underestimated. The combination of these two errors produces one of the most frequent urban crashes: a turning car striking a motorcyclist who has the right of way. A motorcyclist has no protective shell, so injury severity in such a collision is several times higher. Key takeaway: an additional-section arrow never grants priority; it only allows entering a specific trajectory provided the path is clear. Whenever on the exam you see a main red together with a green arrow, the answer is almost always "must yield." • The motorcycle is moving on the main green without any conditions or reservations: whoever has a full green does not yield. The motorcycle's small size does not diminish its priority in any way.

g6-q8.text: This signal given by the traffic controller means that traffic is permitted for:
options: The blue and green automobiles; traffic is prohibited for the red, yellow, and white automobiles.
The blue, red, and green automobiles; traffic is prohibited for the yellow and white automobiles.
g6-q8.explanation: The blue, red, and green cars are allowed to proceed; the yellow and white ones must stop. Always read the traffic controller's signal relative to their body, not the lines of the street. There are three basic positions, and all three solve any question of this type. First: arms lowered or extended to the sides—from the controller's left and right sides, straight and right movement is open; from the chest and back sides, movement is prohibited for all vehicles. Second: right arm extended forward—from the controller's left side, movement is permitted in all directions; from the chest side, only a right turn is permitted; from the right side and from behind, movement is prohibited. Third: arm raised upward—movement of all vehicles and pedestrians is prohibited in all directions. Therefore, for each car in the image, ask only one question: which side of the controller's body faces that car? Remember that a traffic controller's signal takes precedence over traffic lights, signs, and road markings. • This option puts the red car among those prohibited, whereas its position relative to the controller's body is precisely one where passage is open; the prohibited list in this option is one car longer than in reality.

g6-q9.text: Which vehicles may make a right turn?
g6-q9.explanation: The red and green cars may turn right, having taken the rightmost lanes and turned on their right turn signals (from the left side all directions are permitted, and from the chest side—to the right, according to the controller's signal with the baton extended forward). The blue minibus is in the left lane and cannot turn right, the white car is behind the controller (where pedestrians are also crossing), and the yellow car is on the right side and signals a left turn, so options 1 and 2 are incorrect. (Rules, items 16, 40)

options: To the right through the first passage.
To the right through the second passage.
To the right through the first and second passages.
g6-q10.explanation: Only a right turn, and specifically into the first entrance. The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, and their chest faces the red car. Memorize the meaning of this signal verbatim: from the controller's chest side only a right turn is permitted; from their left side movement is permitted in all directions; from their right side and from behind movement is not permitted at all. This means both going straight and turning left are closed to the driver of this car, and the only remaining option is a right turn. The second half of the question is specifically about the turn itself. The road opening to the right is divided by a green island into two entrances.
