"Turning right" means entering the nearest opening—that is, the first entrance. If you drive past the first entrance to reach the second one, you have in fact driven straight through part of the intersection—the very movement the controller's signal prohibited—and end up entering the roadway intended for oncoming traffic from the wrong side. A short rule for the exam and the street: a right turn is always made into the nearest opening and close to the right edge of the roadway. The safety reason is equally tangible: a short arc along the edge intersects the paths of pedestrians and other vehicles the least, whereas passing the first opening and turning into the second means drawing a long arc through the heart of the intersection that no other driver expects. • Going straight from the controller's chest side when their right arm is extended forward is strictly prohibited: this signal opens only one direction. • The second entrance means first passing the first entrance, and passing it counts as moving straight through the intersection, which is prohibited. • Because the second entrance itself is wrong, the option treating both entrances as permitted is also wrong: only the first opening is available to you.

options: To the right through the first passage.
Straight ahead and to the right through the first passage.
g6-q11.explanation: Only a right turn, and specifically into the first entrance. The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, and their chest faces the red car. Memorize the meaning of this signal verbatim: from the controller's chest side only a right turn is permitted; from their left side movement is permitted in all directions; from their right side and from behind movement is not permitted at all. This means both going straight and turning left are closed to the driver of this car, and the only remaining option is a right turn. The second half of the question is specifically about the turn itself. The road opening to the right is divided by a green island into two entrances. "Turning right" means entering the nearest opening—that is, the first entrance. If you drive past the first entrance to reach the second one, you have in fact driven straight through part of the intersection—the very movement the controller's signal prohibited—and end up entering the roadway intended for oncoming traffic from the wrong side. A short rule for the exam and the street: a right turn is always made into the nearest opening and close to the right edge of the roadway. The safety reason is equally tangible: a short arc along the edge intersects the paths of pedestrians and other vehicles the least, whereas passing the first opening and turning into the second means drawing a long arc through the heart of the intersection that no other driver expects. • Going straight from the controller's chest side when their right arm is extended forward is strictly prohibited: this signal opens only one direction. • The second entrance means first passing the first entrance, and passing it counts as moving straight through the intersection, which is prohibited. • Because the second entrance itself is wrong, the option treating both entrances as permitted is also wrong: only the first opening is available to you.

g6-q12.text: If the traffic controller’s arms are extended to the sides or lowered, traffic of non-rail vehicles is permitted:
options: From the front and rear, to the right only.
From the left and right sides, straight ahead and to the right.
From the left and right sides, straight ahead only.
g6-q12.explanation: From the traffic controller's left and right sides, straight and right movement is permitted. Arms extended to the sides and arms lowered have one meaning and should be memorized together. In both positions, a trackless vehicle approaching from the controller's left or right side may proceed straight or turn right, while a rail vehicle may go only straight. Conversely, from the controller's chest side and back side, movement is prohibited for all vehicles. The logic of this signal is the same as a traffic light's: the controller creates a living phase with their own body. When the arms are extended or lowered, the side axis is open and the chest–back axis is closed. Left turns and U-turns are not allowed from any side because those two maneuvers cross the oncoming stream, and if they were open, two simultaneously open axes would collide. A right turn, however, crosses nobody's trajectory and is therefore left open. Remember two common exam traps. First, omitting the right turn and choosing "straight only": that option is always in the test and is always incomplete. Second, reading the signal relative to the street instead of the controller's body: at the intersection you must see which side of the body the controller faces toward you—chest, back, or side. And most importantly, the controller's gesture takes precedence over traffic lights, signs, and markings: even if the traffic light in front of you is green, if the controller has closed your direction, you have no right to move. • The controller's chest and back sides are the exact two sides this signal closes: no movement is permitted from those two sides—not even right. • "Straight only" is incomplete and leaves out the right turn: the "straight only" restriction applies to rail vehicles, not cars.

g6-q13.text: The driver of the red automobile:
g6-q13.explanation: Must yield. The traffic light in front of the red car shows a lit main red lamp, while next to it in the additional section a green arrow pointing upward (straight movement) is lit. Thus the red car is permitted to go straight, but this permission is conditional: at the same time, the green car is crossing the intersection from the left, and priority belongs to it. Many applicants think an additional section always has a left or right arrow. This picture shows the opposite: the arrow can also point upward. But the direction of the arrow does not change the nature of the rule: as long as the main lamp is red, you are not in your green phase. You are threading through a stream that has a real green, so all responsibility for safety is yours. The reason is the physics of an intersection: a car crossing on a full green neither slows down nor expects a collision. If you enter on a straight green arrow, you will cross its path in the middle of the intersection where neither of you has time to react. A short rule to remember: main red lamp + green arrow = you may go, but you go last. Before starting, you must come to a full stop, check the intersection, and proceed only once the way is clear. • The green arrow in the additional section is tempting because of its green color, but since the main lamp is red, this arrow gives only permission to enter and creates no priority.

g6-q14.text: Which vehicles are permitted to proceed?
options: The green, red, and white automobiles.
g6-q14.explanation: The traffic controller's arms are extended to the sides: the white car is on the chest side and the green car is on the back side, so their movement is prohibited. From the sides, movement is permitted only straight ahead and to the right; therefore, the red car turning right and the yellow car going straight are permitted to proceed, whereas the blue minibus signaling a left turn is prohibited from moving; options 2 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q15.text: Under which traffic signal may the automobile driver complete the U-turn?
g6-q15.explanation: Only on a green signal. The general rule states that a driver who enters an intersection on a permitting signal must complete the maneuver in the chosen direction regardless of the exit traffic light signal. However, this rule has an important exception: if there is a stop line or "STOP" sign before the next traffic light along the route, the driver must obey each traffic light signal separately. The picture shows just such a situation. The red car is making a U-turn, and on the median strip there is a traffic light showing red, with a "STOP" plate directly below it marking the stopping point. This means that traffic light establishes an independent stop for you: you must stop before the stop line and complete the U-turn only when that same traffic light turns green. The safety reason is straightforward: a road with a median strip effectively forms two independent roadways. The green signal that let you through the first half says nothing about traffic on the second half; if you continue without heeding the second traffic light, you will turn straight into a stream that has its own green, resulting in a full-speed side impact. The exam trap is precisely the "finish the maneuver" rule: the presence of an intermediate stop line cancels that rule. • The red traffic light inside the intersection together with the stop plate underneath it orders a stop: continuing a U-turn on red means entering a through stream that has a green light. • "On any signal" is tempting based on the maneuver-completion rule, but the presence of a stop line before the second traffic light nullifies that rule and makes obeying each traffic light separately mandatory.

g6-q16.text: What does the combination of yellow and red traffic signals mean?
options: Traffic is prohibited, and the signals indicate that the green signal will turn on shortly.
A vehicle with a special audible signal and flashing beacons activated is approaching the intersection.
g6-q16.explanation: The image shows the simultaneous illumination of the red and yellow traffic light signals. According to the rules, the combination of red and yellow signals prohibits movement and informs drivers of the imminent activation of the green signal, so options 1 (permitting) and 3 (about special flashing beacons) are incorrect. (Rules, item 7, sub-item 6)

g6-q17.text: In which image is the driver making the turn correctly?
g6-q17.explanation: In the left image. The two images must be read under two different signals. In the left image, the traffic controller's arms are lowered. The meaning of this signal is definite: from their left and right sides only straight and right movement is open, while from the chest and back sides movement is not permitted at all. The driver of the blue car approached from the controller's side and made a right turn—the only turn this signal leaves open—so the maneuver is correct. In the right image, the controller has extended their right arm forward. This signal is stricter and has only three cases: from the controller's left side movement in all directions, from the chest side only a right turn, and from the right side and from behind no movement at all. In that image, the vehicle crossing the intersection approaches from behind the controller, i.e., from the side this signal has completely closed. What is worth remembering for all questions in this category: a right turn is the only turn that traffic controller signals readily leave open because it crosses nobody's stream. Left turns and U-turns are always restricted or prohibited. And at an intersection with tram tracks, even when a signal permits you to move, you must make sure the tramway is clear before crossing the rails: a tram can neither leave the rails nor stop in a short distance. • In the right image, the controller's right arm is extended forward and the vehicle enters the intersection from behind their back: movement from behind the controller under this signal is not permitted in any direction, so that maneuver cannot be correct.

g6-q18.text: When the traffic signal is green, must the tram operator yield to vehicles approaching from other directions?
g6-q18.explanation: Must yield. On the traffic light in the picture, a single red lamp is lit, and next to it is an additional section with a green arrow pointing left. This green is not the green of the main phase: it is merely permission for one specific movement within a phase that is red for your direction. Therefore, even a tram turning left on this signal must yield to vehicles proceeding from other directions. This question is specifically designed to break a mental habit. An applicant memorizes "a tram has priority" and applies it blindly. Yet a tram's priority is conditional: a tram has priority over a trackless vehicle only under equal conditions, i.e., when the signals or priority indicators are the same for both. A tram moving on an additional-section arrow is not in equal conditions and therefore loses its priority. Likewise, a tram exiting a depot yields to everyone. The safety reason is also clear: a tram can neither change its path nor stop in a short distance, so if it enters an intersection relying on an imaginary priority, a vehicle with a full green has no way out. Remember: an additional-section arrow cancels the tram's priority. • This option relies on the general rule "a tram always has priority," but that rule is valid only under equal conditions, and moving on an additional-section arrow does not make conditions equal.

g6-q19.text: This traffic signal is used to regulate traffic:
options: Across the entire width of the roadway.
In roadway lanes where the direction of traffic may change to the opposite direction.
Only in lanes designated for public transit vehicles.
g6-q19.explanation: On roadway lanes where the direction of traffic may be reversed. The two square lenses you see in the picture—one with a red cross and the other with a green downward arrow—are a special traffic light for reversible lanes. It is mounted above each lane and governs that specific lane directly: a red cross means entry into this lane is prohibited, while a green downward arrow means this lane is open in your direction of travel. It is used on roads where traffic volume shifts at different times of day: heavy into the city center in the morning, and the opposite in the evening. Instead of building a wider road, the direction of one or more middle lanes is reversed using these traffic lights. The inherent hazard of such a layout is oncoming traffic sharing the same lane, so permission to enter must be announced minute by minute overhead rather than by a permanent sign. Remember two points: if a yellow diagonal arrow is lit, you must change lanes in the direction the arrow points and vacate the lane; and if these traffic lights are off or out of order, you have no right to enter the reversible lane unless its boundary markings permit it. The exam trap is confusing the cross and arrow with special bus-lane traffic lights. • This traffic light does not govern the entire width of the roadway: each lens governs only the lane directly beneath it. • A lane reserved for route vehicles is regulated by its own sign, marking, and special traffic light; the cross and vertical arrow are features of a reversible lane.

g6-q20.text: If the traffic controller’s right arm is extended forward, traffic of non-rail vehicles from the controller’s left side is permitted:
g6-q20.explanation: In all directions. When the traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, whoever approaches the intersection from their left side is in the freest position: they can go straight, turn left, turn right, and make a U-turn. To remember this case properly, view the controller's body as a living sign. The extended arm separates the flow on their left side from oncoming traffic and effectively plays the same role as a full green signal. In this same position, whoever approaches from the controller's chest side has the right only to turn right, while movement from their right side and from behind is not permitted at all. The safety logic of this separation is keeping intersecting trajectories apart: one stream is made completely free, and no other permitted movement crosses it. Since only a right turn is permitted from the front and no one moves from the other two sides, the way from the left side remains open in all directions. A common trap is the "straight and left" option: drivers subconsciously compare this position to a traffic light and omit the right turn and U-turn. Remember that a controller's signal takes precedence over traffic lights and signs, so memorize all four cases completely. • "Straight and left" is incomplete: in this position, a driver approaching from the controller's left side is also permitted to turn right and make a U-turn, so limiting the answer to two directions is wrong.

g6-q21.text: Which vehicles are permitted to proceed under this traffic signal?
options: The tram, the yellow automobile, and the red automobile.
g6-q21.explanation: The yellow and red cars. Look closely at the traffic light itself: on the main green lamp there is an upward arrow, the right additional section is also lit with a green arrow, and the left additional section remains dark. That means at this intersection only straight movement and a right turn are permitted, while any movement to the left, including a U-turn, is prohibited. Now evaluate each vehicle by its intention. The yellow car goes straight without an indicator: the green upward arrow permits this. The red car signals right: the right additional section is lit, meaning it is permitted. The blue car signals left, and the tram rails also turn left at the intersection: since the left additional section is dark, neither the blue car nor the tram has the right to move. The key rule is this: when an arrow is drawn on the green lamp, the green applies only to the indicated directions, not all directions; and an unlit additional section means movement in that direction is strictly prohibited, not "conditionally" allowed. The safety reason is the left turn—the most dangerous maneuver at an intersection because it crosses oncoming traffic. By keeping the left section dark, the intersection designer completely eliminated that conflict. Common trap: imagining that a lit green lamp means any direction is open. • Adding the tram is tempting because you think of a tram as an exception; however, the tracks go left and the left additional section is dark, meaning the tram also has no permission to move. • "All vehicles" includes the blue car with the left turn signal: movement to the left is prohibited by this traffic light, so this option is wrong from the start.

g6-q22.explanation: The traffic controller's arms are extended to the sides: movement of the blue car and the tram, which are on the chest side, is prohibited. The motorcycle approaching from the right side is permitted to proceed straight ahead and to the right, so only the motorcycle is allowed to move, which rules out options 1 and 3. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q23.text: If the traffic controller’s arms are extended to the sides or lowered, traffic of non-rail vehicles from the controller’s left and right sides is permitted:
options: Straight ahead and to the right.
g6-q23.explanation: Straight and right. When the traffic controller's arms are extended to the sides or lowered, a non-rail vehicle approaching from their left or right side may proceed straight or turn right. And nothing more: left turns and U-turns are not permitted from any side. For a rail vehicle, the permission is narrower, leaving only straight movement. The difference between these two is the main trap of the question. The "straight only" option sounds right because drivers remember it from the tram rule, yet for cars it is incomplete. An easy way to distinguish them is to remember that a tram cannot leave its rails: allowing a tram to turn right makes no sense if the rails do not go right. For a car, however, a right turn is the shortest and least conflicting maneuver at an intersection. The safety reason behind this entire rule fits in one sentence: with their body, the controller creates one open phase and one closed phase and does not allow movement that crosses the other open axis. Left turns and U-turns cross the width of the intersection and must stay closed; a right turn always stays along the edge of the road and crosses nothing. And always remember that this gesture takes precedence over traffic lights, signs, and markings: the final decision belongs to the controller, not the traffic light. • "Straight only" is the restriction for rail vehicles: for a car and motorcycle from the controller's side, a right turn is also permitted, and this option left it out.

g6-q24.text: Which vehicle driver has the right-of-way?
g6-q24.explanation: The tram driver. At this intersection, green is lit for the tram's route and the tram is entering the intersection; the red car approaches this same intersection from a secondary road on the left. Priority belongs to the tram, and the car must stop and allow the rails to clear. The governing rule has two layers, and both lead to the same conclusion. First layer: the main green is lit for the tram's direction, meaning the tram's path is open. Second layer—more importantly—under equal conditions, a rail vehicle has priority over a trackless vehicle regardless of its direction of travel. That is, even if the tram approaches from your left rather than your right, and even if it intends to turn, it still goes first. The technical reason for this priority is clear and compelling: a tram cannot swerve to avoid an obstacle, its path is fixed by the rails, and due to its heavy mass its braking distance is several times longer than that of a passenger car. Thus, the most practical and safest allocation of duty is for the car—which is more maneuverable and stops faster—to yield. Also remember the exceptions: a tram moving on an additional-section arrow or exiting a depot does not have this priority. Neither of those two cases applies in this image. • The car approaches from a secondary road toward an intersection whose rail route is open: neither the traffic light nor the rule on rail vehicle priority allows it to go first. Rushing to "dash in front of the tram" is precisely the behavior that causes these crashes.

options: The white, blue, and green automobiles.
g6-q25.explanation: The traffic controller's arms are extended to the sides: movement from the chest side (white car) and from the back side (green car) is prohibited, while from the sides non-rail vehicles are permitted only straight ahead and to the right. The blue truck is on the side but has switched on its left turn signal, so movement is prohibited for the white, blue, and green vehicles (the red and yellow ones are permitted), which rules out options 1, 3, and 4. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q26.text: When this traffic signal is red, traffic is prohibited:
options: Across the entire width of the roadway.
At a speed not exceeding 50 km/h.
In the lane over which the signal is located.
g6-q26.explanation: The image shows a reversible-lane traffic light with a red "X"-shaped signal and a downward arrow on a white plate. The red signal of a reversible-lane traffic light prohibits movement only along the lane above which it is located, rather than across the entire width of the roadway (option 1) or with a speed limit (option 2). (Rules, item 13)

g6-q27.text: What is the meaning of the circular flashing green traffic signal?
options: It indicates that entering the intersection is prohibited.
It permits traffic and indicates that its display period is ending and a prohibitory signal will be activated shortly.
g6-q27.explanation: A round flashing green traffic light signal permits movement and at the same time informs drivers that its active duration is expiring and a prohibiting signal will soon be switched on. By itself, it does not prohibit entering the intersection. (Rules, item 7, sub-item 2)

g6-q28.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The tram, the red automobile, the green automobile.
The red automobile, then the tram simultaneously with the green automobile.
The tram simultaneously with the green automobile, then the red automobile.
g6-q28.explanation: The red car, then the tram simultaneously with the green car. The traffic light on the side of the tram and green car shows a lit main red lamp, and only the additional section glows with a green upward arrow; the red car passes unobstructed along the intersecting road. This means both vehicles moving on the arrow must first yield to the red car and only then enter. Why do the tram and the green car go simultaneously? Because there is no conflict between them: the tram goes straight on its rails, and the green car also goes straight in the lane next to the rails. Their trajectories are parallel, not intersecting; and since both move under the same signal, neither has priority over the other. Two traps are built into this question at once. First, the yellow diamond (main road) on the same post: as long as the traffic light is operating, priority signs have no force, and the traffic light has the final say. Second, the supposedly permanent priority of the tram: a tram moving on an additional-section arrow does not have this priority and, like everyone else, must yield. The safety logic is the same: an additional-section arrow does not stop the stream that has a full green, so whoever enters on an arrow must see that the intersection is clear. • This order is built on the "tram always goes first" principle: yet the tram is moving on an additional-section arrow and must yield to the red car, so it cannot be first. • It is true that the tram and the green car go simultaneously, but not before the red car: their main signal is red, and priority belongs to the cross-traffic stream.

g6-q29.text: Which answer correctly identifies the vehicles that are permitted to proceed?
g6-q29.explanation: The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, and all vehicles are on their left side. From the left side, non-rail vehicles (the red car, the truck, and the motorcycle) are permitted to move in all directions, whereas the tram is permitted only to the left; however, the tram tracks run straight ahead, so movement is prohibited for the tram; options 2 and 3 are incorrect. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q30.text: If the traffic controller’s right arm is extended forward, traffic of non-rail vehicles from the controller’s left side is permitted:
options: Straight ahead and to the left.
g6-q30.explanation: In all directions. When the traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, whoever approaches the intersection from their left side is in the freest position: they can go straight, turn left, turn right, and make a U-turn. To remember this case properly, view the controller's body as a living sign. The extended arm separates the flow on their left side from oncoming traffic and effectively plays the same role as a full green signal. In this same position, whoever approaches from the controller's chest side has the right only to turn right, while movement from their right side and from behind is not permitted at all. The safety logic of this separation is keeping intersecting trajectories apart: one stream is made completely free, and no other permitted movement crosses it. Since only a right turn is permitted from the front and no one moves from the other two sides, the way from the left side remains open in all directions. A common trap is the "straight and left" option: drivers subconsciously compare this position to a traffic light and omit the right turn and U-turn. Remember that a controller's signal takes precedence over traffic lights and signs, so memorize all four cases completely. • "Straight and left" is incomplete: in this position, a driver approaching from the controller's left side is also permitted to turn right and make a U-turn, so limiting the answer to two directions is wrong.

options: The blue-and-yellow automobile when proceeding to the left.
The blue-and-yellow automobile when proceeding straight ahead, and the red automobile when proceeding straight ahead and to the right.
g6-q31.explanation: The traffic controller's arms are lowered, which is the same as arms extended to the sides, and both cars are on their left side. From the left side, non-rail vehicles are permitted to move only straight ahead and to the right, so the blue-and-yellow car is prohibited from turning left, while straight (for both) and right (for the red car) are permitted, which rules out options 2 and 3. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q32.text: In which direction is traffic permitted?
options: Straight ahead and to the right through the first passage.
To the right through the first passage.
To the right through the second passage.
To the right through the first and second passages.
g6-q32.explanation: The main red traffic light signal prohibits moving straight ahead, while a green right-pointing arrow is lit in the additional section. Since the traffic light is installed before the first intersection of roadways, its permitting arrow applies only to turning right at the first passage, whereas driving straight ahead and turning at the second passage on a red signal are prohibited. (Rules, items 8, 91)

g6-q33.text: Which vehicle will proceed through the intersection first?
g6-q33.explanation: The green car. The traffic light facing the blue and red cars shows a lit main red lamp, and only the additional section glows with a green arrow pointing right. The green car is crossing the intersection from the intersecting road on the left under its own traffic light's permission. That means it passes first. Break down the position of each of the three vehicles. The blue car is going straight, and no permitting signal is lit for its direction: it must remain behind the stop line. The red car is signaling right, and the additional-section arrow permits it to turn, but this permission is conditional: it must yield both to traffic approaching from other directions—that is, the green car—and to pedestrians on the crosswalk of the road it is entering. In the image, pedestrian crosswalks are marked on all four sides of the intersection and lie directly on the red car's turning path. The safety reason for this order is important: a right turn on an arrow is made quickly without stopping, and the turning driver's gaze is directed left to find a gap; at that very moment, a pedestrian stepping onto the crosswalk to their right is in a blind spot. Therefore, turning on an arrow always begins with "stop, look, then move." • The red car only has permission to turn right, not priority: it must yield to the green car and pedestrians, so it cannot be the first vehicle. • The blue car is going straight and its main traffic light is red: the additional-section arrow applies only to a right turn and gives no permission for straight movement.

g6-q34.text: In which image is the driver making the turn correctly?
g6-q34.explanation: In the left image. The two images must be read under two different signals. In the left image, the traffic controller's arms are lowered. The meaning of this signal is definite: from their left and right sides only straight and right movement is open, while from the chest and back sides movement is not permitted at all. The driver of the blue car approached from the controller's side and made a right turn—the only turn this signal leaves open—so the maneuver is correct. In the right image, the controller has extended their right arm forward. This signal is stricter and has only three cases: from the controller's left side movement in all directions, from the chest side only a right turn, and from the right side and from behind no movement at all. In that image, the vehicle crossing the intersection approaches from behind the controller, i.e., from the side this signal has completely closed. What is worth remembering for all questions in this category: a right turn is the only turn that traffic controller signals readily leave open because it crosses nobody's stream. Left turns and U-turns are always restricted or prohibited. And at an intersection with tram tracks, even when a signal permits you to move, you must make sure the tramway is clear before crossing the rails: a tram can neither leave the rails nor stop in a short distance. • In the right image, the controller's right arm is extended forward and the vehicle enters the intersection from behind their back: movement from behind the controller under this signal is not permitted in any direction, so that maneuver cannot be correct.

g6-q35.text: The red automobile will proceed through the intersection:
g6-q35.explanation: Last. Green is lit for both directions of this road. The red car has both left indicators on, meaning it intends to turn left; to its left, the tram goes straight along the rails, the blue car goes straight in the right lane, and the green and yellow cars come straight from the oncoming direction. In this layout, the red car crosses the intersection last. The reason is that a left turn intersects all other paths, and the driver turning left must yield to two groups: to the tram, because under equal conditions a rail vehicle has priority and the turning path crosses the rails; and to the green and yellow cars, because an oncoming vehicle going straight has priority over one turning left. The blue car going straight in its lane does not stop at all and passes without conflict. The safety logic is straightforward: a car turning left slows down and is exposed in the middle of the intersection to a side impact from oncoming traffic, while a tram can neither swerve nor stop quickly. Therefore, the burden of waiting is placed on the turning driver. Common trap: assuming a green signal means priority; green is merely permission to enter the intersection. • The red car is turning left and must yield to the tram and oncoming traffic: there is no scenario in which it goes first. • "Second" would only be true if one vehicle had priority ahead of it, whereas the tram and two oncoming cars pass before it. • "Third" also overlooks one vehicle: the tram, green car, and yellow car—all three cross the intersection before the red car.

g6-q36.text: The automobile will proceed through the intersection:
g6-q36.explanation: First. The traffic light in front of the car shows a solid green, while the traffic light on the tram's side shows a lit main red lamp and only the green right arrow in the additional section is glowing. Thus the order of passage is determined: first the car, then the tram. The rule is that moving on an additional-section arrow while the main red lamp is lit creates no priority: it only permits entering a specific trajectory, and the driver must yield to vehicles approaching from other directions on the main signal. This provision knows no exception even for a tram. There is an important learning point here worth locking into memory: a rail vehicle's priority is not absolute. A tram has priority over a car only under equal conditions—that is, when the signals or priority indicators are the same for both. In this picture the signals are not equal: one has a full green, the other only a conditional arrow. The safety reason is the usual one: a car with a full green does not slow down and does not expect an obstacle. If the tram enters relying on an imaginary priority, the car will realize it when there is no braking distance left. Remember: a full green has priority over an additional-section arrow regardless of vehicle type. • "Second" means treating the tram as having priority: yet the tram is moving on an additional-section arrow under a lit main red lamp and must yield to the car that has a full green.

options: The blue-and-yellow automobile straight ahead, and the red automobile to the right.
The red automobile straight ahead and to the right, and the blue-and-yellow automobile straight ahead.
g6-q37.explanation: The traffic controller is standing with lowered arms and sideways to the approaching cars, which permits non-rail vehicles approaching from their side to proceed straight ahead and to the right. The red car in the right lane may continue straight ahead and to the right, whereas the blue-and-yellow car in the left lane may only go straight, since turning left under this signal is prohibited. (Rules, items 16, 40)

options: The tram and the red automobile.
g6-q38.explanation: The red car. The traffic controller has extended their right arm forward, and their chest faces the red car. The meaning of this signal is exact and worth memorizing: from the controller's chest side only a right turn is permitted; from the controller's left side movement is permitted in all directions, except a tram has the right only to turn left; from the controller's right side and from behind their back any movement is prohibited. Now read the scene using this rule. The red car approaches from the controller's chest side and is signaling right, meaning it is the only vehicle permitted to move. The motorcycle approaches from the controller's right side and is completely prohibited. The blue truck approaches from behind the controller's back and is also prohibited. The tram, which is going straight, under this signal had permission only to turn left, meaning it has no right to go straight. The safety reason for these signals is clear: the controller creates a living "traffic-light phase" with their body and lets through only one low-conflict stream. A right turn from the chest side crosses nobody's path. Crucial point: the controller's command takes precedence over traffic lights, signs, and markings. If the traffic light is green, but the controller has prohibited your direction, you have no right to move. • The motorcycle approaches from the controller's right side, and with the right arm extended forward, movement from the right side is not permitted in any direction. • Adding the tram is tempting, but under this signal the tram could only turn left, and the straight path is closed to it. • The tram by itself is also wrong: the tram's permission is limited to a left turn, while in this scene it is going straight. • The blue truck approaches from behind the controller's back, and movement from behind the controller is always prohibited.

g6-q39.text: Is it permitted to proceed along the indicated path when the reversible traffic signals are off?
options: Permitted for the purpose of passing.
Permitted if there are no oncoming vehicles.
g6-q39.explanation: The image shows reversible traffic lanes marked on both sides with marking 1.9, above which the reversible-lane traffic lights are turned off. When the signals of a reversible-lane traffic light located above a lane marked on both sides with marking 1.9 are turned off, entering this lane is strictly prohibited—even to overtake or when there are no oncoming vehicles. (Rules, item 13)

g6-q40.text: In this situation, which vehicles are permitted to continue?
options: The passenger car straight ahead, the patrol vehicle in all directions, and the bus to the right only.
Only the patrol vehicle, in all directions.
The patrol vehicle in all directions and the bus to the right only.
g6-q40.explanation: The patrol car in all directions and the bus only to the right. The traffic controller has extended their right arm forward. Memorize the three provisions of this signal accurately: from the controller's left side a non-rail vehicle may move in all directions; from their chest side only a right turn is permitted; and from the right side and from behind movement is not permitted at all. Break down the scene by these three provisions. The patrol car approaches from the controller's left side, meaning it can go in any desired direction. The bus faces the controller's chest, so its only choice is a right turn, and if it goes straight or turns left it commits a violation. The red passenger car is on the side that this signal has completely closed, and must stop. Yet the most important lesson of this image is something else: in the same frame a green traffic light is lit and a yellow "main road" sign is posted, and neither of them decides anything. The controller's gesture takes precedence over traffic lights, signs, and markings. The reason is functional: a controller steps into an intersection when the situation is abnormal—traffic-light failure, crash, gridlock, or passage of a convoy—and if drivers could cite the traffic light, the whole point of the controller's presence would be destroyed. Therefore, look first at the controller's body, then at the traffic light. • Here the passenger car is also treated as permitted, whereas it enters from the side completely closed when the right arm is extended forward: the green signal changes nothing. • The patrol car is indeed permitted, but this option leaves out the bus: the bus approaches from the controller's chest side and has the right to turn right.

g6-q41.text: What does the traffic signal indicate?
options: When proceeding through the intersection, drivers must follow the requirements of the traffic sign.
Drivers must wait for a permissive traffic signal.
g6-q41.explanation: You must wait for the permitting signal. In the image to the right of the intersection, the traffic light has lit both the red and yellow lenses simultaneously. This combination is an independent and completely definite signal: movement is still prohibited, and the only thing this signal does is inform you of the imminent activation of the permitting signal. That means your duty is to remain behind the stop line and wait for green. The rationale is practical: warned a few seconds before green, the driver has time to engage a gear, release the parking brake, and prepare to pull away. The result is an orderly start of the queue, preventing stalling in the middle of the intersection, and less stress when green appears. Yet this preparation must not turn into premature movement: at that exact moment a car from the cross direction may still be clearing the intersection or a pedestrian may be taking their last steps. The exam trap is reading red with yellow as a "get ready to go" light and equating it with permission to proceed. The sign of a malfunctioning traffic light is different—complete blackout or flashing yellow—and it is in that condition that you must act according to signs and priority rules. As long as two steady lenses are lit, the traffic light is working properly and ordering a stop. • A malfunctioning traffic light is not indicated by two steadily lit lenses: a malfunction typically appears as a complete blackout or a flashing yellow. • Obeying signs is appropriate when the traffic light is off or operating on flashing yellow; here the traffic light is active and giving its own command.

g6-q42.text: Is the passenger-car driver permitted to pass the bus when the reversible traffic signal is off?
options: Permitted if the bus is moving at 30 km/h.
Permitted if there are no oncoming vehicles.
g6-q42.explanation: Prohibited: when the reversible-lane traffic light is off, this lane cannot be used to pass the bus. A reversible-lane traffic light changes the lane's direction at different times. The basic rule is this: until this traffic light gives a permitting signal—meaning it is off or malfunctioning—entry into the reversible lane is prohibited, and the driver must stay in the right-hand lanes. Thus you cannot use this lane to pass the bus or any other slow or stopped vehicle. The technical reason is clear: with the traffic light off, no one knows which direction the lane is assigned to at that moment, and oncoming traffic may legally be traveling in that same lane; the outcome of entering is a head-on collision at high relative speed—the most dangerous kind of crash. The reversible lane is separated from the others by a special double marking, and that very feature serves as a reminder to be cautious. The fact that the path ahead looks clear changes nothing: permission to enter comes from the traffic light, not the driver's split-second judgment. • "Permitted" ignores the fundamental condition: entry into a reversible lane is possible only on a permitting signal from that traffic light. • The speed of the bus plays no role in whether the reversible lane is open or closed: the state of the traffic light decides. • The absence of an oncoming car at that moment creates no permission: the lane is closed, and oncoming traffic could legally enter it at any second.

options: The motorcycle and the passenger car.
g6-q43.explanation: The traffic light at the intersection is operating (the green signal is on), so the intersection is controlled, and sign 2.4 "Give Way" and plate 8.13 do not apply. On a green traffic light signal, the bus turning left must yield to the motorcycle and passenger car proceeding straight ahead from the oncoming direction. (Rules, items 90, 173)

g6-q44.text: The following drivers are permitted to continue along the indicated paths:
options: The bus driver and the truck driver.
The passenger-car driver and the bus driver.
g6-q44.explanation: The traffic controller is standing with lowered arms—facing the passenger car with their chest and the truck with their back. In this position, movement from the chest and back sides is prohibited, while non-rail vehicles approaching from the side are permitted to proceed straight ahead and to the right; therefore, only the bus driver has the right to continue along the indicated path. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q45.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The tram, the passenger car, the bus.
The passenger car, the tram, the bus.
The passenger car, the bus, the tram.
g6-q45.explanation: The passenger car enters the intersection on the main green traffic light signal, while the tram and the bus move in the direction of the green arrow in the additional section lit simultaneously with the red signal, so they must yield to traffic from other directions. The passenger car will pass first, followed by the tram under equal conditions (since it has priority over a trackless vehicle), and finally the bus. (Rules, items 91, 92)

g6-q46.text: In which direction may the driver continue?
options: To the right through the first passage.
To the right through the first and second passages.
To the left through the first passage.
g6-q46.explanation: Only right and only into the first entrance. The main traffic light in the image is red, and next to it the additional section is lit with a green arrow pointing right. A green additional-section arrow permits movement only in the direction of that arrow and gives no permission to go straight. Since going straight is prohibited, you cannot pass the first entrance at all to reach the second one; therefore, the only accessible destination is that very first entrance on the right, visible in the image between the green islands. The safety reason for this layout is stream separation: the additional section permits a right turn while the straight and left streams are still held behind the red signal. If drivers mistook the green arrow for permission to go straight, they would enter an intersection where cross traffic has green—the exact angular collision the traffic light prevents. Two points to remember: first, moving on an additional-section green arrow grants no priority, and you must yield to vehicles proceeding from other directions on the main green. Second, you must approach the traffic light already positioned in the right lane: turning right from another lane is a violation even when the arrow is lit. • To reach the second entrance, you would first have to drive straight past the first one, and the red signal specifically prohibited that straight movement. • The green arrow permits only its own direction: a left turn is covered by neither the right arrow nor the main red signal.

g6-q47.text: When making a right turn, the driver must yield to:
options: The driver may continue without stopping.
g6-q47.explanation: When turning right on a green traffic light signal and exiting the intersection, the driver must yield both to pedestrians crossing the roadway and to a cyclist riding along a bicycle path. Proceeding without stopping or yielding to only one of them violates the rules for exiting an intersection. (Rules, item 87)

g6-q48.text: The vehicles will proceed through the intersection in the following order:
options: The tram, the bus, the truck, the motorcycle.
The bus, the truck, the tram, the motorcycle.
The bus, then the tram and the motorcycle, then the truck.
g6-q48.explanation: In the image, the traffic light is off, so the intersection is uncontrolled, and sign 2.4 "Give Way" is posted on the motorcycle's side. The bus going straight will cross the intersection first, after which the tram going straight and the motorcycle turning right will pass simultaneously (their paths do not intersect), and finally the truck turning left, yielding to the oncoming tram and crossing directions. (Rules, items 95, 96, 99)

g6-q49.text: In this situation, to which tram operator must you yield?
g6-q49.explanation: The main green traffic light signal is on, and our car is about to turn right. When traffic light signals permit simultaneous movement of a tram and non-rail vehicles, the tram has priority regardless of the direction of movement, so we must yield to both trams. (Rules, item 92)

g6-q50.explanation: The driver of the passenger car. The traffic light facing the passenger car has lit the green lens of the main section, and in the additional section the green left-turn arrow is also lit: meaning this driver's path is completely open and they enter the intersection on the main green. On the left side of the image, the bus is stopped behind the stop line, and the traffic light for that direction is red. The governing rule is simple: only a green signal of the main section gives a full right of passage. A driver who has a main red signal—even if a green arrow in an additional section allows them to turn—gains no priority and must yield to all vehicles proceeding from other directions. Permission to move and priority are not the same thing: this single sentence is the key to most traffic-light questions. The safety logic of this distinction is clear: if moving on an arrow combined with red were treated as equal to green, two intersecting streams would enter the intersection simultaneously—each convinced "I have green"—and the result would be an angular collision in the middle of the intersection, the crash that causes the greatest harm to occupants because the impact hits the side of the car. The exam trap in this question is vehicle size. The bus is larger and heavier and carries public-transit passengers, yet none of that creates priority in right-of-way rules. The only real exception is an emergency-service vehicle with an active flashing beacon and siren, and there is no trace of one in this image. • The bus is stopped at the intersection, and its size creates the impression that the road should be cleared for it, yet its direction's traffic light is red: neither a vehicle's size nor its public nature creates priority.

g6-q51.text: In this situation, when making a left turn:
options: I will yield to the tram.
I will proceed through the intersection first.
g6-q51.explanation: On the "T"-shaped traffic light regulating tram traffic, the top three signals are lit without the bottom signal, which prohibits tram movement. At the same time, for our car the green traffic light signal and the additional section with the left arrow are lit, so we will pass through the intersection first without yielding to the tram. (Rules, items 8, 14)

g6-q52.text: What should you do in this situation?
options: Enter the intersection and, after yielding to the passenger-car driver, proceed through the intersection.
Wait before the “Stop Line” until the passenger-car driver has proceeded through the intersection.
g6-q52.explanation: Enter the intersection, yield to the oncoming car inside the intersection, and then complete the left turn. The traffic light ahead of you is green, you have signaled left, and a green left arrow is lit on the dashboard. The purple car opposite is going straight. Green means "permission to enter the intersection," not "permission to cut across oncoming traffic": you must enter the intersection, pull forward toward the point where paths meet, wait there with straight wheels, and complete the turn after oncoming traffic clears. Why is waiting behind the stop line wrong? Because the stop line defines your duty with respect to a red signal and a "stop" sign, not green. Stopping behind it on green blocks the cars behind you that have the same green, creates a rear-end collision risk, and causes only one or two cars to manage a left turn per light cycle. Worth remembering: if after you legally enter an intersection the light turns red, you have the right and duty to clear the intersection—drivers who just received green must let you clear first. That is why entering the intersection and waiting inside it is both legal and safe. The exam trap is the outwardly cautious option. On the exam, any option containing "I will wait" is not necessarily right: the criterion is the rule, not a feeling of caution. • Stopping behind the "stop line" seems cautious, yet that line applies to a red signal and a "stop" sign: stopping behind it on green halts the stream behind you and destroys intersection capacity. • "Go first" means ignoring the oncoming car going straight: a left turn never has priority over straight oncoming traffic.

g6-q53.text: Which driver violates the traffic rules when making the turn?
g6-q53.explanation: Before the intersection, mandatory signs 4.1.1 "Proceed straight" are installed on both sides, requiring traffic to travel straight ahead only. Traffic light signals override only priority signs, not mandatory signs, so both drivers—of the passenger car turning left and the motorcycle turning right—violate the rules. (Rules, item 173, sign 4.1.1)

g6-q54.text: In this situation, when making a right turn, must you yield?
g6-q54.explanation: Must yield: moving on an additional-section green arrow grants no priority. In the image, the main traffic light is red, while in the additional section—next to the bottom lens—the green right-turn arrow is lit. Your car's right indicator is blinking as well. This arrow says only one thing: "you may move in the direction of the arrow." It says nothing about priority. Governing rule: when moving in the direction of an arrow lit in an additional section simultaneously with a red or yellow signal, the driver must yield to vehicles proceeding from other directions. In the image, the light-colored car on the right is crossing along the intersecting road—in a direction whose traffic light permits movement—meaning it goes first and you go after it. Safety reason: the green arrow is designed solely so the right-turn stream does not sit idle during red; if that same arrow also gave priority, the turning car would drive straight under the wheels of a stream that has a full green and enters the intersection at normal speed. The result is a side impact at the exit point of the intersection. A short formula to remember: "green arrow on red = you may go, but you are at the end of the priority line." In practice, this means turning your head before turning to check cross traffic, rather than simply trusting a lit arrow. • This option confuses the green color of the arrow with priority: since the main signal is red, the arrow's trajectory is only opened, while priority still belongs to traffic from other directions.

g6-q55.text: Is a right turn permitted in this situation?
options: Yes, provided you do not interfere with pedestrians.
g6-q55.explanation: Yes, provided you do not obstruct pedestrians. In the image, the traffic controller faces you sideways with both arms lowered. In this position, for drivers viewing them from the side, straight movement and a right turn are open, and pedestrians also have the right to cross the roadway. That is why a group of pedestrians in the image is walking across the crosswalk: their presence is a sign of that very permission, not a sign that your maneuver is prohibited. Therefore, a right turn is permitted, but conditionally: at the end of the turn you enter the roadway across whose markings pedestrians are walking, and you must let them finish crossing. The fact that the controller's signal permitted you to move does not allow you to press pedestrians: permission to move and priority are two different things. What to remember about controller signals: when arms are lowered or extended to the sides, only those who see them from the left or right side may move, and only straight and right. If the controller faces you with their chest or back, movement is prohibited altogether. A common exam trap is mistaking the sight of walking pedestrians for a reason a right turn is banned. • "No" would be correct if the controller stood facing you with chest or back; however, the image shows them from the side, and in this position a right turn is not closed.

g6-q56.text: In this situation, must you yield to the tram operator?
g6-q56.explanation: Must yield: you must give way to the tram. The tram on the left has signaled and wants to cross in front of you. The governing rule is simple: when a signal permits movement for both of you, **the rail vehicle has priority**—whether it approaches from your left or your right, and whether you are going straight or turning. If your movement is on an additional-section green arrow, the requirement is even stricter: an additional-section arrow gives "permission to move," not "priority." A driver entering an intersection on an additional-section arrow must yield to all vehicles moving from other directions on a permitting signal. Thus, by both lines of reasoning, the conclusion is the same: tram first. The safety reason is also technical: a tram cannot leave its track, and its braking distance is several times longer than a passenger car's. If you pull forward thinking "it's coming from the left, so I'm right," the tram will be unable either to swerve or to stop in time. Therein lies a common exam trap: the right-hand rule does not apply to a tram. The two exceptions that cancel a tram's priority—neither of which applies here—are a tram moving on an additional-section arrow on red and a tram exiting a depot. • "Do not have to yield" is true when the tram itself moves on an additional-section arrow on red or exits a depot: neither is visible in this image. The mere fact that the tram approaches from the left does not eliminate its priority.

g6-q57.text: When the green traffic signal turns on, the driver:
options: Must yield to the truck driver.
g6-q57.explanation: When the green traffic light signal turns on after the combination of red and yellow signals, the driver must yield to the truck that is inside the intersection completing a left-turn maneuver. Starting immediately before the intersection clears is not permitted. (Rules, item 94)

g6-q58.explanation: You pass first. The traffic light to your right is green, and the additional section next to it is dark: meaning you have permission to go straight, and as the rails show, your path runs straight through the intersection. The blue-and-white tram to your left is moving in the same direction as you, and its side indicator is lit: meaning it wants to leave its straight path and change direction. The main point of this question is correcting a belief: a tram's priority is not absolute. A tram has priority over trackless vehicles when the traffic light permits movement for both the tram and you simultaneously and your paths intersect in different directions at an intersection. However, a tram moving alongside you in the same direction that wants to change its trajectory is performing a maneuver; and a maneuver, regardless of the vehicle performing it, creates no priority. Priority belongs to whoever travels straight without changing direction. The safety reason for this order is obvious: a car moving straight at normal speed does not expect someone beside it to cut across in front of it; its braking distance is not calculated for such a surprise. The burden of decision must lie on the one changing the state of affairs. Nevertheless, in practice never hug a tram or linger in its blind spot. A tram cannot swerve and its braking distance is very long: having priority does not prevent a collision. • This option relies on the memorized phrase "a tram always has priority." That priority is conditional and does not extend to a same-direction tram changing trajectory: here, you are the one proceeding without changing direction.

g6-q59.text: When proceeding straight through the intersection, the driver:
g6-q59.explanation: You must yield to the tram. The traffic light on the right is green, and you are driving straight through the intersection. From the oncoming direction, the red-and-white tram and the white passenger car have both signaled and want to turn. Instinct says "I'm going straight, so both must yield to me"; yet regarding the tram, that instinct is wrong. The rule is this: when the traffic light permits movement for a tram and non-rail vehicles simultaneously, the tram has priority regardless of its direction of movement. That means even a tram approaching from the oncoming direction and turning left has priority over you going straight. However, the white car is an ordinary vehicle, and to turn left it must yield to vehicles coming straight from the oncoming direction—meaning it stays behind you. The reason for this exception is physics. A tram runs on fixed rails, cannot swerve or pull aside, weighs tens of tons, and has a braking distance several times longer than a passenger car's. The only way to prevent a collision is for others always to accommodate the tram, not the other way around. Moreover, a tram usually carries dozens of standing passengers who get injured during sudden braking. Worth remembering: in this question two vehicles signaled simultaneously, and that pairing is the trap. The right comparison is "rail versus non-rail," not "straight versus turning." • This uses the valid "straight has priority over turning" rule, but that rule is overridden in front of a tram: a tram has priority regardless of its direction of movement. • Here the white car is also treated as having priority, whereas to turn left it must yield to you going straight from the oncoming direction.

g6-q60.text: When making the turn, the driver must yield to:
g6-q60.explanation: Both the cyclist and the pedestrian. You have signaled right, and the traffic light is green. On the right side of the image there is a round blue sign with a bicycle and a downward arrow—a dedicated cycle path—and a marking of dashed squares is applied on the roadway—a bicycle crossing. The cyclist is crossing this very crossing, while several pedestrians are standing at the pedestrian crosswalk. Rule: when turning, the driver must yield both to pedestrians crossing the roadway of the target street and to cyclists crossing it on a dedicated path or bicycle crossing. Your right turn takes you across both markings, meaning both groups have priority. Safety reason: a cyclist travels at around 20 km/h, roughly three times faster than a pedestrian. A turning driver usually casts only a quick glance in the mirror and over the right shoulder, and at that exact moment the cyclist is in the car's side blind spot: this is precisely the classic "right hook" crash scenario onto a cyclist. Worth remembering: before every right turn, two separate checks are needed—the right mirror and blind spot for a bicycle, and a direct look at the pedestrian crosswalk. The exam trap is the options naming only one of the two. • The pedestrian has priority, but this option leaves out the cyclist crossing the bicycle crossing: the dedicated cycle path is marked by the round blue sign. • The cyclist has priority, but this option sets pedestrians aside: the right turn crosses the pedestrian crosswalk as well.

g6-q61.text: When making a right turn, must you yield to the driver approaching in the oncoming lane?
g6-q61.explanation: The traffic light is operating at the intersection (the green signal is on), so the requirements of sign 2.4 "Give Way" and plate 8.13 do not apply. When turning right on a green traffic light signal, we are not required to yield to the driver approaching from the oncoming lane and making a left turn, because that driver is the one required to yield to oncoming traffic going straight and right. (Rules, items 90, 173)

g6-q62.text: When proceeding straight through the intersection:
options: We must yield to the passenger-car driver.
g6-q62.explanation: You must yield to the driver of the blue passenger car. Look closely at the traffic light on the right: the main red is lit, and below it in the additional section a green arrow pointing upward is lit. This combination means straight movement is permitted for you, not on a full green, but on an additional-section arrow while the main red is lit. The governing rule applies precisely to this state: whenever you move in the direction of an arrow lit in an additional section while the main signal is simultaneously red or yellow, you must yield to vehicles proceeding from other directions. That is why the blue passenger car, entering the intersection from the road on the left and having green for its direction, has priority. The safety logic of this rule lies in the fact that an additional-section arrow is not a "protected path." A full green means the signal system has stopped intersecting directions. By contrast, an additional arrow on red is only a conditional permission: it opens the path without guaranteeing that nobody is crossing transversely. If a driver does not know this difference, they enter the intersection at full-green speed and end up right in the middle of cross traffic. A key point very frequent on the exam: always read the color of the main signal together with the additional-section arrow. Green arrow + main red means "go, but yield." Green arrow + main green means "go, priority is yours." That single difference changes the answer to dozens of questions. • This assumes a green arrow is the same as a full green. Yet an additional-section arrow together with a main red gives conditional permission and requires you to yield to other directions.

g6-q63.text: When making a left turn, you must yield to:
options: The passenger-car driver and the pedestrians.
g6-q63.explanation: Both the oncoming driver and the pedestrians. The traffic light is green, you have signaled left, and a green left arrow is lit on the dashboard. A left turn is the most dangerous urban maneuver because in one motion it crosses two independent streams: oncoming traffic and pedestrians crossing the roadway of the target street. In this image both hazards are present at once: the green car is coming straight from the oncoming direction, and three pedestrians have stepped onto the pedestrian crosswalk on the left. Thus the order of action is this: first let oncoming traffic pass, then enter the turn and, before reaching the crosswalk, yield to the pedestrians. Rule: when turning left, you must yield to vehicles going straight or turning right from the oncoming direction, and after that to pedestrians crossing the roadway of the street you are entering. Safety reason and key practical point: the real danger is giving all your attention to the oncoming car, finding a gap in traffic, and entering the turn with brisk acceleration; at that exact second the car's front pillar and turning angle hide the walking pedestrian from you. Therefore a left turn must be executed in two stages, not one continuous sweep. The exam trap is the two options starting with "only," which force you to forget one of the two hazards. • It is true that you must yield to the oncoming car, but the word "only" leaves out the pedestrians walking across the crosswalk of the street you are turning onto. • Pedestrians indeed have priority, but this option ignores the straight oncoming stream: a left turn is not permitted before it passes.

g6-q64.text: In this situation, is a right turn permitted?
options: Yes, provided you do not interfere with the pedestrian.
g6-q64.explanation: Yes, provided you do not obstruct the pedestrian. In the image, the traffic controller has extended their right arm forward, and you see them from the left side. In this position, movement in all directions is open for vehicles on rubber tires—meaning a right turn is unconditionally permitted. The pedestrians visible on the right of the image may also cross the roadway behind the controller's back. Yet permission to move is not the end of the matter. Turning right, you enter a roadway with a pedestrian crosswalk: a pedestrian who started crossing before you has priority, and you must stop until they finish. The safety reason is simple: at the moment of turning, the car's front pillar blocks the very angle from which a pedestrian steps onto your path, while low turning speed creates a false impression of no danger. To remember, place the three cases of "right arm extended forward" side by side: from the controller's left side all directions are open, from the chest side only a right turn, and from the right side and from behind movement is prohibited. First identify which side of the controller you see; without that, any answer is guesswork. • "No" assumes the controller's signal has closed your path: yet you see them from the left side, which is the freest state of the signal, not the most prohibited.

options: You must yield to the tram operator.
You will proceed through the intersection first.
g6-q65.explanation: You must yield to the tram. In the image, the tram is to your left on rails laid down the middle of the roadway, and the overhead sign shows the direction of travel for each lane. The basic rule is this: under equal conditions, a rail vehicle always has priority over rubber-tired traffic—both inside and outside intersections, and regardless of whether the tram approaches from the right or the left. The reason for this priority is the physics of braking, not administrative preference. A tram cannot change its path, does not leave the rails, and due to its heavy mass and low steel-on-steel friction, its braking distance is several times longer than a passenger car's. The only one in this equation who can maneuver is you, so the law places the burden of decision on you. Practical point when turning left: your maneuver inevitably crosses the rails, and for those few seconds your car is exposed to being hit by the front of the tram. Before turning the steering wheel, check the rail track in both directions and never wait on the rails for the road to clear. A common exam trap is extending the "yield to the right" rule to a tram as well: that rule does not apply to a rail vehicle. • "You cross the intersection first" is true when the tram is in unequal conditions or a signal has prohibited its movement; here neither is the case, and priority belongs to the rail vehicle.

g6-q66.text: Which traffic signs do not apply when their requirements conflict with traffic signal indications?
g6-q66.explanation: When the meanings of traffic light signals contradict the requirements of priority signs, drivers must follow the traffic light signals, meaning priority signs do not apply. Meanwhile, prohibitory and mandatory signs continue to apply as usual. (Rules, item 173)

g6-q67.text: In this situation, who must yield?
g6-q67.explanation: The tram driver. The traffic light on the right has lit the red lens, while in the additional section the green right-turn arrow is lit. The red-and-white tram stands on the rails ahead of you with a blinking right indicator: meaning it wants to turn in the direction of this arrow. On the left side of the image, a passenger car is passing along the intersecting road because the traffic light for that direction is green. Rule: when moving in the direction of an additional-section arrow lit simultaneously with a red or yellow signal, a driver—and equally a tram driver—must yield to vehicles proceeding from other directions. A rail vehicle's usual priority does not operate in this state and is canceled. The second point in the image is also important: under the traffic light there is a yellow diamond "main road" sign, yet as long as the traffic light is operating, priority signs do not apply. That means you cannot cite that yellow diamond to treat yourself or the tram as having priority. Safety reason: at an intersection where one direction has a full green, vehicles enter at normal speed expecting no obstacle. If a heavy tram pulls out under a green arrow relying on its "rail priority," a collision with the green stream is virtually inevitable because the tram can neither swerve nor stop quickly. Exam trap: the memorized phrase "a tram always has priority." • This option extends the general priority of a rail vehicle to all cases, yet the passenger car approaches from a direction whose traffic light is green while the tram moves on an arrow combined with red: in this combination the tram yields, not the car.

options: We must yield to the tram operator.
We will proceed through the intersection first.
g6-q68.explanation: The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, and they face our car with their left side, which permits non-rail vehicles to proceed in all directions (including right). In this position, a tram is permitted to proceed only left (and movement from the controller's right side is prohibited altogether); therefore, the tram cannot go straight ahead, and we will pass through the intersection first. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q69.text: You intend to make a left turn. To whom must you yield?
options: The automobile driver and the tram operator.
g6-q69.explanation: Both oncoming vehicles—both the tram and the car beside it. The traffic light is green, you have signaled left, and two vehicles are approaching from the oncoming direction: a red-and-white tram on the rails and a light-colored car to its left. Both are moving in a direction permitted by their traffic light, meaning both have priority ahead of you. The rule has two layers, and they must be seen together. First layer: a driver turning left must yield to vehicles coming straight or turning right from the oncoming direction. Second layer: when traffic lights permit movement for a tram and a trackless vehicle simultaneously, priority belongs to the tram regardless of its direction of movement. Combining these two means you cannot ignore either of the two oncoming vehicles. Safety reason: a left turn crosses the paths of both, and the tram is the more dangerous of the two because it has no ability to swerve; the only thing it can do is brake, and a loaded tram's braking distance is measured in tens of meters. A driver who turns assuming the path is clear has usually underestimated the tram's speed and distance. Worth remembering: during a left turn, "oncoming traffic" means all oncoming vehicles, not just the most noticeable one. The exam trap is the "tram only" and "neither" options, which remove one of the threats. • It is true that the tram has priority, but "only" is wrong: the oncoming car is also moving on green, and a left turn crosses its path as well. • "Neither" means treating green as absolute priority: green permits you to turn, not to cut across oncoming traffic.

options: I will complete the maneuver without stopping.
After entering the intersection, I will stop before the second “Stop Line” and wait for the green signal.
g6-q70.explanation: In our direction, the green traffic light signal is on, allowing entry into the intersection; however, in the direction of the left turn inside the intersection, there is a second "Stop line" marking (1.12) before a red traffic light. In such a case, the driver must follow the signals of each traffic light, so it is necessary to stop before the second "Stop line" and wait for the green signal. (Rules, item 93)

g6-q71.text: In this situation, must we yield to the truck driver?
g6-q71.explanation: Yes, you must yield to the truck driver. A green left arrow is lit on the dashboard, meaning you intend to turn left. The traffic light on the right is green, and a blue truck is approaching from the oncoming direction: its right indicator is also on, and it wants to turn onto the adjoining street. Rule: a driver turning left must yield to vehicles going straight or turning right from the oncoming direction. Here both cases lead to the same result: whether the truck goes straight or turns right, your path crosses its path, and you yield. Even when you both enter the same street, priority belongs to the right turn because that turn is shorter and does not cross oncoming traffic. Safety reason specific to trucks: drivers underestimate the distance and speed of large vehicles; a larger object appears "farther away and slower." That is why the classic "left turn versus truck" crash always starts with "I thought I'd make it," whereas a loaded truck can neither stop in time nor swerve. Worth remembering: an active turn signal on an oncoming vehicle guarantees nothing. Until its maneuver has actually begun, it does not lose priority; a mistakenly turned-on or forgotten indicator is one of the most frequent causes of intersection crashes. • "No" usually stems from thinking that since the truck signaled right, "it will leave the road anyway"; yet an indicator is a statement of intent, not a waiver of priority, and the one turning left still yields.

g6-q72.text: In this situation, when making a left turn, you must:
options: Enter the intersection and wait for the traffic controller’s signal permitting a left turn.
Stop before the “Stop Line” pavement marking and wait for the traffic controller’s signal permitting a left turn.
Enter the intersection and, after yielding to the driver approaching in the oncoming lane, proceed through the intersection.
g6-q72.explanation: The traffic controller is standing with lowered arms and sideways to us, which permits movement only straight ahead and to the right, while a left turn is prohibited. On a prohibiting signal, the driver has no right to enter the intersection and must stop before the "Stop line" marking (1.12), waiting for a controller signal permitting a left turn. (Rules, items 16, 18)

g6-q73.text: In which case may you proceed through the intersection without yielding to another road user?
g6-q73.explanation: On a green traffic light signal, when turning right we must yield to pedestrians crossing the roadway, and when turning left we must yield to the tram moving from the left along tracks in the same direction. Only when going straight ahead does our trajectory intersect neither pedestrians nor the tram, so we can proceed without yielding. (Rules, items 87, 92)

g6-q74.text: When making a right turn, you must:
options: Stop before the “Stop Line” so as not to interfere with pedestrians.
Enter the intersection and stop so as not to interfere with pedestrians.
Proceed through the intersection without stopping.
g6-q74.explanation: The green traffic light signal permits entering the intersection, so there is no requirement to stop before the "Stop line." However, when exiting the intersection by turning right, the driver must not obstruct pedestrians crossing the roadway; therefore, the driver must enter the intersection and stop before the pedestrian crosswalk to yield to them. (Rules, items 87, 105)

options: You must yield to the passenger-car driver.
You will proceed through the intersection first.
g6-q75.explanation: Under the traffic controller's signal, our direction for turning right is permitted (from the chest side with the right arm extended forward, movement to the right is permitted).
