At the same time, for the passenger car making a U-turn along the intersecting road, at the point where trajectories intersect we approach from the right side, so that driver must yield and we will pass through the intersection first. (Rules, items 16, 45)

g6-q76.text: After the permissive traffic signal turns on, we may enter the intersection:
options: Only when making a turn or a U-turn.
g6-q76.explanation: Ahead, immediately beyond the intersection, a traffic jam has formed in the straight direction. The rules prohibit entering an intersection if the resulting congestion will force the driver to stop and obstruct the movement of other vehicles; therefore, after the permitting signal turns on, one may enter the intersection only to make a turn or U-turn where there is no congestion. (Rules, item 88)

g6-q77.text: When the green traffic signal turns on, we must:
options: Make sure that there are no pedestrians who have not finished crossing in the part of the pedestrian crossing that is not visible.
Immediately start moving in accordance with the traffic signal.
g6-q77.explanation: The truck stopped on the right blocks visibility of the right side of the pedestrian crosswalk. At controlled pedestrian crosswalks, after the green signal turns on, the driver must give pedestrians the opportunity to finish crossing the roadway, so one must first make sure there are no pedestrians in the obscured part of the crosswalk and must not start moving immediately. (Rules, item 105)

g6-q78.text: In this situation, when making a left turn, you must yield to:
options: The bus driver and the pedestrian.
g6-q78.explanation: The traffic light at the intersection is operating (the green signal is on), so signs 2.1 "Main Road" and 8.13 do not apply. When turning left on a green signal, the driver must yield both to the bus coming straight ahead from the oncoming direction and to pedestrians crossing the roadway after the turn. (Rules, items 87, 90, 173)

g6-q79.text: Must you yield to the bus?
g6-q79.explanation: Our car is making a right turn on the green arrow of the additional section lit simultaneously with the main red traffic light signal. In this case, the driver must yield to vehicles approaching from other directions, and therefore must yield to the bus. (Rules, item 91)

g6-q80.text: In this situation, when making a U-turn, must you yield to the other driver?
g6-q80.explanation: The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward—with their chest toward the blue car and their left side toward us, which permits us to proceed in all directions (including a U-turn), and the blue car to turn right. While making the U-turn, the blue car turning right ends up on our right side, so we must yield to it. (Rules, items 16, 45)

g6-q81.text: In which direction or directions may the driver continue in this situation?
options: Straight ahead and to the right.
Straight ahead and to the left.
g6-q81.explanation: The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward and they face us with their left side, which permits movement in all directions. However, turning right is prohibited because sign 5.7.2 establishes one-way traffic to the left on the intersecting road, while turning left and making a U-turn are prohibited from the right lane (we have not taken the leftmost lane), so we may continue only straight ahead. (Rules, items 16, 40, sign 5.7.2)

g6-q82.explanation: Although the red signal is on at the traffic light, traffic at the intersection is directed by a traffic controller, whose instructions take precedence over traffic light signals. The controller is standing with their right arm extended forward and their left side toward the cars, which permits movement in all directions from the left side, so both the bus turning left and the passenger car turning right may proceed. (Rules, items 16, 20)

g6-q83.text: Proceeding across the railroad crossing is:
g6-q83.explanation: Permitted: the flashing white signal is lit, and the red signals are off. In the image to the right of the road, the cross-shaped railway crossing sign is visible along with the special crossing traffic light. The two side red signals are off, while the top white signal is lit; the barrier is not lowered, and the track is clear. This combination means the crossing is open and passage is permitted. The key point is that a flashing white signal is a permitting signal, not a warning of prohibition; conversely, flashing of either red signal—even with the barrier raised and no train in sight—means an absolute stop. Completely dark signals are not permission either, and you must cross with utmost caution and only after making sure no train is coming. The reason for strictness at crossings is plain: a train can neither swerve nor stop in a short distance—its braking distance is measured in hundreds of meters. That means the entire burden of prevention falls on the car driver. Even when passage is permitted, follow these rules: look both ways along the track before entering; do not stop on the crossing and do not enter if there is no clear space beyond it; do not shift gears or overtake on the crossing. The exam trap is seeing the cross-shaped sign and imagining a prohibition: that sign is a warning sign, not a prohibitory one. • A prohibition applies when a red signal is flashing, the barrier is lowered, or the crossing attendant signals to stop: none of those appears in the image.

options: Prohibited from proceeding through the intersection.
Permitted to proceed through the intersection in all cases.
Permitted to proceed through the intersection if the driver cannot stop before the “Stop Line” without sudden braking.
g6-q84.explanation: The traffic controller's raised arm prohibits movement despite the permitting signal of the traffic light's right section. However, drivers who at the moment the arm is raised are unable to stop before the "Stop line" without sudden braking are permitted to continue moving and pass through the intersection. (Rules, items 16, 19, 20)

g6-q85.text: When complying with the traffic signal, where must the driver stop?
g6-q85.explanation: The prohibiting red traffic light signal is operating, and sign 6.16 "Stop line" is mounted on the traffic light pole (there is no road marking). Under a prohibiting traffic light signal, the driver must stop before sign 6.16 "Stop line"—that is, right before the traffic light—and has no right to move forward to the intersecting roadway. (Rules, item 18, sign 6.16)

options: From the lane indicated in the image.
g6-q86.explanation: At the exact spot shown in the image. The overhead panel with a cross and arrow is a reversible-lane traffic light, and the double dashed line on the roadway marks the boundary of the reversible lane. This marking has a strict rule: you may cross it only when it is to your right. In the position shown, that line is to your left—meaning within the reversible-traffic section you have no permission to veer left and therefore to turn left. Thus, the left turn must be made where the marking breaks and the intersection allows the maneuver—right at that spot ahead of you in the image where the traffic light is green. That is the exact safety reason: the direction of travel in a reversible lane changes depending on time and traffic load, and the very lane you are tempted to enter may at that moment be assigned to oncoming traffic. Crossing a double dashed line in the wrong place means driving straight into the jaws of oncoming traffic. Worth remembering: before any maneuver on such a road, read the reversible-lane traffic light first. Until a green downward arrow is lit for that lane, the lane does not exist for you; and even with a green arrow, a left turn is made only at a permitted location, not at any point along the section. • "From the reversible-traffic lane" is the exact place where you must not cross the double dashed line: this marking is to your left, and crossing it is not permitted.

options: Straight ahead and to the right.
g6-q87.explanation: Straight movement and a right turn are permitted. The traffic controller stands before you with lowered arms and angled sideways to you: meaning you are entering the intersection from their side. With arms lowered or extended to the sides, from the controller's left and right sides a non-rail vehicle may go straight or turn right. Left turns and U-turns are closed. The blue rectangular sign on the right agrees with the same conclusion: its arrow points right and says that the road opening to the right is one-way, and the permitted direction of travel on it is to the right. Thus, a right turn not only matches the controller's signal but is also, from the sign's standpoint, the correct entry onto that road. If that same one-way road ran the opposite way, turning onto it would mean entering a prohibited path. Keep two points together. First, from the controller's side you always have two options, not one: the "straight only" option is the perennial trap in questions of this class. Second, the controller's gesture takes precedence over signs and markings, yet that precedence matters only where there is a conflict. Here there is none: the controller opened two directions and the sign confirms that same right direction, meaning both directives must be obeyed together. • "Straight only" is the restriction for rail vehicles: for a car from the controller's side, a right turn is open as well. • "Right only" is true when you face the controller's chest and their right arm is extended forward; in this image the arms are lowered and you approach from their side.

options: Straight ahead and to the right.
g6-q88.explanation: Only a right turn. This scene is governed simultaneously by two directives, and they must be read together. The first is the traffic controller's signal: their arms are lowered and you enter the intersection from their side, meaning from their standpoint both straight movement and a right turn are open. The second is the road marking: the car is in the right lane, and the arrow painted in that lane is a right-turn arrow, whereas the adjacent lane has a "straight and left" arrow. These two directives do not contradict each other. The controller permitted two directions, and your lane's marking puts only one of those two at your disposal. When two requirements do not clash, both must be obeyed: the result is that from this lane you may only turn right. If you wanted to go straight, you needed to change lanes before approaching the intersection. The reason for lane arrows is visible right here: their purpose is so drivers behind know where the car ahead will go. Someone sitting in a right-turn lane who suddenly goes straight cuts off the stream in the lane that expected clear passage. The exam trap is thinking the controller's presence completely cancels road markings: the priority of a controller's gesture kicks in only in cases of conflict, not under any circumstances. • "Straight and right" is precisely what the controller's signal allows, yet the arrow of the lane you are standing in took straight movement away from you. • "Straight only" agrees with neither your lane's arrow nor the single direction remaining after combining the two directives: your lane is the right-turn lane.

g6-q89.text: The arrows shown in the green traffic signal indicate that:
options: Traffic to the right is controlled by an additional traffic-signal section.
g6-q89.explanation: The black outline arrows (straight and left) shown on the main green traffic light signal inform drivers of the presence of an additional section and indicate that movement to the right is controlled by the additional section. They do not prohibit a right turn (which is performed when the green arrow of the additional section is lit). (Rules, item 10)

g6-q90.explanation: On the reversible-lane traffic lights located above the two left lanes of the road with sign 5.8 "Reversible traffic," the red "X"-shaped signals are lit. They prohibit entering those lanes, and on a four-lane two-way road crossing onto the oncoming side is prohibited altogether, so overtaking the truck is not permitted. (Rules, items 13, 53)

g6-q91.text: In which direction or directions may the driver continue in this situation?
options: The driver must wait for a permissive signal.
To the left and by making a U-turn.
g6-q91.explanation: The car is in the leftmost lane, from which sign 5.15.1 and marking 1.18 permit turning left. Simultaneously with the main red signal, the left arrow of the additional section is lit, and an arrow permitting a left turn (in the absence of a corresponding prohibitory sign) also permits a U-turn, so the driver may continue to the left and in the opposite direction. (Rules, item 8)

g6-q92.text: In this situation, entering the reversible traffic lane is:
options: Permitted only for the purpose of passing.
g6-q92.explanation: The reversible-lane traffic light located above the reversible-traffic lane displays a green downward-pointing arrow. This signal permits entering that reversible lane and driving along it, without being limited solely to the purpose of overtaking. (Rules, item 13)

g6-q93.text: Proceeding straight ahead from the indicated lane is:
options: Permitted only after the main green signal turns on.
g6-q93.explanation: Our car is in the right lane, and sign 5.15.1 "Lane directions" installed before the intersection indicates that from the right lane movement is permitted only to the right (straight and left only from the left lane). Consequently, driving straight ahead from that lane is prohibited even after the main green traffic light signal turns on. (Rules, item 51, sign 5.15.1)

options: Straight ahead and to the right.
g6-q94.explanation: The traffic controller's right arm is extended forward, and they face our car with their left side. Under this controller signal, non-rail vehicles approaching from the left side are permitted to move in all directions—straight ahead, right, left, and in the opposite direction. (Rules, item 16)

g6-q95.explanation: The traffic controller is standing with their back to our vehicle (right arm extended forward). From the back side of the traffic controller, movement of all vehicles is prohibited. (Rules, item 16)

g7-q1.text: Which vehicles are permitted to park?
options: The passenger car and the motorcycle.
g7-q1.explanation: Only the passenger car and the motorcycle. The sign on the left of the image is "No Parking" (a blue circle with a red border and one diagonal slash), yet underneath it is a plate depicting a truck. That plate narrows the scope of the prohibition: the parking ban applies only to trucks, not to all vehicles. Therefore, the yellow passenger car and the motorcycle may park here, whereas the blue truck marked "4 t" may not. The "Type of vehicle" plate is one of the most frequent exam topics because it changes the entire meaning of the main sign. Looking only at the round sign and choosing "all vehicles" is the most common mistake on such questions: always read the lower plate before deciding. The reason such selective restrictions exist is practical too. A parked truck occupies a substantial share of the road width, completely blocks visibility for drivers and pedestrians, and makes exiting a parking area or side road hazardous; whereas a passenger car or motorcycle in the same spot creates no such problem. Instead of closing the spot completely, the lawmaker removed only the source of obstruction. • "Only the motorcycle" needlessly prohibits the passenger car as well: the plate singled out only the truck. • "Only the truck" is the exact opposite of the answer: the truck is the one vehicle not allowed to park here. • "Only the passenger car" baselessly excludes the motorcycle: the motorcycle is also outside the ban and may park. • "All vehicles" is the error that happens when ignoring the plate: without it that option would be incorrect in the other direction, and with it the truck must be excluded.

options: On bridges, elevated roadways, and overpasses.
Under bridges, elevated roadways, and overpasses.
In all of the listed cases.
g7-q2.explanation: In all listed cases—both on bridges and overpasses, and underneath them. Parking is prohibited both on bridges and overpasses and underneath them, so the correct choice is "in all listed cases." Why is it prohibited on a bridge? A bridge's roadway is usually narrower than the road leading to it, so a parked car creates a sudden bottleneck right where a driver has neither room to maneuver nor a long line of sight. Why is it prohibited underneath? Supports and retaining walls block visibility, and a car parked there cannot be seen until the last moment. The official question bank has many "parking is prohibited" questions, and "all listed" often turns out right, yet do not rely on that as a shortcut. Evaluate each option on its merits. • Correct, but incomplete: parking under a bridge is also prohibited. • Correct, but incomplete: parking on a bridge is also prohibited.

g7-q3.text: Is it permitted to drop off a passenger at a location where a solid yellow line is marked on the upper surface of the curb and a “No Stopping” sign is posted?
options: Permitted if no public transit vehicles are present.
Permitted only for public transit vehicles.
g7-q3.explanation: Prohibited. The solid yellow line painted along the top of the curb marks on-site the zone of the "No Stopping" sign. The two mean the same thing and reinforce each other: within this zone not even a brief stop is permitted. Dropping off a passenger without stopping is impossible, so this action falls under the same ban. Keep clearly in mind the difference between "No Stopping" and "No Parking," because most errors come from right there. Where parking is prohibited, stopping to board or drop off passengers or load goods is still allowed. Where stopping is prohibited, however, stopping even for a few seconds is a violation, and the only exceptions are forced stops—such as stopping behind congestion or at an officer's direction. The reason for such strictness goes back to where the sign is placed. This sign is usually put in spots where a stopped car blinds visibility or blocks passage width: near an intersection, on a curve, in front of driveways, or on a single-lane street. A passenger getting out there steps onto the roadway inside traffic and in a blind spot, while your stopped car forces drivers behind to swerve abruptly into the next lane. To drop off a passenger, you must drive to the end of the sign's zone. • "Permitted" assumes a brief stop is an exception, whereas the "No Stopping" sign specifically targets such brief stops. • The absence of route vehicles creates no exception: the sign's effect does not depend on whether other vehicles are present or absent. • This option ties the restriction to public transit, whereas for a private car driver the ban is absolute and covers dropping off a passenger as well.

g7-q4.text: Does the prohibitory sign apply to the section of road where the driver has stopped?
g7-q4.explanation: In the image, after sign 3.27 "No Stopping," there is a break in the median strip marked by sign 6.3.1 "U-turn area," after which the truck has stopped. The effective zone of sign 3.27 extends up to the nearest intersection and is not interrupted at U-turn points or breaks in the median strip, so the prohibitory sign applies to this section as well. (Rules, sign 3.27)

g7-q5.text: Is parking the automobile at the indicated location permitted?
g7-q5.explanation: Permitted. The sign on the right is "End of one-way road": a blue square with a white upward arrow crossed out by a red diagonal line. The presence of this sign means the section where the car is parked is a one-way road. Within a built-up area on a one-way road, parking on the left side of the roadway is permitted for passenger cars and motorcycles; and the red car in the image is parked right along the left edge, along the building. The reason it differs from two-way roads is clear. On a two-way road, left-side parking means a departing driver must cross the oncoming lane and cut across oncoming traffic at the moment of pulling out with minimal visibility. On a one-way road there is no such oncoming stream: all vehicles travel the same way, so left-side parking neither blinds visibility nor requires maneuvering against traffic. Thus the law grants this permission only on a one-way road. Worth remembering: this permission has limits. Trucks exceeding the permitted mass may stop on the left side of a one-way road only for loading and unloading, not for parking. And all general bans—intersections, pedestrian crosswalks, route-vehicle stops—remain in force. • "Prohibited" seems right if you treat "park only on the right" as absolute; yet the one-way road sign activates the exact exception that allows a passenger car to park on the left.

g7-q6.text: Within what distance of a railroad crossing is parking prohibited?
g7-q6.explanation: Under the rules, parking closer than 50 m to railway crossings is prohibited. Among the listed options, only 25 m is a distance under 50 m, whereas at distances of 50 m, 100 m, 150 m, and 300 m parking is permitted. (Rules, item 86, sub-item 3)

g7-q7.text: In this situation, is stopping to drop off a passenger permitted?
options: Permitted if it does not interfere with the movement of public transit vehicles.
g7-q7.explanation: The lane for public transport (route) vehicles marked by sign 5.14 and marking "A" is separated from the rest of the roadway by a dashed marking. The rules permit entering a lane with such marking to drop off and pick up passengers, provided this does not obstruct the movement of route vehicles. (Rules, item 124)

g7-q8.text: Which driver is required to stop?
g7-q8.explanation: The driver of the passenger car. In the image, two pedestrians who got off the red bus are walking across the pedestrian crosswalk, while the yellow passenger car approaches that same crosswalk. The pedestrians are on the marking and in the car's path, so the car driver must stop before the crosswalk and let them finish crossing. The bus, however, has already passed the crosswalk and is stopped at the bus stop: the pedestrians are walking behind it and do not cross the bus's path, meaning it has no duty to stop again. Identifying who is actually in the pedestrians' path gives the whole answer. This situation is one of the most dangerous urban scenes and should be an alarm bell for you: wherever a bus stops at a bus stop, the likelihood of a pedestrian suddenly appearing in front of or behind it is high, and the bus body completely blocks your view. In such a spot, even if the crosswalk looks empty, you must slow down and be ready to stop. The general rule also states: at an uncontrolled pedestrian crosswalk, priority always belongs to a pedestrian who has stepped onto the crosswalk, and the driver must yield to them. • "The bus driver" sounds right if we assume the bus has not reached the crosswalk yet; yet the bus has passed the crosswalk and stopped at the stop, and the pedestrians do not cross it. • "Both drivers" is excessive caution: only the vehicle whose trajectory meets the path of pedestrians on the crosswalk must stop, and here that is only the passenger car.

options: To the left and by making a U-turn.
Straight ahead, to the left, and by making a U-turn.
g7-q9.explanation: In the leftmost lane, horizontal marking arrow 1.18 pointing left is shown. Marking permitting a left turn from the leftmost lane also permits a U-turn (driving in the opposite direction), whereas driving straight ahead is prohibited. (Rules, marking 1.18)

g7-q10.text: Which vehicles are permitted to park within the area where this traffic sign is in effect?
options: Vehicles driven by persons with disabilities and taxis with the taximeter activated.
g7-q10.explanation: On the right side of the road, sign 3.28 "No Parking" is installed. The effect of this sign does not extend to vehicles driven by (or transporting) persons with disabilities and taxis with a running taximeter, so only those vehicles are permitted to park within the sign's effective zone. (Rules, sign 3.28)

g7-q11.text: What does this pavement marking indicate?
options: A place for picking up and dropping off passengers.
A public transit vehicle stop and taxi parking area.
g7-q11.explanation: A stopping and parking place for route vehicles. The blue sign depicting a bus marks a stop for route (public transport) vehicles—that is, the point where buses and trolleybuses are allowed to stop to board and disembark passengers. This sign is a dedicated permission for route transit, not a general spot for any car wanting to drop off a passenger. This distinction has an important practical consequence for you. Within the stop zone, stopping and parking by other vehicles is prohibited, and the only narrow exception is picking up or dropping off passengers—and even then only if you do not obstruct route vehicles. The reason is tangible: a bus must be able to pull right up to the curb so passengers do not board from the roadway; a parked car forces the bus to stop in the second lane and let passengers out in the middle of the street. The question's trap is the other two options. "A place for boarding and disembarking passengers" is overly broad and omits that this spot is intended specifically for route transport. Adding taxis is also wrong because a taxi stand has its own separate sign with a different symbol. Behind the wheel, read the appearance of this sign as a warning: the chance of a bus stopping suddenly and pedestrians stepping out in front of or behind it is high, so slow down and keep your distance. • This description is too broad: the sign marks a stopping place for route vehicles, not a general boarding and alighting place for any vehicle. • Taxis have no place in this sign: a taxi stand has its own independent sign and symbol.

g7-q12.text: What does the solid yellow horizontal pavement marking indicate?
options: A location where stopping and parking of vehicles are prohibited.
A location where stopping is permitted to drop off passengers or unload the vehicle.
A location where parking of vehicles is prohibited.
g7-q12.explanation: Solid yellow horizontal marking line 1.4 marks places where both stopping and parking of vehicles are prohibited (unlike dashed yellow line 1.10, which prohibits only parking). It may be applied independently or together with sign 3.27. (Rules, marking 1.4)

g7-q13.text: Is the driver permitted to cross the solid pavement marking that indicates the boundaries of vehicle parking spaces?
g7-q13.explanation: Permitted. The image shows T-shaped solid white lines dividing parking spaces. Crossing these lines is not prohibited: if it were prohibited, pulling into a parking space would be impossible altogether. The main point of this question is breaking a mental habit: "a solid line means you cannot cross it" applies only to lines that separate traffic streams, mark lane boundaries, or mark the edge of the roadway. Parking-space markings serve a different function: they merely organize space and show where and how each car should stand. The safety reason here is the reverse of the first case. In a parking lot speeds are low, and there is no oncoming stream from which a line needs to separate you. The real hazard in that lot is sloppy parking, one car straddling two spaces, and doors suddenly opening in tight quarters—and that is precisely what this marking prevents. For the exam, identify each line's meaning by its function, not by whether it is solid or dashed. Wherever a line is the boundary of a parking space, crossing it is part of the act of parking itself. • "Prohibited" comes from overgeneralizing the rule about a solid line separating traffic lanes: if that generalization were true, entering any parking space would be impossible.

g7-q14.text: In which direction or directions indicated by the arrows is traffic permitted?
options: To the left and by making a U-turn.
Straight ahead, to the left, and by making a U-turn.
g7-q14.explanation: Straight only. A double solid line is painted down the middle of the roadway. The meaning of this marking is straightforward: crossing it for any reason is prohibited. Any maneuver requiring you to cross this line—a left turn and a U-turn—is thereby prohibited, and the only path remaining for the blue car is straight ahead. A double solid line is typically applied where there is either more than one lane in each direction or insufficient visibility to cross oncoming traffic. That is the exact safety reason: to turn left or make a U-turn you must cross the full width of the oncoming stream, and on a road where cars travel at steady speed, that means entering the path of someone who does not expect you and will not be able to brake in time. A common exam trap is seeing no prohibitory sign in the image and assuming everything is allowed. Yet a road marking, just like a sign, is a legal directive and can prohibit a maneuver on its own. Practical point: to make a U-turn or go left, drive to the nearest permitted spot—such as an intersection where the marking breaks or a spot where the line becomes dashed—and maneuver there rather than jumping across a solid line mid-road. • Both a left turn and driving in the opposite direction require crossing the double solid line, and this single marking closes both maneuvers. • Straight movement is stated accurately, but adding a left turn and U-turn invalidates that option: a double solid line does not allow crossing the oncoming path.

g7-q15.text: What does this pavement marking indicate?
options: A pedestrian crossing where traffic is controlled by a traffic signal.
A location where a bicycle path crosses the roadway.
A location where a pedestrian path crosses the roadway.
g7-q15.explanation: A place where a cycle path crosses the roadway. In the image, two parallel rows of small squares are visible crossing the width of the roadway like a corridor with an empty middle. This pattern is characteristic of where a cycle path intersects a roadway. Telling it apart from a pedestrian crosswalk is easy if you look at the shape of the stripes: a pedestrian crosswalk is applied in wide, long bars along the car's direction of travel and looks like a striped band from afar, whereas a bicycle crossing is marked only by two dotted borders. The practical importance of this distinction lies in approach speed. A cyclist reaches the roadway several times faster than a pedestrian and can appear suddenly from behind a tree, hedge, or parked car—meaning a sight distance sufficient for a pedestrian is insufficient for a bicycle. Seeing this marking, slow down before reaching it and watch both sides. The exam trap is the option that adds the word "traffic light": the marking itself says nothing about whether the location is controlled by a traffic light or not. The type of marking identifies the type of road user, not the method of traffic control. • This option contains two errors at once: the marking pattern does not belong to a pedestrian crosswalk, and a marking never announces the presence of a traffic light. • A pedestrian crosswalk is applied in wide solid bars along the car's direction of travel, not in two rows of small squares.

g7-q16.text: How many lanes does a road have when traffic flows in opposite directions are separated by double solid lines?
g7-q16.explanation: Four lanes or more. The marking of two parallel solid lines you see in the image separates opposing traffic streams on roads with four or more traffic lanes. In other words, the moment you spot such a marking on the roadway, without counting lanes, you know there are at least two in each direction. The safety logic of this choice is speed and volume. On a wide road with four or more lanes, speeds are higher and speed differences between lanes are greater: if stream separation were done with a single line, any slight drift would mean a high-speed head-on collision. Beyond the legal ban, two solid lines create a wider, more noticeable band that reduces perception errors. For a driver, the practical rule matters more than the lane count: crossing two solid lines or straddling part of them is prohibited in all cases—neither for passing, nor for a U-turn, nor for a left turn. If you want to go left, you must reach the first intersection or permitted spot where the marking breaks. The exam trap is the "two" and "three" lane options: on such roads a single solid or dashed line is normally applied, not two solid lines. • On a two-lane road a single solid or dashed line is normally enough for separation: two solid lines are not meant for that width. • "Two or three" combines two rough guesses, repeating the same error under a guise of caution. • On a three-lane road the middle lane must stay accessible to both directions: two solid lines eliminate that very possibility.

g7-q17.text: What do the arrows marked on the roadway warn about?
options: They warn the driver of an approaching hazardous section of road.
They warn of an approaching end of the traffic lane.
They indicate the direction of a hazardous turn in the road.
g7-q17.explanation: Warns of approaching the end of a lane. In the image, several curved arrows are painted on the roadway leading from your lane into the adjacent lane, and to their left a solid line separating streams is visible. The meaning of these arrows is a single message: the lane you are in ends ahead, so change lanes into the adjacent one in advance. The reason for this warning is to buy time. A safe lane change requires a suitable gap in the neighboring stream, and finding that gap at speed takes several seconds. If a driver notices it only at the taper point, they will have either to brake hard or dart into the adjacent lane with a sharp turn of the steering wheel—two moves that lead to chain-reaction crashes in dense traffic. Proper behavior after spotting the arrows: adjust speed, check your mirror and blind spot, turn on your indicator, and change lanes at the first safe opportunity, rather than driving to the very last meter only to squeeze into the line. The exam trap is confusing markings with signs: warnings about a "dangerous section" and "direction of a dangerous curve" are given by signs, not pavement arrows. Wherever a message is painted on the roadway surface, look for a meaning related to lane organization. • Warning about a dangerous road section is the job of warning signs: pavement arrows speak about lane organization. • The direction of a dangerous curve is shown by a special sign and roadside devices, not by arrows painted along the lane.

g7-q18.text: Which of these pavement-marking lines is used to designate lanes with reversible traffic?
g7-q18.explanation: Line 2—that is, two parallel dashed lines. Four samples are shown side by side in the image: line 1 is two parallel solid lines, line 2 is two parallel dashed lines, line 3 is a single dashed line, and line 4 is a yellow dashed line. The boundaries of lanes in which traffic is reversible are marked by two parallel dashed lines—sample number two. The choice of this shape is not accidental. The doubling tells you there may be oncoming traffic on the other side of the boundary, while the dashing means this direction is not permanent and changes depending on time. A double solid line conveys nothing like that because its meaning is a permanent, impassable boundary. A practical point that often appears on the exam: on a road with reversible lanes, the permitted direction is determined by special traffic lights above the lanes. When those traffic lights are turned off, entry into a lane bounded on both sides by such marking is not permitted—meaning an off traffic light is not permission. When comparing options, look first at the number of lines, then at whether they are solid or dashed. The yellow color in sample 4 does not relate to lane boundaries at all and indicates stopping and parking restrictions near the roadway edge. • Two parallel solid lines permanently separate opposing flows on wide roads and cannot be crossed: such a boundary cannot mark a lane whose direction changes. • A single dashed line is an ordinary lane boundary and in no way indicates a change in traffic direction. • Adding line 3 to the answer ruins the defining feature: line 3 is not doubled, meaning it cannot be the boundary of a reversible lane. • The yellow line in the image relates to stopping and parking restrictions near the roadway edge, not lane boundaries: combining it with line 3 compounds two errors.

g7-q19.text: Where is the solid yellow line indicating locations where stopping and parking are prohibited marked?
options: Near the edge of the roadway.
Near the edge of the roadway or on the upper surface of the curb.
Only on the upper surface of the curb.
g7-q19.explanation: At the edge of the roadway or along the top of the curb. A solid yellow line—the one shown in the image as continuous, with no breaks—marks places where stopping and parking are prohibited. Two placements are possible for it: it is applied either at the edge of the roadway or on the top face of the curb along the street. Both cases are equivalent, and the absence of one does not mean the ban is invalid. The reason for such flexibility is practical: on streets with a high continuous curb, curb paint withstands snow, mud, and vehicle tires better and is visible from farther away; where the curb is unsuitable, the line is applied directly on the asphalt at the roadway edge. Worth remembering, and where the exam trap lies: a solid yellow line is never applied down the middle of the roadway between traffic lanes—separating directions and lanes is the job of white markings. Yellow at the edge means "do not stop here." Its counterpart is the dashed yellow line, which prohibits only parking and leaves brief stopping permitted: do not confuse solid with dashed. • "On the roadway" is the place for white markings separating traffic lanes: the yellow no-stopping line is never painted in the middle of the roadway. • "Only at the edge of the roadway" is half the answer, omitting the common case of applying this line to the curb. • "Only along the curb" is the other half: on streets without a suitable curb, the same line is applied at the roadway edge and is completely valid.

g7-q20.text: With which traffic sign may a broken yellow pavement marking be used?
options: “No Parking on Odd-Numbered Days of the Month.”
g7-q20.explanation: Together with the "No Parking" sign. Near the curb or roadway edge there are two yellow markings, and they should be memorized as a pair. A dashed yellow line marks on-site the effective zone of the "No Parking" sign, whereas a solid yellow line marks the effective zone of the "No Stopping" sign. The shape of the marking reflects the strictness of the ban: dashed is less strict, solid is stricter. This cue simplifies a driver's everyday work. If you missed the sign or it was hidden behind a tree or truck, the color of the curb defines your position. A dashed yellow line means you may stop briefly to pick up or drop off passengers or load goods, but you have no right to park the car. A solid yellow line means not even a brief stop is permitted. The safety logic of this distinction is equally clear. Where parking is banned, the problem is long-term occupancy of space and reduction of usable road width: a short, controlled stop is still tolerable. Where stopping is banned, however, even those few seconds blind visibility or block traffic—near an intersection, on a curve, on a bridge, or in a tunnel. The trap in the third option is that even/odd-day parking signs have no accompanying yellow marking and are not indicated by curb markings. • The "No Stopping" sign is accompanied by a solid yellow line, not a dashed one: a stricter ban has a continuous marking. • Signs for parking on certain days of the month are not accompanied by this marking: their restriction is time-based, not a zone marked on the curb.

g7-q21.text: Which vehicles are permitted to proceed in the right lane of the roadway?
g7-q21.explanation: Only route (public transport) vehicles. The letter "A" on the roadway marks a lane dedicated to route vehicles, and in this image that lane is separated from the rest of the roadway by a solid line. A solid line means a closed boundary: no other car has the right to enter this lane, and only route vehicles operating along a designated route may use it. The purpose of such dedication is to maintain public-transit speed during rush hours. A bus stuck behind a line of passenger cars falls off schedule, and the very commuters who could travel without a car get back behind the wheel. Yet for a driver, the safety point is more important: traffic in this lane has a different flow pattern—frequent stops at bus stops and slow acceleration. A passenger car entering such a lane both violates the rules and creates a rear-end collision risk. What to remember for the exam: do not confuse a solid line with a dashed one. When this lane's boundary is solid, entry is prohibited in all cases. Where the boundary is dashed, other cars may enter only to turn right or near the roadway edge to pick up or drop off passengers, and even then without obstructing route vehicles. • "All motor vehicles" destroys the very function of a dedicated lane: if everyone were allowed in, there would be no need to mark it with "A." • A taxi, as hired transport, is not considered a route vehicle operating on a designated route: adding it to the list is tempting, but wrong. • A bicycle is not the subject of this marking at all: a cycle lane has its own separate marking and its own sign.

g7-q22.text: This pavement marking has the following meaning:
options: It indicates curbside parking spaces where the positioning of motor vehicles is specified.
It indicates locations where stopping of motor vehicles is prohibited.
It indicates public transit vehicle stops and taxi parking areas.
g7-q22.explanation: Marking stops for route vehicles and taxi stands. The zigzag shape you see in the image is painted along the edge of the roadway and marks the zone of a bus stop and taxi stand. Its broken shape is intentionally different from every other marking so it can be recognized from afar, even at night and in rain. The safety function of this marking is to keep the roadway edge clear. If private cars stop in the stop zone, the bus is forced to let passengers off away from the curb and effectively in the middle of the roadway: the passenger then steps out between two rows of cars, and a driver in the next lane cannot see them. A substantial share of urban pedestrian collisions happens in this exact scenario. Thus, within this marking's zone, stopping and parking by other vehicles are not permitted: the only exception is boarding and disembarking passengers, and only if it does not obstruct route vehicles. The exam trap is the "marking parking spaces" option: both relate to a stationary car, which is why they seem similar. Distinguish by shape: a parking space is bounded by straight lines, a stop by a zigzag. • Parking spaces are bounded by straight, even lines: a broken zigzag line is never used to show how to park. • This option confuses a consequence of the marking with its purpose: it is true that parking is banned in a stop zone, yet the main message of the marking is to identify the stop's location, not to declare a general no-parking zone.

options: A narrowing of the roadway where the number of traffic lanes in the given direction decreases.
A location where the driver must stop, if necessary, to yield to vehicles proceeding on the intersecting road.
An approach to a location where stopping is prohibited.
g7-q23.explanation: The place where, if necessary, you must stop to yield. In the image, across the width of the lane, a row of white triangles is painted pointing toward the driver. This marking is the asphalt equivalent of "Give Way": it shows the point before which, if necessary, you must stop to yield to vehicles on the intersecting road. The key words are "if necessary." Unlike a stop line, which accompanies a "stop" sign and requires a full, unconditional stop, this marking requires you to slow down to full control and stop only when the way is not clear. If the cross stream is empty, stopping is not mandatory. The placement of the triangles is not accidental either: they are applied at the point where the driver has the best view of the intersecting road while not yet having entered its travel path. Every meter you stop beyond this line means both occupying part of the intersecting roadway and losing sight angle. The exam trap is confusing this pattern with a roadway-narrowing warning: narrowing and lane endings are announced by curved arrows, not triangles. • Roadway narrowing and a reduction in lanes are warned of by curved arrows on the asphalt, not a row of triangles. • A stopping ban is announced by a longitudinal marking along the roadway edge and a corresponding sign: transverse triangles speak of priority, not parking.

g7-q24.text: Is it permitted to enter a channelizing island marked with wide white lines?
g7-q24.explanation: Channelizing islands marked with wide white stripes (markings 1.16.1–1.16.3) serve to separate traffic flows and are outlined by solid lines. Driving onto such channelizing islands (including for stopping or reversing) is prohibited. (Rules, markings 1.16.1–1.16.3)

g7-q25.text: What should the driver do when approaching an intersection with a “Stop Line” pavement marking and a green traffic signal?
options: Stop at the “Stop Line” and then resume driving.
Proceed through the intersection without stopping.
g7-q25.explanation: Continue through the intersection without stopping. A "stop line" by itself is not a command to stop: it merely marks the spot where you must stop if stopping becomes necessary. The duty to stop is created by a red signal, a yellow signal, a "stop" sign, or a police officer's signal—not by the pavement marking. When the traffic light is green, movement is permitted and you must pass through the intersection without stopping. The safety reason for this rule lies in traffic-flow continuity. A driver approaching from behind at urban speed expects the queue to move on green; stopping suddenly at a stop line is one of the most frequent causes of rear-end collisions at intersections. Moreover, every unnecessary stop wastes several seconds of limited green time and stretches the queue back to the previous intersection. Worth remembering: a stop line is a "stopping place," not an "order to stop." Therein lies the exam trap: the line's name nudges the mind toward stopping. Naturally, a green signal is not an unconditional permit: if there is congestion beyond the intersection and you risk getting stuck in the middle, you have no right to enter; you must also yield to pedestrians finishing a crossing and to vehicles whose maneuver in the intersection is unfinished. • Stopping at a stop line is mandatory only when a prohibiting signal or sign is present: on a green signal, stopping is neither necessary nor safe because the car behind expects movement.

g7-q26.text: What does this pavement marking indicate?
options: A location where a bicycle path crosses the roadway.
A location designated for driving livestock across the road.
g7-q26.explanation: Horizontal marking 1.15, consisting of white squares arranged in two rows, indicates the place where a bicycle path crosses the roadway. A pedestrian crosswalk is marked with marking 1.14.1 or 1.14.2 (wide stripes). (Rules, marking 1.15)

g7-q27.text: Where must the driver stop the vehicle when this pavement marking is present?
options: At least 5 m before the pavement marking.
g7-q27.explanation: Directly before the marking. The white triangles painted across the width of the lane in the image are your stopping boundary: if you need to stop, you must stop before them—not on top of them and not several meters back. The reason is sight-line geometry. This marking is applied at a point that is both outside the path of vehicles on the intersecting road and gives the best viewing angle onto that road. If you pull past the line, the front of your car enters someone else's path, and the main-road driver will have to brake or swerve. If you stop noticeably early, your view of the intersecting road is blocked and you will have to pull forward in two stages, needlessly lengthening the line behind you. One more point: "if necessary" means a full stop is not always mandatory—if the intersecting road is empty, slowing down and continuing raises no objection. But if you decide to stop, the stopping point is this line. The exam trap is the number "5 meters." It comes to mind from other rules, such as stopping restrictions near a pedestrian crosswalk or intersection, and has nothing to do with this marking. Whenever you see a precise numerical option, verify that the number is actually written for this exact situation. • Stopping right on the marking means the front of the car has entered the conflict zone: in that position both your own view is limited and you obstruct the intersecting road. • The number "5 meters" was carried over into this question from other stopping restrictions: no numerical distance is set for this marking, and stopping farther back only blinds your view.

g7-q28.text: What does this pavement marking mean?
options: A traffic lane designated for public transit vehicles.
A traffic lane designated for special-purpose vehicles.
It indicates the boundaries of traffic lanes where reversible traffic control is in effect.
g7-q28.explanation: The boundaries of traffic lanes in which reversible control is implemented. The image shows two parallel dashed lines. This exact combination—doubling plus dashing—has a specific meaning: the boundary of a lane whose direction of travel is not permanent and changes under reversible control. A reversible lane is used on roads where traffic demand runs in opposite directions morning and evening: instead of widening the road, one middle lane is given to the busier direction during each period. The permitted direction is announced by special traffic lights mounted above that lane. Two practical points for the exam: first, when reversible traffic lights are off, entering a lane bounded on both sides by such marking is not permitted—an off traffic light does not mean the lane is free. Second, before entering or leaving such a lane, verify that the overhead traffic light confirms your movement. The reason for strictness is clear: an error in determining direction in such a lane leads at worst to a head-on collision. Therefore this marking's shape is intentionally distinct from any ordinary boundary so it can be recognized at a glance. • A dedicated lane for route vehicles is marked by the letter "A" on the roadway and a single longitudinal line, not two parallel dashed lines. • This option exists solely to resemble the right answer: double dashed marking relates to reversing traffic direction, not to a specific vehicle class.

g7-q29.text: Is it permitted to make a U-turn at the indicated location?
g7-q29.explanation: Permitted: the center marking is dashed and may be crossed. In this image, the decisive factor is the type of marking down the middle of the road: the center line is dashed, and a dashed line may be crossed from either side. Since there is no sign prohibiting a U-turn, no intersection, no pedestrian crosswalk, no bridge, and no tunnel in the image, nothing prevents a U-turn. A common error is that an applicant treats a U-turn as inherently a "prohibited act." A U-turn is permitted except at specified places: those places are a pedestrian crosswalk, a tunnel, a bridge or overpass and the space beneath them, a railway crossing, a route-vehicle stop, and any place where road visibility in at least one direction is less than 100 meters. In the image the road is straight and open, and none of those conditions applies. Yet "permitted" does not mean "safe." Before making a U-turn, signal left, check mirrors and blind spot, hug as close to the right edge as possible, and then complete the maneuver without lingering stationary across the oncoming path: throughout the maneuver, priority belongs to vehicles moving in the oncoming direction. Worth remembering: dashed means "may be crossed," solid means "do not cross." Identifying the marking type by itself resolves the answer to many questions about U-turns and passing. • Treating a U-turn as prohibited here comes from thinking U-turns are banned in principle; whereas with a dashed marking and none of the prohibited locations present, there are no grounds for a ban.

g7-q30.text: When this pavement marking is present, is the driver of a bus operating on a tourist route permitted to enter the lane marked “A”?
g7-q30.explanation: The lane for route (public transport) vehicles marked with the letter "A" is separated from the rest of the roadway by a dashed marking. When entering (turning onto) a road with such a lane, a bus operating on a tourist route is permitted to enter that lane provided it immediately changes into the adjacent lane. (Rules, item 124)

g7-q31.text: What does the wide broken-line pavement marking indicate?
options: The boundary between the roadway and the shoulder.
The boundary between a main traffic lane of the roadway and an acceleration lane.
The boundary between a main traffic lane of the roadway and a deceleration lane.
g7-q31.explanation: The boundary between an acceleration lane and the main roadway. In the image, an entrance ramp approaches the main roadway from the left past a painted island, and from the end of that island the boundary between the added lane and the main roadway is marked by a wide dashed white line. It is specifically the width of the strokes that distinguishes this line from an ordinary lane boundary. The message of this marking is simple: the lane you are in is auxiliary, not main. If you are coming from the entrance ramp, your task is to build up to the speed of the main stream along this lane and then merge into a suitable gap. Entering at low speed is the most dangerous thing you can do at a merge point, because a large speed difference leaves little reaction time for a driver approaching from behind. That is why the boundary is painted dashed: crossing it is part of the merge maneuver itself. There is a practical rule for the other side too: if you are driving on the main roadway, expect entering vehicles at such points and yield space when possible. The exam trap is confusing this line with the shoulder boundary: the boundary between the roadway and shoulder is marked by a solid edge line and is neither wide nor dashed. • The boundary between the roadway and shoulder is marked by a solid edge line: in the image the line is wide and dashed and is painted where the entrance ramp joins, not along the outer edge of the road. • The geometry of the image shows an entrance ramp joining the main roadway—that is, a place where the driver needs to gain speed: a deceleration lane is used at a roadway exit point, not at a merge point.

g7-q32.text: Which automobile is permitted to stop within the area where these signs are in effect?
options: The yellow automobile displaying the “Disabled” identification sign.
g7-q32.explanation: The yellow car with the "Disabled" sign. The round blue sign with a red cross is "No Stopping," and within its zone not even a brief stop is permitted. However, underneath it is a plate bearing the wheelchair symbol: the meaning of this plate is that the ban above does not apply to vehicles displaying the "Disabled" sign. Thus there are two cars in the scene, and their status differs. The red car has no badge and is stopped inside the sign's effective zone, meaning it is committing a violation. The yellow car displays the "Disabled" sign and is precisely the vehicle the plate exempted from the ban, meaning its stop is lawful. General rule to take away from this question: plates under a main sign alter its scope of application, and without reading them you cannot judge the main sign. A plate may define the effective zone, effective hours, vehicle type, or an exempted group. Make it a habit to read every sign together with the plate below it, not in isolation. A practical point matters too: the exemption belongs to a vehicle bearing the official "Disabled" sign, and arbitrarily placing that sign on a car that does not meet the legal requirements is itself a violation. • The red car has no exempting sign and is stopped inside the "No Stopping" sign's zone. • "Both cars" means you treated the red one as permitted too, whereas the exemption applies only to the vehicle with the "Disabled" sign. • "Neither" ignores the plate beneath the main sign: it is precisely that plate that exempts the vehicle with the "Disabled" sign from the ban.

g7-q33.text: In which image has the driver stopped correctly to drop off passengers?
g7-q33.explanation: In the left image. Stopping on a pedestrian crosswalk and closer than 5 meters before it is prohibited, and dropping off a passenger creates no exception to this ban. In image 1, the car is stopped by the curb and outside the prohibited zone: the "5 m" arrow shows the exact minimum distance required by law. In image 2, the blue van has stopped directly on the yellow pedestrian marking and blocked the pedestrians' path, forcing a pedestrian to walk around the car and step out into the roadway. The safety reason for this rule is "visibility." A car stopped near a crosswalk acts like a curtain: a pedestrian stepping out from behind it cannot be seen until the last moment, and a driver in the next lane has no time to brake. Those few meters of clearance are what give both sides reaction time: most pedestrian strikes at crosswalks begin with precisely such blocked visibility. A common exam trap is taking stop duration as the criterion and thinking "a few seconds to drop off a passenger won't hurt." The law's criterion is the stopping location, not its duration: the moment your wheels are on the crosswalk, the violation has already occurred. • Tempting because both cars are parked neatly against the curb, yet image 2 shows stopping on a pedestrian crosswalk, which is unacceptable in any way. • In the right image, the van stopped directly on the pedestrian crosswalk: that is the most obvious form of prohibited stopping, not the correct one.

g7-q34.text: The signal to stop a train is:
options: A circular motion of the arm (during daylight, with a brightly colored cloth or another clearly visible object; at night, with a torch or lantern).
An arm raised above the head holding a disk or red flag.
An arm extended forward and moved up and down.
g7-q34.explanation: In the event of a forced stop on a railway crossing, the stop signal given to the train driver is a circular motion of the arm (during the day with a piece of brightly colored cloth or any clearly visible object; at night with a torch or lantern). Arm signals extended or waved in any other way do not constitute a stop signal. (Rules, item 112)

g7-q35.text: In populated areas, on roads with one traffic lane in each direction and no tram tracks in the center, stopping and parking on the left side of the road are:
g7-q35.explanation: Permitted. Within a built-up area, on a road that has only one traffic lane in each direction and no tram tracks in the middle, stopping and parking on the left side of the roadway are permitted. This is the only standard two-way case where the law allows stopping on the left. The logic of the rule comes down to traffic-flow behavior. On a narrow road with one lane per direction and at low urban speeds, a car stopped on the left creates no surprise for any driver: it is seen from afar, and passing around it is straightforward. Yet as soon as there are two or more lanes per direction, the situation changes: there, a driver traveling at speed in the left lane suddenly encounters a stationary obstacle and is forced to swerve lanes abruptly. Tram tracks in the middle are a separate reason: a stopped car blocks the tramway, and a tram cannot swerve. Worth remembering: three conditions must be met simultaneously—a built-up area, one traffic lane per direction, and no tram tracks in the middle. If even one of the three is missing, the answer flips. Remember that outside a built-up area there is no such permission at all. • This option extends the "always stop on the right" rule to everything, whereas the law carved out an explicit exception for this exact case: built-up area, one lane per direction, no tram tracks.

g7-q36.text: At what distance from the “Stop Line” or the “STOP” sign must a vehicle be stopped in order to yield to an approaching train?
options: Immediately at the “Stop Line” and/or the sign.
g7-q36.explanation: Directly before the "stop line" or the "Stop without stopping prohibited" (STOP) sign. The stopping point at a railway crossing is determined not by a number in meters, but by the on-site marking or sign. If a stop line is painted or a "Stop" sign is installed, you must stop directly before them. If neither is present, then the standard safe distance from the rails becomes the criterion. The reason for this order is engineering. The stop line and sign are placed at the exact point where the driver has the best view along the railway line in both directions while still remaining outside the clearance danger zone of a passing train. The crossing designer accounted for grade, road curvature, trees, and buildings when picking this point. If you stop several meters farther or closer based on your own estimate, you will either enter the train's clearance envelope or lose sight distance. What to remember for the exam: whenever a question puts several numbers in front of you and one option says "directly before the stop line or sign," that option is the answer. Numbers are needed only when there is no marking or sign at all. And in practice this stop must be a full stop, not a mere slowdown: at a crossing a train can neither swerve nor stop in a short distance, so the entire burden of judgment is on you. • 1.5 m is a number invented for this situation: when there is a stop line or sign, distance in meters is meaningless. • 2.5 m is wrong for the same reason: the stopping point is defined by the marking/sign, not the driver's guess. • 5 m applies to other situations and is not a standard for stopping past a stop line or sign. • 10 m is a number that takes effect only in the absence of a stop line and sign, and is measured relative to the nearest rail, not relative to the stop line or sign itself.

g7-q37.text: Is stopping at the indicated location permitted?
g7-q37.explanation: Prohibited. The solid yellow line painted at the edge of the roadway along the curb prohibits stopping along its entire length. In the image, the red car is stopped right on this yellow line close against the curb, meaning it is committing a violation. This marking is applied where even one car stopping creates a pinch point—in front of a courtyard or building entrance, in bottlenecks, before curves, and where the roadway is narrow. In this very image, the building comes straight out to the roadway, and a stopped car both blocks passing drivers' visibility and takes away their room to maneuver. Unlike a sign, which applies only from where it is posted, a yellow marking is valid from where it begins to as far as it continues, and the driver must watch its extent on the ground. The key point that recurs repeatedly on the exam is the difference between the two yellow lines at the curb: solid yellow means no stopping, even for a few seconds to pick up or drop off, whereas dashed yellow means no parking while allowing a brief stop. If you confuse them, you will miss half the questions in this section. • The car is stopped neatly beside the curb, and that tidy look is deceptive, yet the solid yellow line beneath its wheels is the very ban that makes that appearance irrelevant.

g7-q38.text: Is the automobile permitted to stop at this location?
options: Prohibited because the distance between the broken pavement marking and the stopped vehicle is less than 3 m.
Prohibited on even-numbered days of the month.
g7-q38.explanation: Permitted. The round blue sign with a red border and one diagonal slash mounted on the post by the building is "No Parking," not "No Stopping." This sign closes only long-term parking and leaves short stops open—for picking up or dropping off passengers and loading or unloading. In the image, the driver has stopped at the sidewalk and a passenger is about to get in—precisely what the sign does not prohibit. Tell these two signs apart by the number of diagonal lines: one line means no parking, a cross (two lines) means no stopping. That single glance solves half the questions in this chapter. The lawmaker's logic is that a stopped car with a driver behind the wheel can pull away at any moment and creates no permanent obstruction; whereas a car abandoned for hours deprives everyone else of curb space and blocks driveways and sight lines. Pay attention to the option mentioning "a distance of less than 3 meters": that rule exists, but it applies only when the center marking of the road is solid. The marking on this street is dashed, meaning it simply does not apply here. • The 3-meter rule exists, but applies to a solid marking: the marking on this road is dashed and creates no such restriction. • Even- and odd-day parking has no such status in Armenia's traffic rules, and no sign in the image refers to the day of the month.

g7-q39.text: Which vehicle driver has violated the parking rules?
options: The driver of the blue automobile.
The driver of the red automobile.
Both drivers have violated the rules.
Neither driver has violated the rules.
g7-q39.explanation: Both drivers. Two separate violations are combined in a single image. The round blue sign with a red border and one diagonal slash is "No Parking," and it covers the side of the road on which it is posted: the blue car is parked right next to this sign inside its effective zone. The square blue sign with an upward arrow further announces that the road has one-way traffic. That one-way traffic sign is the main trap of the question: drivers have learned that in a built-up area on a one-way road parking on the left is also permitted, and immediately excuse the red car. However, that permission applies only to stopping beside the roadway, not climbing onto the sidewalk; and the red car is parked completely on the sidewalk, tight against the building. The safety reason is plain: the sidewalk is the pedestrian's only safe space. When a car occupies it, a pedestrian—or worse, a stroller, a wheelchair, a child—is forced onto the roadway, and because of the very parked car that hides them from drivers' eyes. Rule to remember: the "No Parking" sign closes only its own side, whereas the ban on parking on a sidewalk needs no sign and applies everywhere. • It is true that the blue car is parked inside the "No Parking" sign's zone, yet choosing only it means ignoring the red car up on the sidewalk. • The red car indeed violated, yet the blue one is parked directly under the "No Parking" sign and cannot be considered blameless. • The one-way traffic sign creates the impression that parking is open on both sides: yet neither the "No Parking" sign nor the ban on standing on a sidewalk may be ignored.

g7-q40.text: Outside populated areas, where is parking for extended rest, overnight stays, or other purposes permitted?
options: On the shoulders of the road.
In areas designated for parking or outside the boundaries of the road.
On the right side of the roadway, provided it does not interfere with other vehicle traffic.
On the left side of the road, provided road traffic safety is ensured.
g7-q40.explanation: Outside built-up areas, parking for long-term rest, overnight stays, and similar purposes is permitted only at designated rest areas or off the road. On road shoulders or roadway edges, parking for long-term rest or overnight stays is prohibited. (Rules, item 82)

g7-q41.text: Stopping is prohibited if the distance between the solid line and the stopped vehicle is:
g7-q41.explanation: In the image, the arrow indicates the distance between the stopped car and the solid line. According to the rules, stopping is prohibited if the distance between the stopped vehicle and a solid line (except a line marking the edge of the roadway) is less than 3 m, and among the given options the only prohibited value is 2.5 meters. (Rules, item 84, sub-item 3)

g7-q42.text: If traffic across a railroad crossing is prohibited and there are no traffic signals, traffic signs, pavement markings, or barrier gate, the driver must stop:
options: At least 5 m from the nearest rail.
At least 7 m from the nearest rail.
At least 10 m from the nearest rail.
g7-q42.explanation: At least 10 meters from the nearest rail. For a railway crossing, the law sets a priority chain of "stopping places." If there is a traffic light, a "stop" sign, a stop marking, or a barrier, you must stop before that element. Yet when none of these is present and passage is prohibited, the only remaining reference point is the rail itself, and you must stop at least 10 meters from the nearest rail. The safety reason for this distance is simple and purely physical: a train's body and cars overhang the width of the rails, sway sideways at speed, and the slipstream behind a train can pull in light objects. Ten meters also gives you an adequate view both ways along the track and, if the car stalls, leaves a safe margin to push or reverse it clear. Stopping right up against the rail means any slight braking error or slip puts you in the path of a train whose braking distance is measured in hundreds of meters. A common exam trap is mixing up the numbers 5 and 10. Remember it this way: 5 meters goes with the barrier, 10 meters goes with the rail. Whenever the word "rail" appears in a question and there is no crossing equipment, the answer is 10 meters. • 5 meters is a real number in crossing rules, but it is the stopping distance from a barrier, not from a rail: that exact substitution is the most common error on this question. • 7 meters is not set for any stopping case at a crossing and is included only to fill the gap between 5 and 10.

g7-q43.text: Within what distance of a railroad crossing is vehicle parking prohibited?
g7-q43.explanation: 15 m—the only distance in this list that lies inside the prohibited zone. The rule says: on a railway crossing and closer than 50 meters to it, parking is prohibited. The question does not ask for the number in the rule, but at which of these four distances parking is prohibited. 150 and 100 meters are clearly outside the strip. 50 meters is the boundary itself, and the "less than 50 meters" ban does not include it. That leaves 15 meters—squarely inside the prohibited strip. The safety reason is keeping the area around the rails clear. A driver approaching a crossing must see the rails in both directions as well as the crossing signs and traffic lights: an abandoned car blocks that exact view. More importantly, if a car stalls on the rails or a queue behind the barrier grows, clear space must remain to back up and clear the crossing. A train can neither swerve nor stop in a short distance. Keep two points separate: this number applies to **parking**; **stopping** right on the crossing is prohibited under all circumstances, even for a few seconds. This same question also sometimes appears with the list 300/150/100/50/25, where the answer is 25 meters: the rule is the same 50 meters, only the single number inside the strip changed. If you memorize the rule rather than the list, you will answer both versions correctly. • 50 meters is the rule's own number and thus the most tempting option: yet the legal wording is "less than 50 meters," meaning parking at exactly 50 meters is not prohibited. • 100 meters is twice the prohibited strip, and parking there is allowed. • 150 meters is virtually the length of a city block: at that distance from a crossing there is no parking ban.

g7-q44.text: Which answer correctly identifies the drivers who have violated the stopping rules?
options: The drivers of the red automobile and the motorcycle.
The driver of the blue automobile.
The drivers of all the vehicles.
g7-q44.explanation: The drivers of all vehicles. The round blue sign with a red border and a cross is "No Stopping"—meaning neither parking nor even a brief stop. The plate beneath it with arrows pointing both up and down announces that you are inside the sign's effective zone and that the ban continues both before and after the sign. All three vehicles in the image—the blue pickup truck, the red passenger car, and the yellow motorcycle by the sign—are stopped in this interval, meaning all three drivers have committed a violation. Being close to or far from the sign post makes no difference: what matters is being inside the declared zone. Such a sign is usually installed where even one car stopping breaks road capacity or blinds visibility—near driveways, in bottlenecks, and along busy routes. When several cars stop in such an interval, traffic is forced to swerve lanes abruptly, and that is where rear-end and side collisions happen. Two common traps: first, confusing the cross with the single-slash "No Parking" sign; second, thinking a motorcycle is exempt because of its small size. No-stopping signs have nothing to do with vehicle type. • This option sees the two vehicles closer to the sign and misses the blue pickup truck stopped in the same interval. • Picking only the blue car assumes the others are outside the sign's zone, whereas the plate's two-way arrow says the opposite. • The motorcycle indeed violated, yet the stopping ban is not tied to it and covers any vehicle in that same stretch.

g7-q45.text: Which vehicle drivers have stopped incorrectly to drop off passengers?
options: The motorcycle operator and the bus driver.
g7-q45.explanation: The drivers of the motorcycle and the bus: both stopped in the prohibited zone of the pedestrian crosswalk. Stopping on a pedestrian crosswalk and closer than 5 meters before it is prohibited; after the crosswalk, however, there is no such ban. This single rule determines the status of all three vehicles in the image. The motorcycle is stopped right on the edge of the crosswalk's yellow marking—at worst, stopping directly on the crosswalk. The green van stopped 2 meters before the crosswalk, which is clearly inside the prohibited five-meter zone. The red car, however, is stopped 1 meter after the crosswalk, and what it is doing is not a violation. Why is the law sensitive to "before the crosswalk" and not sensitive to "after it"? Because the main hazard is blocking visibility. A car stopped before a crosswalk hides from an approaching driver's eyes a pedestrian stepping onto the roadway from the sidewalk on that side: the pedestrian emerges from behind it, and the driver has only a split second to react. This is the classic "hidden pedestrian" crash, whose victims are most often children. A car stopped on the far side of the crosswalk hides no pedestrian from an approaching driver's view. Worth remembering: the number 5 meters is one-sided—only before the crosswalk. • The passenger car is stopped 1 meter after the crosswalk, and the five-meter ban applies only before the crosswalk: its stop is lawful. • The motorcycle committed a violation, but it is not the only violator: the green van is also stopped 2 meters before the crosswalk. • The bus committed a violation, yet the motorcycle stopped directly on the crosswalk marking committed an even more obvious violation and cannot be left out. • "All drivers" is wrong because the red car's stop after the crosswalk falls under no ban.

g7-q46.text: If traffic across a railroad crossing is prohibited and there are no traffic signals, traffic signs, or pavement markings, the driver must stop:
options: At least 5 m before the barrier gate.
At least 3 m before the barrier gate.
g7-q46.explanation: No closer than 5 meters from the barrier. In this case the crossing has a barrier, but no traffic light, sign, or marking: that means your stopping reference is the barrier itself, and you must stop at least 5 meters from it. Notice that as soon as a barrier is present, the ten-meter distance from the rail no longer applies: the barrier is placed in front of the rail and serves as your stopping boundary. The reason for those 5 meters is easy to see in practice: as the barrier arm lowers it traces an arc, and if a car's bumper or hood sits beneath it, the arm lands on the car or breaks. More importantly, if a car stops tight against the barrier and a line builds up behind you, you will have no room at all to back up and exit the danger zone. Five meters is the exact reserve that gives you a retreat path. Worth remembering: at a railway crossing, always measure distance from the nearest control element. The priority order is: traffic light or "stop" sign and marking, then barrier, and in the absence of all of these, the rail. The number 5 goes with the barrier, and the number 10 goes with the rail: memorize these two pairs together so you do not swap them on the exam. • 3 meters is a number that merely looks "less than five" and sounds plausible, yet at that distance neither room for the barrier arm nor space for the car to maneuver is ensured, and no such limit exists in the rules. • Stopping right up against the barrier is tempting because it feels like "stopping before the obstacle," yet the moving barrier arm and lack of retreat space are precisely what make it prohibited.

g7-q47.text: What does the letter “A” marked in a traffic lane of the roadway mean?
options: A special lane designated for public transit vehicles.
A special lane designated for category A vehicles.
g7-q47.explanation: A special lane dedicated to the movement of route (public transport) vehicles. The letter "A" painted in white on the roadway in the image is a dedicated marking with a permanent meaning: this traffic lane is intended for route vehicles. A matching blue sign is also usually mounted above this lane or beside the road to mark the start of the lane. "Route vehicle" refers to what carries passengers along a designated route with marked stops: a route bus, trolleybus, or route minibus. A private car, taxi, and tourist bus do not fall under this definition. The reason for separating this stream is the difference in motion pattern: a route vehicle stops near the right edge every few hundred meters and pulls out again. Mixing those stops with through traffic increases rear-end collisions, and passengers step into the gap between the bus and moving cars—the most dangerous situation possible for a pedestrian. Worth remembering: not every letter or number you see on asphalt is a road number. On the exam, "A" always refers to a dedicated route-transport lane and has nothing to do with driver's license categories. • A road number appears on roadside markers and as a route code, not as a single letter on the roadway surface. • Driver's license category "A" applies to motorcycles, and no lane dedicated by asphalt marking is provided for license categories.

g7-q48.text: Is the vehicle permitted to stop at the indicated location to drop off passengers?
options: Permitted, but only by driving onto the sidewalk.
g7-q48.explanation: Prohibited. The white arrow in the image points to the right edge of the roadway, and at that exact spot a solid yellow line is applied to the curb.
